Introduction and motivation

A common mycorrhizal networkDefinition: common mycorrhizal network forest ecology and mycology A set of fungal threads that colonise the roots of two or more plants at once and so may link them below ground. Excludes claims about what such a network does, such as moving carbon or signals between trees, which are the matters in dispute. full definition is a set of fungal threads that colonise the roots of two or more plants at once. Popular accounts have described such networks as channels through which trees share carbon and warnings. Karst, Jones and Hoeksema [1] reviewed the field evidence and the way it is cited. They read the later citations of 18 field studies, which we call focal studiesDefinition: focal study our usage, following Karst and colleagues One of the 18 field studies on these networks whose later citations the original authors read and coded, 11 on network function and 7 on network structure. Excludes the citing papers, which are the units counted inside each focal study. full definition, and coded each citation as supported or not by what the focal study found. In their abstract they report that unsupported citationsDefinition: unsupported citation citation analysis, as coded by Karst and colleagues A citation that credits a focal study with a claim that the original authors judged the study's results do not support. Excludes any judgement of ours: every coding in this paper is the original authors'. full definition "have doubled in the past 25 years". An Author Correction followed [2].

The paper drew replies. Klein and colleagues [4] accepted that some of its criticism is justified and argued that evidence for carbon transfer between trees through these networks is solid and growing. Simard, Ryan and Perry [5] replied to three of its critiques; among other points they called its rationale for counting citations by year vague. Neither reply, as far as we read them at abstract and summary level, reanalysed the deposited numbers.

The doubling figure is a statistic, and the authors deposited the table behind it under CC0. That makes it checkable at low cost. Our question was narrow: on that table, does the rate of unsupported citations double over the study period for both kinds of claim, and does the answer hold when each year is weighted by how many citations it holds? The decision the reread informs is how our own work may quote the figure. Searches run on 9 November 2026 for a numeric reanalysis of the deposit returned none. That is what the searches returned; it does not show that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition was hash-locked at 06:07:12 UTC on 31 October 2026, before the table was analysed. It was not blind, and it lists what had been seen: the deposit's metadata in full, the header row of the table, and one data row printed by accident while checking the header. From an earlier reading of ours we also knew the per-year numerators in the paper's supplementary Note 3 and the method in its Note 2: a negative binomial regression of the percentage on indexed year. The article body and its main figure were behind a paywall and unread, so the authors' fitted curve and their own definition of doubled were not available to us.

The plan fixed a definition. Doubled means: the ratio of the fitted rate at the end of each group's span to the fitted rate at its start has a 95 percent interval, from resampling focal studies, that excludes 1 and covers 2, and the point estimate beats year-shuffled rates. Function and structure are read separately.

The plan named five measures, set out in the methods, with a verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition for each and a calibration on planted data. Kill conditionsDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition, without discretion:

  • If the calibration fails, no doubling verdict stands.
  • If the authors' model fails in both groups, the fitted curve does not support doubling on this table.
  • If the authors' model passes and the within-study model fails, the rise comes from a change in which studies are cited.
  • If the citation-weighted model fails beside a pass of the authors' model, the rise depends on thin early years.

The plan also recorded our own forecasts, set against the outcomes in Table 2.

Data and provenance

The data are the authors' Dataverse deposit [3], released under CC0. Its table gives, for each focal study and each citing year, the study-year rateDefinition: study-year rate our usage for the deposited table The share of one focal study's citations in one calendar year that were coded unsupported, as stored in the deposit without its denominator. Excludes a count of citations, which the deposit does not hold. full definition of unsupported citations. A "Count" column holds 100 times the rate, a percentage. The file holds 272 rows; 4 had a blank rate and were skipped and counted, leaving 268 rates: 158 for 11 function studies over 1997 to 2022 and 110 for 7 structure studies over 1999 to 2022. The year 2022 is incomplete.

The table holds no denominators. We built each rebuilt denominatorDefinition: rebuilt denominator our usage in this study The number of citations a focal study received in a year, recovered by finding the whole number n for which a published count k gives the deposited rate k over n. Excludes a count read directly from any source; years with a rate of zero share what remains of the study's total and are the least certain. full definition from the per-year numerators printed in the paper's supplementary Note 3: for a nonzero rate and a known numerator k, the whole number n with rate k/n. Where no whole number fits, the reduced fraction's denominator was used as a lower bound. Years with a rate of zero carry no numerator information and shared what remained of the study's reviewed total, the weakest step in the rebuild. The supplement is copyrighted, so this paper reports only derived values from it.

Methods

Integrity and rebuild

Two checks came first. The integrity check required the Count column to equal 100 times the rate, the expected numbers of studies, and group means of the yearly rate within 1.5 points of the means stated by the authors, 32.2 and 14.8 percent. The rebuild check required at least 0.7 of nonzero rates to give a whole-number denominator and a median gap of at most 0.2 between rebuilt numerators and the totals in the paper's tables. A failed rebuild would void only the citation-weighted measure.

The authors' model as deposited

Following Note 2, a negative binomial modelDefinition: negative binomial model statistics (count regression) A regression for counts whose variance can exceed their mean, fitted here with a log link so that the fitted rate changes by a fixed factor per year. Excludes models that weight each year by how many citations it holds. full definition with a log link was fitted to the percentage in each study-year on the indexed year t, using every row including the incomplete 2022:

ln⁡μt=a+βt(1)

The ratio over a group's span T (25 years for function, 23 for structure) is

R=eβT(2)

The same fit without 2022 is reported beside it. This model gives every study-year equal weight, a year with one citation as much as a year with thirty.

Within study

New focal studies enter the pool over time, so a pooled rise could come from which studies are cited when. The within-study modelDefinition: within-study model statistics (fixed effects) A regression with its own baseline level for each focal study, so the year slope is estimated only from change inside studies. Excludes change that comes from which focal studies happen to be cited in early and late years. full definition gives each focal study s its own level:

ln⁡μst=as+βt(3)

fitted as a quasi-Poisson fitDefinition: quasi-Poisson fit statistics (count regression) A log-linear count regression whose standard errors are scaled by the observed spread, used here for the within-study model. Excludes a full probability model for the counts. full definition. It passes if the slope is above 0 and above the 95th percentile of its year-shuffled control.

Citation-weighted

The citation-weighted share modelDefinition: citation-weighted share model statistics (logistic regression) A regression of the number of unsupported citations out of all citations in each study-year on the year, so a year with thirty citations counts thirty times as much as a year with one. Excludes the equal weight per study-year that a model of the deposited percentages gives. full definition fits the rebuilt count k of unsupported citations out of n in each study-year by a binomial logistic regression on year:

ln⁡pt1−pt=a+βt(4)

and reports the ratio of the fitted share at the last year to the share at the first:

Rw=pendpstart(5)

Intervals and reported quantities

Intervals for the ratios come from study resamplingDefinition: study resampling statistics (cluster bootstrap) Drawing focal studies with replacement, refitting the model each time, and taking the middle 95 percent of the refitted ratios as the interval. Excludes resampling single study-years, which would ignore that citations of one study move together. full definition, because citations of one focal study move together. Reported without a verdict: the pooled share in each group's first ten years against 2012 to 2021, the rate in the first five indexed years against the last five up to 2021, and growth in total citations over the last five years against the five before.

Controls and planted checks

The year-shuffled controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition permutes the rates across years inside each focal study, 1,000 times, and refits the authors' model and the within-study model. A real ratio or slope must beat the control's 95th percentile. Its p value is a p value from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition, so with 1,000 draws the smallest possible value is 1 in 1,001.

The planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition kept the real studies, years and rebuilt denominators and drew new counts from a known truth: a study effect (lognormal, standard deviation 0.4) and a true ratio of 1 or 2 over the span. It ran 60 simulations per group per truth, 120 per truth in all, with 150 study resamples each. The calibration passed if a flat truth was called a rise at most 0.15 of the time, the doubled truth gave a median ratio between 1.6 and 2.4, and its interval covered the truth at least 0.8 of the time.

The authors' stated means were recovered. Row means came out at 33.2 and 15.3 percent against the stated 32.2 and 14.8, within the 1.5 point allowance. The mean of study means gave 32.3 and 14.7, which identifies the definition the authors used.

The rebuild passed: 143 of 169 nonzero rates, 0.846, gave a whole-number denominator, and the rebuilt numerators matched the paper's table totals with a median gap of 0. The per-study totals are in Appendix B.

The calibration met its preregistered bar. With a flat truth the pipeline called a rise 0.092 of the time. With a doubled truth the median ratio was 2.11 and the interval covered the truth 0.89 of the time, against a bar of 0.8. The intervals are narrower than their stated level: they are 95 percent intervals, and they covered a planted doubling about 0.89 of the time where 0.95 was claimed. Read every interval on this page as somewhat too narrow. The calibration also measured statistical powerDefinition: statistical power statistics The chance that a test detects an effect of a given size when that effect is real, measured here on planted data with a known doubling. Excludes the chance that an effect is real given that the test detected it. full definition: with a true doubling, the interval excluded 1 only 0.425 of the time.

Results

Table 1 gives the ratios from all three models and Figure 1 draws them.

On the authors' negative binomial model, unsupported citations rose by a factor of 2.19 for network function (0.86 to 4.14) and 2.84 for network structure (1.18 to 6.62).c1 Both beat their year-shuffled controls. By the letter of the plan, function fails because its interval reaches below 1, and structure passes. Dropping the incomplete 2022 gave 2.26 and 2.43.

Inside individual focal studies the rate rose for both: 3.0 times for function (p 0.001) and 3.5 times for structure (p 0.009).c3 The slopes, 0.044 and 0.054 per year, beat their shuffled cuts of 0.022 and 0.036. The rise does not come from which focal studies happen to be cited early and late.

Weighted by citations, the rise was 1.77 for function (0.52 to 2.99) and 1.54 for structure (0.85 to 5.81), and neither interval excludes 1.c2 The fitted share went from 0.205 to 0.363 for function and from 0.113 to 0.175 for structure. In pooled shares, function went from 21.5 percent in its first ten years to 34.9 percent in 2012 to 2021, about 1.6 times; structure went from 13.6 to 14.7 percent, about 1.1 times. Figure 2 shows why the weighting matters: the early structure years hold few citations each.

What this means for a reader

Newton's table of rings at slanting light is usually read as a set of measurements. Set beside exact optics, the rows split in two. The shallow rows track the physics, and the steep rows track an arithmetic rule Newton states on the same page. In any old table, a row that agrees with its author's formula more closely than the instrument could measure is more likely computed than observed.

Objection

Which rows Newton measured and which he computed is our reading. The text cannot settle it, and a historian should check it against his manuscripts and his optical papers.

What would change the call. Read Shapiro 1993 and Optical Papers vol 2 on Obs 7, plus Newton's manuscripts.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

In Book II of the Opticks, Newton gives a table of the air thickness at a coloured ring for thirteen viewing angles, and beside it a rule he fitted to the table. We put every row beside exact thin-film optics and beside his rule. From perpendicular light to 60 degrees in the air, his table matches the secant law of modern optics within 0.41 percent.c1 From 65 to 90 degrees every row matches his own 106-means rule within 1 percent, and at 85 degrees his tabled thickness sits 26.7 percent below the secant.c2 Exact theory says the secant holds at every angle below the critical one, so the steep rows follow his rule and not the light. Our reading is that those rows were computed from the rule; the text alone cannot settle it. The same model checks his best-known number: under standard daylight weighted by the eye, the first dark ring falls at 275.7 nm, 3.4 percent below Newton's 1/89000 inch (285.4 nm).c3 All five preregistered predictions held and both controls failed as required.

Introduction and motivation

Newton's ringsDefinition: Newton's rings optics The bright and dark circles seen where a curved lens rests on flat glass, made by light reflected from the two faces of the thin air gap between them, whose thickness grows with distance from the point of contact. Excludes rings made by diffraction at an edge or an aperture. full definition are the bright and dark circles seen where a curved lens rests on flat glass. In Book II, Part I of the Opticks [1], Newton measured them with a lens of known curvature and turned ring diameters into thicknesses of the air gap. In Observation 6 he gives the gap at the first dark ring as 1/89000 inch for light near the perpendicular. In Observation 7 he tilts the view and tabulates the thickness at one ring for thirteen values of the obliquityDefinition: obliquity optics, in Newton's usage The angle between the light's path and the perpendicular to the glass. Newton's table gives it twice, once inside the glass and once in the air gap. Excludes the tilt of the glass itself, which stays fixed. full definition, scaled so that perpendicular light gives 10. He says his values came "partly by measuring" and partly by other means, including two prisms for the steepest angles.

Below the table he states a rule he "seem[s] to gather" from it. We call it the 106-means ruleDefinition: 106-means rule history of optics; Newton's own rule in Opticks, Book II Newton's statement that the thickness goes as the secant of an angle whose sine is the first of 106 arithmetical means between the sines of incidence and refraction, counted from the bigger sine. Excludes the secant law, which uses the air angle alone. full definition: the thickness goes as the secant of an angle whose sine is the first of 106 arithmetical means between the sines of incidence and refraction, counted from the bigger sine. Modern optics gives a simpler answer, the secant lawDefinition: secant law thin-film optics The statement that the air thickness at which a given ring appears grows as one over the cosine of the light's angle in the air gap, scaled here so that perpendicular light gives 10. Excludes any rule built from the angle in the glass. full definition: the thickness at a fixed ring grows as one over the cosine of the angle in the air.

The two agree at shallow angles and part at steep ones. At 90 degrees in the air the secant is infinite, and Newton's last row reads 122 and a half. The question is which of the two his rows follow, and from which angle on.

The literature check for this paper ran three searches on 9 November 2026. Shapiro's study of Newton's theories of coloured bodies and fits [3] works from Newton's manuscripts and the experiments behind Book II, and is the most likely place for an earlier analysis of this table; we found its catalogue and publisher records and did not read it. Morizot [4] traces how Thomas Young turned Newton's ring thicknesses into the first wavelengths; we read its abstract. Lee and Lee [5] give open code for the colours of layered thin films from the same multiple-beam sums we use; we read its abstract. None of the searches returned an analysis of the Observation 7 table against exact theory. That is what the searches returned, and it does not show that no such analysis exists.

Preregistration and design

The design was written in a dated preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition on 28 October 2026. The file states that it was written before the model or the study ran. It was not hash-locked at the time, and its result section was appended to the same file after the run, so the hash given in the reproduction section is of the file as it now stands.

One check came before the file. We had computed the rule by hand at the 90 degree row and found about 122.9 against Newton's 122 and a half. The preregistration says so, and that check is why prediction E exists.

The five predictions, with their bounds:

  • A, the first dark ring in white light lies within 5 percent of Newton's 285.4 nm.
  • B, the first four bright rings in white light stand as 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 within 3 percent.
  • C, for light of one wavelength, 571 nm, the thickness at the first dark ring follows the secant of the air angle within 0.1 percent from 0 to 85 degrees.
  • D, Newton's thickness column matches the secant within 1 percent for rows from 0 to 60 degrees.
  • E, Newton's thickness column matches his 106-means rule within 1.5 percent at every row, 65 to 90 degrees included.

The file also names two controlsDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition that had to fail, given in the controls section. If E holds and D fails beyond 60 degrees, the steep rows follow the fitted rule, and C says the true thickness keeps growing as the secant.

Data and provenance

The primary text is the fourth edition of the Opticks, 1730, as transcribed by Project Gutenberg (ebook 33504) [1], with the Newton Project transcription as a second copy [2]. Both are public domain. The thickness column, the glass angles and the air angles of Observation 7 were typed by hand from that text into the study script. Table 2 gives every value that entered.

The white light is the CIE D65 daylight table and the eye's weighting is the CIE 1931 2 degree observer, both from the official CIE data tables [6]. The glass is N-BK7, with an index of 1.5175 at 571 nm from the model's own refraction table.

Methods

The stack and its reflectance

The model is a glass, air gap, glass stack, the geometry of Newton's lens on a plate over the small area of one ring. For light of wavelength λ crossing a gap of thickness d at angle θa in the air, write ca for the cosine of θa. The phase delay between successive beams is

δ=4πdcaλ(1)

Let r1 be the amplitude reflection coefficient from glass into air and r2 that from air into glass, each from the Fresnel equations for one polarisation. Write C for the cosine of δ. Summing every reflected and re-reflected beam gives the Airy reflectanceDefinition: Airy reflectance optics; named after George Airy The share of light power a thin layer reflects when every reflected and re-reflected beam inside it is summed, rather than only the first two. Excludes the two-beam approximation, and absorption in the glass. full definition

R=(r1)2+(r2)2+2r1r2C1+(r1r2)2+2r1r2C(2)

computed for s and p polarisationDefinition: s and p polarisation optics The two directions of the light's electric field relative to the plane that holds the ray and the perpendicular to the surface: s across that plane and p within it. Unpolarised light is their average. Excludes circular polarisation, which this study does not model. full definition and averaged. For this stack r2=−r1. That sign change is the half-wave flipDefinition: half-wave flip optics The change of sign of the reflected wave at one face of the air gap and not the other, which makes the centre of the rings dark in reflected light. Excludes the phase delay from the path across the gap. full definition, and it makes the point of contact dark.

White light

For white light the reflectance is weighted by the CIE D65Definition: CIE D65 colour science (International Commission on Illumination) A standard table of the power in average midday daylight at each wavelength, used as the white light in this study. Excludes the measured spectrum of any one day's sunlight, and Newton's own light. full definition power S(λ) and by the eye's brightness curve y(λ), from 380 to 780 nm in 1 nm steps:

Y(d)=∑R(d,λ)S(λ)y(λ)∑S(λ)y(λ)(3)

Y is the reflected luminanceDefinition: luminance colour science The brightness of light as the standard eye weighs it, computed by weighting power at each wavelength with the CIE 1931 2 degree observer's brightness curve. Excludes hue and saturation, which the study does not score. full definition as a share of the incoming. The study stepped d from 0 to 2,000 nm in 0.1 nm steps and read off the minima and maxima of Y. A dark ring is a minimum of Y and a bright ring a maximum.

The obliquity laws

With thickness scaled to 10 at perpendicular light, the secant law is

tsec=10ca(4)

For Newton's rule, let sa and sg be the sines of the angles in the air and in the glass that his table lists. The first of 106 arithmetical means between them, counted from the bigger, divides the interval into 107 equal steps, and its value sϕ is the sine of the angle in Newton's secant:

sϕ=sa−sa−sg107(5)
trule=101−(sϕ)2(6)

At 90 degrees in the air, sa=1, and eq. 6 stays finite where eq. 4 does not.

Each row's deviation is the absolute difference between Newton's value and the law, divided by the law's value. Prediction C was scored on the model alone: the first dark ring at 571 nm was found at each air angle and its thickness divided by the thickness at perpendicular light.

Controls and planted checks

No planted data were used. The check with a known answer is prediction B: textbook theory places the bright rings at odd multiples of a quarter wavelength, so a model that missed 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 would be wrong before Newton entered.

Two controls had to fail, and both did.

  • With the half-wave flip removed, the centre turns bright and the first minimum moves to 137.7 nm, 52 percent from Newton's value.c4 So the dark-ring match depends on the physics the model carries.
    c4 observed, evidence for claim 4
    The numbers in claim 4
    137.7; 52 matches the result file, 2026-11-09
    Chart 3
    The five predictions and two controls, each against its bound.
    Chart 4
    Air thickness at the first dark ring in white light: the model with and without the half-wave flip, against Newton's value.
    Basis
    observed: measured in this study, with a result file
  • With the thickness column shuffled across rows 200 times, his rule failed the 1.5 percent bound at 7 or more rows in every shuffle, with a median of 12. So the match to the rule depends on the rows being in Newton's order.

One error of ours was caught before grading. The first run gave prediction C a ratio of exactly 1 at every angle, because the dark-ring search started at 1 nm, where reflectance is still rising out of the dark centre, and stopped at once. The search was changed to take the first minimum after the first maximum, and the study was run again. The model was not changed.

Results

All five predictions held. Table 1 gives each against its bound.

From perpendicular light to 60 degrees in the air, his table matches the secant law of modern optics within 0.41 percent.c1 From 65 to 90 degrees every row matches his own 106-means rule within 1 percent, and at 85 degrees his tabled thickness sits 26.7 percent below the secant.c2 Figure 2 draws the three curves and Figure 3 the deviations row by row. Table 2 lists them.

The 60 degree row equals the secant to the printed precision and sits 0.99 percent from the rule. From 65 degrees on, the order flips: every row is closer to the rule than to the secant, and the gap to the secant grows with angle, to 9.27 percent at 80 degrees and 26.72 percent at 85.

The model itself keeps the secant. At 571 nm the first dark ring follows the secant of the air angle within 0.0075 percent at every angle from 0 to 85 degrees. The two phase shifts at the faces of the gap cancel at every angle below the critical one, so nothing in the physics bends the curve toward the rule.

Under standard daylight weighted by the eye, the first dark ring falls at 275.7 nm, 3.4 percent below Newton's 1/89000 inch (285.4 nm).c3 The first four bright rings fall at 137.7, 413.8, 692.8 and 973.5 nm, and the first four dark rings at 275.7, 553.2, 832.8 and 1112.7 nm.

Discussion

The split in Table 2 has a plain reading. Newton measured the rings at shallow angles, fitted a rule to those rows, and filled the steep rows from the rule. He wrote that the values came "partly by measuring" and partly by other means, which allows that reading. It is an inference. A rule fitted to the shallow rows would match them, and a row computed from the rule would match it to within the rounding of the printed fractions. Rows that were measured at steep angles and happened to fall on the rule would look the same in the table. Only his manuscripts could tell the two apart.

The rule itself is a good fit to his shallow data and a wrong law. Up to 60 degrees the rule and the secant differ by under 1 percent. Beyond that the rule bends away, and the error reaches 27 percent at 85 degrees.

The 3.4 percent gap at the first dark ring depends on the light and on what counts as dark in a coloured fringe. Our daylight is a modern standard table, and our dark ring is a luminance minimum. Newton's 285.4 nm corresponds to light centred near 571 nm rather than the 551 nm our weighting gives, a shift that sunlight could plausibly give and an eye judging "the darkest Part" of a fringe. We did not test it. Two related studies of ours, on his thick-plate rings and on his colour limits, also find his 1/89000 inch a few percent off, which is a pattern to test and not yet a result.

Young's wavelengths were taken from Newton's ring thicknesses, as Morizot describes [4]. Our result bears on those perpendicular values only through the 3.4 percent gap.

Limitations

  • Which rows Newton measured and which he computed is our reading. The text cannot settle it, and a historian should check it against his manuscripts and his optical papers.
  • The literature search was short. Shapiro's 1993 study [3] was not read and may already cover this table.
  • The table was typed by hand from the transcription and was not checked against a scan of the 1730 printing.
  • The 3.4 percent gap depends on the light source and on how an eye judges the darkest part of a coloured fringe. The preregistration planned a second check under a solar spectrum; it was not run, and no perceptual model was run.
  • The 90 degree row was checked against the rule by hand before the preregistration was written, as that file states.
  • The preregistration was not hash-locked at the time it was written.
  • Scoring was done by our own code and was not blind.

Evidence

Held. Prereg check on a primary text with exact theory. The rings part is known physics. The reading that steep rows were computed needs a historian's check, since Newton states the rule himself.

What this means for a reader

If a discovery tool shows you a ranked list of "missing links", ask how it does against a list that simply pairs the most common terms. In our test the common-terms list won on every corpus. The shared-neighbour idea is not empty: among pairs that are equally common, it does pick out the ones that later appear together more often than chance. Its weakness sits at the top of the list, which is where a reader looks first.

Objection

A later co-occurrence is an attention event. A hit means two concepts were later used together; it does not show that a link between them is true or new to science.

What would change the call. Preregister Adamic-Adar on a citation corpus with dated held-out links.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Tools that promise to find undiscovered connections often rank unlinked pairs of concepts by the neighbours they share: if A goes with B and B goes with C, perhaps A goes with C. We tested that ranking against the plainest baseline there is, which pairs the most popular concepts. Each corpus was cut by date, and a ranker scored a hit when a pair it proposed from the early documents appeared together at least twice in the next stretch of documents. Ranking unlinked pairs by shared neighbours found fewer later links than ranking them by popularity on all three corpora: precision in the top 200 of 0.127 against 0.268 on our research notes, 0.018 against 0.088 on Biology Stack Exchange and 0.007 against 0.043 on Skeptics Stack Exchange.c1 On degree-preserving rewired graphs the shared-neighbour score reached a 95th percentile of 0.164, above its real score of 0.127, so at the top of the list it added nothing we could detect beyond popularity.c2 Among pairs of similar popularity the shared-neighbour score still separated later links from the rest: area under the curve 0.569 on the research notes, 0.757 on Biology and 0.696 on Skeptics.c3 Three of four preregistered verdicts failed.

Introduction

Swanson [1] described knowledge that is public and still undiscovered: two bodies of literature that each hold half of an argument and never cite each other. His method, now called literature-based discoveryDefinition: literature-based discovery information science, after Swanson The search for connections that no single document states but that follow from linking what separate documents say. Excludes finding links that some document already states, which is ordinary retrieval. full definition, looks for a term C that is linked to a term B in one literature while B is linked to A in another, so that A and C become a candidate pair. Later work recast the problem as link predictionDefinition: link prediction network science Ranking pairs of nodes that are not yet joined in a network by how likely they are to become joined later. Excludes recovering links that exist but were hidden at random from the same snapshot. full definition, the ranking of node pairs in a network by how likely they are to become joined. Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg [2] set out the problem on coauthorship networks, built rankers from measures of how close two nodes sit in the network, and found that subtle proximity measures can outperform direct ones. One such measure is the Adamic-Adar index [3]. Kastrin, Rindflesch and Hristovski [4] applied proximity measures, among them common neighbours, the Adamic-Adar index and preferential attachment, to a network of co-occurring MeSH terms with its history of link formation, and reported that supervised methods outperform the unsupervised ones.

Krenn and Zeilinger [5] built a semantic network of quantum physics concepts from 750,000 papers, linked two concepts when one article studies both, and trained a neural network to predict which concept pairs researchers will study in the next five years. Krenn and colleagues [6] later built a benchmark, Science4Cast, from about 143,000 papers on artificial intelligence and compared ten prediction methods on it; in the authors' public summary, the most effective methods used a curated set of network features.

This study asks a narrower question that sits under all of that work. Before a gap ranking is trusted to point at undiscovered connections, does it beat a ranking that knows only how popular each concept is? The shared-neighbour score in our test discounts popular concepts on purpose, in the form used for time-sliced tests by Krenn and Zeilinger. The baseline is preferential attachmentDefinition: preferential attachment network science A ranking of unlinked pairs by the product of the two concepts' degrees, so the most popular pairs come first. Excludes any use of which neighbours the two concepts share. full definition, the product of the two concepts' degrees.

Preregistration and design

The design was written and hash-locked on 31 October 2026 as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, before any score of the study was computed. Exploration before the lock read schemas, field names and date ranges only. The locked file names the corpora, the slicing, the vocabulary rules, the definition of a link and of a target, the ranker and its baseline, both controlsDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition, the measures, four verdicts, the forecasts and one kill condition. The preregistration's SHA-256 is given in the reproduction section.

Each verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition is a rule read off by code:

  • Beats popularity: the bootstrap interval of the shared-neighbour precision minus the popularity precision lies above zero on the research notes.
  • Beats controls: the shared-neighbour precision on the research notes lies above the 95th percentile of both controls.
  • Holds with popularity fixed: the within-decile area under the curve on the research notes lies above 0.55.
  • Replicates on Biology: the same interval as the first verdict lies above zero on Biology Stack Exchange.

The kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition reads: if the ranking fails to beat popularity and also fails with popularity fixed, absent-link scores say nothing beyond how common a word is, and its top gaps get reported only as prompts for reading.

Data and provenance

Three corpora were used. The first is our own research notes: entries of our findings ledgerDefinition: findings ledger our records The append-only, dated list of every result we have recorded, numbered F1, F2 and on. Corrections are added as new dated lines and old entries are never rewritten. Excludes a curated list of successes. full definition, the titles of saved readings, a catalogue of laws and a table of checks, each dated. They are internal records and are not public, so no one outside can reproduce that arm. Their dates span days of reading, not years, so a slice of them is a stretch of attention, not a stretch of a field's history.

The other two are the question posts of Biology Stack Exchange (28,798 questions) and Skeptics Stack Exchange (11,202 questions), 2011 to 2024, taken from the sites' public data dump. Each question's tags serve as its concepts. Stack Exchange content is licensed CC BY-SA [7]; this paper reports statistics only.

Each corpus was ordered by date and cut into five time slicesDefinition: time slice forecast evaluation One of five blocks of equal document count cut from a corpus ordered by date. A fold trains on the early slices and tests on the next one. Excludes random splits, which let later documents inform the training graph. full definition of equal document count. The fifth slice was held back for a later study and was not read here. A vocabulary was built from the training slices only: at most 1,500 concepts, each appearing in at least four documents and in no more than 10 percent of them, with each document keeping at most 40 concepts by tf-idf weight. On the research notes the concepts are single words and word pairs; on the Stack Exchange sites they are tags.

A linkDefinition: link our usage for this study Two concepts appearing in the same document. A concept here is a question tag on the Stack Exchange sites and a word or word pair on the research notes. Excludes any judgement that the two concepts are related in fact. full definition is two concepts in one document. A targetDefinition: target our usage for this study A pair of concepts never linked in the training slices that appears together in at least two documents of the next slice. Excludes pairs that appear together only once in the test slice, and any check that the later pairing is true. full definition is a pair with no link in the training slices that appears together in at least two documents of the test slice.

Methods

Folds

Three folds trained on slice 1, slices 1 to 2 and slices 1 to 3, and each tested on the slice after its training block. Every number in the results is the mean over the three folds unless a fold is named.

The rankers

Let A be the training graph, di the degreeDefinition: degree network science The number of other concepts a concept is linked to in the training graph, our measure of how popular it is. Excludes how many documents mention the concept. full definition of concept i, and E the number of edges. Each edge between i and k gets a weight that falls as both ends become popular, floored at zero:

wik=ln⁡2Edidk(1)

The A-B-C rankingDefinition: A-B-C ranking literature-based discovery, after Swanson Scoring an unlinked pair A and C by the intermediate concepts B that each is linked to. Here a cosine over shared neighbours with each edge weighted down when both of its ends are popular. Excludes methods trained on known outcomes, and the expert reading that Swanson applied to each candidate. full definition scores an unlinked pair i and j by the cosine of their weighted neighbour rows, so that it is high when the two concepts share specific neighbours:

Sij=∑kwikwjk∑kwikwik∑kwjkwjk(2)

The popularity baseline is

Pij=didj(3)

The Adamic-Adar indexDefinition: Adamic-Adar index network science A count of the neighbours two nodes share in which each shared neighbour is weighted by one over the logarithm of its own degree. Excludes the popularity discount on edges that the A-B-C score uses. full definition was reported beside them as a secondary measure. It was not in the preregistration, and its result is read as a lead only:

AAij=∑k1ln⁡dk(4)

where the sum runs over the neighbours k that i and j share. Ties in any score are broken by a fixed small noise term, the same in every run.

Measures

The main measure is precision in the top 200Definition: precision in the top 200 information retrieval The share of a ranker's 200 highest-scored unlinked pairs that turn out to be targets. Excludes how the ranker orders pairs below the top 200. full definition:

P200=h200(5)

where h is the number of targets among a ranker's 200 highest-scored unlinked pairs. It is set beside the base rateDefinition: base rate statistics The share of all unlinked candidate pairs that are targets, the precision a random ranking would reach on average. Excludes the precision of any particular ranker. full definition, the share of all unlinked candidate pairs that are targets.

The interval for the difference in precision comes from a document bootstrapDefinition: document bootstrap statistics (resampling) Redrawing the test slice's documents with replacement, recomputing which pairs are targets, and rescoring the fixed top-200 lists each time, so the interval shows how much the result depends on which documents happened to arrive. Excludes uncertainty from the training graph, which is held fixed. full definition: 200 times, the test slice's documents are reweighted by a multinomial draw, the targets are recomputed, and both fixed top-200 lists are rescored. The difference is averaged over the three folds within each draw, and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 200 averages form the 95 percent intervalDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition.

The second measure holds popularity fixed. Candidate pairs are split into tenths by the product of their degrees, and the area under the ROC curveDefinition: area under the ROC curve statistics and machine learning The chance that a randomly chosen target scores above a randomly chosen non-target. 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect. Excludes how the top of the list performs, which precision in the top 200 measures. full definition is computed inside each tenth from 40,000 sampled pairs of a target and a non-target. The within-decile AUCDefinition: within-decile AUC our usage for this study The area under the ROC curve computed separately inside each tenth of the candidate pairs ranked by degree product, then averaged with weights equal to each tenth's number of targets. Excludes any advantage that comes from ranking popular pairs above unpopular ones. full definition is their weighted mean:

Astrat=∑bnbAb∑bnb(6)

where Ab is the area in tenth b and nb its number of targets.

Controls and planted checks

Two controls were run on the research notes, 20 draws each, scored against the true targets of each fold. Degree-preserving rewiringDefinition: degree-preserving rewiring network science, after Maslov and Sneppen Repeatedly swapping the ends of two randomly chosen edges, so every concept keeps its degree while who is linked to whom is scrambled. Excludes changes to any concept's popularity. full definition attempts two random double-edge swaps per edge on the training graph, skipping any swap that would duplicate an edge. Every concept keeps its popularity and loses its real neighbourhood. If the shared-neighbour score finds anything beyond popularity at the top of the list, it must beat this control. Node-label permutationDefinition: node-label permutation statistics (permutation test) Shuffling which concept sits at which node of the training graph, so the graph's shape stays and its link to the real concepts is broken. Excludes any change to the shape of the graph. full definition keeps the graph's shape and breaks its tie to the real concepts. It is the weaker control: a score that loses to it would be worse than noise. The 95th percentile of each control's null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition is the bar.

There was no planted check. No corpus with a known set of future links was built, so the study cannot say how often the instrument misses a real effect.

Results

Table 1 gives the main measure on each corpus and Figure 1 draws it. Ranking unlinked pairs by shared neighbours found fewer later links than ranking them by popularity on all three corpora: precision in the top 200 of 0.127 against 0.268 on our research notes, 0.018 against 0.088 on Biology Stack Exchange and 0.007 against 0.043 on Skeptics Stack Exchange.c1 All three bootstrap intervals for the difference lie below zero.

Figure 2 sets the research-notes score against its controls. On degree-preserving rewired graphs the shared-neighbour score reached a 95th percentile of 0.164, above its real score of 0.127, so at the top of the list it added nothing we could detect beyond popularity.c2 The rewired draws had a mean of 0.146, and 19 of 20 met or beat the real score (p value from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition 0.95). The score did beat the node-permuted graphs, whose 95th percentile was 0.048 (p 0.048, the smallest value 20 draws allow).

Among pairs of similar popularity the shared-neighbour score still separated later links from the rest: area under the curve 0.569 on the research notes, 0.757 on Biology and 0.696 on Skeptics.c3 Over all candidate pairs, without holding popularity fixed, its area was 0.739 on the research notes against 0.782 for popularity, 0.810 against 0.815 on Biology, and 0.762 against 0.836 on Skeptics.

Adamic-Adar, not preregistered, matched or beat popularity: 0.273 against 0.268 on the research notes and 0.122 against 0.088 on Biology.c4 No interval was computed for that comparison.

0.273; 0.268; 0.122; 0.088 matches the result file, 2026-11-09

The folds explain much of the research-notes result. Table 2 shows that the first fold, with 285 concepts and a base rate of 0.094, holds almost all of the hits. The later folds have 1,500 concepts and base rates near 0.001, and the shared-neighbour score found no target in its top 200 in either of them.

Table 3 sets the forecasts written before the run against the outcomes.

What this means for a reader

Adding terms to a model of choice will almost always improve its fit a little. The fair test is whether the new terms beat a version of the old theory given a similar number of extra parameters, three against our four. Ours did not, so the terms we named after information, threat and drive describe where prospect theory misfits, and they do not add a new account of why people choose. The loss aversion we measured sits near 1, well below the classic 2.25, which says this number depends on the task that measures it.

Objection

Entropy, loss probability and the mean and mean square of outcomes are one reading of information, threat and drive. Another reading could score differently, so the result covers this operationalisation only.

What would change the call. Person-level data and a preregistered reading of information gain.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

We had written a single value formula for risky choice: prospect value plus a term for the information a gamble resolves, a term for the threat of a loss, and a term for drive toward a setpoint. We tested it on the public choices13k data, 1,928 problems answered without outcome feedback and 9,831 answered with it, against cumulative prospect theory and against a flexible prospect theory with comparable room to absorb misfit (three extra parameters against our four). The kill rule was fixed before any real fit. The combined formula never beat the flexible prospect theory by the preregistered margin: cross-validated R² 0.634 against 0.645 without feedback and 0.597 against 0.596 with it, against a bar of 0.005.c1 Without feedback, the joint gain of the four added terms, 7.6 in deviance, sat below the 95th percentile of both null controls, 52.0 and 58.9.c2 With feedback two of the terms help as corrections to prospect theory, and the drive term does not. The kill rule fired, and the formula is retired as a model of risky choice. Fitted loss aversion was 1.16 (1.05 to 1.30) without feedback and 0.89 (0.86 to 0.93) with feedback.c4

Introduction

Cumulative prospect theoryDefinition: cumulative prospect theory (CPT) behavioural economics A model of choice between gambles with a value function concave for gains and steeper for losses, a loss aversion coefficient and a probability weighting function applied to cumulative probabilities. Here six parameters. Excludes any account of the feelings or brain processes behind a choice. full definition [2] describes a choice between gambles with three ingredients: a value function that is concave for gains and steeper for losses, a loss aversionDefinition: loss aversion behavioural economics The factor lambda by which a loss weighs more than an equal gain in the value function. 1 means losses and gains count alike. Excludes a dislike of risk as such, which curvature and weighting carry. full definition coefficient λ that scales losses, and a weighting functionDefinition: probability weighting function behavioural economics A function that maps a stated probability to the weight a choice gives it, so that small chances can count for more than their size and large ones for less. Excludes a person's belief about the odds, which in these problems are stated. full definition that bends probabilities. The theory comes from behavioural economics and describes choices; it gives no account of the feelings behind them. Loss aversion is the factor by which a loss weighs more than an equal gain, so 1 means losses and gains count alike, and it says nothing about a dislike of risk as such. The weighting function maps a stated probability to the weight a choice gives it, so small chances can count for more than their size; it is no belief about the odds. Tversky and Kahneman reported a median λ of 2.25 from their own experiment. Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer [3] collected 607 estimates of λ from 150 articles published from 1992 to 2017 and pooled them in a meta-analysisDefinition: meta-analysis statistics, research synthesis The statistical pooling of published estimates of one quantity into a summary and a measure of their spread. Excludes collecting new data. full definition, the statistical pooling of published estimates of one quantity, which collects no new data of its own.

Peterson, Bourgin, Agrawal, Reichman and Griffiths [1] ran the largest risky choice experiment to that date, choices13k, with choice rates on 13,006 problems collected online. They used it to compare classical decision theories with machine-learning models and to search for better theories. Thomas and colleagues [6] argued that the choice behaviour in choices13k contains structured decision noise when compared with a laboratory data set, which bears on how much of the gap between theories and flexible learners is psychology.

The data set also separates problems answered with and without feedback on outcomes. Hertwig, Barron, Weber and Erev [5] reported that people choose as if they overweight rare events when choosing from descriptions and underweight them when choosing from experience, the pattern later called the description-experience gapDefinition: description-experience gap decision research The pattern that people choose as if they overweight rare events when choosing from stated odds and underweight them when they learn the odds from sampled outcomes. Excludes differences in the gambles themselves. full definition. In decision research the term means that difference between choices from stated odds and choices learned from sampled outcomes; it excludes any difference in the gambles themselves. We analysed the two settings apart for that reason.

Our own starting point was a combined value formulaDefinition: combined value formula (COMB) our usage CPT's value difference plus four added terms in one choice rule: entropy for information, loss probability for threat, and the mean and mean square of outcomes for drive toward a setpoint. Ten parameters. Excludes any claim about mechanisms in the brain, and any reading of the terms other than this operationalisation. full definition from earlier notes in this project, a name of ours for prospect value plus four added terms in one choice rule, standing for three ideas: information, threat and drive, which makes no claim about mechanisms in the brain. It adds to prospect value a term for the information a gamble resolves, a term for the threat of a loss, and a term for reduction of a drive toward a setpoint. This paper is a test of that formula, and the formula is ours to retire.

Preregistration and design

The design was written and hash-locked on 31 October 2026 at 08:02 UTC as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, a practice from clinical trials and psychology: a dated plan fixed before any result is seen, so a plan revised after a look at the outcome does not qualify. Before writing it we had seen the file schemas, the row counts and outcomes simulated by the study code. No real outcome had been fitted.

The locked file names the data, the two settings, every model, the scoring, the planted checksDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition, both controlsDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition, the forecasts and the kill ruleDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition. A planted check runs data with a known answer through the same analysis first, to show the analysis can find an effect when it is there, which no check on real data can show. A control is a version of the data with the structure under test removed, scored the same way as the real data; a published number from another study is no control. The kill rule decides against the claim when it is met, with no room for judgement after the run. The question it states is whether the combined formula predicts human risky choice better than cumulative prospect theory, and better than a richer pure prospect theory that could absorb the same misfit. Nothing was added after the run. The preregistration's SHA-256 is given in the reproduction section.

Kill and void conditions, as written:

  • If the combined formula fails to beat the flexible prospect theory in both settings by 0.005 in cross-validated R² with a quasi-binomial BIC change below -10, the formula is retired as a model of risky choice, and its added terms are read as patches for prospect theory misfit whatever their permutation p values say.
  • If the planted check fails, every other verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition is voidDefinition: void research method (our usage) The verdict of a run whose planted check failed or whose sample fell below its stated minimum. It says nothing for or against the claim. Excludes a null result, which comes from a working instrument. full definition. A verdict, in our usage, is the pass or fail of one preregistered rule set read off by code. A void verdict says nothing for or against the claim, unlike a null result from an instrument that works.

Data and provenance

The data are choices13k [1], the selections table and the problems file from the authors' public repository. Each row gives, for one problem, the share of participants who chose option B over option A, the number of participants and the between-person standard deviation of that share. There is no person-level input.

We kept rows marked unambiguous and split them by the feedback flag: 1,928 problems answered without outcome feedback, which we call the description settingDefinition: description setting our usage, after decision research The 1,928 choices13k problems answered without outcome feedback, where people chose from stated odds alone. Excludes the 9,831 problems answered with feedback on outcomes. full definition because people chose from stated odds alone and learned no outcomes along the way, and 9,831 answered with feedback. In each setting each problem appears once. The repository states no licence. We used a local research copy and report only statistics computed from it.

A join check ran before the lock. The problems file uses row positions in the selections table as its keys, and problem identifiers do not match them. On a dry run with simulated outcomes the join by identifier matched 0.015 of rows; after the fix the match was 1.0 in both settings, checked by recomputing each problem's expected value from both files.

Methods

The choice rule

Every value model predicts the log oddsDefinition: log odds statistics For a rate p, the natural log of p divided by 1 minus p. 0 at an even split and unbounded toward certainty. Excludes any information beyond the rate, of which it is a rescaling. full definition of choosing B from the difference in value between the options. The log odds of a rate p is ln⁡(p/(1−p)), a statistics rescaling that is 0 at an even split and adds no information to the rate:

ln⁡PB1−PB=b0+τ(VB−VA)(1)

where PB is the predicted rate, b0 an intercept and τ a sensitivity. Models were fitted by binomial likelihoodDefinition: binomial likelihood statistics Fitting by choosing the parameters under which the observed counts of B choices are most probable, treating each choice as an independent draw at the predicted rate. Here five choices per listed participant. Excludes extra scatter between problems, which the dispersion handles. full definition on the observed rates, the statistics method that picks the parameters under which the observed counts of B choices are most probable, treating each choice as an independent coin with the predicted rate, counting five choices per listed participant, the count the study code uses for each problem.

The models

The expected valueDefinition: expected value (EV) probability theory The probability-weighted average payoff of a gamble, used here as the baseline value model. Excludes any allowance for risk, loss or probability weighting. full definition baseline (EV), the probability-weighted average payoff from probability theory with no allowance for risk or loss, uses V=∑ipixi for outcomes xi with probabilities pi. Cumulative prospect theory (CPT) uses rank-dependent weightsDefinition: rank-dependent weights decision theory Decision weights that depend on where an outcome ranks among a gamble's outcomes, taken as differences of the weighting function at cumulative probabilities. Excludes weighting each outcome's probability on its own, as the original 1979 prospect theory did. full definition πi, decision weights that depend on where an outcome ranks among the gamble's outcomes and are taken as differences of the weighting function at cumulative probabilities, which excludes weighting each probability on its own, and a value function that for gains is

v(x)=xα(2)

and for losses is v(x)=−λ(−x)α, with V=∑iπiv(xi). The weights come from the Tversky and Kahneman weighting function applied to cumulative probabilities, with its own γ for gains and for losses:

w(p)=pγ(pγ+(1−p)γ)1/γ(3)

CPT has six parameters. The flexible prospect theory (FLEX) has separate curvature for gains and losses, λ, and the two-parameter Prelec weighting functionDefinition: Prelec weighting function decision theory A two-parameter probability weighting function, exp of minus delta times minus log p to the power gamma, that sets the curvature and the crossing point of the curve separately. Excludes the one-parameter Tversky and Kahneman function used in CPT. full definition [4] on each side, nine parameters in all. Prelec's function, from decision theory, sets the curvature and the crossing point of the weighting curve separately, a shape the one-parameter function cannot take:

w(p)=e−δ(−ln⁡p)γ(4)

The combined formula

The combined formula (COMB) keeps CPT and adds four terms to the log odds of eq. 1, each the value for option B minus the value for option A:

ln⁡PB1−PB=b0+τ(VB−VA)+β1(HB−HA)+β2(TB−TA)+β3(MB−MA)+β4(QB−QA)(5)

Here H is the Shannon entropyDefinition: Shannon entropy information theory Minus the sum of p log2 p over a gamble's outcomes, in bits: how uncertain the outcome is before it happens, 0 for a sure thing. Excludes the sizes of the payoffs. full definition of the outcome distribution in bits, read as the information gained when the gamble resolves. In information theory entropy measures how uncertain an outcome is before it happens, 0 for a sure thing; it ignores the sizes of the payoffs:

H=−∑ipilog⁡2pi(6)

T is the probability of a loss, read as threat. M is the mean outcome and Q the mean squared outcome. Those two carry the drive term: for a setpoint S, the drive reductionDefinition: drive reduction motivation psychology, our operationalisation For a setpoint S, the quantity S squared minus (S minus x) squared for an outcome x, whose expectation is linear in the mean and mean square of outcomes. Excludes any measured need or state of the people choosing. full definition of an outcome is

S2−(S−x)2=2Sx−x2(7)

so its expectation is linear in M and Q. Drive reduction is a term from motivation psychology, here only the quadratic form above, and it excludes any measured need or state of the people choosing. The mean was divided by 10 and the mean square by 1,000 before fitting. COMB has ten parameters. Three reduced models add each term alone: CPT+H (entropy), CPT+T (loss probability) and CPT+D (mean and mean square).

Scoring

Each model was scored by 10-fold cross-validated R²Definition: cross-validated R² statistics and machine learning One minus the squared error of out-of-fold predictions over the variance of the observed rates, with 10 folds grouped by problem: the share of variance that predictions made without seeing those rates account for. Excludes in-sample R², which rewards fitting noise. full definition on the rates, with folds grouped by problem. Cross-validated R², from statistics and machine learning, is the share of variance in the observed rates that predictions made without seeing those rates account for, so it does not reward fitting noise as in-sample R² does. With out-of-fold predictions qi, observed rates yi and their mean my,

R2=1−∑i(yi−qi)2∑i(yi−my)2(8)

Each model was also scored by a quasi-binomial BICDefinition: quasi-binomial BIC statistics, model selection The Bayesian information criterion with the log-likelihood divided by the dispersion: a score that trades fit against the number of parameters, lower being better. Excludes an absolute test of a model, since it only compares models on the same data. full definition, with the dispersionDefinition: dispersion statistics, quasi-likelihood The factor phi by which observed rates scatter more than independent binomial choices would allow, taken from the COMB fit in each setting. Excludes a parameter of choice behaviour. full definition ϕ taken from the COMB fit in each setting (5.70 without feedback, 7.58 with it):

Bq=−2ln⁡Lϕ+kln⁡n(9)

where L is the binomial likelihood, k the number of parameters and n the number of problems. The Bayesian information criterion, a statistics score, trades fit against the number of parameters, lower being better; it compares models on the same data and gives no absolute test. The dispersion scales the likelihood for rates that scatter more than independent choices would allow, the quasi-binomial adjustment, and it is no parameter of choice.

Two references bound the value models. Gradient-boosted treesDefinition: gradient-boosted trees machine learning A predictor built by adding many small decision trees, each fitted to what the previous ones missed. Here a flexible learner's score on the same folds. Excludes a theory of choice, since it states no value function. full definition, fitted to the raw problem parameters and the four added terms with the same folds, give a flexible learner's score. The method, from machine learning, adds many small decision trees each fitted to what the previous ones missed; it predicts well and states no theory of choice. A sampling ceilingDefinition: sampling ceiling our usage, after reliability analysis One minus the mean sampling variance of the observed rates over their variance across problems: the share of variance not explained by finite samples of participants. Excludes noise of other kinds, such as the structured decision noise reported for these data. full definition, our bound, is the share of variance across problems not explained by sampling noise, C=1−ms/vy. Here ms is the mean over problems of the squared between-person standard deviation divided by the number of participants, and vy is the variance of the observed rates.

Tests on the added terms

Each added term was tested with the fitted CPT log odds held as a fixed offsetDefinition: offset regression A part of the prediction fixed in advance and never refitted. Here the fitted CPT log odds, so an added term can only explain what CPT leaves over. Excludes refitting CPT together with the added term. full definition: the term was standardised, fitted by iteratively reweighted least squaresDefinition: iteratively reweighted least squares statistics, generalised linear models The standard routine for fitting a logistic model by repeated weighted least-squares steps. Excludes any effect on what is tested, since it is only the fitting method. full definition, and its devianceDefinition: deviance statistics, generalised linear models Twice the log-likelihood shortfall of a model against a perfect fit. A deviance gain is the fall in deviance when a term is added. Excludes any penalty for the added parameter. full definition gain was compared with 200 fits on the same term permuted across problems. An offset, in regression, is a part of the prediction fixed in advance and never refitted, so the term can only explain what CPT leaves over. Iteratively reweighted least squares is the standard fitting routine for such models, a means of fitting with no effect on what is tested. Deviance is twice the log-likelihood shortfall of a model against a perfect fit, so a deviance gain is the improvement in fit from the term, before any penalty for its parameter. The p valueDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition is a p value from draws, as in permutation statistics, and assumes no textbook distribution; it counts one added to the numerator and the denominator:

p=k+1n+1(10)

where k is the number of permuted gains at or above the real one and n the number of permutations. The smallest possible value at 200 permutations is 0.005. The six p values, three terms in two settings, were corrected by Benjamini and Hochberg's procedureDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics, multiple testing A rule that adjusts a set of p values into q values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call. full definition at q 0.05. That multiple-testing rule keeps the expected share of false calls among the tests called significant at or below q, which is looser than the Bonferroni bound on any false call; the corrected values are q values.

The loss aversion intervalDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition comes from refitting CPT on problems resampled with replacement: 100 resamples without feedback and 30 with feedback, with the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles reported. This is a bootstrapDefinition: bootstrap statistics Refitting a model many times on problems resampled with replacement to read how much an estimate varies. Excludes an interval from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition, the statistics method that reads a number's spread from resampled data with no distribution assumed, and the interval holds the middle 95 percent of the resamples; it is no statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability.

Controls and planted checks

The planted check ran on the description problems with their real participant counts. Three data sets were simulated from CPT with λ 1.6, and three from CPT plus an entropy term with coefficient 0.25, each with extra-binomial noiseDefinition: extra-binomial noise statistics Scatter in a choice rate from problem to problem beyond what independent choices would give, simulated here with a Beta distribution. Excludes a bias in the rate. full definition drawn from a Beta distribution. That is scatter in the choice rate from problem to problem beyond what independent coin flips would give, the kind of spread real aggregate rates show, and it adds no bias to the rate. Selection between CPT and COMB was by the quasi-binomial BIC. The rule required the right model in at least 5 of 6 data sets and λ recovered within 0.3 in at least 2 of 3. Model selection picked the true model in 6 of 6 planted data sets and recovered loss aversion within 0.3 in 3 of 3.c5 The three recovered values were 1.64, 1.55 and 1.59. The check passed, and no verdict was voided.

c5 observed, evidence for claim 5
The numbers in claim 5
6; 0.3; 3 matches the result file, 2026-11-09
Chart 1
How the test was built: five models, one planted check and two null controls.
Chart 2
Every rule fixed in advance, the value it tested and the bar it had to clear.
Basis

Two null controls ask whether the description setting's joint gain from the four added terms is larger than chance would give. Their draws form a null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition, drawn from these data and never assumed from theory, whose 95th percentile is the bar the real gain must clear. The first permutes the four terms together across problems with CPT held fixed (200 draws). The second simulates outcomes from the fitted CPT at the observed dispersion and fits the four terms to those (100 draws). The second is a false-success checkDefinition: false-success check our usage A run of the full procedure on data simulated with no added effect, showing how large a gain the procedure finds when there is nothing to find. Excludes a planted check, which asks whether a real effect is found. full definition: on data with no added effect, it shows how large a gain the procedure finds anyway.

Results

Table 1 gives every model's score in both settings, and Figure 1 draws the main rows. Prospect theory improves on expected value by a wide margin in both settings. The flexible prospect theory improves on CPT by 0.017 without feedback and 0.012 with it.

What this means for a reader

If a published effect cleared p below 0.05, expect a replication to find it smaller, and expect the chance of a successful replication to be well below what the original's own numbers imply. A model of the significance filter turns that expectation into a number that is far better than trusting the original. It does not tell you which single finding will hold. On these data the plain original z value, read through a small regression, is the stronger tool for picking claims to check.

Objection

Fisher z standard errors ignore design, and unsigned rows assume direction.

What would change the call. Lock the two-normal prior and review the conversions by hand on a sample.

From the strongest objection recorded in our publication register.

Abstract

Published effects that cleared a significance threshold tend to be overstated, and replications of them succeed less often than their own statistics suggest. We asked whether one model of that filter, fitted only to the significant originals of other fields, can predict which effects replicate in a field it has not seen. On 1,222 significant originals in 307 replication projects, pooled from the Reproducibility Project Psychology and the FORRT Replication Database, each of eight fields was held out in turn and forecasts were scored by Brier score. The selection model beat taking the originals at face value by 0.142 in Brier score (95% interval 0.108 to 0.186) and did not beat the base rate, at -0.004 (-0.039 to 0.027).c1 A small logistic model on the original z value and the two sample sizes beat the selection model by 0.037 (0.011 to 0.069).c2 The preregistered kill rule fired, and the claim that the model tells which effects replicate is withdrawn. The reading that significant originals are inflated survives on these data.
