Introduction

The Open Science Collaboration [1] repeated 100 studies from three psychology journals and found that far fewer replications than originals reached significance. Since then, replication results have been gathered into databases. The FORRT Replication Database, FReD, joins earlier collections and pairs original findings with their replications at the level of single effects [4].

One explanation of the gap needs no misconduct. When results are published only if significant, the significance filterDefinition: significance filter (winner's curse) metascience and statistics The selection of published results by a significance threshold, which lets lucky overestimates through more often than underestimates, so the published effects of a set of studies are on average larger than the true ones. Excludes deliberate misconduct, which the filter neither requires nor detects. full definition lets through estimates that happened to land high. Gelman and Carlin [5] named the two resulting errors: the sign of a significant estimate can be wrong (Type S), and its size can be exaggerated (Type M), and both grow as power falls. A replication of the same size then succeeds less often than the original's estimate predicts.

Two families of tools forecast replication. Statistical models of selection, such as z-curve [6], fit the distribution of significant z values and estimate how often exact replications should succeed. Learned models predict from features of the original; Altmejd and colleagues [7] trained such a model on replications in economics and psychology and found, among other things, that interaction effects replicate worse than main effects.

This paper puts a selection modelDefinition: selection model meta-analysis and statistics A model of observed results that writes down both a distribution of true effects and the rule by which results get seen, here the rule that only originals with z above 1.96 in absolute value are seen, and fits both together. Excludes a model that takes the observed results as an unselected sample. full definition in a held-out test against three baselines, with all parameters fitted away from the field being forecast. The question is narrow: does a model of the filter pick out which effects replicate, or does it only set the level? Our search did not find a test of this exact design. That is what the search returned, and it does not show that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The design was written as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition and hash-locked on 31 October 2026 at 08:21 UTC, before any replication outcome was scored. Seen before the lock: column names, counts by category, the number of original statistics that could be converted, and outcomes simulated by the code. The published replication rate of the Reproducibility Project, 36 percent, was known, so the forecast for that field was not blind to its headline.

The locked file names the data, the conversions, the model, the held-out scheme, the baselines, the score, the interval and test methods, the planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition, two data checks, each controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition, the forecasts and the kill conditionsDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition. Nothing was added after the run.

Kill conditions, without discretion:

  • If the selection model fails to beat the base rate on held-out fields, it predicts a rate and not which effects replicate, and the study-level claim is withdrawn.
  • If it fails to beat face value, the winner's-curse reading is dropped for these data.
  • If the planted check or a data check fails, the affected verdictsDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition are voidDefinition: void research method (our usage) The verdict of a run whose planted check failed or whose sample fell below its stated minimum. It says nothing for or against the claim. Excludes a null result, which comes from a working instrument. full definition.

Data and provenance

Two public sets were read through the Open Science Framework's interface: the Reproducibility Project Psychology data [1] [2], released under CC0, and FReD [3], released under CC BY 4.0. Rows of the Reproducibility Project were removed from FReD so that no effect enters twice. Only numeric columns were read from the Reproducibility Project file; names and emails in it were never loaded. Outputs stay at field and project level, and no paper or author is scored or named.

Effects were converted to a correlation from r, d, g, h, standardised beta, odds ratios, eta squared, r squared, f squared, and parsed t, F with one numerator degree of freedom, Z and chi squared with one degree of freedom. Other effect types were dropped. Of 2,164 FReD rows, 1,344 converted. Only originals significant by our conversion entered, since the model conditions on that filter: 201 FReD rows and 18 Reproducibility Project rows were dropped as not significant. That left 1,222 effects, 79 from the Reproducibility Project and 1,143 from FReD, in 307 project clusters, the largest with 156 rows.

Fields are coarse buckets of our own: seven groups of FReD rows (cognitive, economics, management, marketing, other psychology, social and other) and the Reproducibility Project as an eighth. Which effects got replicated was itself selected by the people who chose to replicate them. The results describe this set of replicated effects, not published work at large.

Methods

Effects on one scale

Each effect is put on the Fisher zDefinition: Fisher z statistics The transform of a correlation r to half the natural log of (1 + r) over (1 - r), on which the sampling error is close to normal with standard error 1 over the square root of n minus 3. Excludes the z statistic of a test, which is an effect divided by its standard error. full definition scale, with a standard error from the sample size n:

y=12ln⁡1+r1−r(1)
s=1n−3(2)

An original enters only if y/s exceeds 1.96 in absolute value. A replication succeeds if its own y/s exceeds 1.96 in the original's direction. The same rule is applied to every row, whatever the database's own label says.

The selection model

The true effect θ of an original is either exactly zero, with weight π0, or drawn from a normal distribution with mean zero and spread τ:

g(θ)=π0δ(θ)+(1−π0)ϕ(θ;0,τ2)(3)

where δ is a point mass at zero and ϕ(x;m,v) the normal density with mean m and variance v. The estimate is normal around the true effect, so an original's density before selection is f(y)=∫g(θ)ϕ(y;θ,s2)dθ. Because only significant originals are seen, each original's likelihood is divided by the chance w(s) that an estimate with its standard error would be significant:

L=∏if(yi)w(si)(4)

The parameters π0 and τ are fitted by maximum likelihood on the training fields. The weight π0 is a mixture weight under an assumed prior. It is not the share of false hypotheses, and it measures no misconduct or intent.

Forecasts

For original i, let hi(θ) be the density of the true effect given the original's estimate, and ψi(θ) a replication's statistical power at its own sample size, meaning the chance that it succeeds by the rule above when the true effect is θ. The forecast is

qi=∫ψi(θ)hi(θ)dθ(5)

Five forecasts compete with it, each built only from training rows. The face-value forecastDefinition: face-value forecast forecasting, our usage A forecast that takes each published original effect as the true effect and predicts replication from the power a replication of the given size would have against it. Excludes any correction for how the original was selected. full definition sets θ equal to the original estimate. The base-rate forecastDefinition: base-rate forecast forecasting A forecast that gives every effect in a held-out field the same chance of replicating, the share that replicated in the training fields. Excludes any use of an effect's own statistics. full definition gives every row the training success rate. A logistic regressionDefinition: logistic regression statistics A model in which the log odds of success are a weighted sum of predictors, here the original z value, the log of the original sample size and the log of the replication sample size, fitted by maximum likelihood on the training fields. Excludes any model of how originals were selected. full definition uses the original z value and the logs of the two sample sizes. A normal prior with no spike drops the point mass. A transport term lets the replication's true effect differ from the original's by a normal amount whose variance h is fitted on training replications.

Score and held-out scheme

Forecasts are scored by the Brier scoreDefinition: Brier score forecast verification The mean squared difference between a forecast probability and the outcome coded 1 or 0, from 0 for a perfect forecast to 1 for a confident wrong one. 0.25 is what a forecast of one half always earns. Excludes a ranking measure such as AUC, which ignores whether the probabilities are at the right level. full definition over N held-out rows with outcomes oi of 1 or 0:

B=1N∑i(qi−oi)2(6)

In a leave-one-field-out testDefinition: leave-one-field-out test statistics, cross-validation A test in which each field in turn is held out, every parameter is fitted on the other fields, and forecasts are scored only on the held-out field. Excludes scoring forecasts on the rows that were used to fit them. full definition each of the eight fields is forecast with every parameter fitted on the other seven, and the held-out scores are pooled. Skill over the base rate is Bbase−Bsel, so a positive value favours the selection model.

Intervals and tests

Each comparison is a difference in pooled Brier score, the competitor's minus the selection model's. Its 95% intervalDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition comes from a project-cluster bootstrapDefinition: project-cluster bootstrap statistics An interval made by recomputing a statistic many times, here 2,000, on samples of whole replication projects drawn with replacement, so rows from one project stay together. Excludes resampling single rows as if they were independent. full definition with 2,000 draws. Its p value comes from a sign-flip permutation testDefinition: sign-flip permutation test statistics A test that sums the per-project differences between two forecasts' scores, then flips the sign of each project's difference at random many times, here 4,000, to see how often a sum as large arises with no true difference. Excludes a test that treats rows inside one project as independent. full definition over projects with 4,000 draws, and the four comparisons are adjusted together with the Benjamini-Hochberg correctionDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics, multiple testing A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05. The adjusted values are called q values. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call. full definition. The prior's shape was compared by BICDefinition: BIC statistics, model comparison The Bayesian information criterion, minus twice the maximised log likelihood plus the number of parameters times the log of the number of rows. Lower is better, and a difference of 10 is the usual bar for strong preference. Excludes a test of whether either model is right. full definition on all originals against a single normal and a two-normal mixture.

Controls and planted checks

The planted check used the real sample-size pairs with outcomes simulated from the model at three known settings of π0 and τ: 0.5 and 0.25, 0.05 and 0.35, 0.8 and 0.3, five datasets each. Across the 15 planted datasets the fit recovered π0 with mean absolute error 0.051 and the success rate with mean error 0.009, and the selection model beat face value in every one.c3 The rules were an error below 0.1, a rate error below 0.03 and a win in at least 90 percent. The fit was weakest at π0 of 0.05, where two of five datasets gave estimates near 0.18.

c3 observed, evidence for claim 3
The numbers in claim 3
15; 0.051; 0.009 matches the result file, 2026-11-09
Chart 1
The planted check: the fit run on simulated data where the answer is known.
Basis
observed: measured in this study, with a result file

Two data checks tested the conversions. The Reproducibility Project rows we kept carried 34 reported successes against the 35 published, within the rule of 4. FReD rows labelled successful by the database had a success rate by our rule of 0.86, and rows labelled failed 0.15, a gap of 0.71 against a rule of at least 0.3. By our own uniform rule, 27 of the 79 kept Reproducibility Project rows succeeded.

Two controls give the null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition of skill over the base rate. Shuffling replication outcomes across rows (500 draws) gave a 95th percentile of -0.110. Shuffling original statistics across rows while keeping each replication's size (200 draws) gave -0.092 and measures how much skill comes from replication size alone. Both sit far below zero, because a confident forecast paired with the wrong outcome is punished hard. Beating them shows that the real pairing carries signal. The base-rate comparison is the test that decides.

Results

Table 1 and Figure 1 give the pooled held-out Brier scores. The selection model at 0.260 sits next to the base rate at 0.256, far ahead of face value at 0.402 and behind the logistic model at 0.223.

Table 2 gives the four preregistered comparisons. What this means for a reader

When a benchmark says a new nature-inspired optimiser wins, check two things: whether the test functions have their best point at the centre of the search box, and whether the standard methods it beat were run correctly. Our own first run failed the second check, and the result looked like a win for the nature-inspired group. Two popular methods in that group did well only when the answer sat at the centre. A good result on centred test functions can come from a method that guesses the centre. A stricter score, which counts a run only when it gets within 1e-8 of the optimum and then asks how fast it got there, keeps CMA-ES first and moves L-BFGS up to second.

Objection

Seven functions, 10 dimensions, one budget of 20,000 evaluations and 15 repeats. Other functions, dimensions or budgets could reorder the methods.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Optimisers named after slime moulds, wolves, bees and ants are often reported to beat standard methods. Our first preregistered benchmark seemed to agree: the biologically labelled group had the better mean rank, 5.04 against 6.20. Tracing a poor CMA-ES score showed a bug in our own code, and several other methods had a related fault. We kept that run, fixed the box handling for every method, wrote a new preregistration and ran again on seven test functions in 10 dimensions. After the fix, CMA-ES ranked first on the shifted functions with a mean rank of 2.00, and the best method with a biological label, ACOR, ranked second at 3.14.c1 Moving the optimum away from the centre cost the slime mould method 12.1 and the grey wolf method 13.6 decades of median error, while ACOR, IWO and PSO lost 0.0006, 0.07 and 0.42 decades.c2 Without random search the plain group's mean rank was 3.98 against 5.54 for the biologically labelled group; with random search counted as plain the groups were 5.45 and 5.54, a gap that sat inside the label-permutation range (p 0.45).c3 The group contest does not settle much in either direction. The method-level results do. On 18 November 2026 we scored the same grid again with a success target of the optimum plus 1e-8, ranking methods by successes and then by evaluations spent. Under the fixed target, CMA-ES stayed first at a mean rank of 2.71 against 3.86 for L-BFGS, and it was first in all 2,000 bootstrap resamples.c5

Introduction

A metaheuristicDefinition: metaheuristic optimisation A general recipe for searching for the minimum of a function by sampling and updating a set of candidate points, used when the function gives no gradient or has many local minima. Excludes exact methods that come with a proof of finding the minimum. full definition is a general recipe for searching a function for its minimum by sampling and updating candidate points. Sörensen [1] described a flood of "novel" metaheuristics built on metaphors of natural or man-made processes and argued that the trend threatens to lead the field away from scientific rigour. Camacho-Villalón, Dorigo and Stützle [2] took six widely used metaphor-based methods for continuous problems apart into components, the grey wolf optimiser among them, and reported that none of them proposes a new idea; one section of their paper is titled "The grey wolf optimizer is PSO".

Kudela [3] pointed to a defect in how such methods are tested. Several common test functionsDefinition: test function optimisation benchmarking A formula with a known minimum, chosen to be easy or hard in a known way, on which optimisers are compared by how close they get. Excludes real engineering problems, whose minimum is unknown. full definition have their minimum at the centre of the feasible set, and a method whose update rule has a centre biasDefinition: centre bias evolutionary computation benchmarking, after Kudela A tendency of a method's update rule to pull candidates toward the centre of the search box, which helps on any function whose minimum happens to sit there. Excludes good performance that survives when the minimum is moved. full definition solves those functions easily. Comparisons between such a method and one without the bias on centred functions say little.

The no free lunchDefinition: no free lunch optimisation theory, after Wolpert and Macready The result that, averaged over all possible functions, every search method that never revisits a point does equally well, so any advantage on one class of functions is paid for on another. Excludes claims about any one class of functions, such as the test functions here. full definition theorems of Wolpert and Macready [4] give the background for any optimiser comparison: averaged over all possible functions, no method beats another, so an advantage on one class is paid for on another.

This study tested biologically labelled methodsDefinition: biologically labelled method our usage for this study An optimiser whose published description is framed by an animal, plant or other organism, here slime mould, grey wolf, particle swarm, bee colony, ant colony and invasive weed. Excludes any claim that the method works the way the organism does. full definition against plain ones with the optimum moved off the centre. It became a study of our own error as well. The first run's headline came from a bug in our CMA-ESDefinition: CMA-ES evolutionary computation, after Hansen and colleagues Covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy: it samples candidates from a multivariate normal distribution and adapts the distribution's centre, shape and step size from the best samples. Excludes the larger-population restart schedule known as IPOP, which our version did not use. full definition code. CMA-ES, the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy, samples candidates from a normal distribution and adapts the distribution's centre, shape and step size. Auger and Hansen [5] described a version that restarts with a doubled population each time, known as IPOP. Ours restarts with the same population size.

Preregistration and design

The study ran twice, each time under its own preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition. The first (here, the first run) was hash-locked on 31 October 2026 before any result of the run was seen; only smoke runs (short trial runs that check the code executes) in 3 dimensions with small budgets had been made, to fix crashes, and no rankings were read from them. It named the methods, the functions, the measures, two controlsDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition, the forecasts and the kill conditionsDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition. The decision it informs was written in it: no slime or plant-labelled optimiser becomes a default search method in our tools unless it beats differential evolution and CMA-ES on the shifted functions.

The second (the rerun) was hash-locked on 31 October 2026 after the first run had been read in full. It records what went wrong, the fix, and new forecasts. Its own kill condition reads: if CMA-ES fails to bring the median error on the shifted ellipsoid below 1, it is still broken and the study stops. It also commits to reporting any biologically labelled method that beats the best plain one, whatever we expected.

Both preregistrations' SHA-256 hashes are in the reproduction section.

Data and provenance

No external data were used. All results come from our own implementations of ten optimisers and seven standard test functions, run on one desktop computer. The method update rules were written from their published descriptions with default settings and no tuning. Every number in this paper is read from the two runs' result files, apart from the fixed-target scoring, whose numbers are read from its own analysis file. That scoring's code, all 1,260 runs, its analysis and its preregistration addendum are published in the site's repository beside this page, under the repository's licence, which lets anyone read and review them [7].

Methods

Methods compared

The plain group is random search, L-BFGS-B with restarts and a numeric gradient, differential evolution (rand/1/bin) and CMA-ES with restarts. The biologically labelled group is the slime mould algorithm (SMA), the grey wolf optimiser (GWO), particle swarm optimisation (PSO), artificial bee colony (ABC), ant colony optimisation for continuous domains (ACOR) and invasive weed optimisation (IWO). Every method gets the same budget of 20,000 function evaluations; a numeric gradient spends evaluations from that budget.

Functions and arms

The seven functions are the sphere, an ellipsoid with a condition number of one million, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin, Ackley, Griewank and Schaffer F7, each in 10 dimensions with a minimum value of 0. The search boxDefinition: search box optimisation The allowed region, here every coordinate between -100 and 100. A method may only propose and keep points inside it. Excludes constraints other than simple bounds on each coordinate. full definition allows every coordinate from -100 to 100. On the shifted armDefinition: shifted arm our usage for this study The version of each test function whose minimum is moved to a random point with every coordinate between -70 and 70 and whose axes are turned by a random rotation, the same for every method within one repeat. Excludes the unshifted arm, with the minimum at the centre and the axes aligned. full definition each base function g is evaluated as

f(x)=g(R(x−s))(1)

where s is a random shift with every coordinate drawn from -70 to 70 and R a random rotation. Every method sees the same s and R within one repeat. On the unshifted arm s is zero and R is the identity, so the minimum sits at the centre of the box. Each method ran 15 repeats on each function on each arm.

Measures

For method m on function f, let Mfm be the median best error over the 15 repeats on the shifted arm and Ufm the same on the unshifted arm, each floored at 10−12. Methods are ranked on each function by the base-10 logarithm of Mfm rounded to two decimals, with ties sharing their average rank. Call that rank ρfm. The mean rankDefinition: mean rank benchmarking statistics Each method's rank on each function by median final error, averaged over the seven functions. 1 is best and 10 is worst. Excludes how large the differences in error are. full definition is

rm=17∑fρfm(2)

The change in error from moving the minimum, in decadesDefinition: decade measurement A factor of ten. A change of one decade in error is a change of one in its base-10 logarithm. Excludes a difference on a linear scale. full definition, is

δfm=log⁡10Mfm−log⁡10Ufm(3)

and a method's shift penaltyDefinition: shift penalty our usage for this study For one method, the median over the seven functions of how many decades its median error grows when the function moves from the unshifted arm to the shifted arm. Excludes effects of the rotation alone, which the design does not separate from the shift. full definition Dm is the median of δfm over the seven functions. The group gap is

G=rbio−rplain(4)

where rbio and rplain are the averages of rm over each group, so a positive gap means the plain group did better.

The bug and the fix

In the first run CMA-ES scored a median error of 14 million on the ellipsoid. Tracing it showed that the distribution's centre had left the box (its norm reached 498 against a box half-width of 100). Every sample was clipped to the same corner, the step size fell to about 10−8, and the method never restarted. Differential evolution, ABC, ACOR and IWO also kept candidates outside the box in their internal state. These were errors in our code.

For the rerun every method keeps its candidates inside the box. CMA-ES adds a quadratic penalty for any part of a sample outside the box,

F=f+10000(1+a)∑ieiei(5)

where a is the absolute value of f and ei is how far coordinate i lies outside the box, zero inside. It restarts from a random point when its step size falls below 10−11. No method's parameters were tuned.

Controls and planted checks

Two planted checksDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition guard the instrument. CMA-ES must bring the shifted sphere below 10−8. A centre cheatDefinition: centre cheat our usage for this study A dummy method that only samples points within a tiny distance of the centre of the box, so it solves any function whose minimum sits there and nothing else. Excludes any real optimiser. full definition, a dummy method that samples only points next to the centre, must solve the unshifted sphere (error below 0.001) and fail the shifted one (base-10 logarithm of its error above 3). The cheat shows that the unshifted arm can be won by guessing the centre and that the shifted arm cannot.

The label permutationDefinition: label permutation statistics (permutation test) Shuffling which method name goes with which rank within each function, 2,000 times, to see how large a gap between the two groups' mean ranks arises by chance. Excludes uncertainty from the random repeats of each run. full definition control shuffles method names within each function's ranks 2,000 times and records the group gap each time. A real gap must clear the 95th percentile of that null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition.

The no-free-lunch check runs every method on a test function in which each integer cell of the box gets an independent random value, with a budget of 5,000 evaluations and 30 repeats. No method can exploit such a function, so the methods should tie. Ties are tested with the Kruskal-Wallis testDefinition: Kruskal-Wallis test statistics A rank-based test of whether several groups of numbers come from the same distribution. Excludes a test of which group is better. full definition, with L-BFGS left out because it can stall on a flat cell, on the best value found and, in the rerun, on the best of the first 500 distinct cells visited.

In the rerun CMA-ES reached a median error of 1.6e-15 on the shifted sphere, written in the e-notation used in the tables. The centre cheat reached 7.2e-7 on the unshifted sphere and an error whose base-10 logarithm is 4.27 on the shifted sphere. Both planted checks held.

Results

Table 1 gives every method's mean rank in both runs and its shift penalty in the rerun, and Figure 1 draws the ranks. After the fix, CMA-ES ranked first on the shifted functions with a mean rank of 2.00, and the best method with a biological label, ACOR, ranked second at 3.14.c1 The fix moved CMA-ES from 4.86 to 2.00 and PSO, the first run's leader, from 2.79 to 4.57.

With the minimum at the centre, SMA ranked first (2.07) and GWO second (2.43). Figure 2 shows what moving the minimum did to each method. Moving the optimum away from the centre cost the slime mould method 12.1 and the grey wolf method 13.6 decades of median error, while ACOR, IWO and PSO lost 0.0006, 0.07 and 0.42 decades.c2 The centre bias described by Kudela [3] shows in two of the six labelled methods and not in the other four.

Table 2 gives the group contest. Without random search the plain group's mean rank was 3.98 against 5.54 for the biologically labelled group; with random search counted as plain the groups were 5.45 and 5.54, a gap that sat inside the label-permutation range (p 0.45).c3 The preregistered label-permutation control was computed only for the gap with random search included. The gap of 1.56 without it has no control of its own.

In the first run the labelled group's lead of 1.16 ranks came partly from our bug and partly from counting random search as plain, and it sat inside its own label-permutation range.c4 The first run's preregistration had a kill condition we did not apply when we first read it: if the no-free-lunch check fails to tie, the ranking is void. That check failed (p 0.0015), so by its own rule the first run's ranking was voidDefinition: void research method (our usage) The verdict of a run whose planted check failed or whose sample fell below its stated minimum. It says nothing for or against the claim. Excludes a null result, which comes from a working instrument. full definition. In the rerun the methods tied on that function, at p 0.13 on the best value and p 0.74 on the best of the first 500 distinct cells. The rerun's preregistration traced the first run's failure to converged methods revisiting the same cells, which the theorem does not count; in the rerun IWO visited a median of 2,870 distinct cells in 5,000 evaluations, against 5,000 for random search and ACOR.

Second scoring: a fixed target and average runtime

On 18 November 2026 we scored the shifted arm again under a rule Nikolaus Hansen suggested to us in cor

What this means for a reader

A simulation can match a known answer for the wrong reason. Ours produced a clean threshold for when cooperation survives, close to a number from the theory literature, and we credited the theory. The match came from a coding choice that let each cooperator keep part of its own contribution, which turns cooperation into private investment. If you build or read individual-based models of microbes, markets or teams, check whether the "cooperators" are paid by their own act.

Objection

One update rule, fitness-proportional and synchronous, with invented numbers. Other update rules, asynchronous timing, other neighbourhood sizes or a parent window separate from the goods box could let producers persist.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Microbes that release costly products into their surroundings are exposed to cheaters that take the benefit and skip the cost. A standard result in social evolution says that when relatives stay near each other, producers can persist anyway. We tried to reproduce that on a simple grid model before using the idea in our own writing, and in the second of three preregistered rounds the model seemed to succeed, with a threshold that matched a rule from the theory literature. It had a flaw: each producer received a share of its own goods. The shuffled control, which should have collapsed, kept producers at a mean share of 0.37 (95th percentile 0.52), and with a 3 by 3 goods box a producer recovers a ninth of its own output, so producing paid for itself whenever the benefit-to-cost ratio passed 9.c1 The third round paid goods to others only. With goods paid to others only, local producers ended at a share of 0.03 at a benefit-to-cost ratio of 100, 0.19 at 200 and 0.48 at 400, and never reached the preregistered bar of 0.5.c2 Under this update rule, space alone gave producers no foothold at any benefit-to-cost ratio up to 50, where their share was 0.00.

Introduction

Many bacteria release a public goodDefinition: public good social evolution and economics A product that costs its maker something and benefits others nearby, such as an enzyme or iron-scavenging molecule a microbe releases into its surroundings. Excludes products the maker keeps for itself. full definition, a product that costs its maker something and helps others nearby. Iron-scavenging siderophores are a studied case. In a population where everyone meets everyone, a cheaterDefinition: producer and cheater social evolution A producer pays a cost to make the public good. A cheater makes none and still gains from the goods of producers near it. Excludes any intention on either side; the words name two fixed strategies. full definition that makes none and takes the benefit should win. Kin selection gives one way out: if producers mostly help relatives, which are also producers, production can spread.

Space is the usual route to relatedness in microbes, because daughter cells stay near their parents. Nadell, Drescher and Foster [1] review how the spatial arrangement of clones and species in biofilms shapes cooperation and competition. Space also has a cost. Taylor [2] showed with an inclusive fitness model that in a patch-structured population the benefit of helping relatives and the cost of local competitionDefinition: local competition social evolution, after Taylor and after Griffin and colleagues Competition for space or resources among neighbours, which, when neighbours are relatives, can cancel the benefit that helping relatives brings. Excludes competition spread over the whole population. full definition among them can cancel exactly, the same result Wilson, Pollock and Dugatkin [3] reached by simulation. Griffin, West and Buckling [4] tested it in the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa by setting relatedness and the scale of competition independently, and found that cooperation rose with relatedness and fell when competition was more local.

On graphs, Ohtsuki, Hauert, Lieberman and Nowak [5] found that selection favours cooperation when the benefit-to-cost ratio exceeds the average number of neighbours. We used that rule in our second round to forecast a threshold, and the forecast came true for a reason the rule had nothing to do with.

Preregistration and design

The study ran in three rounds on 31 October 2026, each under its own preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, hash-locked before that round ran and written after reading the round before. The decision they inform was stated in the third: whether our own writing may say that space protects cooperators on the strength of our own model, or must only cite published work for it.

  • Round one asked whether producers persist under local rules at b of 2 and c of 0.3 and collapse when mixed or shuffled. Its kill conditionsDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition: if the mixed arm does not collapse or its early decline misses a closed form, the model is wrong; if the shuffled arm keeps producers, space was not the cause.
  • Round two, after round one missed, swept the benefit-to-cost ratioDefinition: benefit-to-cost ratio social evolution The benefit b that one producer's goods give in total divided by the cost c it pays, written b/c. Excludes the net payoff to any one cell, which also depends on its neighbours. full definition from 5 to 16 at b of 1, 2 and 4 and forecast that persistence would begin between ratios of 7 and 12. Its kill conditions: a mean-field error above 0.03, or a shuffled arm that keeps producers.
  • Round three, after reading round two's control, ran goods to others only beside the old version, at ratios from 2 to 400. It had no kill condition: it said in advance that whatever it gave would be the report.

The SHA-256 of each preregistration is in the reproduction section.

Data and provenance

No external data were used. The model and all its numbers are our own and invented for the check. It describes no organism. Every number in this paper is read from the three rounds' result files.

Methods

The model

A torus gridDefinition: torus grid simulation A square grid whose opposite edges are joined, so every cell has the same number of neighbours and there is no border. Excludes grids with edges, where border cells have fewer neighbours. full definition of 100 by 100 cells holds producers and cheaters, starting half and half at random. Let z be 1 for a producer and 0 for a cheater. A cell's fitness is

W=1+bϕ−cz(1)

floored at a small positive value, where ϕ is the share of producers in the cell's goods boxDefinition: goods box our usage for this study The square of cells over which one producer's goods are spread, 3 by 3 at range 1 and 5 by 5 at range 2. Excludes the 3 by 3 window from which parents are drawn, which stays fixed. full definition. Each generation is a synchronous updateDefinition: synchronous update simulation Every cell of the grid is replaced at once in each generation, from the fitnesses of the previous generation. Excludes asynchronous updating, where one cell at a time is replaced. full definition by fitness-proportional replacementDefinition: fitness-proportional replacement evolutionary dynamics The update rule in which a cell's next occupant is copied from a parent drawn with chance in proportion to the parent's fitness, here among the 3 by 3 window around the cell including the cell itself. Excludes other update rules, such as death followed by birth from neighbours only, or imitation of the best neighbour. full definition: every cell's next occupant is copied from a parent drawn from the 3 by 3 window around the cell, the cell included, with chance in proportion to fitness.

In rounds one and two the producer share counts the cell itself:

ϕ=nN(2)

where n is the number of producers in the box, the cell included, and N the number of cells in the box, 9 for a 3 by 3 box. In round three, goods reach others only:

ϕ=n−zN−1(3)

Arms

The local arm uses the rules above. The mixed armDefinition: mixed arm our usage for this study The version of the model in which every cell gains from the producer share of the whole population and parents are drawn from the whole population, so neighbours mean nothing. Excludes any spatial structure. full definition sets ϕ to the producer share of the whole grid and draws parents from the whole grid. The shuffled armDefinition: shuffled arm our usage for this study The version of the model in which all positions are shuffled at random before each generation and the local rules then apply, so neighbours are strangers. Excludes the clustering of relatives that the local arm allows. full definition shuffles all positions before each generation and then applies the local rules, so neighbours are strangers.

The flaw

Under eq. 2 a producer is one of the N cells its own goods reach, so it receives b/N of its own output. Producing then pays the producer directly whenever

bN>c(4)

that is, whenever b/c exceeds N, which is 9 for a 3 by 3 box. That is a private return. It needs no relatives nearby, so it survives in the shuffled arm too. In round three it did so from a ratio of 20 (a share of 0.37) and fully from 30; at ratios of 12 and 16 the shuffled producers ended at 0.00 while local producers ended at 1.00, so in that band clustering still mattered.

Measures

The final producer shareDefinition: final producer share our usage for this study The share of producers in the grid at the end of a run, averaged over the replicate runs. A run stops early when one type takes the whole grid. Excludes the share of runs in which producers survived. full definition is the share of producers at the end of a run, averaged over replicate runs; a run stops early when one type fills the grid. A ratio counts as persistence when that average reaches 0.5. Round one ran 1,500 generations and 8 replicates; round two 1,200 generations and 6 replicates; round three 1,000 generations and 5 replicates.

Controls and planted checks

The shuffled arm is the controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition on which the study turns. If space is what keeps producers alive, removing space must make them collapse. Rounds two and three ran it 20 times at the most favourable setting.

Round two added a known answer for the mixed arm. Producers have fitness 1+bp−c and cheaters 1+bp, where p is the producer share, so the mean-field recursionDefinition: mean-field recursion population genetics An exact formula for next generation's producer share in the mixed arm, used here as a known answer the simulation must match. Excludes the local and shuffled arms, which have no such formula. full definition is

pt+1=pt(1+bpt−c)1+bpt−cpt(5)

The simulated mixed arm, on a 300 by 300 grid averaged over 8 runs, had to match it within 0.03 over the first 20 generations. It did, with a maximum error of 0.0019.

Round one's known answer for the mixed arm was a closed-form slope for the early decline of the producer share on the log-odds scale. It failed, with an error of 0.117 against a bar of 0.05. The closed form was our mistake: it held the producer share fixed at one half while the share fell. Round two replaced it with eq. 5.

Results

Round one

At b of 2 and c of 0.3, a ratio of 6.7, local producers collapsed in every run, against our forecast of a final share of 0.6. The mixed and shuffled arms collapsed too. The cost sweep at b of 2 kept producers at c of 0.1 and 0.2, ratios of 20 and 10, and lost them from 0.3 up. Read with eq. 4, that pattern already fits the flaw.

Round two

Figure 1 shows the threshold. Local producers first reached a final share of 0.5 at a ratio of 9 for every value of b: 0.52 at b of 1, 0.66 at 2 and 0.88 at 4. We had forecast 7 to 12 from the rule that cooperation wins when the ratio exceeds the number of neighbours, 8 here, and counted it a pass.

The control did not hold. The shuffled control, which should have collapsed, kept producers at a mean share of 0.37 (95th percentile 0.52), and with a 3 by 3 goods box a producer recovers a ninth of its own output, so producing paid for itself whenever the benefit-to-cost ratio passed 9.c1 The control ran at a ratio of 20 with 20 draws; its 5th percentile was 0.26. The same round's goods-range sweep at a ratio of 20 kept producers at range 1 and lost them at range 2, where the box holds 25 cells and the private return b/25 falls below c. The threshold was the size of the goods box.

Round three

Table 1 and Figure 2 give the side-by-side run at b of 2. With self-benefit put back, local producers reached a share of 0.70 at a ratio of 9 and 1.0 from 12 up, and shuffled producers reached 1.0 from a ratio of 30 up.c3 The artefact reproduced.

items.title: F204: Backward and contrary checks caught 39 of 47 quiet faults in eight small simulated instruments
items.description: In a mutation simulation on eight small instrument models, running a model backward and against its contrary caught 39 of 47 faults that had passed a calibration point, where a wide forward test caught 29. Half the faults came from one instrument, and a model that is wrong in a self-consistent way passed everything.

What this means for a reader

If you maintain code that models a physical instrument, a test that runs the model forward and then backward costs little and needs no trusted answer, and in this simulation it found faults that many forward reference points missed. It has a blind spot that matters: a model that is wrong in a self-consistent way inverts itself perfectly and passes. So keep at least one absolute reference, and never calibrate with every scale factor set to 1. The numbers come from eight small models and planted faults, and a test on a real code base with real bugs is what would confirm or sink them.

Objection

This is a simulation on planted faults. Mutants are arithmetic slips made by rule, and no study here shows that they resemble the faults people make in instrument code.

What would change the call. The same test on a real code base with real faults, checked by someone outside the project.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

A numerical instrument model is usually tested forward: feed it a case with a known answer and compare. We asked how much two checks that need no known answer add: running the model backward against itself, and running it against its contrary. The study is a simulation. Code planted one fault at a time at every arithmetic site of eight small instrument models we wrote, and scored which tests noticed. Among 47 single faults that passed one calibration point, the backward and contrary checks together caught 39 (83 percent) and a wide forward test caught 29 (62 percent); sign-flip p 0.003, corrected to 0.013 within the study and 0.009 across the 84 tests of the nine-study set.c1 The advantage sits in three of the eight instruments, and one of them, the Radon projector, supplies 23 of the 47 faults; without it the counts are 16 and 12 of 24.c2 Seven faults passed every test: four divide by a grid spacing that every test set to 1, and three leave a wrong wave propagator that still inverts itself exactly.c3 On pairs of faults the order reversed with no clear difference: the wide test caught 27 of 30 and the backward and contrary checks 24 of 30, p 0.12.c4 Nothing here was measured on hardware or on code written by anyone else.

Introduction

Scientific code often has no cheap source of right answers. Software testing calls this the oracle problem, and metamorphic testingDefinition: metamorphic testing software engineering (testing) Testing a program by checking a relation that must hold between the outputs of several related runs, used when no trusted expected output is available. Excludes a test that compares one output with a stored expected value, and any proof that an output is correct. full definition is the standard response: check a relation that must hold between several runs of the program. The term comes from software engineering and covers any test that compares outputs of related inputs with each other; a test that compares one output with a stored expected value is outside it. Segura and colleagues surveyed 119 papers on the method [1], and a later article by the same first author warns that a satisfied relation does not confirm that an output is right [2].

Physics supplies such relations for free. A lossless film transmits the same from either side. A wave run forward and then backward in time returns to its start. A projector and its adjointDefinition: adjoint linear algebra and inverse problems The partner of a linear map that carries vectors from the output space back to the input space so that the inner product of an output with a vector equals the inner product of the input with the partner's result. Excludes the inverse, which undoes the map; an adjoint exists for maps that cannot be undone. full definition satisfy an inner-product identity. The adjoint, in linear algebra and inverse problems, is the partner map that moves a vector from the output space back to the input space so that the two inner products agree; it is a different thing from the inverse, which undoes the map. Claerbout's dot-product test, which compares two scalars computed with random vectors, has been a routine check of such pairs in geophysical imaging for decades, and his texts say a failure condemns the code while a pass leaves correctness unproven [3]. A recent tutorial on adjoint gradients names the same blind spot we met here: the test checks mutual consistency, so a wrong derivative with a matching wrong transpose passes [4].

None of this is new, and we claim no novelty. The question was a practical one for our own work: how much weight a reference-free check should get beside a forward test when a new numerical kernel is written. The decision it informed was whether the check enters our catalogue of default checks. We priced it with mutantsDefinition: mutant software engineering (mutation testing) A copy of a program with one small fault planted by rule, such as a plus swapped for a minus, used to measure whether a test notices. Excludes a bug written by a person; mutants stand in for such bugs and may not resemble them. full definition. A mutant, in mutation testing, is a copy of a program with one small fault planted by rule; it is a stand-in for a bug and may not resemble the bugs people write. The survey above describes the share of mutants a test detects as a common measure of test strength [1].

Preregistration and design

The study ran twice on 31 October 2026, each time under a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition: a plan with forecasts and rules, hash-locked before the run.

The first run compared four test sets on every mutant of every function. It gave the backward and contrary checks 79 of 89 false passes (89 percent) against 29 of 89 (33 percent) for the wide forward test. Reading the 51 faults that only the reference-free checks caught showed that most sat in functions the forward tests never called, or in an output the forward film test never read. The result was partly a gap in our own forward tests. That run is kept as it ran, and its headline is not claimed here.

The second preregistration was written after the first result was seen, and says so in its text. It scores only faults in functions that the forward tests call, makes the forward film tests read both outputs, reports faults in inverse functions apart, and adds pairs of faults. Its forecasts were that the wide forward test would catch more than the reference-free checks, on single faults and on pairs. Its kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition, the outcome fixed in advance that would end the claim, was a catch rate under 30 percent for the reference-free checks on single faults. Each forecast became a rule that code reads off the result as a verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition.

The first preregistration also covered a re-reading of two earlier studies of ours with the same three-way idea. That part was post hoc and is not reported in this paper.

Data and provenance

There is no external dataset. The material is eight instrument models written for this study in plain Python with NumPy, each a few lines long so that every arithmetic site can be changed: a normal-incidence thin film by characteristic matrices; an angular-spectrum wave propagator; a leapfrog wave equation in one dimension; a blur with its adjoint and a regularised deblur; a pixel-driven Radon projector with its adjoint; an explicit heat-diffusion step; ray transfer matrices; and a Stokes analyzer row with a least-squares inversion. The faults were generated by rule from that source. The forward reference values are closed-form results from textbook physics, coded by us. All of it is our own work, written the same day as the tests.

Methods

Planting faults

A program walked the syntax tree of each model and listed every site of seven kinds: a plus or minus, a times or divide, a unary minus, a complex conjugate, a numeric constant (twice: add 1, and double), and an inequality. Each mutant changes one site: plus and minus swap, times and divide swap, the unary minus or the conjugate is dropped, the constant changes, the inequality flips. We did not choose which faults to plant.

A mutant can leave the program's behaviour unchanged; mutation testing calls that an equivalent mutantDefinition: equivalent mutant software engineering (mutation testing) A mutant whose change leaves the program's behaviour the same on every input, so that no test can or should fail on it. Excludes a fault that a weak test happens to miss. full definition, and it is no fault at all. A differential oracleDefinition: differential oracle software engineering (testing) A judge of behaviour that runs two versions of a program on the same inputs and reports whether their outputs differ. Here it marks a mutant as a fault when it differs from the original on random inputs. Excludes any statement that the original program is right. full definition separated the two cases: the mutant and the original ran on random inputs wider than any test uses, and any difference in output beyond a relative tolerance of 1e-9, or a change of array shape, marks a fault. This is a comparison of two programs and says nothing about whether the original is right.

Four test sets

Each instrument has four tests, written before any mutant was scored and adjusted until the original code passed all of them.

  • The calibration pointDefinition: calibration point our usage, from instrument practice A single forward test case with a known closed-form answer, standing for the one check a new instrument model often gets. Excludes a calibration of hardware against a physical standard. full definition: one forward case with a closed-form answer, such as the reflectance of a quarter-wave film. It stands for the single check an instrument often gets.
  • The wide forward testDefinition: wide forward test our usage A set of 4 to 15 forward test cases with closed-form answers at random parameter values, all of which must pass. Excludes any check that runs the model backward or against a complement, and any reference taken from measurement. full definition: 4 to 15 forward cases with closed-form answers at random parameter values.
  • The backward checkDefinition: backward check our usage, from physics symmetries A test that runs an instrument model in reverse against itself, by time reversal, reciprocity, an adjoint identity or an inverse, and needs no reference value. Excludes a comparison with a known answer. full definition: the model against itself in reverse. Transmission through a film stack from the other side; a wave propagated out and back; a wave run on with its last two states swapped; blur then deblur; the inner-product identity for the projector and its adjoint; ray matrices for the elements in reverse order; analyzer rows inverted to recover a known Stokes vector. Diffusion has no time reversal, so one small step with the diffusivity negated stood in for it.
  • The contrary checkDefinition: contrary check our usage, from physics symmetries A test that runs an instrument model against its opposite or complement, such as an aperture and its complementary screen or a lens and its negative, and needs no reference value. Excludes a comparison with a known answer, and the backward check, which reverses the same case. full definition: the model against its opposite or complement. A half-wave absentee layer that must leave reflectance unchanged, with energy conserved; an aperture and its complement summing to the open field (Babinet's principle); source and receiver swapped; a lens followed by its negative; crossed polarizers reading zero.

The last two use no reference value. The three-way testDefinition: three-way test our usage The backward and contrary checks taken together after a forward calibration. A fault is caught three-way when either check fails. Excludes the wide forward test, which is scored apart. full definition is our name for the backward and contrary checks taken together after a forward calibration: a fault is caught three-way when either one fails.

The score

A false passDefinition: false pass our usage A planted fault, confirmed by the differential oracle, that still passes the calibration point. Excludes equivalent mutants, and mutants that crash a test. full definition is a mutant that the oracle marks as a fault and that still passes the calibration point. These are the quiet faults. For a test set that fails on k of the N false passes, the catch rate is

c=kN(1)

Mutants that crashed any test left the count, since a crash is noticed without a test.

The two rates were compared on the same faults. For each false pass let di be 1 when only the three-way test caught it, minus 1 when only the wide test caught it, and 0 otherwise. A sign-flip testDefinition: sign-flip test statistics (permutation tests) A paired test that gives each difference a random sign many times and counts how often the mean of the re-signed differences reaches the real mean. Excludes a test that assumes a normal distribution, and any comparison of unpaired groups. full definition drew 4,000 random sign patterns for the di and counted how many gave a mean at or above the real one:

p=j+1n+1(2)

with j that count and n = 4,000. The four p values of the run (each direction, on singles and on pairs) were corrected with the Benjamini-Hochberg correctionDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics (multiple testing) An adjustment of a family of p values that limits the expected share of false discoveries among the tests called significant. Excludes control of the chance of any single false discovery, which is the stricter Bonferroni aim. full definition [5], which limits the expected share of false discoveries among the tests called significant, and again across all 84 tests of the nine simulation studies run together that day.

Pairs

Two errors can cancel at a calibration point. The run drew 400 random pairs of sitesDefinition: compensating pair our usage Two planted faults in one function, drawn at random, kept in the score when together they still pass the calibration point. Excludes pairs chosen by hand to cancel. full definition, each pair inside one forward function, from a fixed seed, planted both faults and scored the result the same way. Draws from a function with a single site were skipped, which left 344 pairs.

False alarms

A reference-free check that fails on a correct program would be useless. Two things bound that: every test passes on the original code, and in the first run neither test failed on any equivalent mutant. With 0 failures in m = 9 equivalents, the one-sided 95 percent upper bound on the false-alarm rate is

u=1−0.051/m(3)

which is 0.28.

Controls and planted checks

The controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition permuted the fault labels among the mutants of each instrument 200 times and recomputed the three-way catch rate. It gave a mean of 0.726 with a 95th percentile of 0.76, below the real 0.830 (p 0.005). The preregistration calls this a weak check, and it is: only 9 of the 148 scored mutants are equivalent, so permuting labels changes little.

The first run carried a planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition: with the conjugate dropped in the blur adjoint, the forward tests had to pass and the contrary check had to fail. Both happened.

All four tests passed on the original code of all eight instruments in both runs.

Results

The second run planted 200 single faults in the eight forward functions. Of these, 52 crashed a test and left the count, 148 were scored, 9 were equivalent, and 47 were faults that passed the calibration point.

Among 47 single faults that passed one calibration point, the backward and contrary checks together caught 39 (83 percent) and a wide forward test caught 29 (62 percent); sign-flip p 0.003, corrected to 0.013 within the study and 0.009 across the 84 tests of the nine-study set.c1 Taken alone, the backward check caught 33 and the contrary check 28. Eleven faults fell only to the three-way test and 1 only to the wide test. All three test sets together caught 40. Figure 1 gives the rates.

The total hides how uneven the instruments are. The advantage sits in three of the eight instruments, and one of them, the Radon projector, supplies 23 of the 47 faults; without it the counts are 16 and 12 of 24.c2 The split without the projector was computed after the result was seen. Table 1 and Figure 2 give every instrument. In three instruments the three-way test caught nothing.

Seven faults passed every test: four divide by a grid spacing that every test set to 1, and three leave a wrong wave propagator that still inverts itself exactly.c3 The four are the single false pass in the wave code and all three in the heat code; each swaps a division by the grid spacing for a multiplication, which changes nothing when the spacing is 1. The three in the angular-spectrum code are two sign changes inside the term under the square root and one division by the transfer function where the code should multiply. Each of those leaves a propagator that conserves power, obeys Babinet's principle and undoes itself when run backward, so the reference-free checks pass, and the forward tests read only a beam width that the fault does not change. The one-step undo that stood in for time reversal in the heat code caught none of its 3 false passes.

On pairs of faults the order reversed with no clear difference: the wide test caught 27 of 30 and the backward and contrary checks 24 of 30, p 0.12.c4 Of the 344 pairs, 155 crashed, and 30 of the remaining 189 were faults that passed the calibration point. Three fell only to the wide test, none only to the three-way test, and 3 passed everything.

Faults in the inverse and adjoint functions were scored apart. All 34 scored mutants there were false passes, the three-way test caught 32 of them and the wide forward test caught 0. The zero could not have come out otherwise, because no forward test calls those functions. The 32 show only that a pairing test reaches code a forward test does not.

Table 2 sets the forecasts against the outcomes. The forecast that the wide test would win on single faults was wrong.

Discussion

The two kinds of test fail in different places. A forward test sees only the outputs it reads at the parameter values it visits; the thin-film and projector faults it missed were visible to a symmetry. A symmetry test sees only departures from the symmetry; a model that is wrong and still symmetric is invisible to it. The seven survivors are the useful part of the result, because each names a habit to change. Four of them existed only because every test used a grid spacing of 1, where multiplying and dividing agree. Three existed because a propagator with the wrong dispersion is still unitary.

That gives two working rules, which we adopted: calibrate at values other than 1, and keep one absolute reference beside any reference-free check. The catalogue entry for our own kernels now asks for both kinds of test.

The size of the advantage should not be carried anywhere. It depends on which instruments are in the sample, and one instrument holds half the faults. On pairs of faults, where two errors cancel at the calibration point, the wide test did at least as well.

Limitations

  • This is a simulation on planted faults. Mutants are arithmetic slips made by rule, and no study here shows that they resemble the faults people make in instrument code.
  • The eight instruments are small models we wrote ourselves, and we wrote the tests too, on the same day. A stronger forward test or a weaker symmetry test would move both rates.
  • One instrument, the Radon projector, supplies 23 of the 47 faults. The three-way test caught 0 of the 7 faults in the angular-spectrum, wave and heat code.
  • 52 of 200 single mutants and 155 of 344 pairs crashed a test and left the count, so the rates describe quiet faults only.
  • The false-alarm rate is bounded loosely: 0 failures on 9 equivalent mutants allows a rate up to 0.28.
  • The second design was written after the first result was seen. It was made to remove an advantage the first design gave the three-way test, and it is still a design chosen with knowledge of the data.
  • The split without the Radon projector is post hoc.
  • The label-permutation control is weak, as the preregistration says.
  • Scoring was by our own code and was not blind. Nobody outside the project has checked the code or the result.

Evidence

Mixed. The forecast that a wide forward test would win on single faults failed (29 against 39 of 47). On 30 pairs of faults the wide test caught 27 and the backward and contrary checks 24 (p 0.12). The backward and contrary checks caught 0 of the 7 false passes in the angular-spectrum, wave and heat code, and 7 faults passed every test. False alarms are bounded only below 0.28 (0 of 9).

Figures

These are the paper's own figures, numbered as in the PDF, and each "Figure" reference in the text points here. The charts on this page redraw the same results from the result files and carry their own numbers.

Tables

Appendix A. The preregistered verdicts

Each verdict is a rule written before the second run. Values are read from that run's result file. Five rules hold and two fail. The pairs rule holds on the point values alone; the difference behind it has p 0.12.

Numbers recorded in our publication register

WhatValue
Sample47 single faults that passed a calibration point, of 148 scored; 30 such pairs of 189
Main estimate and intervalno interval; backward and contrary checks 39 of 47 against the wide forward test 29 of 47, sign-flip p 0.003
Forecast against outcomeDid not hold: the forecast that a wide forward test would win on single faults (29 against 39 of 47). On pairs the wide test caught 27 of 30 and the backward and contrary checks 24

As recorded in the publication register, the summary row each finding gets; the paper's own numbers above were re-read from the result files.

What lowers it

  • blinding Not blind. The second design was written after the first result was seen; the models and the tests were written by the same project. from our publication register, on blinding
  • depth of reading The cited literature was read at the level of search snippets; full texts were not read. from the Verified section

What holds it up

  • scoring Scored by code against rules fixed in advance. from our publication register, on who scored it
  • preregistration Preregistered and hash-locked before the run (sha256 d82bfea0). from the Reproduce section
  • control Controls: 9 equivalent mutants raised no false alarm, which bounds the rate below 0.28; the label-permutation control is weak, as the preregistration says. from our publication register, on controls

Where the claim stands

  1. lead
  2. hypothesis
  3. thesis
  4. conjecture
  5. theorem
  6. law candidate
  7. killed

A preregistration with pass-or-fail rules is on file, which this rung needs. The next rung needs a named rival reading beaten by a decisive observation, and none is on file. Tier B: A real signal in simulation and a useful blind spot. The next step is the same scoring on real instrument code with a reader outside the project.

Trail

Versions

  1. v2 2026-11-14, paper version 1.0, first published PDF sha256 620e36d626e7a7ac
  2. v1 2026-10-31, entered in the findings ledger

Corrections

  1. 2026-11-14 scope found by the publication pass

    The re-reading of two earlier studies, which the ledger entry lists, was left out because it was post hoc and needs those studies to be read.

  2. 2026-11-14 wording found by the publication pass

    The per-instrument split was added beside the headline count, because the three-way test caught none of the false passes in three instruments.

  3. 2026-11-14 number found by the publication pass

    The ledger entry gives one corrected value, 0.009; this paper prints both the within-study value, 0.013, and the across-studies value, 0.009, and says which is which.

  4. 2026-10-31 wording found by the study itself, before publication

    The first run's result, 89 percent against 33, was traced to forward tests that did not reach the inverse functions or the film's transmittance. now The second run was preregistered to remove that, and its numbers replace the first run's.

Each correction is a dated note; the findings ledger is never rewritten, and a note governs where it differs.

What this means for a reader

A sensitive growth recorder also records the room. In this simulation a dead shoot on a lever shows more apparent growth than the live shoot has, purely from the warming and dampening we assumed, and a dead partner shoot fixes the average while leaving single readings loose. The second half carries the wider warning: a method for spotting the day a tree stops growing looked perfect until the simulated tree stopped obeying the method's own equations, and then it raised an alarm on about half of the trees that were still growing. Real stem records with independently dated growth stops are what would settle how these detectors behave.

Objection

Nothing was measured. Every parameter is assumed from memory, including the growth rates, the swing, the drift ranges and the rain store.

What would change the call. Real stem records with independently dated growth stops.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

In 1920 A. D. Waller told the Royal Society that the plant movement shown on J. C. Bose's crescograph could come from heat, moisture and handling. We simulated that objection, and then the modern form of the same problem: telling growth from swelling in the stem of a tree. Everything here is a simulation with assumed parameters, and no plant was measured. With the assumed room drift, a lever on a dead shoot reads a mean of 5.2 micrometres an hour over 300 simulated runs, against a true growth of 2.0 on the live shoot, and 94 percent of dead runs read above 1.c1 Subtracting a paired dead shoot recovers the mean, 2.04 micrometres an hour, with a spread of 1.03, so 67 percent of single runs land within 1 of the truth.c2 When the simulated stem follows the detector's own model, neither growth-stop detector raises a false alarm in 200 runs, and the stop is flagged after a median of 1 day by a regression detector and 2 days by a daily-maximum detector.c3 Under misfit at 5 micrometres a day, the daily-maximum detector raises a false alarm on 62 percent of stems that never stop and the regression detector on 46 percent; at 1 micrometre a day both alarm on every stem.c4 The clean result came from testing a detector on data made by its own model.
