Introduction

Jagadis Chandra Bose built the crescographDefinition: crescograph plant physiology (history of instruments) An instrument built by J. C. Bose from about 1917 that magnifies the lengthening of a plant shoot with compound levers, or in a later version a magnetic needle and a light beam, and records it as a trace. Excludes modern optical or electronic growth sensors, which touch the plant far less. full definition to make plant growth visible in seconds. The instrument, from plant physiology, magnifies the lengthening of a shoot with compound levers and writes it as a trace. Bose's 1927 account gives a magnification of 10,000 times by two levers for the high magnification version and far more for a later magnetic version [2]. A report in Nature of the Royal Society meeting of 13 May 1920 records Waller's objection after a demonstration at a claimed ten-million-fold magnification: he judged the demonstration illusory, and held that effects with no physiological cause, visible at a thousand-fold, could hide or imitate the physiological ones [1]. The title of his paper extended apparent growth to inanimate materials.

The objection is a statement about a control. A recorder that cannot tell growth from thermal expansion or moisture swelling needs a specimen that does everything a living shoot does except grow. A dead shoot is the plain candidate. We wanted to size the problem: how large the drift is against the growth under stated assumptions, and how well a dead partner removes it when the partner is not an exact twin.

The modern form of the question is asked of trees. A dendrometerDefinition: dendrometer forest science A gauge that records the size of a tree stem, here an electronic sensor reading the stem radius many times a day. Excludes any direct count of new wood cells; the gauge records size, which also changes with the water held in the stem. full definition records the radius of a stem through the day. In forest science the term covers any gauge of stem size, from a band read by eye to an electronic point sensor; it records size and cannot by itself say which part of a change is new wood. Stems shrink by day as water is drawn out and swell at night, and this swing can be many times the daily growth. The zero-growth conceptDefinition: zero-growth concept tree physiology The rule, due to Zweifel and colleagues, that a stem is counted as growing only while it exceeds its own previous maximum radius, with every reading below that maximum treated as water deficit. Excludes the linear-growth alternative, in which growth is assumed to continue through periods of shrinkage. full definition of Zweifel and colleagues counts growth only when the stem passes its previous maximum and treats everything below that maximum as water deficit [3]. A practical question follows: how soon after growth stops for the season can a record show it. The decision this study informed was whether to spend effort on a detector that models the daily swing, or to stay with the running maximum.

Our searches found the historical report and the zero-growth literature. They did not look for published tests of cessation detectors on simulated stems, so we make no claim that this comparison is new.

Preregistration and design

There was no preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, meaning no dated plan locked by a hash before the run. Forecasts were written to a file on 31 October 2026 before any simulation ran, and the file says so in its own first line. It holds four forecasts for this study: that a dead shoot on a lever would read as growing (probability 0.9), that the daily-maximum detector would flag a stop after 5 days, that the regression detector would flag it after 3, and that the regression detector would beat the daily maximum (probability 0.5).

No kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition, an outcome fixed in advance that would end the claim, was set, and no pass or fail rules. Our register records that the first version of the stem test had only the matched case, in which the detector's model is the generator's model, and that the misfit scenarios were added after that result was seen. The misfit scenarios are therefore a correction made after a first look, and are reported as that.

Data and provenance

There is no external dataset. Every input is an assumed parameter, chosen from memory and not checked against a measurement: shoot elongation of 2 micrometres an hour, a daily stem swing of 100 micrometres, radial growth of 5 micrometres a day, and the drift ranges given below. The simulation is a short Python program with NumPy, run once with a fixed seed. The historical facts come from the two sources cited in the introduction.

Methods

The lever and the dead shoot

Each of 300 runs is a 10-minute record sampled every 5 seconds, in micrometres of displacement at the specimen. The lever's magnification does not enter; the lever is represented by its dead bandDefinition: dead band mechanical engineering and instrumentation The range of input movement to which a mechanism gives no output, from slack or friction in its joints. Here 0.05 micrometres at the specimen. Excludes random noise, which moves the output both ways. full definition, a mechanical slack of 0.05 micrometres below which the pointer does not follow the specimen.

A live shoot's displacement is the sum of four parts: growth at 2.0 micrometres an hour; thermal expansion of a 10 cm frame and tissue with a coefficient of 1.2e-5 per kelvin, for a room warming by 0.02 to 0.2 K over the record; hygroscopic swellingDefinition: hygroscopic swelling materials science and plant anatomy The change in size of a material as it takes up water vapour from the air. Plant tissue, wood and gut strings all lengthen or swell this way with no living process involved. Excludes growth, which adds new cells or enlarges living ones, and thermal expansion. full definition of 0 to 1.5 micrometres over the record, which is the lengthening of tissue as it takes up moisture from the air; and a small random walk for handling. Warming and swelling are drawn uniformly from those ranges for each run and rise linearly in time. A dead shoot has no growth, its own handling noise, and the same warming and swelling scaled by a factor drawn between 0.7 and 1.3, because a dead shoot is not a twin of the live one.

The reading s is the least-squares slope of the pointer trace over the record. The paired estimate of growth is

g=slive−sdead(1)

The mean drift the assumptions imply can be written down without a simulation. With a mean warming of 0.11 K and a mean swelling of 0.75 micrometres, the common displacement over the record is

1.2×0.11+0.75=0.88(2)

micrometres, where 1.2 micrometres per kelvin is the coefficient times the 10 cm length. Over a record of 595 seconds that is about 5.3 micrometres an hour. The swelling term supplies most of it.

The stem

A stem is simulated hourly for 60 days. Its radius is

y=G−A(1+0.5D)T+S+e(3)

Here G is growth, rising at a fixed rate per day until the stop and flat after it. A is the swing, 100 micrometres. T is the water tension: a daytime half-sine of vapour pressure deficitDefinition: vapour pressure deficit meteorology and plant physiology The difference between the water vapour pressure of saturated air at the current temperature and the vapour pressure the air has. A measure of how strongly the air draws water from a plant. Excludes relative humidity, which is a ratio and does not scale with drying demand across temperatures. full definition, scaled by a weather factor that changes from day to day, and smoothed by an exponential memory with time constant τ. Vapour pressure deficit, from meteorology, is the gap between the water vapour the air holds and what it could hold, and here it stands for the drying demand on the tree. D is a drying term that grows after the stop in the scenarios that include it. S is rain: a store that refills on random days and drains over about three days. e is sensor noise of 1 micrometre.

Each scenario simulates 200 stems that stop growing on day 40 and 200 that never stop.

Two detectors

The daily-maximum detector takes each day's largest radius, keeps the running maximum, and flags a stop when the running maximum has gained no more than 0.5 micrometres for 4 days in a row. It is a simplified reading of the zero-growth concept written for this study, and is not the published method or its software.

The regression detector fits each 8-day window with the vapour pressure deficit smoothed at a 4-hour time constant, a straight-line trend, and a daily sine and cosine, and flags a stop when the fitted trend falls below 0.3 of the growth rate. It is told the true growth rate, which favours it. Both detectors start after a 15-day baseline.

A false alarmDefinition: false alarm signal detection A detection reported when the event did not happen. Here a growth stop flagged on a simulated stem that never stops growing. Excludes an early flag on a stem that does stop later, which is counted apart. full definition is a flag on a stem that never stops. An early flag is a flag before day 40 on a stem that does stop. The lag is the flag day minus 40, and its median is taken over flags that are not early.

Matched and misfit scenarios

In the matched scenarios the generator uses the same 4-hour time constant as the regression detector, no rain, and a vapour pressure deficit measured with noise of 0.05. Testing an inverse method on data made by its own forward model is known in the inverse-problems literature as an inverse crimeDefinition: inverse crime inverse problems (applied mathematics) Testing a reconstruction or detection method on synthetic data produced by the same model the method assumes, which makes the method look better than it is on real data. Excludes tests on data from a different or richer model, and tests on measurements. full definition, because it hides every error of the model. The misfitDefinition: misfit statistics and modelling A difference between the process that made the data and the model the analysis assumes. Here a slower water memory, an unmodelled rain store and a noisier humidity record. Excludes measurement noise alone, which the matched scenarios also contain. full definition scenarios break the match in three ways at once: the generator's time constant is 7 hours, rain is on, and the vapour pressure deficit is measured with noise of 0.2. They were run at growth rates of 5 and 1 micrometres a day.

Controls and planted checks

The stems that never stop are the controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition for every detector: any flag on them is false. The matched scenarios serve as the known-answer case, since there the regression detector's model is exactly right and the stop day is known.

There is no control for the lever simulation beyond the arithmetic of eq. 2, which the simulated dead reading should and does come close to. No noise-only or shuffled version of the stem series was run.

Results

The lever

With the assumed room drift, a lever on a dead shoot reads a mean of 5.2 micrometres an hour over 300 simulated runs, against a true growth of 2.0 on the live shoot, and 94 percent of dead runs read above 1.c1 The live shoot on the same lever reads a mean of 7.2 with a standard deviation of 2.6, more than three times its true growth. The dead reading of 5.2 sits close to the 5.3 that eq. 2 gives, so this number restates the assumed drift ranges and could not have come out far from them. What it shows is the size of drift that would bury the growth: under 1 micrometre of swelling and a tenth of a kelvin in ten minutes.

Subtracting a paired dead shoot recovers the mean, 2.04 micrometres an hour, with a spread of 1.03, so 67 percent of single runs land within 1 of the truth.c2 The spread is half the growth rate. It follows from the assumed mismatch of up to 30 percent between the two shoots. Figure 1 shows the three readings.

The stem

When the simulated stem follows the detector's own model, neither growth-stop detector raises a false alarm in 200 runs, and the stop is flagged after a median of 1 day by a regression detector and 2 days by a daily-maximum detector.c3 That is the scenario with drying after the stop. Without drying both detectors take a median of 2 days.

Under misfit at 5 micrometres a day, the daily-maximum detector raises a false alarm on 62 percent of stems that never stop and the regression detector on 46 percent; at 1 micrometre a day both alarm on every stem.c4 Those shares are 124 and 92 of 200 stems. The regression detector's count is lower by 32 stems, and it is still wrong on nearly half the stems that never stop. On stems that do stop, the detectors flag before the stop in 49 and 35.5 percent of runs. Table 1 gives all five scenarios and Figure 2 the false alarms.

Neither detector missed a stop in any scenario; every stopping stem was flagged, early or late.

Table 2 sets the forecasts against the outcomes. The first forecast was a probability and the outcome beside it is a share of runs, so the two are of different kinds.

Discussion

The lever result is a sizing exercise. If a cut shoot in a lecture room swells by a micrometre in ten minutes, a lever reads several times the growth, and it does so on dead tissue. Whether real shoots swell that much is a question for a measurement, and our ranges are guesses. The pairing result has a practical edge: a dead partner removes the average drift, and the single-run error is set by how alike the two specimens are. An experimenter would need many pairs, or a better twin, before trusting one trace.

The stem result is the one we would act on. With the generator matched to the detector, the regression detector looked a day faster with no false alarms. That was the inverse crime at work. Once the stem had a slower water memory than the detector assumed, rain the detector had no term for, and a noisier humidity record, both detectors flagged stops that never happened on about half the stems, and at a slow growth rate on all of them. The regression detector's lower false-alarm share under misfit is real in these counts and has no practical use at that level.

Two things follow for our own work. A detector of this kind gets no credit from a matched simulation. The next test has to use recorded stems with a stop date known from another method.

Limitations

  • Nothing was measured. Every parameter is assumed from memory, including the growth rates, the swing, the drift ranges and the rain store.
  • The dead-shoot reading follows from the assumed drift ranges by arithmetic, so it is an illustration of the objection and no evidence about Bose's instrument or his results.
  • The lever is modelled only by a dead band. Friction, creep of the levers and the contact with the plant are left out.
  • The simulated instrument is the 10,000 times lever version. Waller's objection, as reported, was to a demonstration at a claimed ten-million-fold magnification.
  • The daily-maximum detector is our simplification of the zero-growth concept. Its failure here says nothing about the published method on real data.
  • The regression detector is told the true growth rate, and the misfit scenarios change three things at once, so the result does not say which misfit does the damage.
  • One seed, one run. The shares rest on 200 or 300 simulated runs, and no interval was computed in the study.
  • The misfit scenarios were added after the matched result was seen.
  • Scoring was by our own code and was not blind. Nobody outside the project has checked it.

Evidence

Mixed. Under misfit at 5 micrometres a day the daily-maximum detector raised false alarms on 124 of 200 stems that never stop and the regression detector on 92 of 200; at 1 micrometre a day both alarmed on all 200. The forecast that the regression detector beats the daily maximum held only by 1 day in the matched case with drying, and no claim is made under misfit. The paired dead shoot left a spread of 1.03 micrometres an hour on a growth of 2.0.

These are the paper's own figures, numbered as in the PDF, and each "Figure" reference in the text points here. The charts on this page redraw the same results from the result files and carry their own numbers.

Reproduce

Steps

  1. Data: no external dataset. The inputs are the assumed parameters listed in the Methods section; the simulation code is not yet in a public repository.
  2. Lever: for each of 300 runs, build a 10-minute trace every 5 seconds from growth, thermal expansion, swelling and a random walk, pass it through a dead band of 0.05 micrometres, and fit a slope. Do the same for a dead shoot with the drift scaled by a factor between 0.7 and 1.3, and apply eq. 1.
  3. Stem: simulate eq. 3 hourly for 60 days, 200 stems with a stop on day 40 and 200 without, in the five scenarios of Table 1.
  4. Run both detectors on every stem and count false alarms, early flags and lags.
  5. Random numbers: NumPy default generator, seed 20261036.
  6. No preregistration exists, so there is no preregistration hash, plan hash or run id. The forecast file carries a written date and no hash.

Cost. The simulation took about 6 s on one desktop CPU. The simulation was not re-run for this paper.

What this means for a reader

A lens whose index must vary smoothly sounds impossible to make, and for decades that was the stated obstacle. In this simulation the smoothness matters much less than it looks: shells about one wavelength thick focus almost as well as a perfect gradient, and thicker shells lose the focus by degrees. The second lesson is about our own first reading. A lens whose outer layers cannot reach an index of 1 looked ruined, and it was only ruined because we cut the ideal profile off and did not redesign it. A solver for the full sphere, and then a measurement on a stepped lens at microwave wavelengths, would test both results.

Objection

This is a simulation in two dimensions with a scalar field. A sphere, the other polarisation, absorption and scattering at rough shell boundaries were not modelled.

What would change the call. A solver for the full sphere, then a measurement on a stepped lens at microwave wavelengths.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

A Luneburg lens focuses a plane wave to a point on its far surface, and needs a refractive index that falls smoothly from 1.41 at the centre to 1 at the rim. Built lenses approximate that with shells of constant index. We asked how thick the shells can be. The study is a simulation: a scalar wave solution for a layered cylinder in two dimensions, with no sphere, no absorption and no measurement. At a radius of 50 wavelengths, 30 equal shells, each 1.67 wavelengths thick, keep 0.93 of the continuous lens's focal peak; 50 shells keep 0.99 and 10 shells keep 0.54.c1 With shells 1.67 wavelengths thick the share is 0.84 at a radius of 25 wavelengths and 0.97 at 100; with shells 1 wavelength thick it is 0.97 and 0.99.c2 Clipping the Luneburg profile at a minimum index destroys the focus quickly: a floor of 1.05 keeps 0.76 of the peak, 1.1 keeps 0.31, 1.2 keeps 0.09 and 1.3 keeps 0.035.c3 We first read that as a hard limit set by the rim index. A second run the same day showed otherwise. That loss belongs to the clipping: a quadratic profile refitted to the rim index keeps 0.53 at 1.1, 0.41 at 1.3 and 0.38 at 1.5.c4

Introduction

The Luneburg lensDefinition: Luneburg lens optics and antenna engineering A sphere, or in two dimensions a cylinder, whose refractive index falls from the square root of 2 at the centre to 1 at the surface, so that a plane wave from any direction is focused to a point on the opposite surface. Excludes a uniform ball lens, and modified profiles whose focus lies inside or outside the surface. full definition is a sphere, or in two dimensions a cylinder, whose refractive index n depends on the distance r from the centre as

n=2−r2R2(1)

where R is the radius. It is the best known gradient-indexDefinition: gradient-index optics Describing an optical element whose refractive index changes smoothly through the material, so that light bends inside it along curved paths. Excludes a conventional lens of one material, which bends light only at its surfaces. full definition lens, an optical element that bends light by a smooth change of index inside the material; a conventional lens, which bends light only at its surfaces, is the contrasting case. Every direction is an optical axis, so the lens has no off-axis aberration, which is why it is used as a wide-angle antenna at microwave frequencies.

No material offers that profile directly. The usual answer is the stepped lens: concentric shells, each of one index. Stepped lenses arose because graded materials were not available, and built examples often have 4 to 10 layers. Fuchs and colleagues treated the choice of shell number, thickness and index as an optimisation problem, and work citing them reports that directivity stops improving beyond a certain shell count [2]. A ray-tracing study of an optical all-sky lens considers up to 40 glass layers [3]. On the rim index, Gutman's modified Luneburg lens of 1954 moves the focus inside the sphere [4], and a later generalised profile carries the edge index as an explicit parameter, with a silicon example at an edge index of 2.2 [5].

So both of our questions have long histories in antenna engineering, and we claim nothing new. The study began from a census of instruments that were proposed and then set aside, where a 1989 patent text named the manufacture of graded material as the obstacle for gradient lenses [1]. The decision it informed was small and practical: which controls a teaching model of the lens should expose, and what numbers to put beside them. The questions were how coarse the shells can be before the focus fails, whether that depends on the size of the lens, and what happens when the outer index cannot go down to 1.

Preregistration and design

There was no preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, meaning no dated plan locked by a hash before the run, and no kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition, an outcome fixed in advance that would end the claim. Forecasts were written to a file on 31 October 2026 before any simulation ran, and the file says so in its own first line. Three of them concern this paper: that a lens 1,000 wavelengths in radius would need 50 shells to reach the diffraction limit, that a uniform ball would be worse by a factor of 50, and that an index floor of 1.3 would break the lens (probability 0.8).

The first pass used a ray trace and gave an answer the wave solver then overturned, as the results section describes. The check of other lens sizes and the refitted rim profile were both added after the first numbers were seen. The refit had its own forecasts written before it ran: 0.6 of the peak at a rim index of 1.1 and 0.25 at 1.3.

Data and provenance

There is no external dataset. The inputs are the index profiles defined in the methods and three lens sizes. The numbers come from three result files written by the study's own Python code on 31 October 2026: the main run at a radius of 50 wavelengths, the size check at 25 and 100, and the refitted rim profile at 50.

Methods

The wave solution

The model is a cylinder of radius R in vacuum, uniform along its axis, lit by a plane wave of unit amplitude with its electric field along the axis. This is a scalar problem in two dimensions. The field is written as a sum of angular orders m, and for each order the radial part u obeys

d2udr2+1rdudr+(k2n2−m2r2)u=0(2)

with k the wavenumber in vacuum and n the index at radius r. The code integrates eq. 2 outward from near the axis with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme, 120 steps per wavelength of radius, and matches the result at the surface to the incident wave plus an outgoing wave. This is the standard partial-waveDefinition: partial-wave wave physics (scattering theory) Describing a solution in which the field around a round object is written as a sum of angular orders, each order is solved along the radius alone, and the orders are added up. Excludes ray tracing, which follows paths and carries no wavelength, and grid methods that sample the whole field. full definition treatment of scattering by a cylinder, in which each angular order is solved by itself and the orders are summed; it includes every reflection between shells, and it is exact up to the numerical integration. Orders up to 1.1kR+25 are kept.

What is read off

The intensity is computed along the rear surface of the cylinder, within 0.3 radian of the point opposite the source (0.2 radian in the size check), on a grid of 0.001 radian. Two numbers are read: the focal peakDefinition: focal peak our usage The largest intensity found on the rear surface of the lens within the arc examined, reported as a share of the same quantity for the continuous lens of the same size. Excludes the total power delivered, the gain of an antenna, and any peak that forms off the rear surface. full definition, which is the largest intensity on that arc, and the width of the peak at half its height, in wavelengths of arc. Every lens is reported as its focal peak divided by the focal peak of the continuous lens of eq. 1 at the same size.

The lenses

  • Continuous: eq. 1.
  • Stepped: N shells of equal thickness R/N, each with the index eq. 1 gives at the middle of the shell.
  • Clipped: eq. 1 with every index below a floor raised to the floor, for floors of 1.05, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 and 1.4. This stands for a material that cannot be made lighter than the floor.
  • Refitted: a profile of the same quadratic form with the rim index fixed and the centre index free,
n2=nc2−(nc2−nr2)r2R2(3)

where nr is the rim index and nc the centre index. For each rim index the centre index was chosen with a ray trace so that rays meet at the rear surface, and the wave solver then scored the result. The centre indices came out between 1.45 and 1.72.

  • Uniform: a cylinder of index 2 throughout, whose paraxial focus also falls on its rear surface.

The ray trace

The first pass traced 25 rays through stepped spheres with Snell's law at every shell boundary, for a lens taken to be 1,000 wavelengths in radius, and measured how far each ray lands from the focal point. It is reported because its answer was wrong in an instructive way.

Controls and planted checks

The known-answer check is an empty cylinder. With an index of 1 everywhere there is no lens, and the field on the surface must equal the incident plane wave, with magnitude 1. The solver returned a mean magnitude of 0.996 and a largest deviation of 0.026. That bounds the solver's error at about 2.6 percent in amplitude, or about 5 percent in intensity, at a radius of 50 wavelengths.

The continuous lens is a second check: its peak falls at the point opposite the source, as the theory requires, with a width of 0.40 wavelength. The ray tracer was checked the same way; rays through the continuous profile met the focal point within 4e-7 of the radius.

No controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition in the statistical sense applies, because the calculation has no random element.

Results

Shell thickness

At a radius of 50 wavelengths, 30 equal shells, each 1.67 wavelengths thick, keep 0.93 of the continuous lens's focal peak; 50 shells keep 0.99 and 10 shells keep 0.54.c1 Table 1 gives all nine shell counts. The peak keeps its width of 0.40 wavelength from 10 shells upward; with fewer shells it also broadens.

With shells 1.67 wavelengths thick the share is 0.84 at a radius of 25 wavelengths and 0.97 at 100; with shells 1 wavelength thick it is 0.97 and 0.99.c2 Thickness in wavelengths is therefore a fair first guide and is not the whole rule: at a fixed thickness the larger lens does better. With shells 2.5 wavelengths thick the shares are 0.64, 0.76 and 0.87 at radii of 25, 50 and 100 wavelengths, and with shells 5 wavelengths thick they are 0.53, 0.54 and 0.60. Figure 1 shows the three sizes.

Table 2 lists the size check, with the nearest rows of Table 1 in its middle column.

The ray trace had pointed the other way. For a lens 1,000 wavelengths in radius it found no shell count up to 1,000 that brought the rays within the diffraction radius: at 1,000 shells the root-mean-square miss was 0.0098 of the radius against a diffraction radius of 0.00061. At that size 1,000 shells are 1 wavelength thick, which is where the wave solution keeps 0.97 to 0.99 of the peak at the three sizes it was run. Tracing rays through layers about one wavelength thick is outside the range where ray optics holds. The wave solver was not run at a radius of 1,000 wavelengths, so the forecast of 50 shells at that size was not tested at its own size.

A uniform cylinder of index 2 at the same size reaches 0.14 of the peak.c5 That is a factor of 7 below the continuous lens, against a forecast factor of 50.

The rim index

Clipping the Luneburg profile at a minimum index destroys the focus quickly: a floor of 1.05 keeps 0.76 of the peak, 1.1 keeps 0.31, 1.2 keeps 0.09 and 1.3 keeps 0.035.c3 At a floor of 1.3 the peak is 5.3 wavelengths wide. At 1.4 the largest intensity is no longer opposite the source.

That loss belongs to the clipping: a quadratic profile refitted to the rim index keeps 0.53 at 1.1, 0.41 at 1.3 and 0.38 at 1.5.c4 The refitted lenses keep a narrow focus, 0.4 to 0.6 wavelength wide. Table 3 and Figure 2 set the two side by side. The refitted profile still loses about half the peak once the rim index reaches 1.1, so a raised rim has a cost; it is a far smaller one than the clipped numbers suggested.

Discussion

The shell result has a plain physical reading. A wave averages over structure finer than its wavelength, so steps about a wavelength thick act much like the gradient they replace, and the focus degrades smoothly as the steps grow. A ray has no wavelength and sees every step as a prism, which is why the ray trace kept reporting failure. For a lens tens of wavelengths across, the number of shells that matters is set by the wavelength and to a lesser degree by the size.

The rim result is a correction to ourselves. The first entry in our ledger said the rim index was the harder limit, on the strength of the clipped profile. Clipping leaves the inner part of the lens designed for a rim that is no longer there. Refitting the same simple form to the new rim recovers a sharp focus at about 0.4 to 0.6 of the peak for rim indices of 1.1 and above, with no optimisation at the wave level. The literature we found afterwards treats lenses with a rim index above 1 as a known family, so the refit rediscovers a small part of it.

For the teaching model the outcome was two controls: a shell count, and an edge index that redesigns the profile and does not cut it.

Limitations

  • This is a simulation in two dimensions with a scalar field. A sphere, the other polarisation, absorption and scattering at rough shell boundaries were not modelled.
  • The field was read only on the rear surface. A stepped or refitted lens may focus slightly inside or outside that surface, and the peak share would then understate it.
  • The solver's own error is about 2.6 percent in amplitude by the empty-cylinder check, so peak shares closer than about 0.05 to each other should not be ranked.
  • Widths are read on a grid of 0.05 wavelength and are coarse.
  • Shells have equal thickness and mid-shell indices. No shell design was optimised, so a designed lens with the same count could do better.
  • The refitted centre index was chosen by a ray trace at one size, and only one size was run for the rim results.
  • The size check and the refit were added after first results were seen, and there was no preregistration.
  • The ray trace and the wave solver were run at different lens sizes, so their disagreement is argued from shell thickness and was not shown at one size.
  • The literature was read at the level of search snippets, and the results are likely to be known in antenna engineering.
  • Scoring was by our own code and was not blind. Nobody outside the project has checked it.

Evidence

Mixed. The statement that the rim index is the harder limit did not hold. Clipping the profile keeps 0.31 of the peak at a rim index of 1.1 and 0.035 at 1.3; a quadratic profile refitted to the rim keeps 0.53 and 0.41. The forecast of a factor of 50 for a uniform cylinder missed (factor of 7), and the forecast of 50 shells for a lens 1,000 wavelengths in radius was not tested at that size.

Figures

These are the paper's own figures, numbered as in the PDF, and each "Figure" reference in the text points here. The charts on this page redraw the same results from the result files and carry their own numbers.

What lowers it

  • blinding Not blind. No preregistration; the size check and the refit were added after first results were seen. from our publication register, on blinding
  • depth of reading The cited literature was read at the level of search snippets; full texts were not read. from the Verified section

What holds it up

  • scoring Scored by code against rules fixed in advance. from our publication register, on who scored it

Where the claim stands

  1. lead
  2. hypothesis
  3. thesis
  4. conjecture
  5. theorem
  6. law candidate
  7. killed

An observation with a source. No prediction with a kill condition was on file before the run, which the next rung needs. Tier B: A clean known answer for the ideal lens, in two dimensions only; the result is likely known in antenna engineering.

Reproduce

Steps

  1. Data: no external dataset. The inputs are the index profiles in the Methods section; the simulation code is not yet in a public repository.
  2. For each angular order up to 1.1kR+25, integrate eq. 2 from 0.001 of the radius to the surface with 120 Runge-Kutta steps per wavelength of radius, and match to Bessel and Hankel functions outside.
  3. Sum the orders on the rear surface, take the largest intensity and its width at half height, and divide the peak by that of eq. 1.
  4. Repeat for stepped profiles of 4 to 100 shells at a radius of 50 wavelengths, for thicknesses of 5, 2.5, 1.67 and 1 wavelengths at radii of 25 and 100, for clipped profiles, for eq. 3, for an index of 2 and for an index of 1.
  5. No preregistration exists, so there is no preregistration hash, plan hash or run id. The forecast files carry a written date and no hash. The wave calculation uses no random numbers.

Cost. The main run, ray trace included, took about 18 s on one desktop CPU. The simulation was not re-run for this paper.

In a 30-year log experiment, western redcedar heartwood lost density slowest of four species, and in a large forest inventory, wind damage ranked well but forecast almost nothing.

What this means for a reader

The picture of a forest wired to large "mother trees" needs a comparison before it carries meaning. In the one public map we tested, the hub pattern is what you get from how many root tips were dug up on each tree and how many links each tree has, with nothing extra left for hubs to explain. A shared fungus also shows only that one fungal individual reached two root systems; whether anything passed between them is a separate question these data cannot answer. Cedar's reputation holds for its heartwood and not for its sapwood. Wind damage in inventory records is too rare for a model to say which tree will break, though it can say which trees to look at first.

Objection

The network sample is small: 26 trees had a measured diameter, in one forest type and one region, sampled once. Plots of 13 to 41 trees cannot establish or exclude a power-law tail.

What would change the call. Apply the same nulls to Beiler 2010 and other mapped networks, with a model that separates root extent from effort.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Three popular forest claims were tested on public data with rules fixed in advance. The first is that large trees act as hubs in fungal networks below ground. In a mapped network of 166 Douglas-fir trees and 56 Rhizopogon fungal individuals in six plots, bigger trees carried more fungal partners (Spearman rho 0.45, 26 trees), but the number of root tips sampled per tree tracked partners at rho 0.87. Once sampling was controlled, the size link fell to a partial rho of 0.20 (p 0.067), and hub concentration and nestedness sat inside 1,000 degree-preserving shuffles in 6 of 6 plots.c1 The second claim is that western redcedar decays slowly. In the 530-log HJ Andrews experiment, cedar heartwood lost density at 0.0026 per year (95% interval 0.0016 to 0.0038), the slowest of four species, while cedar sapwood ranked third of four.c2 The third is that inventory data can say which trees wind will damage. Among 488,499 live trees in Washington and Oregon, 506 (0.10 percent) carried recorded wind damage; a model ranked risk with a held-out AUC of 0.77 but gained a Brier skill of only 0.0014 over the base rate.c3 Bigger, more slender and recently cut trees were not more damaged, against our forecasts.

Introduction

A mycorrhizaDefinition: mycorrhiza mycology and plant ecology A root tip of a plant enclosed by a fungus that lives with it, the fungus taking sugars from the plant and passing it water and soil nutrients. Here the tuberculate root tips that Rhizopogon fungi form on Douglas-fir. Excludes fungi that rot wood or cause disease, and fungal threads in the soil away from a root. full definition is a root tip enclosed by a fungus that trades soil water and nutrients for the plant's sugars. When one fungal individual, a genetDefinition: genet population genetics of clonal organisms One genetic individual of a fungus, recognised by its microsatellite profile, which may spread through the soil and colonise many root tips. Excludes a species, and a single fungal thread or fruiting body. full definition, colonises the roots of several trees, the trees are linked through it. Beiler and colleagues mapped such links for Rhizopogon genets on interior Douglas-fir in one 30 by 30 m plot [1]. They reported that tree size went with connectivity and called the network scale-free. A second study [2] mapped six smaller plots on dry and moist sites and released the data. It reported a steeper rise of tree links with diameter on dry sites and argued that the networks would withstand random losses but not the loss of large trees or fungal genets. These maps fed the popular "wood wide web" with large hub trees at its centre.

Karst, Jones and Hoeksema [4] reviewed the field evidence and judged that the claims that such networks are widespread, and that transfer through them helps seedlings, are not supported well enough in the field. They found no peer-reviewed field evidence that mature trees preferentially send resources or signals to their offspring. They also found that papers with positive results were cited more than those without.

Hub structure in a network has a standard test. A degree-preserving shuffleDefinition: degree-preserving shuffle network ecology A control that rewires the links of a network at random while every tree keeps its number of genets and every genet its number of trees, drawn here by the curveball algorithm 1,000 times per plot. Excludes a shuffle that also changes how many links each node has. full definition rewires the links at random while every node keeps its number of links. Structure that survives the shuffle comes from the pattern of who links to whom; structure that the shuffle reproduces comes from the link counts alone. The curveball algorithm of Strona and colleagues [5] draws such shuffles uniformly and fast. A search we ran on 9 November 2026 found no reanalysis of the Beiler 2015 data against degree-preserving shuffles with a sampling-effort control. That is what the search returned; it is not proof that none exists.

The second study uses the long-term log decay experiment at the HJ Andrews Experimental Forest in Oregon. Harmon [6] laid out 530 logs of four conifer species at six old-growth sites in 1985 for a study planned to last 200 years. A Pacific Northwest Research Station summary found by our search gives a whole-log half-time of about 15 years for Pacific silver fir and 100 years for western redcedar. We asked whether that order holds for heartwood and sapwood separately, and whether decay can be forecast for logs not yet sampled.

The third study asks whether the USDA Forest Inventory and Analysis records can say which trees wind damages. It was written as a forecast test on held-out plots, with three predictions drawn from common forestry expectations: bigger trees, more slender trees and trees in recently cut stands should carry more wind damage.

Preregistration and design

All three studies were written as one preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition on 29 October 2026, before any confirmatory analysis. Its hash was recorded at once. The file discloses what had been seen: per-plot counts of samples, genets and trees in the network data; sample counts by species and time in the log data; and counts of wind-damaged trees by year and state in the inventory. No relation between any outcome and any predictor had been computed.

One addendum, on slendernessDefinition: slenderness forestry and tree biomechanics Tree height divided by stem diameter at breast height, both in the same units. Excludes the height-to-diameter ratio measured at the base of the stem. full definition and the buckling limit, was appended while the wind script was running and before any of its scores, coefficients or rates had been printed. The old hash was kept and a new one recorded. Both hashes are in the reproduction section.

Each test has a forecast with a numeric pass rule. The network forecasts were that the degree tails would not support a power lawDefinition: power law (scale-free) network science A degree distribution whose tail falls as a fixed power of the degree, so that a few nodes have very many links. A network with such a tail is called scale-free. Excludes skewed distributions with an exponential tail, which also have a few well linked nodes. full definition, that tree diameter would correlate with genets per tree, that sampling effort would correlate with genets per tree at rho above 0.5, and that hub concentration and nestedness would sit inside the shuffled range in at least 4 of 6 plots. Two forecasts pointed the other way: that modularity would exceed the shuffles in at least 4 of 6 plots, and that moist plots would be more connected than dry plots. The decay and wind forecasts are listed with their methods in Section Methods. Forecasts of log density at years 40 and 50 were written to a separate file and hash-locked before the results were written, so they can be scored when those logs are sampled.

Data and provenance

Fungal network

Beiler, Simard and Durall [2] typed 758 tuberculate mycorrhizas from six 10 by 10 m plots of interior Douglas-fir in British Columbia: plots 1 to 3 on dry (xeric) sites and 4 to 6 on moist (mesic) sites. Each root tip was assigned by microsatellites to one genet of Rhizopogon vesiculosus or R. vinicolor and one Douglas-fir genotype. Tree diameter at breast height and age come from a second deposit of tree data for the same plots; 26 of its 35 trees match a tree in the network data. Both deposits are on Dryad under CC0 [3].

Log decay

The log data are the HJ Andrews TD014 long-term log decay experiment [7], principal investigator Mark E. Harmon, under CC BY 4.0. The licence asks for this credit line: Data were provided by the HJ Andrews Experimental Forest research program, funded by the National Science Foundation's Long-Term Ecological Research Program (DEB 1440409), US Forest Service Pacific Northwest Research Station, and Oregon State University.

The four species are Pacific silver fir, Douglas-fir, western redcedar and western hemlock, about 50 cm in diameter, laid on six old-growth sites in 1985. At each sampling a different set of logs is cut. The quantity used is apparent density of heartwood, sapwood, inner bark and outer bark. The local copy of the metadata file was damaged and did not decompress, so the codes were read from the Andrews online metadata page. A wildfire in 2023 burned three of the six sites; this comes from news and Andrews sources and was not checked against site records.

Forest inventory

The wind data are the USDA Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis DataMart tree, plot and condition tables for Washington and Oregon [8], which are in the public domain. The population is live trees of 5 inches diameter and over on forested conditions, inventory years 2013 to 2024, when the national damage codes are recorded. That gives 488,499 tree records on 16,128 plots. Records are unweighted, so results describe the sampled trees and not population totals.

Methods

The network tests

One bipartite networkDefinition: bipartite network network science A network with two kinds of node, here trees and fungal genets, in which a link joins a tree to a genet found on at least one of its root tips and never joins two nodes of the same kind. Excludes a network of measured flows between trees. full definition was built per plot, with a link where at least one root tip joins a tree and a genet; both Rhizopogon species are combined. In the tree-tree view, two trees are linked when they share at least one genet. A node's degreeDefinition: degree network science The number of links a node has: the genets on one tree, the trees one genet reaches, or, in the tree-tree view, the other trees that share at least one genet with a tree. Excludes the strength or direction of a link. full definition is its number of links.

Degree distributions pooled over plots were fitted by maximum likelihood to a geometric (discrete exponential) form, a discrete power law and a zero-truncated Poisson, and compared by AICDefinition: AIC statistics (model selection) The Akaike information criterion, twice the number of fitted parameters minus twice the log-likelihood. Between two models fitted to the same data the lower value is preferred, and a gap of 2 or more is the usual bar. Excludes a test that one model is true. full definition. A power law counts as supported only if it beats the geometric form by 2 AIC units or more.

Tree size was tested with Spearman rhoDefinition: Spearman rho statistics The correlation between the ranks of two quantities, from -1 to 1, which counts any steadily rising or falling relation and is not pulled by single extreme values. Excludes the slope of a relation, and evidence of cause. full definition between diameter and genets per tree for the 26 matched trees, with a one-sided p value from 10,000 permutations of diameter within plots and a bootstrap intervalDefinition: bootstrap interval statistics An interval made by recomputing a number many times on units drawn with replacement from the data, here trees, logs or inventory plots, and keeping the middle 95 percent of the results. Excludes an interval that also covers doubt about the model's form. full definition over trees. Sampling effort was controlled with the partial Spearman rhoDefinition: partial Spearman rho statistics The Spearman correlation between two quantities after the ranks of a third, here the number of root tips sampled per tree, have been regressed out of both. Excludes a causal effect, and a correction that is known to be the right size. full definition given the number of root tips sampled per tree.

Hub concentrationDefinition: hub concentration network science, our usage The share of all tree-tree links held by the top 10 percent of trees ranked by their number of tree-tree links. Excludes a measure of how much a hub tree passes to others. full definition, nestedness (NODF)Definition: nestedness (NODF) network ecology The degree to which the partners of poorly linked nodes are a subset of the partners of well linked nodes, scored from 0 to 100 by the NODF index (nestedness based on overlap and decreasing fill). Excludes modules, which are groups of nodes linked mostly among themselves. full definition and modularityDefinition: modularity network science Newman's Q: how far links fall inside groups of nodes rather than between groups, beyond what random links with the same degrees would give. Here the best of 20 Louvain runs. Excludes spatial clumping of samples, which can produce modules without any network structure. full definition were each compared with 1,000 curveball shuffles per plot [5], which form the controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition. The null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition of each measure is the spread over those draws. Each plot is reported as inside or outside the central 95 percent of the draws and as a z score against the nullDefinition: z score against the null statistics The real value minus the mean of the control draws, divided by their standard deviation. Values beyond 2 in size are rare under the control. Excludes a p value, and a measure of effect size in the units of the data. full definition. Dry and moist plots were compared with the exact permutation test over the 20 ways to split six plots into two groups of three.

The decay tests

For each log, tissue and sampling time, relative densityDefinition: relative density wood science and decomposition ecology The apparent density of a log tissue at a sampling time divided by the same log's density of that tissue when the log was laid out in 1985. Excludes mass loss and carbon loss, which also count the volume a log loses as it fragments. full definition r is the mean density divided by the same log's density at time zero. Three models were fitted per species and tissue by nonlinear least squares on years 1 to 16. The single exponential is

r=e−kt(1)

where t is years since 1985 and k is the decay rateDefinition: decay rate k decomposition ecology The constant k in the single-exponential model, the fraction of remaining density lost per year. A half-life is the natural log of 2 divided by k. Excludes a rate measured from mass, and the rate in the first years of a lag model. full definition. The lag model holds r=1 until a lag L and decays after it:

r=e−k(t−L),t≥L(2)

The Weibull model has a scale a and a shape b:

r=e−(t/a)b(3)

Held-out logs at years 20 and 30 are different physical logs from the fitted ones, so a score is a forecast for new logs of a species. The carry-forward baselineDefinition: carry-forward baseline forecast verification The forecast that a later sampling will show the same mean relative density as the last sampling used for fitting, here year 16. Excludes a forecast from a fitted decay curve. full definition is the species and tissue mean at year 16. Forecast skillDefinition: forecast skill forecast verification One minus the mean absolute error of a model's forecast divided by the mean absolute error of a baseline on the same held-out logs. 0 means no better than the baseline and 1 means perfect. Excludes a score on the logs used to fit the model. full definition is

S=1−MmodelMcf(4)

where Mmodel and Mcf are the mean absolute errors of the model and of the baseline on the held-out logs. Intervals come from 2,000 bootstrap draws over logs. A second baseline fits one single exponential to all four species pooled.

The decay forecasts were these. P2.1: at year 30, at least one model beats the baseline for heartwood, with the lower end of its skill interval above 0, in at least 3 of 4 species. P2.2: the lag or Weibull model has lower held-out error than the single exponential for heartwood in at least 3 of 4 species. P2.3: species models beat the pooled model for heartwood at year 30. For the cedar test, eq. 1 was fitted per species on all years 1 to 30, and the difference in k between each other species and cedar was bootstrapped over logs 2,000 times. P2.4: cedar heartwood has the lowest k, with every difference interval excluding 0. P2.5: cedar sapwood is not the slowest. Only after these fits were frozen were our rates compared with the principal investigator's published heartwood rates.

The wind tests

The outcome is wind damage, national damage code 50013 in any of a tree's three damage fields. The features are species (the 15 commonest, the rest pooled), log diameter, slenderness, crown class, plot elevation, latitude and longitude, slope, aspect as sine and cosine of the angle from south-west, stand age, site class, topographic position, state, and a flag for cutting within 10 years. A random 30 percent of plots, 146,893 trees with 158 wind cases, was held out.

The primary model is logistic regressionDefinition: logistic regression statistics A model that gives the log odds of a yes-or-no outcome, here recorded wind damage, as a weighted sum of the features. Here fitted with an L2 penalty on standardised features. Excludes a model of how much damage a tree has. full definition; gradient boosting and a species-only model are secondary. Scores on held-out trees are log loss, the AUCDefinition: AUC statistics (signal detection) The area under the ROC curve: the chance that a randomly chosen damaged tree is ranked above a randomly chosen undamaged one, with 0.5 for guessing. Excludes how close the predicted probabilities are to the observed rates. full definition and the Brier skillDefinition: Brier skill forecast verification (meteorology) One minus the Brier score of a model divided by the Brier score of always forecasting the base rate, where the Brier score is the mean squared gap between a probability and the outcome coded 0 or 1. Excludes a ranking measure such as AUC, which ignores whether the probabilities are right in size. full definition. The Brier skill is

BSS=1−BmodelBbase(5)

where Bmodel is the model's Brier score and Bbase that of always forecasting the training base rate. Intervals come from 1,000 bootstrap draws over held-out plots. Effects are reported as an odds ratio per SDDefinition: odds ratio per SD statistics The factor by which the odds of the outcome change when a feature rises by one standard deviation and the other features stay fixed. 1 means no change. Excludes a ratio of probabilities, and a causal effect. full definition with intervals from 200 bootstrap refits.

The wind forecasts were these. P3.1: the logistic model beats the base rate, with a Brier skill above 0, a log-loss gain whose interval excludes 0, and an AUC interval above 0.5. P3.2: odds ratios above 1 for log diameter and for slenderness. P3.3: higher odds in stands cut within 10 years. P3.4: higher odds on south-west facing slopes. The addendum added A1.3: slenderness improves held-out log loss beyond species, size and site.

Controls and planted checks

The main control for the network is the degree-preserving shuffle: a plot whose measure sits inside the shuffled range has no hub, nested or modular structure beyond its link counts. The second control is sampling effort, the number of root tips sampled per tree. It was named in the preregistration with its own forecast, so the effort correlation is a tested result and not a later excuse.

For the decay forecasts the controls are the carry-forward baseline and the pooled-species model. For the wind forecasts the control is the base rate on held-out plots, with species alone as a stronger reference.

No planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition was run in these studies: no data with a known answer were passed through the analysis first. The nearest check is a known answer from outside. The principal investigator's published single-exponential heartwood rates were opened only after our fits were frozen, and they give the same order: silver fir 0.043, hemlock 0.029, Douglas-fir 0.008 and cedar 0.003 per year. The lack of a planted check is stated again in the limitations.

Results

The fungal network

Genets per tree had a mean of 1.88 and a maximum of 6 over 166 trees; trees per genet a mean of 5.6 and a maximum of 23 over 56 genets. A typical tree shared at least one genet with about 18 others. The power law fitted worst of the three forms: for genets per tree its AIC was 473.1 against 433.2 for the geometric form, a gap of 40 units. The degree distributions are skewed, with an exponential-type tail, and "scale-free" is not supported here. Networks of 13 to 41 trees cannot settle that question in either direction.

Diameter correlated with genets per tree at rho 0.45 (95% bootstrap interval 0.06 to 0.75; permutation p 0.0075, one-sided) for the 26 matched trees, whose diameters run from 10.8 to 52.8 cm. Across all 166 trees, root tips sampled per tree correlated with genets per tree at rho 0.87. Once sampling was controlled, the size link fell to a partial rho of 0.20 (p 0.067), and hub concentration and nestedness sat inside 1,000 degree-preserving shuffles in 6 of 6 plots.c1 Age showed no link with genets per tree (rho -0.07). Diameter against the number of trees linked gave rho 0.25 (p 0.20).

Table 1 gives each plot's measures, and Figure 1 draws hub concentration against its shuffled range. Plot 2's value sits on the lower edge of its range. Modularity exceeded a z of 2 in 1 of 6 plots (plot 2, z 2.27), so the forecast of modules failed. Samples of the same genet lay closer together than samples of different genets in every plot, so the genets are clumped in space, yet the clumping did not produce modules beyond what the degrees set.

The moist plots were not more connected than the dry ones. Mean trees linked per tree gave an exact p of 0.35, and connectance ran the other way (difference -0.046, p 0.80). With three plots per site type, a failed comparison is not evidence of no difference.

Log decay

At year 30, a decay model beat carrying the year-16 value forward for heartwood in 3 of 4 species, with skill 0.53 to 0.93 (Table 2). Cedar heartwood had barely changed, so carrying the last value forward was already almost right and no model beat it with an interval above 0. At year 20, four years past the fit, only Douglas-fir beat the baseline with an interval above 0 (0.56, 0.45 to 0.74). Short horizons favour the naive forecast.

The lag or Weibull model beat the single exponential for heartwood in 2 of 4 species, so P2.2 failed. In cedar both flexible forms overshot badly: their year-30 errors were 0.22 and 0.53 against 0.04 for the single exponential. Curves fitted to 16 years of almost no change extrapolate to a collapse that had not happened by year 30. Species models beat the pooled model for heartwood, with summed year-30 errors of 0.41 against 1.03.

In the 530-log HJ Andrews experiment, cedar heartwood lost density at 0.0026 per year (95% interval 0.0016 to 0.0038), the slowest of four species, while cedar sapwood ranked third of four.c2 Each other species' heartwood rate exceeded cedar's with an interval that excludes 0: Douglas-fir by 0.0041 (0.0025 to 0.0057), hemlock by 0.0175 (0.0142 to 0.0208) and silver fir by 0.0332 (0.0283 to 0.0383). Figure 2 draws the rates.

What this means for a reader

A person whose mood tends to linger from hour to hour also tends, in these data, to come back more slowly after a big swing. We could not show that these are two different things. That is weak evidence that they are one, because the person-level measures were noisy. If you read a study that reports a strong link between inertia and recovery, check whether both were computed from the same moments; in our data that overlap alone pushes the correlation from about 0.3 to about 0.7.

Objection

Split-half reliability was 0.03 to 0.47, so the factor test had little power, and one dataset could not be fitted at all.

What would change the call. Longer series, an AR(1) null with measurement noise, and test-retest reliability.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Emotional inertia is the carryover of mood from one moment to the next. Recovery is how fast mood returns to a person's usual level after a sharp high or low. We asked whether these are two separate traits or one trait seen twice. In four open phone-survey datasets from the openESM database (71, 49, 99 and 259 eligible people), the two measures were computed on disjoint sets of prompt pairs and correlated across people. Across people, inertia and recovery were negatively correlated in all four datasets, r -0.44, -0.41, -0.28 and -0.29.c1 The coupling was weaker than a one-parameter AR(1) null in two datasets, 0008 clearly and 0018 by 0.001, and sat inside that null in the other two.c2 A factor model with two factors never fit better than one.c3 Split-half reliability ran from 0.03 to 0.47, so the factor test had little power.c4 The preregistered prediction that the two are separate was not supported in any dataset on both of its tests. We report it as an honest nullDefinition: honest null research method (our usage) A working test that found no effect beyond a stated bound, a forecast that failed, or an error of our own found and fixed, reported with the same weight as a positive result. Excludes a void run, and a result left unpublished because it was negative. full definition with low power, and with one methods warning: with the usual all-pairs inertia, which reuses the spike pairs, the correlation reached 0.67 to 0.81 in size.c5

Introduction

Emotional inertiaDefinition: emotional inertia affective science How far a person's mood at one prompt predicts their mood at the next, measured as the lag-one correlation of their own mood series. Excludes average mood, how much mood varies, and any claim about what causes the carryover. full definition was introduced as a person-level property by Kuppens, Allen and Sheeber [2], who found higher inertia of both positive and negative emotions in people with depression and low self-esteem, across two naturalistic studies. Inertia is usually read off as an autocorrelation, so it measures how self-predictable a person's mood is from one prompt to the next.

Koval and colleagues [3] asked how inertia relates to the events people meet. In 200 first-year students, measured in daily life and in a film-clip task, the most consistent result was that higher inertia of negative affect went with slower recovery after negative stimuli. Their abstract reads this as inertia being driven mostly by weaker repair of mood after negative events. Schreuder and colleagues [5] measured recovery more directly: in a preregistered study of 68 adults with burst sampling, they timed returns to baseline after positive and negative episodes with survival analysis, and trait resilience did not predict return time.

A broader caution comes from Dejonckheere and colleagues [4]. Across many datasets, measures of mood dynamics such as autocorrelation added little to the prediction of well-being once mean affect and its variability were known. A dynamic measure has to earn its place as a separate quantity.

Our question sits between these. If inertia and recovery are two traits, they should vary across people more loosely than a model with one parameter would allow. If they are one trait, the coupling should look like what a single parameter produces on the same prompt schedules. The search we ran found adjacent work but no test of this form; that is what the search returned, not proof that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition was written on 29 October 2026, before any inertia, recovery, correlation or factor model was computed on the real data. Before writing it we had seen column names, row counts, the most common raw values of each mood column, and the number of prompts per person. All design choices were tested on synthetic populations first.

The idea and the prediction came from the author, who framed mood as an audio chain: a reverb, how long a feeling rings on, and a compressor release, how fast a large swing returns. The prediction had two parts, tested in each dataset separately:

  • P1, separate variation: the across-person correlation of inertia and recovery has a 95 percent interval inside -0.7 to 0.7, and its size is below the 5th percentile of the same quantity from a one-parameter AR(1) null.
  • P2, two factors beat one: a two-factor model of odd-day and even-day inertia and recovery beats a one-factor model, with a chi-square difference testDefinition: chi-square difference test statistics (model comparison) A test of whether a model with more free parameters fits nested data better than a simpler model, using the drop in the chi-square fit statistic against its degrees of freedom. Excludes comparisons of models that are not nested. full definition p below 0.05 and a lower BIC.

The verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition rules were fixed in advance. A dataset is "supported" when the shuffle check P0, P1 and P2 all pass; "partly" when P0 passes and exactly one of P1 and P2; "null" when P0 passes and both fail; "instrument failure" when P0 fails; "untestable" with fewer than 30 eligible people. There was no pooling across datasets, because their scales and samples differ. The preregistration's SHA-256 is given in the reproduction section.

Data and provenance

The four datasets come from openESM [1], a database of open experience samplingDefinition: experience sampling psychology (methods) A study design in which people answer short questions on a phone several times a day, so that mood is recorded close to the moment it is felt. Excludes one-off questionnaires and recall of past weeks. full definition data, all under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence (CC BY 4.0). Only group statistics are reported here; nothing describes an individual participant.

  • 0018, Bailon 2020 (CoVidAffect, Spain, spring 2020): a valence slider from 0 to 100. There are no prompt numbers, so prompts are ordered by answer time and a pair needs the same day and a gap of at most 6 hours.
  • 0062, Neubauer 2024 (STECCO, German first-year students, 2021): valence is the mean of four positive items minus the mean of four negative items, each 1 to 7, from the five momentary prompts a day. Two 7-day bursts six weeks apart.
  • 0008, Westhoff 2024 (young adults, Germany): a valence item from 0 to 100, five prompts a day for 21 days.
  • 0076, Bayer (mCog, US adults with Android phones, 2019): positive affect from 1 to 5, six prompts a day for 14 days.

The four input files were hashed by the run, and the hashes are in its result file. The samples are convenience samples, each on its own scale, which is why each is analysed alone.

Methods

Pairs, spikes and recovery

A lag pairDefinition: lag pair time-series analysis Two adjacent prompts on the same study day, the earlier one called the lead. A missed prompt or a night breaks the pair. Excludes pairs that cross a night or skip a prompt. full definition is two adjacent prompts on the same study day. For a person with mean m and standard deviation s over all their valid prompts, the deviation at prompt t is

dt=xt−m(1)

A spikeDefinition: spike our usage A lead prompt whose mood sits at least 1.5 of the person's own standard deviations from the person's own mean. Excludes deviations judged against other people or against a population norm. full definition is the lead prompt of a lag pair with a deviation of at least 1.5s in size. For each spike, the share of the deviation that has gone at the next prompt is

ut=1−dt+1dt(2)

clipped to the range -1 to 2. A person's recoveryDefinition: recovery affective science (our operational form) The median, over a person's spikes, of the share of each spike's distance from the person's mean that has gone by the next prompt, with 1 meaning back at the mean and 0 meaning no change. Excludes recovery measured in clock time, and recovery after events that did not produce a spike. full definition is the median of ut over their spikes, so 1 means back at the mean one prompt later and 0 means no change.

Inertia on disjoint pairs

Primary inertia is the Pearson rDefinition: Pearson r statistics The correlation coefficient between two quantities measured on the same units, from -1 through 0 for no linear relation to 1. Excludes non-linear relations and any statement about cause. full definition between xt and xt+1 over the lag pairs whose lead prompt is not a spike. The reason was settled on synthetic data before the run. Inertia over all pairs is dominated by large deviations, so it reads the same spike pairs that define recovery. In a synthetic population with separate rates for small and large deviations, all-pairs inertia still correlated with recovery at -0.77 to -0.83; the disjoint version gave -0.23 to -0.29, against -0.54 to -0.61 in a one-parameter population. All-pairs inertia was kept as a secondary measure.

A person was eligible with at least 30 valid prompts, 20 lag pairs, 15 non-spike pairs and 5 spikes. A dataset was tested with at least 30 eligible people.

The across-person correlation

For each dataset, r is the Pearson correlation of inertia and recovery across eligible people. Its 95 percent interval is a person bootstrapDefinition: person bootstrap statistics (resampling) An interval found by drawing people with replacement many times, recomputing the statistic each time, and taking the middle of the resulting spread. Excludes resampling of single prompts, which would treat one person's prompts as independent. full definition with 2,000 resamples.

The one-parameter null

The decisive comparison is with an AR(1) processDefinition: AR(1) process time-series statistics A series in which each value is the mean plus a fixed fraction of the previous value's distance from the mean, plus fresh random noise. The fraction is the single parameter. Excludes models with separate rates for small and large deviations, and models with measurement noise on top. full definition, in which each person has a single parameter ϕ:

dt+1=ϕdt+ϵt+1(3)

where ϵ is fresh Gaussian noise. Each eligible person is simulated on their exact prompt schedule, with the same days, prompts and missed prompts, a fresh stationary start each day, their own m and s, and values rounded and clipped to the scale. The person's ϕ is their all-pairs inertia corrected for short-series Kendall biasDefinition: Kendall bias time-series statistics The downward bias of a lag-one correlation estimated from a short series, about (1 + 3 phi)/n for a series of n values with true value phi (Kendall 1954). Excludes bias from measurement noise, which is a separate attenuation. full definition,

ϕK=ϕ+1+3ϕn(4)

with n the number of pairs, then shrunk toward the dataset mean so that its spread excludes sampling noise, and clipped to -0.5 to 0.95. The whole pipeline is rerun on the simulated people, and the size of r is recorded. Two hundred draws give the null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition.

The factor test

Each person gives four indicators: inertia and recovery computed on odd study days and on even study days, each half needing at least 10 non-spike pairs and 3 spikes. A one-factor modelDefinition: factor model psychometrics (confirmatory factor analysis) A model that explains the correlations among several measured indicators by a smaller number of unseen common factors, fitted by maximum likelihood. Excludes exploratory searches for the number of factors, and models of change over time. full definition (four loadings, four unique variances, 2 degrees of freedom) is compared with a two-factor model with inertia halves on one factor, recovery halves on the other and a free factor correlation (1 degree of freedom). The two-factor model wins only if the chi-square difference has p below 0.05 and its BICDefinition: BIC statistics (model selection) The Bayesian information criterion, a fit score that charges each extra parameter a penalty growing with sample size. The lower value is preferred. Excludes a test of whether either model is true. full definition is lower. The one-factor model is the two-factor model with the factor correlation at plus or minus 1, a boundary value, so the 1-degree-of-freedom p is conservative. The same halves give each measure's split-half reliabilityDefinition: split-half reliability psychometrics The correlation across people between a measure computed on one half of each person's data and the same measure on the other half. Here the halves are odd and even study days. Excludes test-retest reliability over months, and the validity of the measure. full definition.

p values from draws

Each control's p value is the share of draws at or above the real value, with one added to the count and the number of draws:

p=k+1n+1(5)

At 200 draws the smallest value is 0.005.

Controls and planted checks

Three controlsDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition ran per dataset, 200 draws each, from one random generator with seed 20261029.

  • C1, time shuffle: each person's mood values are permuted over their own prompt slots, and pairs and spikes are recomputed. The real mean inertia must exceed the shuffle's 95th percentile (rule P0). This checks that the instrument reads real carryover.

What this means for a reader

Ask whether some waves can beat the speed of light, and the answer depends on which speed you mean. For light in empty space, the highest-energy photons from a burst 7 billion years away arrived with the low-energy ones, and even our plain reanalysis puts a tight lid on any energy-dependent speed. In a medium, waves have their own limits that bend at short wavelengths by an ordinary, known law. Neither result needs new physics, and the bound from our rerun is weaker than the published one, so quote the published one.

Objection

The bound holds only in the tested band, about 0.1 to 30 GeV, and only for a delay linear in energy. The quadratic form, other energies and other carriers were not tested.

What would change the call. A reader from outside; the full texts behind the values typed by hand from abstracts; an instrument or data of our own where the result is simulated.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Some ideas about quantum gravity predict that light in vacuum travels at a speed that depends slightly on photon energy. A short, distant gamma-ray burst tests this well, because high-energy and low-energy photons leave together and travel for billions of years. We reran the test on the public Fermi Large Area Telescope photons from GRB 090510 with a simple method, fixed in advance. Our rerun bounds any linear energy-dependent change in light speed to less than 7.6e-18 of c at 29.9 GeV, a linear energy scale above 0.32 Planck energies, about 24 times weaker than the published limit of 7.6 Planck energies from the same burst.c1 The value of the rerun is as a reproduction of the method, and the published limits stand. Planted delays from 1 to 10 times our bound were recovered within 0.9 percent, and the fitted slope of zero sat inside the range that shuffled photon energies gave.c2 In the same study we simulated sound, which has a speed limit of its own. Sound in a uniform flow moved at the flow speed plus or minus the sound speed to within 1e-6, and in a simulated condensate the wave frequencies followed the Bogoliubov law within 2 percent, with a short-wavelength packet moving at 2.89 times the sound speed.c3 Twelve of the 15 preregistered verdicts passed; the three that failed were two forecasts of our own bound's strength and one test of a packet near a simulated horizon.c4
