Introduction

Special relativity says every observer measures the same speed of light. Several approaches to quantum gravity allow a small Lorentz invariance violationDefinition: Lorentz invariance violation particle physics and quantum gravity phenomenology Any departure from the rule of special relativity that every observer measures the same speed of light. The form tested here is a speed of light in vacuum that changes with photon energy. Excludes the slowing of light in a medium such as glass or plasma, which is ordinary optics. full definition in which that speed depends on photon energy. The size of such an effect is usually stated as a linear energy scale (E_QG,1)Definition: linear energy scale (E_QG,1) quantum gravity phenomenology The photon energy at which a speed change that grows in proportion to energy would reach the full speed of light. A lower limit on it is the usual way to state a time-of-flight bound. Excludes the quadratic scale, for a speed change that grows with the square of energy, which this paper does not bound. full definition, and the natural reference is the Planck energyDefinition: Planck energy physics The energy built from the constant of gravitation, Planck's constant and the speed of light, about 1.22e19 GeV. Many quantum-gravity models expect new effects near it. Excludes any energy reached by a particle accelerator, which is about fifteen powers of ten lower. full definition. A photon of 30 GeV is about 2.5e-18 of the Planck energy, so the expected effect on its speed is tiny, and only a very long flight can make it visible.

Gamma-ray bursts give that flight. Jacob and Piran [5] derived how an energy-dependent speed turns into an arrival-time delay over a path through an expanding universe; that relation is the one used here. GRB 090510 is a short burst at redshift 0.903, measured from the spectrum of its host galaxy [6]. Abdo and colleagues [2] used the Fermi observation of this burst, with emission up to about 31 GeV, and set a lower limit of 1.2 Planck energies on the linear scale under conservative assumptions about when the photons were emitted. Vasileiou and colleagues [3] analysed four bright Fermi bursts with three complementary methods; their strongest limit, from GRB 090510, is above 7.6 Planck energies at 95 percent confidence for the case where higher energies travel slower. The LHAASO collaboration [4] used the TeV photons of GRB 221009A and reported a linear limit above 10 Planck energies.

We had a narrower aim. A published limit rests on a pipeline most readers cannot run. We asked how close a short, plain analysis of the public photon file comes, with its forecasts and kill rules fixed before the run. The same study asked the companion question for sound: sound in a fluid has its own speed limit, and that limit is known to bend at short wavelength. Trachenko and colleagues [7] proposed an upper bound on the speed of sound in condensed matter, about 36 km per second, built from fundamental constants; it entered our study as one table check.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition and three forecast files were written and hash-locked on 31 October 2026, each before any run or data opening for its item. The hypothesis under test was that some sound and light waves travel faster or slower than c and follow different laws. The decision it informed: if the vacuum form fails, the published limits are quoted and our rerun is used only as a reproduction of method.

The lock records a debug run made before it. That run showed 84 photons in the analysis window and a bootstrap limit weaker than our forecast, so two forecast rows were known to fail. The rows were kept unchanged and are reported as failures. A one-photon bound was added after the debug run, and it is labelled as added wherever it appears. Two simulation settings were retuned in debug: the horizon packet was moved to start near the horizon, and the grid for the frame test was doubled.

Kill conditions, fixed in advance:

  • Vacuum form: killed in the tested band if the arrival-time slope against energy is consistent with zero and the implied speed change at the highest tested energy is below 1e-15 of c. It survives outside the tested band.
  • Medium form: phase and group speeds above c are already known; the form is killed as new physics if every case keeps its signal front at or below c under the ordinary wave equation.
  • Sound form: killed at long wavelength if sound in a moving fluid follows the flow speed plus or minus the sound speed within 1 percent.

Each kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition and forecast became a rule set whose pass or fail is a verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition read off by code.

Data and provenance

The photons are from the Fermi Large Area Telescope public archive at the NASA High Energy Astrophysics Science Archive Research Center [1]: the weekly photon file for mission week 49 (processing P305, Source event class), which holds 1,214,533 photons, together with the trigger folder for bn090510016, all fetched on 31 October 2026. Fermi data are public with no restriction on use. The trigger time was read from the trigger file header. The burst position and the redshift of 0.903 were entered from memory before the run; the trigger header gives the same position to one decimal place, and the redshift matches the published value [6].

Photons were kept if they arrived between 1 s before and 3 s after the trigger, had energy above 100 MeV and zenith angle below 105 degrees, and fell within an energy-dependent radius of the burst, up to 12 degrees at low energy. That radius was set from memory of the telescope's point-spread function; the published response tables were not used. This gave 119 photons. The analysis window, 0.5 to 1.45 s after the trigger, holds 84 of them, with energies from 0.1 to 29.9 GeV. The highest-energy photon carried 29.9 GeV and arrived 0.828 s after the trigger.

The sound part uses no external data. The sound-speed table for the Trachenko check lists 14 materials with values entered from memory.

Methods

The delay model

If the speed of light changes in proportion to photon energy, a photon of energy E arrives later or earlier than a low-energy photon emitted with it by a time proportional to E:

t=t0+τE(1)

where τ is the delay per GeV. This is dispersionDefinition: dispersion wave physics The dependence of a wave's speed on its frequency or energy, written as a relation between frequency and wavenumber. Excludes a delay that is the same at every energy, such as a fixed travel time. full definition in vacuum. Following Jacob and Piran [5], the slope sets the linear energy scale through a cosmological distance factor K:

K=1H0∫1+xM(1+x)3+1−Mdx(2)

with the integral taken from 0 to the redshift 0.903, H0 = 67.4 km/s/Mpc and matter density M = 0.315. The factor came out at 4.58e17 s. A bound τlim on the slope gives

EQG=Kτlim(3)

and the fractional speed change at the top energy Etop is

δ=EtopτlimK(4)

Fitting the slope

For a trial slope τ, each photon's time is shifted back to xi=ti−τEi. If the trial slope is right, the shifted times bunch most tightly. The fit maximises a sharpness score

S=∑∑G(xi−xj)(5)

over all photon pairs, where G is a Gaussian of width 30 ms. The slope was searched on a grid from -250 to +250 ms per GeV in steps of 2 ms per GeV. This is a simple version of the methods in the published analyses, without the instrument response and without a model of the burst's own spectral lag.

The bound

The 84 photons were resampled with replacement 300 times, a bootstrapDefinition: bootstrap statistics Resampling the data with replacement many times and recomputing the estimate each time, so that the spread of the recomputed values gives an interval for it. Excludes an interval taken from a formula that assumes a distribution. full definition, and the slope refitted each time. The 95% intervalDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition of the refitted slopes runs from its 2.5th to its 97.5th percentile, and τlim is the larger of its two ends in size. The added one-photon bound assumes the top photon was emitted no earlier than the trigger, so its delay cannot exceed its arrival time:

τ1=ttopEtop(6)

This form follows the conservative argument of Abdo and colleagues [2] in outline only.

Sound

Three simulations solved the linear wave equation for sound in a moving fluid, in units where the sound speed cs is 1. In a uniform flow of speed u = 0.5, rays should move at

v=u±cs(7)

A frame test checked that a solution transforms between frames under the sound speed and fails under a wrong one. A horizon flow u(x)=−1+0.5tanh(2λx), with λ = 0.4, makes an acoustic horizonDefinition: acoustic horizon analogue gravity The place in a moving fluid where the flow speed equals the sound speed, so that sound travelling against the flow cannot get out. It mimics the horizon of a black hole. Excludes a gravitational horizon, and any place where the flow is slower than sound. full definition at x = 0 with surface gravityDefinition: surface gravity (of a horizon) analogue gravity, after black-hole physics The slope of the flow speed at the acoustic horizon. It sets how fast a trapped wave's wavelength is stretched. Excludes the pull of gravity at a planet's surface. full definition λ; a wave packet was released near it and its position and wavenumber compared with ray predictions.

The fourth simulation solved the one-dimensional Gross-Pitaevskii equation for a uniform condensate and measured the frequency of small plane waves at six wavenumbers. The known answer is the Bogoliubov dispersionDefinition: Bogoliubov dispersion condensed-matter physics (Bose-Einstein condensates) The frequency of small waves in a uniform condensate: equal to the sound speed times the wavenumber at long wavelength and rising faster, towards the free-particle law, at wavelengths near the healing length. Excludes sound in an ordinary gas or solid, whose dispersion is set by other physics. full definition

ω=csk1+k2h22(8)

where h is the healing lengthDefinition: healing length condensed-matter physics The length below which a condensate's density cannot change smoothly. Waves shorter than it stop behaving like sound. Excludes the wavelength of any particular wave. full definition. Its slope, the group velocityDefinition: group velocity wave physics The speed at which a packet of waves, and the energy it carries, moves. It equals the slope of frequency against wavenumber. Excludes the phase velocity, the speed of a single crest, which can differ from it. full definition, rises above cs once kh nears 1.

Controls and planted checks

Two checks were run on the photon fit.

The first controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition shuffled the photon energies among the 84 photons, which breaks any link between energy and arrival time, and refitted the slope 300 times. The shuffled slopes ran from -44 to +76 ms per GeV (2.5th to 97.5th percentile). The real fitted slope, 0, sits inside that range, as forecast.

The planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition added a known delay, τE, to every photon at 1, 3, 5 and 10 times our bound, with both signs, and refitted. Table 1 gives the result: every planted delay came back within 0.9 percent, so the fit sees a delay of the size of our bound when one is there. The result file stores one recovered value for each planted size, a positive delay, and none for the opposite sign. Three of the four planted delays lie outside the search grid of -250 to +250 ms per GeV stated in the methods, so the planted refits searched a wider range than that sentence gives; the file does not record the range.

For sound, the frame test is its own control: under the true sound speed the residual was 4.5e-4, and under a wrong speed 0.78.

Results

Vacuum

Table 2 gives the photon results. The fitted slope is 0, on a 2 ms per GeV grid. The bootstrap interval runs from -117 to +46 ms per GeV, so the bound is 117 ms per GeV. Through eq. 3 that is a linear energy scale of 3.9e18 GeV, or 0.32 Planck energies. Our rerun bounds any linear energy-dependent change in light speed to less than 7.6e-18 of c at 29.9 GeV, a linear energy scale above 0.32 Planck energies, about 24 times weaker than the published limit of 7.6 Planck energies from the same burst.c1 The speed change is below the preregistered 1e-15, so the vacuum form of the hypothesis is killed in the band tested, 0.1 to 30 GeV.

Figure 2 sets our two bounds beside the published ones. The bootstrap bound is weak because resampling often leaves out the single 29.9 GeV photon, which sets most of the fit. The one-photon bound uses that photon directly and reaches 1.36 Planck energies, still a factor of about 5.6 below the published 7.6.

Sound

Table 3 gives the simulation results. Sound in a uniform flow moved at the flow speed plus or minus the sound speed to within 1e-6, and in a simulated condensate the wave frequencies followed the Bogoliubov law within 2 percent, with a short-wavelength packet moving at 2.89 times the sound speed.c3 Figure 3 shows the measured frequencies leaving the sound line as the wavelength nears the healing length.

The horizon packet stayed trapped, and its wavenumber followed the ray prediction within 3.3 percent. Its position lagged the ray by 0.16 in scaled units against a limit of 0.01, which failed. The packet is about as wide as the distance it travels, so a ray, which has no width, is a poor description of it; we did not refine the test after the run.

The Trachenko value computed from constants was 36.10 km per second, inside the forecast band of 36.0 to 36.2, and none of the 14 materials in our remembered table exceeded it; the fastest was diamond at 18 km per second.

Forecasts

Table 4 sets the forecasts written before the run against the outcomes.

Twelve of the 15 preregistered verdicts passed; the three that failed were two forecasts of our own bound's strength and one test of a packet near a simulated horizon.c4 Appendix A lists every rule.

What this means for a reader

When people in a large forecasting tournament said they knew little about a question, their forecast was a little worse, and they had already moved it toward 50 percent. People who answered fewer of the questions open to them scored better on the ones they did answer. Both patterns are associations in people who chose their own ratings and questions. The follow-up study found that the stated probability already carries what the self-rating knows, and that a person who skips more in one year than the last does not clearly score better, so a habit of skipping marks a careful forecaster and is not shown to improve an answer.

Objection

Nothing here is causal. People chose their ratings, their questions and when to forecast.

What would change the call. Read together with F32, and repeat on data that records when a forecaster declined a question.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

A source that can say "I am not sure" or decline to answer is only useful if those signals mean something. We tested both on the public survey forecasts of the Good Judgment Project, where volunteers rated their own expertise from 1 to 5 on each forecast and chose which questions to answer. Within a forecaster-year, one point of self-rated expertise went with a relative Brier score better by 0.0226 (95 percent interval 0.0185 to 0.0270) across 3,780 forecaster-years.c1 Forecasts rated expertise 1 scored 0.0218 worse (0.0155 to 0.0285) than the same person's forecasts rated 2 to 5 and sat 0.055 nearer to 50 percent (0.051 to 0.058), across 1,826 forecaster-years.c2 The preregistered prediction was that low-rated forecasts would be worse and no less hedged, and it failed on the hedging rule. With question-by-time medians the gap fell to 0.0156 (0.0094 to 0.0219), under the preregistered bar of 0.02.c3 At matched forecast count, skip rate correlated with better relative Brier score at rho +0.351 (+0.331 to +0.368) across 9,204 forecaster-years.c4 Inside the same strata skip rate correlated +0.452 with updates per answered question, so this round does not separate skipping from updating.c5 A second round, published as F32, removed the updates and narrowed two of these readings; this paper states what it changed.

Introduction

The Good Judgment Project ran from 2011 to 2015 inside a geopolitical forecasting tournament. Thousands of volunteers gave probabilities for world events, and the project tested training, teaming and tracking as ways to raise accuracy [2]. Its survey forecasts are public, and for the first three years each forecast carries the forecaster's own 1 to 5 rating of their expertise on that question.

Two things in those files bear on a practical design question: how software that collects answers from many sources should treat a source's stated confidence, and whether it should let a source decline. The first is the self-rating. A review of ways to identify skilled forecasters lists the same 1 to 5 item among expertise-based predictors and attributes it to the project's own papers [5]. The second is the choice of questions. Merkle, Steyvers, Mellers and Tetlock [3] pointed out that a Brier scoreDefinition: Brier score forecast verification, from weather forecasting The squared difference between the stated probabilities and the outcomes, here summed over the answer options in the Good Judgment Project form so it runs from 0 to 2. Lower is better. Excludes questions left unanswered, which it does not score. full definition, the squared difference between stated probabilities and outcomes, looks only at the forecasts a person submitted, and asked whether the questions a person selects add information about their ability. A Brier score is lower when better, and it gives no score to a question left unanswered.

We asked two questions of the data. Within one person, does a low self-rating mark a worse forecast, and is that forecast already hedged? Across people, do those who skip more score better on what they answer? The decision the study informed was whether an abstain filter in Flywheel, our accountability software, can use a source's own confidence report or needs an outside measure. Our searches for this paper returned the two works above and the project's own account of its best forecasters [4]; none of the search results gave an effect size for the self-rating inside one person, which is what a search returned and no proof that none is published.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, a dated plan fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen, was written on 29 October 2026 and locked at 14:29:13 UTC that day. Before writing it we had seen file lists, column headers, and counts of questions, forecasts and rating levels with no outcome joined to any forecast. No Brier score had been computed on the real data. The code had been run on synthetic files shaped like the real ones, with effects built in that it recovered, which is a planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition: data with a known answer run through the same analysis first, to show the analysis can see an effect when one is there.

The plan names seven verdictsDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition, each a set of rules that must all hold, read off by code. A verdict in our usage is that pass or fail and never a reading written after the numbers were seen. It also states a prior probability for each main verdict (0.8, 0.25 and 0.35 for the positive control, the low-rating prediction and the skipping prediction) and a mapping from outcomes to the filter design. Appendix A gives every rule.

Data and provenance

The data are the Good Judgment Project survey forecasts for years 1 to 4 and the question file, published on the Harvard Dataverse under CC0 1.0Definition: CC0 1.0 copyright and data licensing The Creative Commons public domain dedication, under which anyone may reuse the work for any purpose without permission. Excludes a licence condition requiring citation, which stays a scholarly courtesy. full definition, the Creative Commons public domain dedication, which allows any reuse and leaves citation as a courtesy [1]. The SHA-256 of each of the five input files was recorded in the run's result file.

The survey files hold 3,143,460 rows, one per answer option. Dropping 43,944 withdrawal rows left 1,234,940 forecasts. We dropped 157,189 forecasts on questions that were voided or had no recorded outcome, 13,381 dated after the question closed and 15 whose probabilities could not be repaired. That leaves 1,064,355 scored forecasts. Self-rated expertise exists in years 1 to 3 only, on 410,451 scored binary forecasts. Only aggregates and distributions were stored; no value for any single forecaster was written to any output.

The files hold no record of a declined question. A skipDefinition: skip our usage A closed question that was open during a forecaster's active window in a year and that they never answered, inferred from the data. Excludes questions outside the active window, and any recorded decision to decline, which the data do not hold. full definition is inferred: a closed question that was open during a forecaster's active window in a year and that they never answered. The word excludes any recorded decision to decline, which the data do not have, so a skipped question may have been unseen.

Methods

Scores

Each forecast is scored with the Brier score in the project's form, summed over the answer options, so it runs from 0 to 2:

B=∑k(pk−ok)2(1)

where pk is the stated probability of option k and ok is 1 if that option occurred and 0 otherwise. The relative Brier scoreDefinition: relative Brier score forecast verification, our usage A forecast's Brier score minus the median Brier score of all scored survey forecasts on the same question. Lower is better. Excludes the difficulty of the question, which subtracting the median removes. full definition of a forecast is B minus the median B of all scored survey forecasts on the same question, so it measures skill against the crowd and leaves out how hard the question was. The secondary form takes the median inside the question and the fifth of its open period in which the forecast was made. ExtremityDefinition: extremity judgment and forecasting research The distance of a binary forecast from 50 percent, from 0 for a coin-flip forecast to 0.5 for a certain one. Excludes whether the forecast was right, and how well calibrated the forecaster is. full definition is the distance of a binary forecast from 50 percent, |p−0.5|, from 0 to 0.5; it measures how hedged a forecast is and says nothing about whether it was right. The unit is the forecaster-yearDefinition: forecaster-year our usage One person's forecasts within one tournament year, the unit for every statistic here. Excludes pooling of different people, and pooling one person's years. full definition, one person's forecasts within one tournament year, so a person active in three years counts three times.

The within-person tests

The positive controlDefinition: positive control experimental design A test of an effect expected to be present, which the instrument must detect for its other readings to be trusted. Excludes a shuffle control, which removes an effect instead. full definition tests an effect that should be there for the other readings to be trusted: that self-rated expertise goes with accuracy at all. For forecaster-years with at least 10 scored binary forecasts using two or more rating levels, relative Brier score and rating were both centred within the forecaster-year, and one slope β was fitted to the pooled data. The reported quantity is −β, so a positive value means a higher rating goes with a better score.

The low-rating test uses forecaster-years with at least 5 forecasts rated 1 and 5 rated 2 to 5. For each it takes

dB=Slow−Srest(2)

where Slow is the mean relative Brier score of the forecasts rated 1 and Srest that of the forecasts rated 2 to 5, and the matching difference in extremity, dE. The statistic is the mean over forecaster-years. The preregistered bar for dB was 0.02 on the 0 to 2 scale.

Skip rate and the matched correlation

A forecaster-year is eligible with at least 10 available questions and 5 answered. Its skip rate is

s=1−nansnav(3)

with nans the available questions answered and nav the number available. Busy forecasters answer more, so the correlation is taken inside each stratumDefinition: stratum survey statistics A group of units alike on the matched variables, here year and twentieth of forecast count, inside which a statistic is computed before averaging. Excludes control for variables that were not matched. full definition h of year and twentieth of forecast count, a group alike on the matched variables, and averaged with weights wh equal to stratum size:

ρM=∑hwhρh∑hwh(4)

where ρh is the Spearman rhoDefinition: Spearman rho statistics The correlation between the ranks of two quantities, from -1 to 1, which counts any steadily rising or falling relation and is not pulled by single extreme values. Excludes the slope of a relation, and evidence of cause. full definition, the correlation of ranks, between skip rate and the negative of the forecaster-year's mean relative score. Strata with fewer than 10 forecaster-years were dropped. Matching controls only the matched variables.

Intervals

Every 95 percent intervalDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition is the middle 95 percent of bootstrapDefinition: bootstrap statistics Recomputing a statistic many times on forecaster-years resampled with replacement to read how much the estimate varies. Excludes an interval from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition draws, a resampling of forecaster-years with replacement that assumes no textbook distribution: 2,000 draws for the low-rating test and 1,000 for the others, the skip test resampling inside strata.

Controls and planted checks

Each controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition is a copy of the data with one link broken by shuffling and scored with the same code; a comparison with another dataset is not a control. Three were fixed in advance, with 1,000 draws each, and the 95th percentile of each one's null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition is the bar the real value must clear.

  • Ratings shuffled within forecaster-year, the null for the mean of dB.
  • Ratings shuffled within forecaster-year, the null for the positive-control slope.
  • Skip rate shuffled within year and forecast-count strata, the null for ρM.

The activity check asks whether matching did its job: the mean correlation of skip rate with forecast count inside strata must be under 0.2 in size. A p value from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition is the share of control draws at or above the real value, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so 1,000 draws cannot give less than 0.001.

Results

Self-rating inside one person

The positive control passed. Within a forecaster-year, one point of self-rated expertise went with a relative Brier score better by 0.0226 (95 percent interval 0.0185 to 0.0270) across 3,780 forecaster-years.c1 The shuffle's 95th percentile was 0.0015 (p 0.001), and the test covered 398,463 forecasts. Each point of rating also went with a forecast 0.037 further from 50 percent (0.034 to 0.040).

Forecasts rated expertise 1 scored 0.0218 worse (0.0155 to 0.0285) than the same person's forecasts rated 2 to 5 and sat 0.055 nearer to 50 percent (0.051 to 0.058), across 1,826 forecaster-years.c2 The sample held 243,486 forecasts, 77,572 of them rated 1. The score gap cleared the shuffle's 95th percentile of 0.0048 (p 0.001) and cleared the 0.02 bar by 0.0018. The verdict still failed, because the prediction was "worse and no less hedged" and the extremity rule required the lower bound of dE to be above -0.02; it was -0.058. The effect is small beside the spread between people: the low-rated forecasts were the worse ones in 55 percent of forecaster-years, and the median gap was 0.018.

With question-by-time medians the gap fell to 0.0156 (0.0094 to 0.0219), under the preregistered bar of 0.02.c3 Figure 1 and Table 1 give the three within-person effects.

Skipping

Across the 9,204 eligible forecaster-years (1,781; 1,114; 1,360 and 4,949 in years 1 to 4) the median skip rate was 0.59. At matched forecast count, skip rate correlated with better relative Brier score at rho +0.351 (+0.331 to +0.368) across 9,204 forecaster-years.c4 The shuffle's 95th percentile was +0.017 (p 0.001). The activity check passed: skip rate correlated -0.613 with forecast count overall and -0.078 inside strata. Matching matters to the size of the number. Unmatched, the correlation was +0.119. Matched on questions answered in place of forecasts it was +0.236 (+0.216 to +0.252), and with question-by-time medians +0.211 (+0.188 to +0.229). Figure 2 draws the four.

Inside the same strata skip rate correlated +0.452 with updates per answered question, so this round does not separate skipping from updating.c5 The preregistration named this before the run: at a fixed forecast count, a person who answers fewer questions must update each one more, and updating goes with accuracy in this tournament.

Table 2 sets the priors against the outcomes.

Discussion

The self-rating means something inside one person: a forecast rated low is a worse forecast. People had also acted on that knowledge already, since the low-rated forecasts sit nearer 50 percent. The decision mapping written before the run read this outcome as "self-report modulates the stated probability and is usable as one input" to a filter. The first-round write-up went one step further and read "worse and hedged" as the rating carrying information past the stated probability.

The second round, F32, tested that step and took it back. It found that forecasts rated 1 are pulled toward 50 percent by about the right amount, with a best rescaling factor of 0.92 (0.79 to 1.06) where 1 means right-sized, and that adding the self-rating to a filter on the stated probability gained 0.0026 in area under the risk-coverage curve against a bar of 0.005, while a rating shuffled within each forecaster-year gained 0.0024. A calibrated forecast from a less informed person scores worse, and its stated probability already says by how much.

F32 also removed the confound on skipping. Counting each person's first forecast on a question only, the matched correlation was +0.286 (+0.264 to +0.303), and +0.195 with timing matched as well, so most of the +0.351 reported here survives the removal of every update. Within the same person across consecutive years it was +0.041 (-0.007 to +0.095) over 1,578 pairs, which shows no benefit to a person from skipping more. The supported reading is a trait: people who answer selectively tend to be better forecasters.

Merkle and colleagues [3] studied question selection in the same tournament. We read their abstract only, in a search snippet that was cut short, so we do not compare signs or sizes with their result.

Limitations

  • Nothing here is causal. People chose their ratings, their questions and when to forecast.
  • Skips are inferred. A question counted as skipped may have been unseen, and "available" means any closed question open during the forecaster's active window.
  • The skip correlation in this round includes updates. F32 puts the first-forecast value at +0.286 and found no within-person effect.
  • The low-rating gap clears its 0.02 bar by 0.0018, with an interval from 0.0155 to 0.0285, and falls under the bar with question-by-time medians. The 0.02 bar was a choice.
  • The reading that the self-rating adds information past the stated probability did not survive F32.
  • Year 4 has no self-ratings, prediction-market trades were not used, and nothing here speaks for language models or for any named person.
  • Scoring was done by our own code and was not blind.

Evidence

Mixed. The prediction that low-rated forecasts are worse and no less hedged failed: they sat 0.055 nearer 50 percent (interval 0.051 to 0.058) against a limit of 0.02. With question-by-time medians the score gap was 0.0156, under the 0.02 bar. The skip correlation of +0.351 includes updates; F32 puts it at +0.286 on first forecasts and found no within-person effect (+0.041, interval -0.007 to +0.095).

Figures

These are the paper's own figures, numbered as in the PDF, and each "Figure" reference in the text points here. The charts on this page redraw the same results from the result files and carry their own numbers.

Tables

Appendix A. The preregistered verdicts

Each verdict is a set of rules written before the run. A verdict passes only when every rule holds. Values are read from the run's result file.

Numbers recorded in our publication register

As recorded in the publication register, the summary row each finding gets; the paper's own numbers above were re-read from the result files.

What lowers it

  • blinding Not blind: the analyst saw the data's shape before the lock. from our publication register, on blinding
  • novelty Nearby work exists; novelty is not shown. from our publication register, on the literature
  • depth of reading The cited literature was read at the level of search snippets; full texts were not read. from the Verified section

What holds it up

  • scoring Scored by code against rules fixed in advance. from our publication register, on who scored it
  • preregistration Preregistered and hash-locked before the run (sha256 723e0f54). from the Reproduce section
  • control Controls: the shuffles worked and the activity check passed; the plan named updating as a confound before the run. from our publication register, on controls
  • open data Public data. from our publication register, on the data licence

Where the claim stands

  1. lead
  2. hypothesis
  3. thesis
  4. conjecture
  5. theorem
  6. law candidate
  7. killed

A preregistration with pass-or-fail rules is on file, which this rung needs. The next rung needs a named rival reading beaten by a decisive observation, and none is on file. Tier B: Large public data with working shuffle controls and a preregistration. The follow-up finding F32 shows the skip correlation is partly updating and timing, and the score gap for low-rated forecasts clears its bar by only 0.0018.

What this means for a reader

When an OEIS entry says "Conjecture" in front of a simple recurrence, the line has usually held far past the terms it was fitted on. In our sample, 212 of 213 such lines held for a median of 967 further terms, and the one that failed had already been marked false by a later contributor. Read such a line as a well-tested guess. It still has no proof behind it, and holding for a thousand more terms does not supply one.

Objection

The lines were fitted to data, so passing is what a correct fit does, and a high-order fit can pass by construction when the b-file is short relative to its order. A passing line stays a conjecture with more range.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Many entries in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences carry a line such as "Conjecture: a(n) = 3*a(n-1) - 3*a(n-2) + a(n-3)". Most such lines were found by fitting the terms known at the time, and the b-file stored beside the entry often lists hundreds or thousands more. We asked how often these conjectures fail on their own b-files and whether the failures are data errors or counterexamples. From the public OEIS data, 23,883 entries mention a conjecture and 1,179 have a line our parser accepts; we drew a random 500 and tested every line that its b-file extends by at least 30 terms. One of 213 tested conjecture lines failed on its b-file, 0.47 percent, with a 95 percent Wilson interval of 0.08 to 2.6 percent.c1 The one failure, A031740, holds for 64 indices and fails at n = 65, and the entry has recorded the conjecture as false since 2016, so the sweep found no new counterexample.c2 Planted errors were caught in 212 of 212 passing lines, and equations applied to other entries' terms passed at a mean rate of 0.005.c3 The sampling frame changed after the preregistered route failed, and the change is recorded. The result says the check is cheap and, on this kind of line, low in yield.

Introduction

The OEISDefinition: OEIS mathematics (reference databases) The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, a public database of number sequences in which each entry carries the first terms, formulas, comments and links contributed by many people. Excludes a peer-reviewed journal; a line in an entry is a contribution, and a conjecture line in it carries no proof. full definition is a public database of integer sequences, online since 1995 and holding over 300,000 entries when Sloane described its recent history in 2018 [2]. Each entry lists the first terms of a sequence in a short data section, with formulas, comments and references contributed by many people. Beside most entries sits a b-fileDefinition: b-file the OEIS A text file stored beside an OEIS entry that lists the sequence's index and term pairs much further than the entry's own data section, often to thousands of terms. Excludes the entry's data section, which holds only the first few dozen terms. full definition, a plain list of index and term pairs that often runs to thousands of terms.

Some entries carry a conjecture lineDefinition: conjecture line the OEIS, our usage A comment or formula line in an OEIS entry that states an equation for the sequence and labels it a conjecture. Most were found by fitting the terms then known. Excludes a line marked as proved, and a statement with no equation. full definition: an equation for the sequence, offered without proof. Many are a linear recurrenceDefinition: linear recurrence mathematics (combinatorics) An equation that gives each term of a sequence as a fixed weighted sum of a set number of earlier terms, possibly with terms in n. Here with integer coefficients. Excludes an equation with a product of earlier terms, and an equation with coefficients that are not integers. full definition with integer coefficients, found by fitting the terms then listed. Fitting of this kind is a standard method in computer algebra. Kauers and Koutschan [3] describe guessing a recurrence from finitely many terms by linear algebra, note that the overdetermination of the linear system is one source of trust in a guess, and show how to guess from fewer terms by restricting the coefficients. In a later search across the OEIS [4] they found conjectured recurrences for sequences not previously known to satisfy one, proved some, and showed that a recurrence exists for others without proving the guessed one.

Our question was smaller. The b-files already hold the data a mechanical check needs. We asked what share of conjecture lines fail on their own b-files, and whether each failure is a data error or a true counterexampleDefinition: counterexample mathematics (logic) A single case where a general statement is false. One is enough to refute a conjecture. Excludes a term that disagrees because the data are wrong. full definition. The decision it informed was whether such lines are worth a routine check as a cheap source of counterexamples, and how to read one when it appears in our own work. Our searches found the guessing literature above and no published sweep of this exact kind; that is what the searches returned, and it does not show that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition was written and hash-locked on 31 October 2026, before any entry was sampled beyond one probe request that returned an unrelated entry. It names the sampling route, the parser rules, the definition of tested and of failed, the planted errors, the control, the forecasts and the kill conditions.

Kill conditions, without discretion:

  • The run is voidDefinition: void research method (our usage) The verdict of a run whose planted check failed or whose sample fell below its stated minimum. It says nothing for or against the claim. Excludes a null result, which comes from a working instrument. full definition if fewer than 99 percent of planted errors are caught, if fewer than 100 lines are tested, or if the real pass rate is at or below the control's 95th percentile.
  • A failure counts only after a second check that the failing term is not a known b-file error.
  • Nothing here proves the passing recurrences; a passing line stays a conjecture with more range.

Each kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition and forecast became a rule set whose pass or fail is a verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition read off by code.

The locked plan sampled entries through the OEIS search pages at random offsets. That route returned only 10 entries, because the site asks for a sign-in past the first 100 search results, and we did not work around it. The first run tested 2 lines and was void under the first kill condition. Having seen only those 2 lines, both passing, we changed the sampling frameDefinition: sampling frame survey statistics The list from which a sample is drawn. A result describes the frame, so a change of frame changes what the result is about. Excludes the sample itself. full definition: the public OEIS data repository, every entry with a parsable conjecture line, then a seeded random 500. The change is recorded as a deviationDefinition: deviation research method (metascience) A dated, recorded change from the preregistered plan, stated with its reason and with what had been seen when it was made. Excludes a change made silently, and a change made after seeing the outcome it would affect without saying so. full definition with its reason and what had been seen. The new frame is wider than the locked one, and the second run used the same locked plan, rules and forecasts.

Data and provenance

The data are the OEIS entries from the public oeis/oeisdata repository and the b-files from oeis.org [1], retrieved on 31 October 2026. OEIS content is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 under the OEIS End-User License Agreement. We used it as data for checks; this paper reports counts and quotes one entry's conjecture and comment lines with attribution.

Of all entries, 23,883 mention a conjecture and 1,179 have a conjecture line our parser accepts. The seeded random 500 entries held 531 lines that mention a conjecture and a term a(n), and 512 of those parsed. Only about 5 percent of the entries that mention a conjecture had a line our parser accepts: 1,179 of 23,883.c4 The result therefore describes simple linear recurrences, not OEIS conjectures in general.

Methods

Parsing

A line was parsed only if it states an equation in n and earlier terms a(n−k) with integer coefficients. A pattern match finds the candidate equation, and a parser whitelistDefinition: parser whitelist computer science (parsing) A rule that turns each line into a syntax tree and accepts it only if every part is on a fixed list: integers, n, the terms a(n-k), addition, subtraction, multiplication and powers. Excludes any line that needs division, sums, named functions or words to state. full definition accepts it only if every part of its syntax tree is an integer, n, a term a(n−k), addition, subtraction, multiplication or a power. Anything else was skipped and counted.

Testing

For each sampled entry, the first conjecture line that parsed and qualified was tested; at most one line per entry was tested. A line qualified when the b-file holds at least 30 more terms than the entry's data section and the equation can be evaluated at 10 or more indices. The equation was evaluated at every index in the b-file's range where all the terms it needs exist. A line fails if its two sides differ at any such index; the first failing index and the number of indices it held for were recorded. This left 213 tested lines, with a median of 967 b-file terms beyond the data section.

The failure rate

With k failures among N tested lines, the failure rate is f=k/N. Its Wilson intervalDefinition: Wilson interval statistics A 95 percent interval for a proportion, found by inverting the score test. It stays inside 0 to 1 and behaves well when the count is small or near zero. Excludes the simple interval of the proportion plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, which fails near zero. full definition [5] at z = 1.96 has centre c and half-width w:

D=1+z2N(1)
c=1D(f+z22N)(2)
w=zDf(1−f)N+z24N2(3)

Controls and planted checks

The planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition raised the first integer coefficient of each passing equation by one and ran the check again. A planted line should fail. Of the 213 tested lines, 212 passed, so 212 planted versions were built. All 212 were caught.

The cross-entry controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition applied each equation to a different, randomly chosen entry's terms, up to index 200. One draw takes 30 equations at random, applies each to another entry's terms, and records the share that pass. This share is the pass rate of an equation on a sequence it was not written for, the chance level of the test. Over 200 draws the mean share was 0.0048, and the 95th percentile of this null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition was 0.033, one equation in 30.

The real pass rate, 0.995, was above every draw. The p value from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition is

p=k+1n+1(4)

with k the number of draws at or above the real pass rate and n the number of draws. Here k = 0 and n = 200, so p = 0.005, the smallest value 200 draws can give.

Results

Figure 1 follows the counts from the whole corpus to the one failure.

One of 213 tested conjecture lines failed on its b-file, 0.47 percent, with a 95 percent Wilson interval of 0.08 to 2.6 percent.c1 Figure 2 places the rate against the forecast of 4 percent and the preregistered 1 percent rule.

The failing line is in entry A031740. Its conjecture, contributed by Colin Barker on 30 September 2012, reads:

a(n)=n(961n+1)(5)
a(n)=3a(n−1)−3a(n−2)+a(n−3)(6)

The entry's data section has 32 terms and its b-file 10,000. The one failure, A031740, holds for 64 indices and fails at n = 65, and the entry has recorded the conjecture as false since 2016, so the sweep found no new counterexample.c2 The stored copy of the entry carries a comment by Chai Wah Wu dated 19 June 2016: the conjecture is false, and 3940288 is a term not of the form m(961m+1). The preregistration asked for a second code path before a failure counts; the result file records no such rerun. The check by hand was reading this comment, which confirms the failure is a true counterexample and not a b-file error.

Table 1 gives the counts and rates.

Table 2 sets the forecasts written before the run against the outcomes.

Discussion

The sweep shows that a mechanical check of OEIS conjecture lines is cheap: the analysis took about 6 seconds once the data were stored. On simple linear recurrences it is also low in yield. The lines held at a rate of 99.5 percent, the failure rate came in an order of magnitude under the forecast, and the single failure had been caught by a contributor four years after it was posted.

Two features of the lines explain much of this. They were fitted to data, so passing on further terms is what a correct fit does. And a recurrence of order d fitted to a few more than d terms is close to determined by them, so the guess is either right or wrong in a way that shows quickly; A031740's conjecture failed just past twice the length of its data section. Kauers and Koutschan [3] point to the same property, overdetermination, as a source of trust in a guessed recurrence. Our pass rate is a measurement of how well that trust held on one class of OEIS line.

The more interesting conjectures are the ones our parser skipped: 95 percent of the entries that mention a conjecture state something our whitelist cannot read; we did not classify what those lines say. A sweep of those would need a different checker for each kind of line.

Limitations

  • The lines were fitted to data, so passing is what a correct fit does, and a high-order fit can pass by construction when the b-file is short relative to its order. A passing line stays a conjecture with more range.
  • Only about 5 percent of conjecture entries parse under our rules, so the rate describes simple linear recurrences with integer coefficients.
  • Many lines come from a few contributors, so the rate also describes their habits.
  • The sampling frame changed after the locked route failed. A later review of our ledger marked this as narrowing the claim. The new frame was chosen after seeing 2 lines, both passing.
  • The preregistered second code path for a failure was not recorded; the single failure was confirmed by the entry's own comment.
  • Scoring was by our own code and was not blind.

Evidence

Honest null. One failure in 213 tested lines, 0.47 percent; the 95 percent Wilson interval runs to 2.6 percent, so failure rates above that are ruled out for lines of this kind.

What this means for a reader

If a paper says a Titius-BodeDefinition: Titius-Bode rule planetary astronomy Any formula that places a system's planets at distances or periods growing by a near-constant ratio from one planet to the next, here fitted in three forms to the log of orbital period. Excludes a physical model of how planets form or migrate. full definition fit predicts a missing planet at a given period, ask what the two neighbouring planets alone would predict. A Titius-Bode rule, in planetary astronomy, is any formula that places a system's planets at distances or periods growing by a near-constant ratio from one to the next; it is a description of where planets sit and carries no model of how they formed or migrated. In our sample the neighbours win. A system's planets do tend to sit at similar spacing ratios, a pattern known from Kepler data as "peas in a podDefinition: peas in a pod exoplanet surveys The pattern, reported from Kepler data, that planets inside one system tend to be alike in size and in the ratios between neighbouring periods. Excludes a rule for the order of the gaps, and any likeness between planets of different systems. full definition" [8], and any rule that fits a geometric sequence will fit such a system well. That good fit is not evidence that the sequence itself is a law. The exoplanet survey phrase covers planets inside one system being alike in size and in spacing ratio; it states no rule for the order of the gaps.

Objection

The three forms were written from memory of the published ones, and a later review of our own ledger flagged that. A published form that differs could score differently, so the result covers these three versions only. Blagg's formula with its periodic term was not tested.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

The Titius-Bode rule says planets sit at distances that grow by a steady ratio, and its generalised forms have been used to predict planets nobody has seen. We asked whether exoplanet spacing follows such a rule beyond what each system's own set of gaps explains. On 122 systems with four or more planets (543 planets) from the NASA Exoplanet Archive, three forms of the rule were scored against two controls fixed in advance. The real systems beat a control that draws gaps from the whole catalogue (p 0.0005, 2,000 draws), and none of the three forms beat a control that keeps each system's gaps and shuffles their order (p 0.85, 0.995 and 0.68).c1 When an interior planet is dropped, the geometric mean of its two neighbours predicts its period better than the rule does: median error 0.107 against 0.131 in log period, a ratio of 1.23.c2 The regularity is real, and it is the regularity of similar gaps inside one system. The order of those gaps adds nothing we could detect. The preregistered law-like verdict failed.

Introduction

Johann Titius noticed in 1766 that the planets then known sit near distances given by a simple doubling sequence, and Johann Bode popularised it. The rule matched Uranus and the asteroid belt and missed Neptune. It has been rewritten many times since. Blagg [2] fitted the Solar System and the moons of the giant planets with a periodic correction to a geometric progression; Richardson [3] gave another version.

The question of whether the rule means anything was put sharply by Hayes and Tremaine [4]. They drew random planetary systems, rejected the ones that would be unstable, and found that the survivors fit a Titius-Bode law about as well as the Solar System. Their conclusion was that stable systems tend to be regularly spaced, and that this is the whole content of the rule.

Exoplanets gave the rule new material. Bovaird and Lineweaver [5] fitted a generalised Titius-Bode relation to multi-planet systems, allowed for unseen planets in the gaps, and predicted 141 new planets. Huang and Bakos [6] searched the Kepler data for 97 of those predictions and found 5. Bovaird, Lineweaver and Jacobsen [7] replied that many predicted planets would not transit and should not be expected in the data, and ranked new predictions by their chance of transiting.

This paper adds one controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition to that argument. A control, in the sense of experimental design, is a copy of the data with one structure removed and scored exactly like the real data; a comparison with another catalogue or a published number would not count as one. A rule about a sequence should beat a version of the same system with its gaps put in a different order. If it does not, the rule describes the sizes of the gaps and nothing about their arrangement.

Preregistration and design

The design was written and hash-locked on 31 October 2026 as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, after the archive file was fetched and its first two rows were seen and before any spacing was computed. The practice comes from clinical trials and psychology: a dated plan fixed before any result is seen, so a plan revised after a look at the outcome does not qualify. The decision it informs was stated in the same file: if the rule fails, it is reported as spacing, and predicted-planet claims built on it get no weight in our work.

The locked file names the data, the three forms, the per-system statistic, the leave-one-outDefinition: leave-one-out prediction statistics, cross-validation Dropping one interior planet, fitting the rule to the others and comparing the predicted period with the true one, repeated for every interior planet. Excludes scoring a planet with a fit that has already seen it. full definition prediction test, the planted systemsDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition, both controls, the forecasts and the kill conditionsDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition. Leave-one-out is a validation method from statistics: drop one planet, fit the rest and predict the one dropped, so no planet is scored by a fit that has seen it. The planted systems are our planted check, synthetic systems with a known regularity run through the same analysis first to show the score can find regularity when it is there, which no check on real data can show. A kill condition is a rule in the plan that decides against the claim when it is met, with no room for judgement after the run. Nothing was added after the run. The preregistration's SHA-256Definition: SHA-256 cryptography A hash function that turns a file into a 64-character fingerprint which changes if any byte of the file changes. A recorded hash shows the file was not edited after it was taken. Excludes encryption, because the hash keeps nothing secret and cannot be turned back into the file. full definition is given in the reproduction section. SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash, a 64-character fingerprint of a file that changes if any byte changes; it shows the plan was not edited and keeps nothing secret, since it is not encryption.

The two controls are our own constructions, set out in the methods. The order-shuffle controlDefinition: order-shuffle control our usage, a permutation control Each system rebuilt from its own innermost period and its own gaps in log period, put in a random order, and scored with the same form and freedom as the real system. Excludes gaps borrowed from other systems, which the pooled-gap control uses. full definition keeps each system's own gaps and puts them in a random order. The pooled-gap controlDefinition: pooled-gap control our usage, a resampling control Each system rebuilt from gaps in log period drawn at random from all systems' gaps, and scored with the same form and freedom as the real system. Excludes planets or gaps from outside the 122 systems in the sample. full definition rebuilds each system from gaps drawn from the whole sample. Neither brings in any planet from outside the 122 systems.

Kill conditions, without discretion:

  • VoidDefinition: void research method (our usage) The verdict of a run whose planted check failed or whose sample fell below its stated minimum. It says nothing for or against the claim. Excludes a null result, which comes from a working instrument. full definition if the planted systems score at or below the pooled-gap control's 95th percentile, or if fewer than 60 systems qualify. A void run, in our usage, says nothing for or against the rule, and differs from a null result, which comes from an instrument that works.
  • Law-likeDefinition: law-like our usage, fixed in the preregistration The verdict that a Titius-Bode form beats the order-shuffle control's 95th percentile and predicts dropped planets better than the neighbour baseline. Excludes regularity that similar gaps alone produce, which beats only the pooled-gap control. full definition only if the plain form beats the order-shuffle control's 95th percentile and the leave-one-out ratio is below 1. Otherwise the rule is reported as explained by spacing. Law-like is our label for a rule whose sequence carries information past the sizes of the gaps; regularity that similar gaps alone produce falls outside it.

Data and provenance

The data are the NASA Exoplanet Archive Planetary Systems Composite Parameters table [1], retrieved on 31 October 2026 through the archive's TAP serviceDefinition: TAP service astronomical data services The Table Access Protocol of the International Virtual Observatory Alliance, the standard query interface through which astronomical archives return table rows. Excludes any selection or cleaning of the rows, which the query itself sets. full definition. TAP, the Table Access Protocol set by the International Virtual Observatory Alliance, is the standard query interface of astronomical archives; it fetches rows and applies no selection of its own. A system qualified with at least four listed planets that have orbital periods and a controversy flagDefinition: controversy flag NASA Exoplanet Archive catalogue fields A catalogue field set to 1 when a planet's existence or confirmation has been questioned in the published literature and 0 otherwise. Excludes independent confirmation, which a flag of 0 does not give. full definition of zero. The archive sets that flag to 1 when a planet's existence has been questioned in the published literature, so 0 means no published dispute, which is weaker than independent confirmation. This gave 122 systems and 543 planets. The archive is public and places no restriction on use.

Two selection effects shape the sample. TransitDefinition: transit survey observational astronomy A search that finds planets by the small dip in a star's light as a planet crosses its disc, which favours short periods and orbits seen close to edge-on. Excludes planets found only by other methods, such as radial velocity or direct imaging. full definition surveys find short periods and planets whose orbits are close to edge-on, so long periods and tilted planets are missing, and the gaps we see are partly survey-shaped. A transit survey, in observational astronomy, finds a planet by the dip in starlight as it crosses its star's disc; planets found only by other methods, such as radial velocity, are outside that term. Multi-planet entries in the catalogue are also a selected set. The order-shuffle control keeps both effects, because it uses the same gaps from the same systems. That is why it is the fair control for a claim about order.

Methods

The three forms

For a system with planets sorted by period, let Pn be the period of the nth planet. The plain form is log-linear in the index:

ln⁡Pn=a+bn(1)

The Blagg-Richardson style form adds an offset period P0, a three-parameter form in period:

ln⁡(Pn−P0)=a+bn(2)

The gapped form, in the style of Bovaird and Lineweaver, replaces the index by integers kn that may skip up to two places, so that up to two unseen planets can be inserted wherever they lower the residual:

ln⁡Pn=a+bkn(3)

All three forms were written from the published descriptions as remembered, not copied from the papers. Blagg's own formula has a periodic correction term that eq. 2 does not carry. The result is therefore about these three versions.

The regularity score

For system s, let σs be the root mean square residualDefinition: root mean square residual statistics The square root of the mean squared difference between fitted and observed log period across a system's planets, a measure of scatter about the fit. Excludes any offset or trend the fit has already absorbed into its parameters. full definition of the fit in ln⁡P, and gs the mean gap in ln⁡P between neighbouring planets. The per-system statistic divides one by the other, so that systems with wide and narrow spacing are compared on one scale. The residual term is from statistics: the square root of the mean squared difference between fitted and observed ln⁡P, a measure of scatter about the fit that leaves out any offset the fit has already absorbed:

rs=σsgs(4)

The sample score S is minus the median of rs over the systems, so a higher score means more regular. Each form has its own score.

Prediction by leave-one-out

For each interior planet j, the planet is dropped, the plain form is fitted to the rest, and the fitted ln⁡Pj is compared with the true value. The baseline predicts ln⁡Pj as the mean of its two neighbours' ln⁡P, which is the geometric meanDefinition: geometric mean statistics For two numbers, the square root of their product, which is the plain average taken on a log scale. Here the neighbour baseline for a dropped planet's period. Excludes the ordinary average of the two periods, which is larger whenever they differ. full definition of their periods. The geometric mean of two numbers is the square root of their product, the plain average taken on a log scale; it is smaller than the ordinary average whenever the two differ. The ratio of median absolute errors is

L=MfitMnb(5)

where Mfit is the median error of the fit and Mnb that of the neighbour baseline. A ratio above 1 means the neighbours win.

Controls

The order-shuffle control keeps each system's set of gaps in ln⁡P and puts them in a random order, then rebuilds the periods from the innermost planet. The pooled-gap control rebuilds each system from gaps drawn at random from all systems' gaps. Each control is scored with the same form and the same freedom as the real data; for the gapped form that includes the inserted planets. The plain form's controls ran 2,000 draws each and the other two forms' order controls ran 200 each.

The p valueDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition reported for each comparison is the share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, counted with one added to both the numerator and the denominator. It is a p value from draws, as in permutation statistics, and assumes no textbook distribution:

p=k+1n+1(6)

where k is the number of draws at or above the real score and n the number of draws. This is why the smallest possible value at 2,000 draws is 0.0005.

Controls and planted checks

The instrument was checked on planted systems before the real data were read. Planted systems have exactly log-linear periods with 5 percent jitter and the same numbers of planets as the real systems. They scored -0.050 against the pooled-gap control's 95th percentile of -0.190, so the score sees regularity when it is there.c3 The void condition did not fire.

The two controls ask different questions, and they are read in that order. Beating the pooled-gap control says the gaps inside a system resemble each other more than gaps drawn from other systems. Beating the order-shuffle control would say the order of those gaps is regular as well. Only the second is a claim about a sequence.

Results

Table 1 gives the score of each form against its controls, and Figure 2 draws the same numbers. The plain form scores -0.157. The real systems are far more regular than systems built from pooled gaps. They are not more regular than their own gaps in a shuffled order: the real score sits inside the order-shuffle range for the plain and gapped forms and below it for the Blagg-Richardson style form (-0.141 against a 5th to 95th percentile range of -0.134 to -0.116).

The Blagg-Richardson style form scores below the 5th percentile of its own order shuffles, and the gapped form sits at its mean.c4 The extra freedom in those forms fits shuffled systems as well as real ones.

When an interior planet is dropped, the geometric mean of its two neighbours predicts its period better than the rule does: median error 0.107 against 0.131 in log period, a ratio of 1.23.c2 Figure 3 shows the two errors.

The Solar System was scored beside the test and is not part of it. It has r of 0.32 on the plain form and 0.17 on the gapped form, against a catalogue median of 0.157 on the plain form. On this statistic the median exoplanet system is more regular than ours.

Table 2 sets the forecasts written before the run against the outcomes.

Discussion

Hayes and Tremaine [4] argued that a Titius-Bode law is what stable spacing looks like. Our result is a direct check of one consequence of that view on exoplanets. If the rule only describes similar gaps, then a system with its gaps shuffled should fit as well as the real one. It does, for three forms.

The prediction test points the same way. A rule that captured a law of sequence should predict a missing planet better than a local average of its neighbours, because it uses the whole system. It predicts worse. Local spacing carries the information, which fits the correlated period ratios of neighbouring planets reported by Weiss and colleagues [8].

This bears on the prediction debate between Bovaird and Lineweaver [5] [7] and Huang and Bakos [6] in one way. A predicted planet in a gap is a claim that the gaps should be more equal than they look. That claim can be useful as a search target. It does not need a law of sequence, and it should be weighed against the neighbour baseline rather than against no prediction at all.

Limitations

  • The three forms were written from memory of the published ones, and a later review of our own ledger flagged that. A published form that differs could score differently, so the result covers these three versions only. Blagg's formula with its periodic term was not tested.
  • Transit surveys miss long periods and tilted planets, so the gaps are survey-shaped. The order shuffle keeps that effect, which is why it is the fair control, but the pooled-gap result is partly a survey result.
  • The catalogue's multi-planet entries are a selected set, and the sample is 122 systems, short of the 150 we forecast.
  • The 200-draw controls for the two richer forms give coarse p values.
  • The finding says nothing about the physics that sets spacing.
  • Scoring was done by our own code and was not blind.
  • The order-shuffle test cannot be passed by an exact geometric law. A system whose log gaps are all equal is unchanged by shuffling them, so the law-like verdict tests only whether unequal gaps come in an ordered sequence. An exact Titius-Bode spacing would show up here as regularity in gap sizes, which the pooled-gap control did detect.

Evidence

Mixed. The spacing signal is real: the systems beat gaps pooled from the whole catalogue (p 0.0005). The order and law-like verdicts are null: against each system's own gaps put in a new order none of the three forms scored above the shuffled range (p 0.85, 0.995 and 0.68).

Figures

These are the paper's own figures, numbered as in the PDF, and each "Figure" reference in the text points here. The charts on this page redraw the same results from the result files and carry their own numbers.

What this means for a reader

If a paper reports a near-perfect stress classifier, look for how it split the data. When neighbouring windows share most of their samples and land on both sides of a random split, the model can score perfectly by recognising the recording, with no stress signal at all. In our test that happened exactly. On the real data the classifier did hold for new people, which is good news for this one laboratory protocol, but only a split that holds out whole people could show it.

Objection

Fifteen people, one laboratory, one protocol, about one hour each. A held-out person is a stranger only inside this sample.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Wearable stress detectors are often scored by cutting recordings into overlapping windows and splitting the windows at random into training and test sets. We tested what that split measures. On planted data built on the same windows and timing as the WESAD recordings, where each person and each condition block carries its own random offsets and nothing carries from one person to the next, a random split over windows scored an AUC of 1.000 and a held-out-person split scored 0.469.c1 On the real chest recordings of 15 people (2,122 windows of 60 s, 30 percent of them stress), the random forest held across people at a held-out-person AUC of 0.966, against 1.000 under the random split.c2 The random split inflated the AUC by 0.033 for the random forest and 0.086 for logistic regression.c3 ECG, EDA and skin temperature together reached 0.97 for a held-out person, and acceleration with EMG reached 0.79.c4 Across the 15 people, the rise in reported anxiety did not follow the size of the bodily change: Spearman rho 0.03 with EDA, 0.02 with heart rate and -0.45 with breathing rate (p 0.09).c5 The first run failed its own planted check because we set its bar at 0.90, within 0.012 of the best score that planted shift allows; a second preregistered run repaired the plant and passed.
