Introduction

WESAD, the Wearable Stress and Affect Detection dataset of Schmidt and colleagues [1], records 15 people with a chest sensor and a wrist sensor during a baseline, amusing film clips and the Trier Social Stress TestDefinition: Trier Social Stress Test psychology and psychoneuroendocrinology A laboratory stressor in which a person prepares and gives a short public talk and then does mental arithmetic aloud in front of an evaluating panel. Excludes daily stress, chronic stress and trauma. full definition, in which a person gives a short public talk and then does mental arithmetic aloud before an evaluating panel. The dataset paper reports classifiers scored with every person held out in turn, and WESAD has since become a common benchmark.

Many later studies score their models with a random split over windowsDefinition: random split over windows machine learning evaluation; called record-wise cross-validation in the clinical literature Assigning windows to training and test sets at random, so that windows from the same person and the same recording block fall on both sides. Excludes any split that keeps all of one person's data on one side. full definition: the windows are assigned to training and test sets at random, so windows from the same person and the same recording block fall on both sides. The windows are usually overlapping windowsDefinition: overlapping windows signal processing Fixed-length stretches cut from a recording at a step shorter than their length, so that neighbouring windows share samples. Here 60 s windows every 15 s share 75 percent of their samples. Excludes windows cut end to end with no shared samples. full definition, fixed-length stretches cut at a step shorter than their length. Here a 60 s window is cut every 15 s, so neighbours share 75 percent of their samples.

The clinical machine-learning literature has argued over this choice. Saeb and colleagues [2] showed on wearable and phone sensor data that record-wise and subject-wise cross-validation can give very different error rates, and traced the gap to the classifier learning to recognise people. Little and colleagues [3] replied that subject-wise splits can also mislead in some settings. Chaibub Neto and colleagues [4] built a permutation test for identity confounding and, on mobile health data, found strong evidence of it under record-wise splits. Our searches on 9 November 2026 also returned recent WESAD studies and open audits that make the same point about random splits; we read those at the level of search summaries and do not cite their numbers.

This paper adds a known answer. We build data in which nothing can carry from one person to another, run it through the same windows, features and models as the real data, and measure what the random split reports. Then we ask three questions of the real data: whether the classifier holds for a person it has not seen, which sensors carry the signal, and whether the size of a person's bodily response follows the size of the stress they report. On the last question, Campbell and Ehlert [5] reviewed acute psychosocial stress studies and asked whether emotional and physiological responses correspond.

Preregistration and design

The design was written as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, a dated plan fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen, on 31 October 2026 at 22:37 UTC. Window features were extracted and fixed before any label was compared with them. The decision it informs was stated in the file: how much to discount a wearable stress classifier reported under a within-person random split, and whether its label reads stress or a protocol.

The locked file names the data, the windows and features, four splits, two models, the sensor groups, the felt-stress test, a planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition (data built so the right answer is known, run before the real data), a controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition (a version of the data with the structure under test removed), forecasts and kill conditionsDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition, rules that decide against the claim with no room for judgement after the run.

Kill conditions, without discretion:

  • If the planted data with nothing to learn fail (random split under 0.8 or held-out person above 0.6), or if the planted data with a real shared shift score under 0.9 for a held-out person, the instrument gets no claim.
  • A leakage claim requires the random forest's random-split AUC to exceed its held-out-person AUC by at least 0.02.

The first run met the second part of the first rule: the planted shift scored 0.824 against a bar of 0.90. By its own rule that run was voidDefinition: void research method (our usage) The verdict of a run whose planted check failed or whose sample fell below its stated minimum. It says nothing for or against the claim. Excludes a null result, which comes from a working instrument. full definition, a verdict that says nothing for or against the claim. A calculation after the run showed the bar left almost no room: for the planted shift of 2 the best possible AUC is about 0.91 (section Methods). A second preregistration, locked at 22:39 UTC the same evening, kept the real-data handling unchanged, tested planted shifts of 2, 3 and 4 on a fresh seed, and required the shift of 4 to reach 0.90 for a held-out person. If it passed, the first run's real-data results were to be credited. It passed. The second plan was written after the first run's results were seen, and its forecasts for the real data copy the first run's values; we report it as a repair, not as a blind test.

Data and provenance

The data are WESAD [1], obtained from the authors' page at the University of Siegen; the UCI repository record (doi:10.24432/C57K5T) points to that page. The terms allow scientific, non-commercial use with credit to the dataset's owners. This paper reports statistics only. Subjects are pseudonymous (S2 to S17; there is no S1 or S12); no attempt was made to identify anyone.

We used the chest device only, recorded at 700 Hz, read from the text files: ECG, EDA, EMG, skin temperature, three-axis acceleration and respiration. The pickled files were not opened. Condition times and the questionnaire answers came from each person's questionnaire file. The task was the binary one of the dataset paper: stress (the Trier test) against baseline and amusement. Windows of 60 s were cut every 15 s inside each condition. Windows with any missing feature were dropped, leaving 2,122 windows from 15 people, 30 percent of them stress.

Electrodermal activity (EDA)Definition: electrodermal activity (EDA) psychophysiology The electrical conductance of the skin, which rises with sweat gland activity under sympathetic nervous control. Excludes a direct reading of emotion; temperature and movement also change it. full definition, used throughout, is the electrical conductance of the skin, which rises with sweat gland activity under sympathetic control.

Methods

Features

Twenty features in six groups were computed per window. ECG: heart rate, the standard deviation of beat intervals, the root mean square of successive interval differences, and the ratio of the two as a rough balance measure. EDA: mean, standard deviation, slope and the count of skin conductance responses. Temperature: mean and slope. Respiration: breath count, amplitude and standard deviation. Acceleration: mean magnitude, its standard deviation and the mean of each axis. EMG: root mean square and 90th percentile of the rectified signal.

Models and score

Two classifiers were scored. A random forestDefinition: random forest machine learning A classifier that averages many decision trees, each grown on a resampled copy of the training data with a random subset of features tried at each split. Here 100 trees with at least 3 windows per leaf. Excludes any model tuned on the test person. full definition averages 100 decision trees grown on resampled data with at least 3 windows per leaf. Logistic regressionDefinition: logistic regression statistics A classifier that models the log odds of the positive class as a weighted sum of the features. Here on standardised features with an L2 (ridge) penalty at strength C = 1. Excludes interactions between features, which it does not model unless they are added by hand. full definition models the log odds of stress as a weighted sum of standardised features. The score is the AUCDefinition: AUC (area under the ROC curve) statistics and machine learning The probability that a classifier gives a randomly chosen positive case a higher score than a randomly chosen negative case. 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect separation. Excludes accuracy at one threshold, and any statement about how well the scores are calibrated as probabilities. full definition, the probability that a randomly chosen stress window gets a higher score than a randomly chosen non-stress window. With ranks ri of the scores, n1 stress windows and n0 others,

A=R1−n1(n1+1)/2n1n0(1)

where R1 is the sum of the stress windows' ranks. AUC is reported two ways: global, over all held-out windows pooled, and within-person AUCDefinition: within-person AUC machine learning evaluation, our usage The AUC computed on one held-out person's windows alone, then averaged over people. It asks whether the classifier ranks that person's stress windows above their other windows. Excludes the global AUC, which pools all held-out windows and also rewards separating people from each other. full definition, computed on each person's windows and then averaged over people.

Splits

  • Random split over windows: five folds assigned at random to windows.
  • Time blocks within a person: in each person's condition block, windows before the block's middle train and windows after it test, with a guard of 37.5 s on each side of the middle so that no test window overlaps a training window.
  • Held-out personDefinition: held-out person (leave one subject out) machine learning evaluation; called subject-wise cross-validation Training on all people but one and scoring on the one left out, repeated so that each person is held out once. Excludes a test on people from another study, lab or protocol. full definition: train on 14 people, score the fifteenth, once for each person.
  • Held-out person with each person's features scaled to that person's own baseline mean and standard deviation.

The leakage gap is the difference between the random-split and held-out-person global AUCs:

G=Arand−Aloso(2)

Planted data

The planted data keep the real windows' people, conditions and timing and replace the features. For window w of person s in condition block c, feature f is

xwf=0.3ϵwf+uscf+dyw(3)

where ϵwf and uscf are independent standard normal draws, the second shared by every window of one person's block, yw is 1 for a stress window and 0 otherwise, and d is a planted shared shiftDefinition: planted shared shift research method, our usage A fixed amount added to one feature in every stress window of every person in planted data, in the same direction for all, so that a classifier tested on a new person has something real to find. Excludes the per-person, per-block offsets, which point in a random direction and carry nothing from one person to the next. full definition added to the first feature only. With d=0 each block has its own offsets in a random direction and nothing carries from one person to the next; a held-out person should score near 0.5. With d>0 a held-out person has something real to find.

For one feature, the stress and non-stress values each have variance 1+0.32=1.09, so the ceiling AUC for a shiftDefinition: ceiling AUC for a shift statistics, our derivation The AUC a perfect reader of the one shifted feature could reach when the stress and non-stress values of that feature are normal with a variance of 1.09 each (a block offset of variance 1 plus window noise of variance 0.09). Excludes the effect of the 19 features that carry no shift, and of the small number of people. full definition is

C(d)=N(d2·1.09)(4)

where N is the standard normal cumulative distribution. At d=2 this gives 0.912, which is why a bar of 0.90 left no room.

Sensor groups

Each sensor group, physiology without motion or breath (ECG, EDA and temperature) and motion alone (acceleration and EMG) were scored by held-out-person within-person AUC with the random forest. Whether each of the six single groups beats chance was tested with logistic regression against 100 block permutations, in which each person's stress label is moved to one of their condition blocks chosen at random, so block structure and the share of stress windows stay. The p value counts permutations at or above the real score, with one added to both counts:

p=k+1n+1(5)

The six p values were adjusted with the Benjamini-Hochberg correctionDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics, multiple testing A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false discoveries stays at or below a chosen level q. Excludes control of the chance of even one false discovery, which is a stricter rule. full definition, which keeps the expected share of false discoveries among the tests called significant at or below q 0.05. For p values sorted in increasing order, the ith of m is scaled to mp(i)/i, and each adjusted value is the smallest scaled value at or after its place in the order.

Felt stress

For each person, the change in the six-item STAIDefinition: STAI, six-item form psychology A short form of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory in which a person rates six statements about how they feel at that moment. Positive items are reverse scored so that a higher total means more anxiety. Excludes a clinical diagnosis, and anxiety as a lasting trait. full definition total, a short state-anxiety questionnaire in which positive items are reverse scored, was taken from baseline to stress. The same person's change in mean EDA, heart rate and breath count from baseline windows to stress windows was compared with it across the 15 people by Spearman rhoDefinition: Spearman rho statistics The correlation between the ranks of two quantities. It runs from -1 to 1 and measures how well one quantity's order follows the other's, whatever the shape of the relation. Excludes the size of the change, and any causal direction. full definition, the correlation of ranks.

Interval on the within-person mean

The second run reports a 95% intervalDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition on the mean within-person AUC by bootstrap by personDefinition: bootstrap by person statistics, resampling Redrawing people with replacement, 2,000 times, and recomputing the mean of the per-person scores each time. The middle 95 percent of those means is the interval. Excludes redrawing single windows, which would treat one person's many windows as many independent people. full definition: people are redrawn with replacement 2,000 times and the mean is recomputed each time.

Controls and planted checks

Planted data with nothing to learn (d=0) were run in both runs. The random split read 1.000 (first run, 0.99999 before rounding) and 1.000 (second run). The held-out-person split read 0.469 and 0.391. Both passed their rules.

The planted shift failed in the first run, at 0.824 against the bar of 0.90 for d=2. In the second run, on a fresh seed, the forest reached 0.692 at d=2 (ceiling 0.912), 0.987 at d=3 (ceiling 0.979) and 0.994 at d=4 (ceiling 0.997). The rule on the shift of 4 passed. The value at d=3 sits 0.008 above its computed ceiling; the ceiling counts one feature and two normal distributions, and we did not trace the difference. The two runs at d=2 differ by 0.13, so this planted check is noisy at small shifts.

The block-shuffle control moves each person's stress label onto one of their own condition blocks at random and scores logistic regression on held-out people. Over 100 draws in the first run it gave a mean of 0.487 and a 95th percentile of 0.656 (p from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition 0.0099); over 40 draws in the second it gave 0.472 and 0.594 (p 0.024). The real logistic score of 0.896 clears both. This control's 95th percentile marks the top of its null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition, the spread of scores the control gives over random draws.

Results

What the random split reports

A random split over windows scored an AUC of 1.000 and a held-out-person split scored 0.469.c1 That is the planted data with nothing to learn, in the first run. The random forest separated stress from non-stress windows perfectly by recognising each block's offsets in windows it had already seen. Figure 1 sets these planted values beside the real ones.

The real recordings

Table 1 gives both models under the four splits. The random forest held across people at a held-out-person AUC of 0.966, against 1.000 under the random split.c2 The second run, on a new seed, gave 0.999 and 0.966. The random split inflated the AUC by 0.033 for the random forest and 0.086 for logistic regression.c3 Scaling each person to their own baseline brought the logistic score from 0.896 to 0.971 and left the forest at 0.964.

The mean within-person AUC for a held-out person was 0.979, with a 95% interval of 0.961 to 0.994 by bootstrap over people. The worst person under the forest read 0.912 (S2); under logistic regression the worst read 0.646 (S15). Figure 2 shows every person and the planted-shift check.

Which sensors carry it

By sensor group, held-out person, random forest, the within-person AUCs were ECG 0.92, EDA 0.89, respiration 0.85, acceleration 0.82, temperature 0.60 and EMG 0.45 (Figure 3). In the logistic permutation test five groups passed the correction at q 0.012 each; EMG did not (q 0.33). ECG, EDA and skin temperature together reached 0.97 for a held-out person, and acceleration with EMG reached 0.79.c4 The Trier test has people stand and speak, so posture and breath move with the label. The classifier does not need them: physiology without motion or breath carries more than motion does.

What this means for a reader

Most people given a free, safe chance to lie for money do not take all of it. Close to half report what they saw, about a quarter claim the top number and the rest shade upward partway. A model in which lying has a fixed cost, one in which people care about looking honest, one in which they follow what others do, and a plain payoff model with enough noise all reproduce those reports almost equally well. To learn which motive is at work, you need experiments designed to pull the motives apart. The distribution of reports alone is not enough.

Objection

The planted check failed, so the near-tie says nothing about which model is true, and the model ranking in Table 1 is not a result.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

In a private die or coin task a person sees a random outcome alone and is paid by the number they report, so a lie pays and cannot be caught. Payoff maximisation says everyone should claim the top outcome. We used the open meta-study data of Abeler, Nosenzo and Raymond: 252 first-round treatments from 58 papers with 27,039 subjects, split by paper so that 19 papers with 9,960 subjects were held out. On held-out tasks with three or more outcomes, reports read as 45 percent honest, 26 percent maximal and 29 percent partial.c1 Six preference models were fitted on the other papers and scored on the held-out ones. All six sit within 0.005 nats per report of each other, and no contrast against the fixed-cost model passes the false-discovery correction.c2 The planted check failed: on data simulated from the reputation model, the reputation model lost to the fixed-cost model by 0.0003 nats per report.c3 By the preregistered rule, no ranking among the models counts. Our subset's mean standardised report was 0.287 against the 0.234 published for the full data, outside the preregistered tolerance of 0.03.c4 The departure from strict self-interest is large; the mechanism behind it is not identified by report distributions.

Introduction

Fischbacher and Föllmi-Heusi [3] made the private reporting taskDefinition: private reporting task (die-under-the-cup) experimental economics and psychology An experiment in which a person observes a random outcome in private, such as a die roll or coin toss, reports it, and is paid by the report, so a lie pays and cannot be caught for any one person. Lying shows only in the distribution of many reports. Excludes tasks where the experimenter can see each person's true outcome. full definition a standard tool. Subjects rolled a die under a cup, reported the number, and were paid by it. No single lie could be detected, and the honest distribution is known, so lying shows in the reports as a whole. They found many fully honest subjects, a smaller group who lied to the maximum, and a large group of partial liars who lied but did not claim the top payoff, which they read as a wish to keep a favourable self-image.

Gächter and Schulz [4] ran the die task in 23 countries and related intrinsic honesty to a national index of the prevalence of rule violations built from corruption, tax evasion and political fraud. They found more honest reporting in subject pools from countries with fewer violations.

Abeler, Nosenzo and Raymond [1] combined data from 90 studies across economics, psychology and sociology and found that people lie surprisingly little. They derived predictions that separate the leading models, tested them with new experiments, and concluded that a preference for being honest together with a preference for being seen as honest best explains the behaviour. They published their data [2].

This paper asks a narrower question of that public data. Without the designed treatments that Abeler and colleagues used to separate the models, can the plain report distributions of ordinary first-round tasks tell the models apart on papers the models have not seen? And what share of reports look honest, maximal or partial?

Preregistration and design

The design was written as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition and hash-locked on 31 October 2026 at 22:02 UTC, before any model was fitted. Two things were seen first, and both are stated in the locked file. The publishers' site gives a mean standardised report of 0.234. Our parsing step printed pooled report distributions over all 252 treatments, held-out ones included, and printed a mean standardised report of 0.287. The forecasts of report shares are therefore not blind to the pooled shape.

The locked file names the data and its filters, the six models and two baselines, the score, the paper-level tests, the three-part reading, the planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition, a reproduction check, a controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition, the forecasts and the kill conditionsDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition. Its assumptions are listed in it: true outcomes are uniform; upward lies come from preference only and downward lies only from mistakes; one population spans countries and subject pools; only first rounds are used; and the norm model has no measured norm input. Nothing was added after the run.

Kill conditions, without discretion:

  • If the planted check fails, no model comparison counts.
  • If the best theory's gain over everyone-honest is not above the shuffle control's 95th percentile, the theories carry nothing beyond chance.

Reproduction check: the mean standardised report over the by-treatment set must lie within 0.03 of 0.234.

Data and provenance

The data are the merged meta-study file and the data-and-programs archive published by Abeler, Nosenzo and Raymond [2] on their resources page and on figshare (files 16211150 and 16211414), downloaded on 31 October 2026. The site states that all its data are released under the CC BY licence, with credit and a link back. The files were read as data; no program in the archive was run. The publishers' site describes the full set as 429 treatments from 90 papers with over 44,000 participants in 47 countries.

A parsing step kept first-round reports from tasks with uniform true outcomes and 2, 3, 6 or 10 possible outcomes. It removed treatments coded in the data as internal lying or as having a victim, treatments that asked subjects about the report distribution, and treatments that told subjects what others reported. That left 252 treatments from 58 papers with 27,039 subjects. Papers were split by a hash of the citation, with 30 percent held out: the held-out papersDefinition: held-out papers statistics, cross-validation Papers kept out of all fitting, chosen by a hash of the citation (30 percent of papers), on which every model is scored once. All treatments from one paper fall on the same side. Excludes a split by treatment or subject, which would let one paper's design appear in both fitting and scoring. full definition were 19 papers with 9,960 subjects, and fitting used 17,079 subjects.

As a check on the parsing, the baseline treatment of Fischbacher and Föllmi-Heusi in our file has counts of 38, 44, 64, 76, 171 and 219 from the lowest to the top payoff. Our results summary records the top report at 36 percent, where honest reporting gives 17.

Methods

Models

Let a task have K outcomes, ranked by payoff, with πr the rank of report r scaled from 0 for the lowest to 1 for the highest. A person who saw outcome s and reports r receives the scaled payoff times a stakes factor

S=(G/5)1−ϵ(1)

where G is the money at stake in the treatment in purchasing-power dollars and ϵ is the stakes elasticityDefinition: stakes elasticity behavioural economics, our parametrisation The parameter epsilon in a stakes factor (G/5) to the power 1 minus epsilon, where G is the money at stake. At epsilon 1 the size of the payment has no effect on reports, and at 0 the pull to lie grows in proportion to the payment. Excludes the effect of payment on whether people take part. full definition. Each person also carries a lying cost c, drawn from a lognormal distribution, ln⁡c=μ+σz with z standard normal, evaluated on a grid of 25 quantiles. Each person picks the report with the highest utility

U=Sπr−car−c(dr)γ+ρcRr(2)

where ar is 1 when r differs from s and 0 otherwise, dr is the payoff distance |πr−πs|, and Rr is the chance that a person making report r is honest. Each model keeps some of these terms:

  • Fixed cost: the first cost term only. A person either reports honestly or claims the top.
  • Size cost: the second cost term only, so the cost grows with the size of the lie.
  • Reputation: the fixed cost plus the value ρ on looking honest. Because Rr depends on everyone's reports, it is solved as a fixed pointDefinition: fixed point (reputation model) game theory A report distribution that, when used to compute how honest each report looks, leads people to make the same distribution of reports. Found here by repeated damped updates starting from honest reporting. Excludes a guarantee that the fixed point found is the only one. full definition by 25 damped updates from honest reporting.
  • Norm: the fixed cost scaled by 1−λL, where L is the share of others who lie, iterated from no lying, which finds the low-lying equilibrium.
  • Full: reputation plus the size cost.

A trembleDefinition: tremble game theory and behavioural economics A parameter that mixes a share of uniformly random reports into a model's prediction, standing for mistakes and inattention. In these models it is the only source of downward lies. Excludes a preference, since the tremble does not depend on payoffs. full definition τ mixes in uniform reports, so a model's prediction for report r is qr=(1−τ)mr+τ/K, with mr the share of the cost grid choosing r. The payoff model has no cost and no tremble. It is a logit choice on money alone with one scale parameter β:

qr=eβGπr∑jeβGπj(3)

Two baselines frame the models: everyone honest, which predicts uniform reports, and the training-average baselineDefinition: training-average baseline forecast verification, where it is called climatology A forecast that gives each held-out treatment the average report distribution of training treatments with the same number of outcomes. Excludes any theory of why people report as they do. full definition. Every model was fitted by maximum likelihoodDefinition: maximum likelihood statistics Fitting a model's parameters by choosing the values that make the observed data most probable under the model. Excludes choosing parameters by hand or by fit to the test data. full definition on the training papers.

Score

Models are scored by log lossDefinition: log loss (nats per report) statistics and forecast verification Minus the average natural log of the probability a model gave to each report that was made. Lower is better, and the difference between two models in nats per report is how much better one predicts each report. Excludes an accuracy count, which ignores how much probability a model gave to what happened. full definition over the N held-out subjects, with ntr the count of report r in treatment t:

ℓ=−1N∑t∑rntrln⁡qtr(4)

A model's gain is the everyone-honest loss minus its own. Each theory model is compared with the fixed-cost model by a paper-level sign permutation testDefinition: paper-level sign permutation test statistics A test that sums each held-out paper's difference in log loss between two models, then flips the sign of each paper's difference at random 5,000 times to see how often a sum as large arises with no true difference. Excludes a test that treats subjects within one paper as independent. full definition, the p values adjusted together by the Benjamini-Hochberg correctionDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics, multiple testing A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call. full definition. The reputation and full models' differences from fixed cost also get a 95% intervalDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition from a paper bootstrapDefinition: paper bootstrap statistics An interval made by recomputing a statistic 2,000 times on held-out papers drawn with replacement, so subjects from one paper stay together. Excludes resampling single subjects as if they were independent. full definition.

Shares of honest, maximal and partial reports

For each task size of 3, 6 or 10, reports are pooled and given a three-part readingDefinition: three-part reading experimental economics, after Fischbacher and Föllmi-Heusi A split of a report distribution into honest reporters, read as the number of outcomes times the share reporting the lowest outcome, maximal liars, the excess at the top over the honest share, and partial liars, the rest. Excludes an observation of any person's lie; it assumes the true outcomes are uniform and that no one lies downward on purpose. full definition. With q1 the share reporting the lowest outcome and qK the share reporting the top,

h=Kq1(5)
m=qK−hK(6)

with h capped at 1, and the partial share is 1−h−m. The three task sizes are combined weighted by subjects. Two-outcome tasks are left out, since they have no partial lie.

Standardised report

For the reproduction check each report is mapped to xr=−1+2(r−1)/(K−1), and the standardised reportDefinition: standardised report experimental economics; the measure Abeler, Nosenzo and Raymond report, computed here by our own code The mean report of a treatment after the outcomes are mapped evenly onto -1 for the lowest-paying report and +1 for the highest, so honest reporting gives 0 in expectation and everyone claiming the top gives 1. Here averaged over treatments without weights. Excludes a share of liars, which the mean alone does not give. full definition is averaged over the T treatments without weights:

M=1T∑t∑rntrntxr(7)

Controls and planted checks

The planted check simulated report counts from the reputation model at known parameters on the same treatments, kept the same split by paper, fitted the fixed-cost, size-cost and reputation models to the simulated training papers and scored them on the simulated held-out papers. The reputation model had to beat both. The planted check failed: on data simulated from the reputation model, the reputation model lost to the fixed-cost model by 0.0003 nats per report.c3 It beat the size-cost model by 0.0005. The fitted reputation parameters also missed the planted ones: the log of the value on looking honest, ρ, was planted at 0.2 and fitted at -0.56. The method cannot recover a known model at this sample size, so by the kill condition no ranking of the real models counts.

The shuffle control permuted report labels within each held-out treatment, and the best model's gain over everyone-honest was recomputed 300 times to give a null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition. Its 95th percentile was -0.086 (mean -0.112). The real best gain of 0.072 lies far above it (p from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition 0.003). The theories carry information beyond chance, and this kill condition did not fire.

The reproduction check failed. Our subset's mean standardised report was 0.287 against the 0.234 published for the full data, outside the preregistered tolerance of 0.03.c4 The two numbers come from different sets: ours uses first rounds only and drops several designs. Our filtered subset does not reproduce the publishers' headline figure, and the 0.287 was printed before the lock, so the outcome of this check was knowable when the plan was written.

Results

Table 1 and Figure 1 give the held-out losses. Every model beats everyone-honest by about 0.07 nats per report. All six sit within 0.005 nats per report of each other, and no contrast against the fixed-cost model passes the false-discovery correction.c2 The reputation model's edge over fixed cost was 0.003 (95% interval -0.001 to 0.008, p 0.40), and the full model's 0.002 (-0.008 to 0.012, p 0.75). The training-average baseline, which has no theory in it, scored the same as the norm model to four places.

The payoff model was forecast to do worse than honest reporting. With its logit noise it did better, by 0.071 nats per report, and finished second. A model with no lying cost at all fits these reports almost as well as the cost models.

The fitted stakes elasticities were 0.89 to 0.96 across the five cost models, so the size of the payment hardly moved reports in these data.

On held-out tasks with three or more outcomes, reports read as 45 percent honest, 26 percent maximal and 29 percent partial.c1 The training papers gave 42, 24 and 34 percent. Table 2 and Figure 2 set those against the shares each fitted model predicts for the held-out tasks.

One held-out paper carries the full model's small edge. In Effron and colleagues' 2015 study (2,151 subjects), the full model beat fixed cost by 0.021 nats per report; without that paper, the full model's edge over fixed cost becomes -0.003. Across the 23 subject pools of Gächter and Schulz [4] in the data, the mean standardised report ranged from 0.18 to 0.58 (standard deviation 0.10).

Two sensitivity refits, scored on matching held-out subsets, are in Table 3. The fixed-cost model scored best of the three theories refitted in both. Among students the training average beat every theory; in the general population it lost to all three. The refit without hand-coded treatments was not run, because too few treatments remained.

Table 4 sets the forecasts written before the run against the outcomes.

Discussion

The departure from strict payoffs is the part that holds. Payoff maximisation predicts that every report is the top one; held-out reports show a top share of about a quarter beyond the honest share and a large honest share, consistent with what Fischbacher and Föllmi-Heusi [3] and Abeler and colleagues [1] report. The reading of those shares rests on the uniform-truth assumption and on there being no deliberate downward lies.

The mechanism is not identified here. Six models built on different motives, and a training average with no motive at all, predict held-out reports to within 0.005 nats per report. The planted check places part of the problem in

What this means for a reader

When a forecaster, a panel or a software system has to choose which answers to withhold, the number it already states is a much better guide than how expert it says it is. In a large public forecasting tournament, a filter on the stated probability cut the error of kept forecasts about six times as much as a filter on self-rated expertise, and the self-rating added nothing a shuffled rating did not also add. People who answer selectively are better forecasters on average, so a habit of skipping marks a careful source. The data does not show that skipping a question makes the remaining answers better.

Objection

Inferred skips may be questions a forecaster never saw; matched strata may explain any difference in sign from Merkle and colleagues, whose sign we have not confirmed; a filter on stated probability rewards confidence by construction.

What would change the call. Replicate on another tournament where question exposure is visible; read Merkle and colleagues in full.

From the strongest objection recorded in our publication register.

Abstract

A source that may decline to answer needs a rule for which answers to hold back. We tested two candidate inputs for that rule on the public survey forecasts of the Good Judgment Project: the probability the forecaster stated, and the forecaster's own 1 to 5 rating of their expertise on that forecast. On 410,451 binary forecasts, filters were scored by the area under the risk-coverage curve, the mean Brier score of kept forecasts as coverage falls from 100 to 10 percent. A filter on the stated probability scored 0.171, a filter on the self-rating 0.259, and random order 0.277.c1 Adding the self-rating to the probability gained 0.0026 (95 percent interval 0.0007 to 0.0046), under the preregistered bar of 0.005, and a rating shuffled within each forecaster-year gained 0.0024 on average.c2 We also asked whether people who skip questions forecast better. On first forecasts only, skip rate correlated with better relative Brier score at rho +0.286 (+0.264 to +0.303) across 9,204 forecaster-years, and +0.195 (+0.174 to +0.212) when timing was matched as well.c3 Within the same person across consecutive years the correlation was +0.041 (-0.007 to +0.095) over 1,578 pairs, so no within-person benefit of skipping was shown.c4 Forecasts rated expertise 1 are pulled toward 50 percent by about the right amount: the best extremising factor was 0.92 (0.79 to 1.06).c5

Introduction and motivation

The Good Judgment Project ran from 2011 to 2015 as one of several research teams in a geopolitical forecasting tournament. Thousands of volunteers gave probabilities for world events, and the project tested training, teaming and tracking of top performers as ways to raise accuracy [2]. The survey forecasts, with each forecaster's self-rated expertise on each forecast for the first three years, are public.

Forecasters in the project chose which questions to answer. That choice is part of the data. Merkle, Steyvers, Mellers and Tetlock [3] asked whether good and poor forecasters choose questions differently, and whether those choices can sharpen estimates of a forecaster's ability beyond what a proper scoring ruleDefinition: proper scoring rule decision theory and forecast verification A score for probability forecasts on which a forecaster does best in expectation by stating their true belief. Excludes scores that pay for shading a forecast toward some answer, and any rule for which questions to answer. full definition reads from the forecasts alone. A proper scoring rule, in decision theory, is a score that a forecaster does best on in expectation by stating their true belief; a rule that pays for shading toward a favoured answer is not proper. Sempere and Lawsen [5] showed that a mean Brier scoreDefinition: Brier score forecast verification, from weather forecasting The squared difference between the stated probabilities and the outcomes, here summed over the answer options in the GJP form so it runs from 0 to 2. Lower is better. Excludes questions left unanswered, which it does not score. full definition gives a forecaster a reason to skip. The Brier score, from weather forecasting, is the squared difference between the stated probabilities and what happened, so lower is better; it scores each answer given and says nothing about questions left unanswered: a forecaster whose average Brier score is b2 should not forecast any question whose true probability lies between b and 1−b, even when they know it exactly. Skipping and scoring are therefore tangled before any data is read.

Machine learning has a matching problem under the name selective predictionDefinition: selective prediction machine learning Prediction with a reject option, where a system answers only the inputs it ranks most likely to be right and declines the rest. Excludes how the kept answers are produced. full definition. A classifier with a reject option keeps the inputs it is most confident on and declines the rest; the term covers that choice of what to answer and leaves out how the kept answers are made. Its quality is drawn as a risk-coverage curveDefinition: risk-coverage curve machine learning, selective prediction The error on kept items against the share kept. Here risk is the mean Brier score of kept forecasts and coverage the share kept. Excludes any score for the forecasts withheld. full definition, the error on kept inputs against the share kept [6]. Here risk is the mean Brier score of kept forecasts and coverage the share kept, so the curve says nothing about the forecasts withheld. We use the same curve to score abstain filters for human forecasts.

The third question concerns the hedge. An earlier round of this study found that a forecast a person rates as expertise 1 is worse than the same person's higher-rated forecasts and sits nearer 50 percent. ExtremisingDefinition: extremising forecast aggregation Pushing a probability away from 50 percent by multiplying its log-odds by a factor a, with a below 1 pulling it inward instead. Excludes changing which side a forecast leans to. full definition, the transformation Baron, Mellers and colleagues studied for aggregated forecasts [4], pushes a probability away from 50 percent by scaling its log-odds by a fixed factor, and a factor below 1 pulls it inward instead; it changes no forecast's direction. It can test whether that pull toward 50 percent is too large, too small or the right size.

The study was built to inform one design choice: how the abstain filter in Flywheel, our accountability software, should rank a source's answers. Should it credit a source for abstaining, and does it need the source's self-rating beside the stated probability?

Preregistration and design

This is the second round of the study. The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, a practice from clinical trials and psychology in which a dated plan is fixed before results are seen, was written on 29 October 2026 after the first round's results and before any second-round statistic was computed on the real data, and it was hash-locked at 14:59:09 UTC that day. A plan revised after a look at second-round outcomes would not have counted as one. It lists what had been seen before it was written: the first round's results and structural counts of conditions, first forecasts and repeat forecasters taken from the survey files with no outcome joined.

The second-round code was checked first on synthetic files shaped like the GJP data, with planted effectsDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition that the code recovered. That is a planted check: data built so the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show the analysis can find an effect when it is there, which no check on real data can show. That check showed that matching on the number of questions answered removes most of the variation in skip rate, because skip rate is one minus answered over available. Matching on forecast count therefore stayed the primary design, as in the first round. This is recorded in the preregistration.

The file names ten verdictsDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition in four parts, each with rules that must all hold, seven shuffle controlsDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition with their draw counts, a prior probability for each verdict, and a decision mapping from outcomes to the filter design. A verdict, in our usage, is the pass or fail of one such rule set read off by code, never a reading written after the numbers were seen. A control is a copy of the data with one link broken, by shuffling, and scored with the same code as the real data; a comparison with another dataset or a published number is not a control. Appendix A gives every verdict and its rule. Nothing was added after the run.

Data and provenance

The data are the Good Judgment Project survey forecasts for years 1 to 4 and the question file, published by Mellers and colleagues on the Harvard Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/BPCDH5) under CC0 1.0Definition: CC0 1.0 copyright and data licensing The Creative Commons public domain dedication, under which anyone may reuse the work for any purpose without permission. Excludes a licence condition requiring citation, which stays a scholarly courtesy. full definition [1]. CC0 is the Creative Commons public domain dedication: anyone may reuse the data for any purpose without permission, and citation is a scholarly courtesy rather than a licence term. The person-level test file and the prediction-marketDefinition: prediction market economics and forecasting A market in which people trade contracts that pay on an outcome, with the price read as a probability. Excludes the individual survey forecasts analysed in this paper. full definition files in the same release were not used; in a prediction market people trade contracts that pay on an outcome and the price is read as a probability, which is a different instrument from the survey forecasts used here. The SHA-256Definition: SHA-256 cryptography A hash function that turns a file into a 64-character fingerprint which changes if any byte changes. A recorded hash shows the file was not altered after it was taken. Excludes encryption, because the hash keeps nothing secret and cannot be turned back into the file. full definition of each of the five input files was recorded before the run and matched after it. SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash, a 64-character fingerprint that changes if any byte of a file changes; it shows the files were not altered and keeps nothing secret.

The survey files hold 3,143,460 rows, one per answer option. Dropping 43,944 withdrawal rows left 1,234,940 forecasts. Of the 617 questions, 498 closed with an outcome and 119 were voidedDefinition: voided question the Good Judgment Project tournament A question the tournament cancelled without scoring, so no forecast on it has an outcome. Excludes a void verdict in our sense, which concerns a failed planted check or a sample below its minimum. full definition. A voided question is one the tournament cancelled without scoring, a tournament term with no bearing on the verdict sense of void. We dropped 157,189 forecasts on voided or unresolved questions, 13,381 dated after the question closed and 15 whose probabilities could not be repaired. That leaves 1,064,355 scored forecasts from 9,914 people, of which 414,570 are a person's first forecast on a question in a year.

Self-rated expertise, 1 to 5 on each forecast, exists in years 1 to 3 only; all 619,380 year 4 forecasts lack it. The abstain-filter sample is therefore every binary scored forecast in years 1 to 3 with a rating: 410,451 forecasts. Experimental conditions 1 and 2 are individuals, 4 teams and 5 superteamsDefinition: superteam the Good Judgment Project design A team made up of forecasters drawn from the top performers of the previous tournament year (condition 5). Excludes ordinary teams (condition 4), formed without selection on past accuracy. full definition. A superteam, in the project's design, is a team made up of forecasters drawn from the top performers of the previous year; ordinary teams were formed without that selection. The prediction-market condition is not in the survey files.

The data hold no record of a declined question. A skipDefinition: skip our usage A closed question that was open during a forecaster's active window in a year and that they never answered, inferred from the data. Excludes questions outside the active window, and any recorded decision to decline, which the data do not hold. full definition is inferred: a closed question that was open during a forecaster's active window in a year and that they never answered. The word is ours for that inferred absence, and it excludes questions that closed before or opened after the forecaster's active window. Only aggregates and distributions are reported here. No score for any named person was stored.

Methods

Scoring

Each forecast is scored with the Brier score in the GJP form, summed over the answer options, so that it runs from 0 to 2:

B=∑k(pk−ok)2(1)

where pk is the stated probability of option k and ok is 1 if that option occurred and 0 otherwise. The relative scoreDefinition: relative Brier score forecast verification, our usage A forecaster's mean, over the questions they answered, of their first-forecast Brier score minus the median first-forecast Brier score on that question. Lower is better. Excludes the difficulty of the question, which subtracting the median removes. full definition of forecaster i on first forecasts is the mean, over the ni questions they answered, of their first-forecast Brier score minus the median first-forecast Brier score on that question. It is our measure of skill against the crowd on the same question, and it leaves out how hard the question was, which the median absorbs:

Si=1ni∑q(Biq−mq)(2)

The time-matched version Si,t takes the median mq only over first forecasts made in the same tenth of the question's open period, drops cells with fewer than 5 first forecasts, and needs 5 or more valid questions per forecaster-yearDefinition: forecaster-year our usage One person's forecasts within one tournament year, the unit for skip rate and relative score. Excludes pooling of different people, and pooling one person's years. full definition, our unit of analysis: one person's forecasts within one tournament year, so a person active in three years counts three times and no two people are pooled. Lower S is better, so the tests correlate skip rate with −S.

Skip rate and the matched correlation

A forecaster-year is eligible with at least 10 available questions and 5 answered. Its skip rate is

si=1−nansnav(3)

where nans is the number of available questions answered and nav the number available. Busy forecasters answer more, so the correlation is taken inside strataDefinition: stratum survey statistics A group of units alike on the matched variables, here year and twentieth of forecast count, inside which a statistic is computed before averaging. Excludes control for variables that were not matched. full definition h of year and twentieth of forecast count, each with 10 or more forecaster-years, and averaged with weights wh equal to stratum size. A stratum, a term from survey statistics, is a group of units alike on the matched variables, so comparisons inside it cannot be driven by those variables; it does nothing about variables left unmatched:

ρM=∑hwhρh∑hwh(4)

where ρh is the Spearman correlationDefinition: Spearman correlation (rho) rank statistics The correlation between the ranks of two quantities, from -1 to +1, which reads any steady rise or fall. Excludes the shape of the relation and the pull of outliers on the raw values. full definition of si with −Si inside stratum h. Spearman's rho, from rank statistics, is the correlation of the ranks of two quantities, so it reads any steady rise or fall and ignores the shape of the relation and the size of outliers. IntervalsDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition come from 1,000 bootstrapDefinition: bootstrap statistics Recomputing a number many times on data resampled with replacement, here within strata or over questions, to see how much it varies. Excludes an interval from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition draws within strata. Each 95 percent interval is the range holding the middle 95 percent of the draws, and it is no statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. The bootstrap, a resampling method from statistics, recomputes the number on data resampled with replacement and assumes no textbook distribution.

The within-person test takes pairs of consecutive years in which a person kept the same majority condition. Inside each year pair it computes the Spearman correlation of the change in skip rate with the change in time-matched score, and averages over year pairs weighted by pair count. Changing condition between years would change the platform and the questions, so mixed pairs are left out of the primary test.

The size of the hedge

For a stated probability p the extremised probability is

p′=papa+(1−p)a(5)

so the log-oddsDefinition: log-odds statistics For a probability p, the natural log of p divided by 1 minus p. 0 at 50 percent and unbounded toward certainty. Excludes any information beyond the probability, of which it is a rescaling. full definition are multiplied by a. The log-odds of a probability p, a term from statistics, is ln⁡(p/(1−p)), which is 0 at 50 percent and grows without bound toward certainty; it is a rescaling of the probability and adds no information to it. A value a above 1 means forecasts were too hedged, below 1 too extreme, and 1 right-sized. The factor is fitted by minimum Brier score on a grid from 0.30 to 4.00 in steps of 0.01. Questions were split once at random into two halves; the held-out gainDefinition: held-out gain machine learning The drop in Brier score from extremising, with the factor fitted on one half of the questions and scored on the other half. Excludes the in-sample improvement any fitted factor gives on the data it was fitted to. full definition is the Brier score at a=1 minus the Brier score at the a fitted on the other half, summed over both halves and taken per forecast. Held-out, in machine-learning usage, means scored on data the fit never saw, which excludes the in-sample improvement any fitted factor gives. The primary contrast uses the first round's within-person sample: forecaster-years with at least 5 forecasts at expertise 1 and 5 at expertise 2 to 5. Intervals come from 1,000 bootstrap draws over questions.

Abstain filters

A filter ranks forecasts by predicted Brier score and keeps the best-ranked share c, the coverage. Its risk R(c) is the mean raw Brier score of the kept forecasts. Each predictor is an out-of-foldDefinition: out-of-fold prediction machine learning, cross-validation A prediction for each item made from a fit on the other folds only. Excludes any use of the item's own outcome to predict it. full definition cell mean, computed for each forecast from the other folds only, so no forecast helps predict itself: the self-rating filter uses the five expertise levels, the probability filter ten bins of distance from 0.5 in steps of 0.05, and the combined filter their 50 crossed cells, falling back to the probability bin where a cell has fewer than 30 training forecasts. Ties are broken by one fixed random key. The summary is the area under the risk-coverage curveDefinition: area under the risk-coverage curve machine learning, selective prediction The mean risk over coverages from 10 to 100 percent in steps of 5, one number for a whole filter. Lower is better. Excludes coverages below 10 percent. full definition, taken as the mean risk over 19 coverages. The area is a selective-prediction summary of a whole filter in one number, lower being better, and it excludes coverages below 10 percent:

A=119∑jR(cj)(6)

with j running from 1 to 19 and cj=0.05(j+1), so coverage runs from 0.10 to 1.00. Lower is better. A random filter keeps the overall mean at every coverage.

Controls and p values

Every shuffle control is scored with the same code as the real data. The p valueDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition of a comparison, a p value from draws as in permutation statistics, assumes no textbook distribution and counts the control draws at or above the real value, with one added to the numerator and the denominator:

p=k+1n+1(7)

where k is the number of draws at or above the real value and n the number of draws. At 1,000 draws the smallest possible value is 0.001.

Controls and planted checks

Seven controls were fixed in the preregistration. Each breaks one link and keeps the rest of the data. The scores a control gives over its draws form a null distribution, whose 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear; it is drawn from these data, never assumed from theory.

  • Skip rate shuffled within year and forecast-count strata, the nullDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition for the first-forecast correlation (1,000 draws), and the same on the time-matched table (1,000).
  • Change in skip rate shuffled within year pair, the null for the within-person test (1,000).
  • The expertise-1 label shuffled within forecaster-year with the question halves fixed, the null for the difference in extremising gain (300).
  • Expertise shuffled within forecaster-year with all predictors refitted, the null for the gain from adding the rating to the probability filter (300). This asks whether the rating carries information about one forecast or only about who is rating.
  • The team label shuffled across forecaster-years within year, the null for the team-against-individual differences in skip effect and in filter gain (300 each).

The random filter is the known floor: Brier 0.277 at every coverage. Before the real data were read, the code recovered planted effects in synthetic files of the same shape: skippers sharper on first forecasts, a within-person change, and over-hedged expertise-1 forecasts. The first round also carried a positive controlDefinition: positive control experimental design A test of an effect already known to be present, which the instrument must detect for its other readings to be trusted. Excludes a shuffle control, which removes an effect instead. full definition that passed, a test of an effect already known to be there, which the instrument must detect for its other readings to be trusted: one point of self-rated expertise improved relative Brier by 0.0226 (0.0185 to 0.0270) within forecaster-years, against a shuffle 95th percentile of 0.0015. Every control in this round had enough spread to be usable.

Results

Abstain filters

Figure 1 draws the three risk-coverage curves and Table 1 gives their areas. A filter on the stated probability scored 0.171, a filter on the self-rating 0.259, and random order 0.277.c1 The probability filter gains 0.107 (0.097 to 0.115) over random, and the self-rating filter 0.018 (0.009 to 0.027), about a sixth as much.

Adding the self-rating to the probability gained 0.0026 (95 percent interval 0.0007 to 0.0046), under the preregistered bar of 0.005, and a rating shuffled within each forecaster-year gained 0.0024 on average.c2 The interval excludes zero, so the combined filter is better than the probability alone by a small amount. The shuffle buys nearly all of it: the small edge comes from who rates themselves high on average. The rating given to one forecast adds nothing past that. The combined filter leads by 0.007 to 0.011 in Brier score up to coverage 0.25, and by 0.004 or less above that. Relative Brier gives the same order: areas 0.124 for self-rating, 0.063 for probability, 0.061 for both and 0.134 for random.

What this means for a reader

People who record sick and healthy cedars also note whether the tree stands on a wet site. Those notes show cedars declining about as often on wet ground as on dry, with a range wide enough to hide a real difference of up to about 75 percent higher odds or 35 percent lower. This is an undecided result from a weak instrument. It does not show that cedar decline ignores water, because every water measure here is a person's judgement at the tree, and people who saw a sick tree filled in that judgement more often.

Objection

Every water measure is an observer's or a crew's call at the tree or plot. No distance to a mapped stream was computed.

What would change the call. Mapped water layers and an elevation model for all 4,184 located cedars, with each declining cedar paired to the nearest healthy one of similar size.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Western redcedar is dying back across the Pacific Northwest, and a field observation by the author holds that the decline follows waterways. A drought reading predicts that water nearby protects a tree. We tested both directions with a plan fixed in advance, on 4,184 located cedar observations from a community science project and 1,545 cedar records from monitored park plots in Seattle. On the primary measure, 87 of 169 cedars on wet sites were declining (51.5 percent) against 347 of 743 on upland sites (46.7 percent), an adjusted odds ratio of 1.11 (95 percent interval 0.65 to 1.75).c1 Compared only with cedars in the same 5 km cell the odds ratio was 0.95, inside the shuffle range of 0.61 to 1.63.c2 By the rule fixed in advance the result is undecided: neither direction passed on any of the four cedar measures.c3 Declining observations answered the hydrology question more often than healthy ones, 64.5 against 52.2 percent, so the primary field is selected on health.c4 Bigleaf maple on water-flagged park plots was stressed in 27 of 463 records (5.8 percent) against 353 of 3,188 (11.1 percent), an adjusted odds ratio of 0.42 (0.17 to 0.88); on the second water measure, wet soil or wetland canopy, the maple odds ratio was 0.84 (0.22 to 2.00).c5 The cedar question stays open, and the paper names the mapped data that would settle it.
