Introduction

Western redcedar (Thuja plicata) has been dying back in Washington and Oregon in recent years. A 2022 report by the Washington Department of Natural Resources with state and federal partners [5] mapped dieback sites and, in the search summaries we read, found them concentrated at low elevation in the urban corridors of western Washington and northwestern Oregon, with low spring precipitation as snow the leading climate predictor on the west side and no site factor tied to worse crown condition in individual trees. A forest health alert issued the same year [6] says cedars are dying in shaded places beside streams and links that to higher temperatures and reduced stream flow.

Those two statements pull in different directions for anyone standing at a stream. If drought is the cause, a tree with water nearby should fare better. If trees beside streams are dying, something about wet sites may add risk: a shallow root system that cannot follow a falling water table, or root disease in wet soil. The author recorded the field observation that cedar decline "follows waterways". An earlier round of this study, ledger entry F25, could not test it: the national forest inventory it used holds no waterway field.

This round asks the narrower question that public data can reach. Among recorded cedars, is decline more common, or less common, on sites an observer called wet? The decision it informs is whether the waterway hypothesis is worth the cost of mapped stream and elevation layers. Our searches returned agency reports and a graduate thesis on topography and drought [7], and no study of decline against distance to water; that is what the searches returned and no proof that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, a dated plan fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen, was locked at 15:06:16 UTC on 29 October 2026. Before it was written we had seen field names, counts per field level and the total number of records in each health class. The code had been run once with health labels shuffled at random. No real health label had been crossed with any water field.

The plan records a prior for the primary measure: probability 0.25 that decline is detectably higher on wet sites, 0.40 that it is detectably lower, and 0.35 that these data can detect no difference. It names twelve verdictsDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition, each a rule set read off by code as pass or fail. An "author" verdict passes when wet sites show more decline and a "drought" verdict when they show less. The overall reading was fixed in advance: supported if the author verdict passes on the primary measure with its observer check and no drought verdict passes elsewhere, opposed if the drought verdict passes on the primary measure, and otherwise undecided.

Data and provenance

Three public sources were used, fetched on 29 October 2026. We report counts and statistics only. No observer name, login, note or photo was read, and records with obscured or private coordinates, 18 in all, were left out.

  • The Western Redcedar Dieback Map [1], a community scienceDefinition: community science ecology (data collection) Records made by volunteers, here photographs of trees with a location and answers to a short form, gathered on a public platform. Excludes a designed sample: volunteers choose which trees to record, so shares in the data are not rates in the forest. full definition project on iNaturalist in which volunteers record a cedar with its location and canopy symptoms; people choose which trees to report, so shares of declining trees are not population rates. Each observation keeps its own licence, mostly CC BY-NC, with about a third all rights reserved. It gave 4,184 usable cedar observations, 1,427 of them declining.
  • The Maple Health Watch project on iNaturalist [2], same terms, with 349 usable bigleaf maple observations.
  • Hulbert's public redcedar repository [3], CC0 1.0 for his own work, which holds 2021 and 2022 exports of the cedar project. The current project no longer carries the site hydrology and slope position fields; these exports hold them for earlier observations, so the primary test covers 2020 to 2022.
  • Green Seattle Partnership Forest Monitoring [4], tree records from plots placed in Seattle parks: 1,545 western redcedar records with 47 rated stressed, and 3,651 bigleaf maple records with 380 stressed. The service names no licence and carries a City of Seattle disclaimer. Trees are not tagged across visits, so one tree can appear twice.

No stream map and no elevation model were available to the study, so distance to water was not computed.

Methods

Outcome and water measures

A cedar observation is healthy when its canopy field says so and declining when it reports thinning, a dead top, branch dieback, browning, yellowing, multiple symptoms or a dead tree. Four cedar measures sort trees into wet and dry:

  • Site hydrology, the primary measure: wet is "seasonally flooded area" or "wetland, lots of water"; dry is "upland or well drained".
  • Slope position: wet is riverbank, floodplain or valley bottom; dry is every other position.
  • Access to water: wet is year-round access, which includes trees watered in summer; dry is no typical access in summer.
  • For park plots, a water flag: the visit's features text names a stream, seep, wetland, lake, spring, creek, pond or wet spot.

Estimates

The main estimate is an odds ratioDefinition: odds ratio statistics The odds of decline on wet sites divided by the odds on dry sites, where odds are the probability of decline over the probability of no decline. 1 means no difference. Excludes a ratio of probabilities, and a causal effect. full definition from logistic regressionDefinition: logistic regression statistics A model in which the log odds of the outcome are a weighted sum of predictors, here a wet-site indicator and site covariates. Excludes any account of which trees came to be recorded. full definition. With π the probability that a tree is declining, w equal to 1 on a wet site and 0 on a dry one, and covariates xj,

ln⁡π1−π=β0+βww+∑jβjxj(1)

and the adjusted odds ratio is the exponential of βw. A value of 1 means the same odds on wet and dry sites; an odds ratio is a ratio of odds and says nothing of cause. Covariates for community observations are site type, disturbance level and observation year; for park plots, stem diameter, edge features, canopy cover, soil compaction and visit period. Each 95 percent intervalDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition is the middle 95 percent of a cluster bootstrapDefinition: cluster bootstrap statistics An interval made by refitting the model many times, here 1,000, on whole sites or plots drawn with replacement, so trees from one place stay together. Excludes resampling single trees as if they were independent. full definition: 1,000 refits on whole sites, or whole plots, drawn with replacement, so trees from one place stay together.

The second estimate compares trees only with their neighbours. A site is a grid cell of 0.05 degrees of latitude by 0.075 of longitude, about 5.5 km square, or a park. The Mantel-Haenszel odds ratioDefinition: Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio epidemiology and statistics One odds ratio pooled across strata, here sites, from the two-by-two table of wet or dry against declining or healthy inside each site. Excludes sites that hold only wet or only dry trees, which add nothing to it, and differences between sites. full definition pools the wet-against-dry comparison across sites:

ORMH=∑sasds/ns∑sbscs/ns(2)

where in site s, as and bs are the declining and healthy trees on wet ground, cs and ds the declining and healthy trees on dry ground, and ns the site's total. Only sites holding both wet and dry trees contribute, so regional differences between cells cannot drive it.

Controls and planted checks

Each controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition is the data with one link broken, scored by the same code.

  • Health labels shuffled within site, 1,000 times per measure, give the null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition of the Mantel-Haenszel estimate. Its 5th and 95th percentiles are the bars for the drought and author verdicts.
  • Bigleaf maple is the comparison species: the same estimate on the same plots and the same access field. A cedar effect counts as specific to cedar only if it lies beyond the 95th percentile of maple's bootstrap.
  • Observer draws: the wet share among declining cedars against random draws of the same size from all cedars with hydrology known.
  • Fill rateDefinition: fill rate survey methods, our usage The share of observations in which the observer answered an optional question, compared between declining and healthy trees. Excludes what the answers were; it measures only who answered. full definition: the share of declining and of healthy observations whose observer answered the optional water question. A gap of 5 points or more means the field is selected on health. This check can show observer bias, which the draws cannot, since they are tied to the main effect by arithmetic.

This study has no planted check, a run on data with a known built-in effect. The shuffle nulls all centred on an odds ratio of 1, with log means within 0.04 of zero.

Results

On the primary measure, 87 of 169 cedars on wet sites were declining (51.5 percent) against 347 of 743 on upland sites (46.7 percent), an adjusted odds ratio of 1.11 (95 percent interval 0.65 to 1.75).c1 Compared only with cedars in the same 5 km cell the odds ratio was 0.95, inside the shuffle range of 0.61 to 1.63.c2 On the 530 observations with an elevation, adding elevation gave 0.98 (0.59 to 1.58). Table 1 and Figure 1 give every measure.

By the rule fixed in advance the result is undecided: neither direction passed on any of the four cedar measures.c3 The access field came nearest. Its within-site odds ratio of 0.66 fell below the shuffle's 5th percentile of 0.69, but the adjusted interval crosses 1, so the drought verdict failed there too, and the field counts a watered garden tree as having access to water. On park plots only 7 stressed cedars stood on water-flagged plots against a required 10, and the features text that carries the flag is blank on 37.7 percent of cedar records. Figure 2 sets each within-site estimate against its shuffle range.

Declining observations answered the hydrology question more often than healthy ones, 64.5 against 52.2 percent, so the primary field is selected on health.c4 The gap is 12.3 points against a limit of 5. For the access field the gap was 2.2 points (22.4 against 20.2 percent), which passed. The observer draws found the wet share among declining cedars at 20.0 percent, against 18.5 percent among all cedars with a hydrology answer and a 95th percentile of 20.7 percent in random draws (p 0.14). Park plots, which a programme placed, put 20.6 percent of cedar records on water-flagged plots, close to the 18.5 percent wet share in volunteers' answers.

Bigleaf maple on water-flagged park plots was stressed in 27 of 463 records (5.8 percent) against 353 of 3,188 (11.1 percent), an adjusted odds ratio of 0.42 (0.17 to 0.88); on the second water measure, wet soil or wetland canopy, the maple odds ratio was 0.84 (0.22 to 2.00).c5 The water-flag interval is the only one in the study that excludes 1, and it is one of nine intervals reported here. Cedar's estimate on the same plots, 0.74, is not beyond the 95th percentile of maple's bootstrap, 0.78, so cedar's response to water is not shown to differ from maple's.

Two exploratory descriptions were planned and not scored. Observers reported heat damage, yes or maybe, on 32 percent of declining cedars on wet sites (31 answers) and 32 percent on dry sites (257 answers). They reported other factors such as insects or disease on 6.5 percent of wet-site cedars (168) against 10.6 percent of dry-site cedars (742). A root disease favoured by wet soil would predict more such reports on wet sites.

Discussion

The outcome fell in the third of the three prior cases, the one given probability 0.35: no difference these data can detect. With 169 wet-site cedars the primary interval runs from 0.65 to 1.75. A real odds ratio of 1.5 in either direction fits inside it. The field observation that decline follows waterways is neither supported nor refuted, and the drought reading is in the same position.

Three features of the instrument limit what any result from it could mean. A wet site is a judgement made by a person at the tree, and it carries no distance to a stream. People recording a declining tree described the site more often, and the direction of the bias that puts into a wet-against-dry comparison is unknown. The hydrology field stopped being collected in 2022, so a pattern that formed later, or one that exists only within a few tens of metres of a channel, would not appear.

The maple result is suggestive and no more. Maple near streams, seeps and wetlands in Seattle parks was stressed about half as often on one measure, which is the direction a drought reading predicts. The second water measure on the same trees shows no clear difference, so the maple result depends on which definition of wet is used.

What would settle the cedar question is a mapped water layer and an elevation model, so that all 4,184 located cedars get a distance to water with no observer call, and a paired design that matches each declining cedar to the nearest healthy one of similar size. The agency work cited above [5, 6] suggests where to look first: low elevations, and stream corridors with reduced summer flow.

Limitations

  • Every water measure is an observer's or a crew's call at the tree or plot. No distance to a mapped stream was computed.
  • The primary field is selected on health: declining observations answered it 12.3 points more often than healthy ones.
  • The interval on the primary measure reaches 1.75 and falls to 0.65, so this is an undecided result and no evidence of absence.
  • Community observations are opportunistic and the project asks for declining trees. The declining shares are not rates in the forest.
  • The hydrology field covers observations from 2020 to 2022 only.
  • "Access to water" mixes summer watering with natural water.
  • Park plots cover forested Seattle parks only and rated 47 cedars stressed; 7 of them were on water-flagged plots.
  • The maple result holds on one of two water measures and is the single interval excluding 1 among nine.
  • There was no planted check.
  • Scoring was done by our own code on observers' calls and was not blind.

Evidence

Inconclusive. Neither direction passed on any of four cedar measures. The primary interval runs from 0.65 to 1.75, so an odds ratio of 1.5 either way is not ruled out. The primary field failed its observer check: declining observations answered it 12.3 points more often than healthy ones, against a limit of 5. The maple result (odds ratio 0.42, interval 0.17 to 0.88) holds on one of two water measures; the other gives 0.84 (0.22 to 2.00).

Figures

These are the paper's own figures, numbered as in the PDF, and each "Figure" reference in the text points here. The charts on this page redraw the same results from the result files and carry their own numbers.

Tables

Appendix A. The preregistered verdicts

Each verdict is a set of rules written before the run and passes only when every rule holds. Odds ratios are shown in place of the stored log values. An "author" verdict needs the interval's lower bound above 1, the within-site estimate above the shuffle's 95th percentile, and a minimum count of declining wet trees. A "drought" verdict needs the upper bound below 1 and the within-site estimate below the shuffle's 5th percentile.

Numbers recorded in our publication register

WhatValue
Sample912 cedars with a site description, 169 of them on wet sites; 4,184 located cedars
Main estimate and intervalodds ratio 1.11 (0.65 to 1.75); maple on water-flagged plots 0.42 (0.17 to 0.88)
Forecast against outcomeNeither the waterways forecast nor the drought forecast passed on any cedar measure. The fill-rate check for the access field passed
Known-answer checknone

What lowers it

What this means for a reader

The public share of the Auger data is small enough that only a large cubic imprint on the arrival directions would have shown up. So the result rules out a strong pattern and says nothing about a subtle one. Anyone citing public cosmic-ray data for or against a grid-like universe should quote the planted sensitivity beside the p value, and the full Auger dataset would do much better than the public share.

Objection

Only the public 10 percent of events was available, which is the main reason the sensitivity is low.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

If space were a fine cubic grid, the highest-energy cosmic rays could arrive in a pattern aligned with its axes, a signature Beane, Davoudi and Savage proposed in 2012. We searched the public Pierre Auger Observatory data for such a pattern with a method fixed in advance. The data are the 25,086 main-array events in the public 10 percent sample and the catalogue of the highest-energy events, cut at 8, 16, 32, 40 and 78 EeV. For each cut we fitted a cube-symmetric pattern over 400 orientations and compared the best fit with skies whose right ascensions were scrambled, which keeps the detector's exposure. No cut shows a cubic pattern: raw p values run from 0.19 to 0.85, and all five read 0.85 after the Benjamini-Hochberg correction.c1 The search could only have seen a strong pattern: at 8 EeV it reaches power 0.9 at a planted strength of 0.2, and at 32 EeV it reaches power 0.97 only at strength 1.0, where the sky along the cube axes is twice the average.c2 The highest-energy event, 166 EeV, bounds the lattice spacing below 3.7e-27 m, an inverse spacing of 5.3e10 GeV, which is 0.53 of the 1e11 GeV bound of Beane and colleagues.c3 This is a null whose value lies in stating how weak it is.

Introduction

Lattice calculations in particle physics put space and time on a grid. Beane, Davoudi and Savage [2] asked what an observer inside such a calculation could detect if the universe itself were computed on a grid with some lattice spacingDefinition: lattice spacing lattice field theory The distance between neighbouring points of a grid on which space is modelled. On a grid, waves shorter than about twice the spacing cannot exist and the speed of a wave depends on its direction. Excludes the Planck length, which is a scale built from constants and not a measured grid. full definition. Their abstract reports that the most stringent bound on the inverse spacing, about 1e11 GeV, comes from the high-energy end of the cosmic-ray spectrum, and their published account predicts that the highest-energy cosmic rays would show the cube symmetry of the grid in their arrival directions.

The particles that could carry that signature are the ultra-high-energy cosmic rayDefinition: ultra-high-energy cosmic ray astroparticle physics A charged particle from space, a proton or heavier nucleus, arriving with an energy above about 1e18 electronvolts. It is recorded through the shower of secondary particles it makes in the atmosphere. Excludes photons and neutrinos, and the far more common cosmic rays of lower energy. full definitions, with energies of many EeVDefinition: EeV physics (units) An exaelectronvolt, 1e18 electronvolts, or 1e9 GeV, carried by a single particle. Excludes the total energy of the shower in a detector, which is spread over many secondary particles. full definition. The Pierre Auger Observatory records them with an array of ground detectors. The Auger Collaboration reported in 2017 a large-scale anisotropy above 8 EeV, a dipole of about 6.5 percent amplitude in 3e4 events, which it reads as evidence that these particles come from outside our galaxy [3]. Since 2021 the collaboration has published 10 percent of its cosmic-ray events, with a catalogue of the highest-energy events added in 2023 [1].

We asked whether the public arrival directions carry a cubic pattern, and what the most energetic event says about the spacing. The decision it informed was how to describe public cosmic-ray data in any work of ours on discretised space: as evidence, or as a weak test. Our searches found the proposal above and the Auger anisotropy results and no published cubic search on the open data; that is what the searches returned, and it does not show that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition and the forecast file were written and hash-locked on 31 October 2026, before the run. They name the baseline (an isotropic sky at the data's declinations), the planted answer (a cubic pattern at random orientation), the controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition (right-ascension scrambles), the outlier checks (the top 3 events and the region around Centaurus A, with and without), the assumption changed (the energy cut and the Centaurus A exclusion), and the kill condition.

The kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition, fixed in advance: if the cubic search gives a corrected p below 0.01, the lattice reading must still survive the Centaurus A exclusion and a second energy cut, or it dies. Each forecast and condition became a rule set whose pass or fail is a verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition read off by code.

Data and provenance

The data are the Pierre Auger Observatory Open Data release of 2024 [1], Zenodo record 10488964, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, fetched on 31 October 2026. We read the event summaries of the main surface array, vertical and inclined showers together with duplicates removed, which gave 25,086 events with direction and energy. This public sample is 10 percent of the recorded events. We also read the catalogue of the highest-energy surface-array events, 109 events with a top energy of 166 EeV. We report statistics only.

The cuts at 8, 16 and 32 EeV use the event summaries, and the cuts at 40 and 78 EeV use the catalogue. Table 1 gives the count at each cut.

Methods

The pattern

For an arrival direction written as a unit vector with components x, y, z, the cubic harmonicDefinition: cubic harmonic mathematics (spherical harmonics) and crystallography The simplest pattern on a sphere with the symmetry of a cube: here x^4 + y^4 + z^4 minus its average, largest along the six cube axes and smallest along the eight diagonals. Excludes a dipole, a single hot spot, or any pattern that a rotation of the cube by a right angle would change. full definition is

C=x4+y4+z4−0.6(1)

The constant 0.6 is its average over the sphere, so C averages to zero on an isotropic sky. It is largest, 0.4, along the six axes of the cube and smallest along the eight diagonals. A grid in space need not line up with our coordinates, so the pattern was rotated through 400 random orientations R.

The statistic

A ground array does not watch the whole sky evenly: its exposureDefinition: exposure astroparticle physics How much of each part of the sky a detector watched over time. A ground array sees some declinations far more than others, so an isotropic sky still looks uneven in its data. Excludes the number of events, which is exposure times the true flux. full definition depends strongly on declination. The baseline sky was therefore built from 60,000 directions with uniform right ascension and declinations drawn from the data. For orientation R, let μR and sR be the mean and standard deviation of C on this baseline, and mR its mean over the N real events. The standardised excess is

ZR=|mR−μR|sR/N(2)

and the statistic T is the largest ZR over the 400 orientations. For cuts with 500 events or fewer, the baseline declinations were drawn from the 8 EeV events.

The null and the correction

Each p value comes from a right-ascension scrambleDefinition: right-ascension scramble astroparticle physics (anisotropy searches) A control sky made by keeping each event's declination and giving it a random right ascension. The Earth's rotation makes a ground array's exposure nearly even in right ascension, so the scramble keeps the exposure and removes any pattern. Excludes a fully random sky, which would ignore the detector's exposure. full definition: each event keeps its declination and gets a random right ascension, which keeps the exposure and removes any pattern. The statistic was recomputed on 300 scrambled skies, and

p=k+1n+1(3)

with k the number of scrambles at or above the real T and n the number of scrambles. The five p values were corrected with the Benjamini-Hochberg correctionDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics (multiple testing) A rule that raises a set of p values to control the expected share of false discoveries among the tests called significant. The smallest raw p is multiplied by the number of tests and larger ones by less. Excludes an uncorrected p value read on its own when several tests were run. full definition [4]: with the raw values sorted so that pi is the ith smallest of M = 5,

qi=Mpii(4)

and each corrected value is the smallest qj at its own rank or above.

Planted patterns

A planted sky keeps the real events' declinations and draws right ascensions from a density proportional to

1+ϵC0.4(5)

at one random orientation, so that the sky along the cube axes is 1+ϵ times the average. The detection powerDefinition: detection power statistics The share of planted skies, each with a pattern of known strength, in which the search finds the pattern at its preregistered threshold. Excludes the chance that a pattern exists in the real sky. full definition at strength ϵ is the share of planted skies whose statistic exceeds the 95th percentile of scrambled skies. At 32 EeV the threshold came from 200 scrambles and each strength had 30 planted skies; at 8 EeV, 60 scrambles and 10 planted skies.

The kinematic reading

On a grid of spacing a, a particle cannot have a wavelength much shorter than the grid. In the simple picture used here, a particle of energy Etop could not propagate unless

a<πQEtop(6)

where Q = 1.973e-16 GeV m is the reduced Planck constant times the speed of light. The inverse spacing in energy units is Etop/π.

Controls and planted checks

The right-ascension scramble is the null for every p value. As a separate control at 32 EeV, 200 scrambled skies gave a mean statistic of 2.32 and a 95th percentile of 3.27; the real statistic, 1.69, sat well inside them (p value from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition 0.87).

The planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition measured the search's power at each strength. Figure 3 and Table 2 give the result. The planted powers are coarse: each is a share of 30 or of 10 trials.

The outlier checks removed the 28 events at 32 EeV within 27 degrees of Centaurus A, and separately the 3 highest-energy events, and recomputed the p value with 200 scrambles each.

Results

No cut shows a cubic pattern: raw p values run from 0.19 to 0.85, and all five read 0.85 after the Benjamini-Hochberg correction.c1 Table 1 and Figure 2 give the values.

Removing the 28 events near Centaurus A or the 3 highest-energy events leaves no pattern at 32 EeV: p 0.38 and 0.71.c4

The search could only have seen a strong pattern: at 8 EeV it reaches power 0.9 at a planted strength of 0.2, and at 32 EeV it reaches power 0.97 only at strength 1.0, where the sky along the cube axes is twice the average.c2

The highest-energy event, 166 EeV, bounds the lattice spacing below 3.7e-27 m, an inverse spacing of 5.3e10 GeV, which is 0.53 of the 1e11 GeV bound of Beane and colleagues.c3 The 1e11 GeV figure was entered from memory before the run; the abstract of Beane and colleagues [2], read for this paper, gives the same value.

The study also ran a toy model of waves on a cubic grid, to check the dispersion a lattice would cause. Along an axis, the phase speed falls short of the continuum value by (ka)2/24, with k the wavenumber, within 0.8 percent for ka up to 0.8. The group speed falls short by (ka)2/8, within 1.3 percent; our forecast had given it the phase speed's coefficient, and that forecast missed. Along a diagonal, waves run faster than along an axis by (ka)2/48, within 1.2 percent, and the model sets the highest energy along a diagonal at 3, 1.73, times that along an axis, from the grid's geometry. This direction dependence is what would imprint a cube on arrival directions.

Table 3 sets the forecasts written before the run against the outcomes.

The event forecast was made from memory of the full dataset; the public release holds a tenth of it.

Discussion

The search found nothing, and the planted skies say how little that means. At 32 EeV, the highest cut with event-level data, only 155 events are public, and the search needs a pattern that doubles the flux along the cube axes before it sees one reliably. At 8 EeV the sample is twenty times larger and the threshold falls to a 20 percent modulation, but at that energy the particles are bent strongly by galactic magnetic fields, which would smear a pattern made at the source.

For scale, the dipole the Auger Collaboration measured above 8 EeV with its full data has an amplitude of about 6.5 percent [3]. A cubic pattern of that size would be far below what our search can see in the public share. The kinematic reading lands within a factor of 2 of the published bound because both rest on the same top energy and the same simple argument; it adds a check of arithmetic and no new information.

The result therefore excludes a large cubic imprint on the public arrival directions and nothing smaller. The same method on the full Auger data would set a stronger limit.

Limitations

  • Only the public 10 percent of events was available, which is the main reason the sensitivity is low.
  • Cosmic rays at these energies are bent by galactic and intergalactic magnetic fields, and we did not model that; a lattice pattern at the source could be smeared before arrival.
  • Only a cubic pattern was tested. Other grid symmetries and other signatures of a lattice were not.
  • The scramble also removes the known dipole from the null skies. With partial sky coverage a dipole is not exactly independent of a cubic pattern, so a dipole could raise the statistic slightly; we did not test this.
  • The planted powers rest on 30 or 10 trials per strength and are coarse.
  • The 1e11 GeV bound was entered from memory and agrees with the abstract read for this paper; the full paper was not read.
  • Scoring was by our own code and was not blind.

Evidence

Honest null. Only strong cubic patterns are ruled out: power 0.9 at planted strength 0.2 at 8 EeV, and at 32 EeV only at strength 1.0, where the sky along the cube axes is twice the average.

What this means for a reader

When a table prints a value plus or minus one sigma, the next edition usually lands about as close as that promise says. Large misses are the problem: shifts of four or five sigma happen far more often than a bell curve allows. If you need 95 percent confidence from a published plus-or-minus, multiply it by three to five, and by more for an astronomical quantity that is still being settled. That multiple describes how these tables behaved in the past, and it will miss when an input shared by many values turns out wrong.

Objection

Later tables reuse inputs from earlier ones (shared inputs), so the later edition is not independent of the earlier one. That flatters every coverage figure here. Editions that share no inputs would be the cleaner test.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

A stated uncertainty is a forecast of where later, better measurements will put a value. We scored that forecast on four reference sources: particle masses and widths in the Particle Data Group tables (2010 to 2025), atomic masses in the Atomic Mass Evaluation (2003 to 2020), the CODATA recommended constants (2002 to 2022) and Huchra's compilation of published Hubble constant values. For each quantity we measured the shift between the first and last edition in units of the first edition's stated sigma. The earlier 1 sigma interval covered 0.68 of later PDG values that moved (n 227) and 0.66 of later AME values (n 2,213, nearly all of which moved), close to the nominal 0.6827.c1 The tails are far heavier than a normal curve. Covering 95.45 percent of later values took 3.8 times the stated sigma for moved PDG values, 4.0 for AME and 4.9 for CODATA.c2 Student t fits to the nonzero shifts gave nu of 1.67 for PDG, 1.22 for AME and 2.17 for CODATA, close to the Cauchy shape.c3 Published Hubble constant values before 1990 covered a proxy truth of 70 km/s/Mpc within 1 sigma in 0.35 of 115 cases.c4 Later tables reuse inputs from earlier ones, which flatters every coverage figure here.

Introduction

A stated 1 sigma uncertaintyDefinition: stated 1 sigma uncertainty metrology (the standard uncertainty of the GUM) and physics data tables The plus-or-minus a table prints beside a value, meant as one standard deviation of the value's error. For a normal error the interval of one sigma either side holds the truth 68.27 percent of the time and two sigma 95.45 percent. Excludes an expanded uncertainty already multiplied by a coverage factor, and any bound meant to hold always. full definition is the plus-or-minus a table prints beside a value, meant as one standard deviation of its error. For a normal error, one sigma either side should hold the truth 68.27 percent of the time and two sigma 95.45 percent. Later editions of the same table give a better estimate of the true value, so the share of later values that fall inside an earlier interval, its coverageDefinition: coverage statistics and metrology The share of cases in which an interval drawn round an earlier value contains the value that later replaced it. Here the interval is one or two of the earlier value's own stated sigma either side. Excludes the share of intervals that contain the true value, which no later table can supply. full definition, can be counted.

Henrion and Fischhoff [5] examined the history of the physical constants, including the speed of light, and found that reported uncertainties were consistently too small, with recommended values often moving by more than their stated errors. Chen, Gott and Ratra [6] built the error distribution of 461 Hubble constant measurements in Huchra's compilation against a central value of 71 km/s/Mpc. They found it non-Gaussian, with 95.4 percent limits at 7.0 times the quoted errors and a shape described by a widened Student t with two degrees of freedom. Bailey [7] analysed about 41,000 measurements of 3,200 quantities from medicine, nuclear and particle physics and interlaboratory comparisons, and found the normalised differences between measurements of the same quantity close to Student t distributions, often almost Cauchy. Its reading is that researchers estimate the size of typical errors well and underestimate the chance of large ones.

This paper asks the same question of edition-to-edition changes in four large tables at once, with a planted check, a normal-world control, a test that removes unchanged values, and forecasts fixed in advance. Bailey's data include nuclear and particle physics. Our searches on 9 November 2026 did not return a study that scores the PDG mass-width files edition against edition; that is what the searches returned, and it does not show that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The design was written as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition dated 31 October 2026 and hash-locked on 1 November 2026 at 01:54 UTC. The forecasts were copied from an earlier forecast file written and hashed before any data were read. Before the lock, the file formats of the PDG, AME and Huchra tables were read; no coverage was computed. The decision it informs was stated in the file: whether stated uncertainties, and our own forecast bands, get a correction factor.

The locked file names the tables and editions, the coverage count, a moved-values armDefinition: moved-values arm research method, our usage The same coverage count repeated after dropping every quantity whose value did not change between the two editions, since an unchanged value counts as covered whatever its stated uncertainty. Excludes a test of whether the unchanged values were right. full definition that drops every quantity whose value did not change (an unchanged value counts as covered whatever its sigma), the proxy truthDefinition: proxy truth research method, our usage A value fixed in advance and used in place of the unknown true value where no later edition settles it. Here three values of the Hubble constant, 67.4, 70 and 73 km/s/Mpc, each reported on its own. Excludes a claim that any of the three is the true value. full definition values for the Hubble constant, a planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition (data built so the right answer is known, run through the same analysis), a controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition (a version of the data with the structure under test removed, scored the same way), the assumptions to be changed one at a time, the forecasts and a kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition, a rule that decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run.

Kill condition, without discretion: if the planted check fails, no coverage claim counts.

The same run also scored our own numeric forecast bands from earlier studies. That arm is reported as a separate finding (F366) and appears here only in the appendix.

Data and provenance

  • Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics, mass and width files for Monte Carlo programs, editions 2010, 2012, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025 [1]. Recent editions are released under CC BY 4.0; the terms for older editions were not read. Asymmetric errors were averaged into one sigma.
  • Atomic Mass Evaluation, editions 2003, 2012, 2016 and 2020 [2]. The 2016 and 2020 files came from the IAEA Atomic Mass Data Center; the 2003 and 2012 files were refused by the live server and taken from Internet Archive copies of the same addresses. No licence was stated on the pages read. Values marked as estimated were removed.
  • CODATA recommended values of the fundamental constants, 2002 to 2022, from the NIST archive of ASCII tables [3]. Values with zero stated uncertainty (exact values) do not enter as earlier values.
  • Huchra's table of published Hubble constant estimates, last updated 7 October 2010 [4], from an Internet Archive copy of 2012. No licence was stated. Asymmetric errors were averaged.

All four are public tables of measured values. The files were read as data. If the PDG 2016 file had been identical to 2014 it would have been dropped; it was not.

Methods

Shift in units of the earlier sigma

For quantity i with value ai and stated sigma si in the first edition and value bi in the last, the shift in units of the earlier sigmaDefinition: shift in units of the earlier sigma statistics, our usage; called a normalised residual in metrology The size of the change in a quantity's value between an earlier and a later edition of a table, divided by the uncertainty stated in the earlier edition. Excludes the sign of the change, and any uncertainty in the later value. full definition is

zi=|bi−ai|si(1)

Only quantities present in both editions with si>0 enter.

Coverage and needed multiple

Coverage at m sigma is the share of quantities with zi≤m:

Cm=N(z≤m)n(2)

where N(z≤m) counts the quantities whose shift is at most m and n is the number of quantities. The needed multipleDefinition: needed multiple metrology, our usage; a coverage factor fitted after the fact The multiple of the stated sigma that would have covered 68.27 or 95.45 percent of the later values. It is the matching percentile of the shifts in units of the earlier sigma, written k68 and k95. Excludes a factor known before the later values were published. full definition k68 is the 68.27th percentile of the shifts and k95 the 95.45th percentile: the multiples of the stated sigma that would have covered those shares. For honest normal errors both coverages sit at 0.6827 and 0.9545 and the two multiples at 1 and 2.

Tail shape

A folded Student t distributionDefinition: Student t distribution and its tail index nu statistics A bell-shaped family with heavier tails than the normal curve. Its degrees of freedom nu set the tail weight, so small nu means large shifts are common, nu of 1 is the Cauchy distribution and nu without limit is the normal curve. Excludes skewed or bounded shapes. full definition with a scale and degrees of freedom nu was fitted by maximum likelihood to the nonzero shifts. Small nu means heavy tails; nu of 1 is the Cauchy distributionDefinition: Cauchy distribution probability The Student t distribution with nu equal to 1, whose tails are so heavy that its mean and variance do not exist. Excludes any distribution with a finite variance. full definition, and a normal curve has nu without limit.

Intervals

The interval on each 1 sigma coverage comes from a bootstrapDefinition: bootstrap statistics, resampling Redrawing the quantities of a table with replacement, here 300 times, and recomputing the coverage each time. The middle 95 percent of the recomputed values is the interval. Excludes uncertainty from the choice of editions or from shared inputs, which resampling quantities does not touch. full definition: quantities are redrawn with replacement 300 times and the coverage recomputed; the 95% intervalDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition is the middle 95 percent of the redrawn values.

The Hubble constant

Huchra's table has no later edition of each entry. Each published value was scored against a proxy truth fixed in advance, 67.4, 70 or 73 km/s/Mpc, reported separately, and the values published before 1990 were scored against 70.

Changes of assumption

Each was run apart: the moved-values arm; the top 1 percent of shifts removed; the last pair of editions alone; and, for CODATA, one row per distinct shift rounded to two decimals, since many constants are derived from the same inputs. A shrink test asked, for each quantity in three or more editions, whether its stated error fell faster than its edition-to-edition steps. An out-of-sample test fitted the needed multiples on the earlier half of the editions and applied them to the later half.

Controls and planted checks

The planted check built 4,000 shifts in a world where the stated sigma is half the true error and the errors follow a Student t with three degrees of freedom. The true k68 is

ktrue=2q3(3)

where q3 is the 0.84135 quantile of that t distribution. On a planted world with stated errors set to half the true error, the method recovered the needed multiple as 2.405 against a true 2.394.c5 The fitted nu was 3.002 against a true 3. The kill condition did not fire.

Results

Table 1 gives every field and Figure 2 draws the same numbers. The earlier 1 sigma interval covered 0.68 of later PDG values that moved (n 227) and 0.66 of later AME values (n 2,213, nearly all of which moved), close to the nominal 0.6827.c1 The 95% intervals on those two coverages are 0.63 to 0.74 for PDG and 0.65 to 0.68 for AME; only 0.3 percent of the AME values did not move. At 2 sigma both fall short of 0.9545, at 0.85 and 0.82.

Covering 95.45 percent of later values took 3.8 times the stated sigma for moved PDG values, 4.0 for AME and 4.9 for CODATA.c2 Student t fits to the nonzero shifts gave nu of 1.67 for PDG, 1.22 for AME and 2.17 for CODATA, close to the Cauchy shape.c3

Over all PDG values, including the 0.35 that never moved, the tables over-cover at 1 sigma (0.79). In the last PDG step, 2024 to 2025, 0.96 of 421 values did not move. Coverage that counts those values says more about which values were carried forward than about how honest the stated errors are.

The CODATA step from 2018 to 2022 covered only 0.47 at 1 sigma. A later reading of this run, made after the lock and recorded as a separate finding, traced most of that step to one input: 99 of the 273 rows moved by 4.2 to 4.7 of their 2018 sigma when the fine-structure constant moved by 4.55 of its own. The CODATA 2022 adjustment reports that move; we did not re-read the report for this paper. The rows are not independent: kept to one row per distinct shift, CODATA has 76 rows, with 1 sigma coverage 0.63 and k95 5.1.

Published Hubble constant values before 1990 covered a proxy truth of 70 km/s/Mpc within 1 sigma in 0.35 of 115 cases.c4 Over all 544 values the needed k95 was 5.4 to 7.7 depending on the proxy, the worst field in the set at every proxy. Ten published speed-of-light values from before 1983, scored against the defined value, covered 0.5 at 1 sigma; six of those came from fetched sources and the rest were transcribed, so we give that row no weight.

Removing the top 1 percent of shifts changed 1 sigma coverage by about 0.01 (PDG 0.80, AME 0.67, CODATA 0.86) and lowered k95 to 2.8 for PDG, 3.6 for AME and 3.2 for CODATA. The largest single shift, the alpha particle molar mass in CODATA at 74 sigma, comes from the 2019 redefinition of the SI changing the molar mass rows. The largest PDG shift (12.7) and the largest AME shift (silicon-32, 64) were not traced.

Needed multiples did not carry forward in time where values moved. Fitted on CODATA 2002 to 2014 and applied to 2014 to 2022, k68 of 0.65 lowered 1 sigma coverage from 0.40 to 0.32, and k95 of 1.46 reached 0.79 where 0.9545 was the aim. In AME, 2016 to 2020 hardly moved, and coverage stayed at 0.94.

The shrink test found stated errors falling faster than the steps between editions in 0.66 of 287 CODATA quantities, 0.52 of 104 PDG quantities and 0.25 of 2,227 AME quantities. No general rule that uncertainty shrinks faster than values settle follows from that.

Table 2 sets the forecasts against the outcomes. Of the ten forecast verdicts in the result file, six held.

Discussion

The pattern matches Bailey [7]: the core of a stated uncertainty is about right and the tails are not. Our fitted nu values, 1.2 to 2.2, sit at or below the heavy end of what that paper describes, and nearer the Cauchy shape. Our Hubble constant result agrees with Chen, Gott and Ratra [6] in kind: they put 95.4 percent limits at 7.0 times the quoted errors against a central value of 71, and we find 6.5 against 70 on a larger version of the same compilation.

In these tables the fault sits in the tails. Bailey draws the same distinction: underestimating every sigma by one factor widens a normal curve without giving it heavy tails. In our tables, the 1 sigma multiple sits near 1 while the 95.45 percent multiple sits near 4. A single scaling of every error bar cannot fix both.

What this means for a reader

A crowd forecast moves steadily toward the right answer as the question nears its end, so its average over the whole period describes no moment of it. Mood reported on a phone is steadier, but in a large minority of people it steps or drifts over the weeks of a study by more than their own hour-to-hour carryover explains. A study that prompts five times a day also cannot see feelings that rise and fade within the hour: they show up as noise. More than half of what we predicted about these data was wrong, and one of our tests was built so that it could not give a positive answer, which we report as a defect.

Objection

Eleven of 20 predictions did not hold, and one that held could not have failed. A further one, that the inventory series are too short to test, is a statement about series length.

What would change the call. Rerun with surrogates that keep each series' own distribution of values and a tie-aware change-point cost on an independent experience-sampling dataset, plus a continuous physiological signal for tests under one hour.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Most statistics for a series of measurements assume the process behind it holds still. We built tests for three ways it can move (a step, a slow drift, a switch between two states), checked each on synthetic series with known answers, and ran them on crowd forecasts and on mood reported several times a day. Twenty predictions were fixed in advance. The ledger scores 9 of the 20 as held and 11 as not held, and one of the 9 held only because its rule could never fire.c1 In 238 forecast questions the drift test fired on 97 percent and 96 percent ended nearer the answer than they began, by a median 0.24 in probability, which is what a crowd converging on an outcome is expected to do.c2 On the two slider datasets the change-point test fired in 22 and 40 percent of people and the drift test in 26 and 43 percent, against about 5 percent per test for a stationary AR(1) series.c3 On the 1 to 7 and 1 to 5 scales the raw change-point rates of 47 and 70 percent fell to 18 and 12 percent once ties were broken, so most of those detections came from the rating scale.c4 The switching test used 19 surrogates, so its smallest p value was 0.05 and the rule "p below 0.05" could never fire; no claim about switching is made.c5 Simulated people whose mood relaxes in 5, 15 or 30 minutes, sampled five times a day for 20 days with no measurement noise, were fitted at the sampling floor or with a noise share of 0.8 or more in 89, 98 and 89 percent of 100 runs, against a preregistered bar of 90 percent.c6

Introduction

A series is stationaryDefinition: stationary probability and time-series analysis A series whose mean and autocovariance do not change over time. Excludes series with trends, level shifts or drifting variance. full definition when its mean and its autocovariance do not change over time, a term from time-series analysis that excludes trends, level shifts and drifting variance. Measures such as an autocorrelation or a spectrum summarise a whole record in a few numbers, and those numbers describe the process only if it is stationary. A recent primer on non-stationarity in psychological time series [4] warns, in the summary we read, that ignoring a trend biases estimates and distorts their sampling distributions.

Mood research meets the problem in experience samplingDefinition: experience sampling psychology (methods) A study design in which people answer short questions on a phone several times a day, so that mood is recorded close to the moment it is felt. Excludes one-off questionnaires and recall of past weeks. full definition, a design in which people answer short questions on a phone several times a day. Such data are sparse and unevenly spaced, and how spacing biases models fitted to them is a studied question [7]. A simulation study found that popular time-series tools lose the dynamics of a toy emotion model once measurements are as sparse as experience sampling, and its authors suspected a mismatch between prompts hours apart and processes that unfold over seconds to minutes [5]. A Monte Carlo study of continuous-time autoregressive models found estimates degraded when the process was observed more slowly than it ran [6].

We asked three things. Which of the processes we hold data on are stationary, by tests that can tell a step from a drift? How widely do people differ in the time their mood takes to relax? And what is the fastest mood process a five-a-day schedule can measure? The decision this informed was which of our own stationary measures may be applied to which data. Our searches returned the work above and no published share of experience-sampling participants whose series fail a stationarity test; that is what two searches returned and no proof that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, a dated plan fixed and hashed before any result is seen, was written on 29 October 2026 and its SHA-256 recorded at 15:54:42 UTC that day, before any measure was run on any real series. Before writing it we had seen file headers, counts of people and prompts, record spans, and the results of the synthetic recovery runs. It fixes 20 predictions, each scored held or not held as written by our own code and reading of the result files, with nothing re-scored after the run and every unplanned analysis labelled exploratory. Each scored prediction is a verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition. Appendix A lists all 20.

Data and provenance

  • Good Judgment Project survey forecasts, years 1 to 4, CC0 1.0 [1]. We kept closed binary questions open for at least 60 days with forecasts on at least 60 days: 238 questions. Each series is the daily median probability given to the outcome that occurred, with empty days carried forward.
  • Four datasets from the openESM database [2], each CC BY 4.0: 0008 (valence on a 0 to 100 slider), 0018 (valence on a slider from -50 to 50), 0062 (happiness, 1 to 7) and 0076 (positive affect, 1 to 5). People with at least 60 usable prompts and 3 distinct values were kept: 113, 70, 34 and 373, in total 590. Only distributions across people are reported.
  • Forest Inventory and Analysis remeasurements for Oregon and Washington [3], a United States Government work in the public domain: annual mortality share and survivor growth by remeasurement year, 14 and 12 years.
  • Two looping animations rendered by our own software, 288 and 144 frames, tiled four times. They are a known periodic control and are not public data.

Methods

The three tests

Each test compares a series with surrogatesDefinition: surrogate series time-series statistics A simulated series that keeps chosen properties of a real one, here its length, mean, standard deviation and lag-1 memory, and nothing else, so a statistic on the real series can be compared with what those properties alone produce. Excludes the real series' distribution of values, which a Gaussian surrogate does not copy. full definition of itself: simulated series from an AR(1) processDefinition: AR(1) process time-series statistics A series in which each value is the mean plus a fixed fraction of the previous value's distance from the mean, plus fresh random noise. Excludes steps, drifting coefficients, switching between states and long memory. full definition fitted to it, in which each value is the mean plus a fraction ϕ of the previous value's distance from the mean plus Gaussian noise et,

xt=μ+ϕ(xt−1−μ)+et(1)

with the same length, mean, standard deviation and ϕ as the real series. A surrogate keeps the memory between neighbouring values and has no step, drift or switching. For a statistic that is k times matched or beaten among N surrogates,

p=1+kN+1(2)

so the smallest possible value is 1/(N+1).

  • Change-pointDefinition: change point time-series statistics A time at which the mean or variance of a series changes. Here found by a penalised search that adds a change only when it improves the fit by more than a fixed penalty. Excludes gradual change, which the drift test reads. full definition test: the number of changes in mean or variance found by a penalised search (PELT, penalty 3ln⁡n, segments of 5 or more), against 99 surrogates.
  • Drift testDefinition: drift test time-series statistics, our usage A comparison of an autoregressive model whose coefficient follows a random walk with one whose coefficient is fixed, by likelihood ratio. Excludes a drift of the mean level alone with a constant coefficient, which this test does not target. full definition: a model whose AR coefficient follows a random walk, ϕt=ϕt−1+ϵt, fitted by a Kalman filter; the likelihood ratio against a fixed coefficient, against 49 surrogates.
  • Switching testDefinition: switching test econometrics (Markov-switching models) A comparison of a model with two hidden states, each with its own level and spread, that the series moves between, with a single AR(1), by likelihood ratio. Excludes a one-way step, which the change-point test reads. full definition: a two-state Markov-switching AR(1) against a single AR(1), likelihood ratio, against 19 surrogates.

A series is labelled switching if the third test gives p below 0.05 with at least 3 switches, else shift if the first does, else drift if the second does, else stationary. In a stationary AR(1) world each test fires about 5 percent of the time.

Timescales

For each person we fitted an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck time constantDefinition: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck time constant stochastic processes The time over which a quantity that relaxes toward its mean loses about 63 percent of a deviation, fitted here from each person's prompts at their real times with a separate noise term. Excludes a second, slower or faster timescale in the same person, which this fit does not model. full definition τ to the real prompt times. The model is a mood that relaxes toward its mean, observed with independent noise, so two prompts d hours apart correlate as

r(d)=(1−ρ)e−d/τ(3)

where ρ is the share of variance that is noise. A person is at the sampling floorDefinition: sampling floor our usage, from sampling theory The condition in which a person's fitted time constant is shorter than their median gap between prompts within a day, so the value is not measured. Excludes a claim that the person's mood is fast; noise gives the same reading. full definition when the fitted τ is shorter than their median gap between prompts within a day; there the time constant is not measured.

The aliasing simulation

AliasingDefinition: aliasing signal processing The misreading that results when a process changes faster than it is sampled, so that the fast change appears in the record as something else, here as noise. Excludes measurement error in the instrument, which is present even with dense sampling. full definition, a term from signal processing, is what happens when a process changes faster than it is sampled: the fast change is recorded as something else, here as noise. We simulated people from eq. 3 with ρ=0 and true τ from 5 minutes to 48 hours, on a schedule of 20 days with 5 prompts a day, 100 runs per value, and fitted them as real people were fitted.

Controls and planted checks

Every measure first had to recover known values from synthetic series, which is a planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition: data built so the right answer is known. Over 40 seeds, the median error had to be below the 5th percentile of a shuffled pairing of recovered and planted values and at most half its median. In the recovery file 15 measures pass every rule. Three are recorded as failing and were not used for claims: a spectral slope on five-a-day sampling (ratio 1.04), variance shares in three bands on records under 90 days, and a fit of two timescales in one person (ratios 0.63 and 0.89).

Two controlsDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition, estimators that should fail, passed at first. A single spectral peak passed the test for a frequency sweep (ratio 0.44) and a single AR coefficient passed the test for a drifting one (0.49), because each correlates with the endpoints. The rule was changed so that every moving case is also scored on the movement itself, where both fail at ratio 1.00. A third control showed that a switching model fitted to a shuffled series still recovers the gap between its two levels from the histogram alone; only the durations of the states need time order.

The change-point search was also run on pure noise, 200 series per setting. It reported a change in 2 to 6 percent of white-noise series, and in 83 to 100 percent of AR(1) series with ϕ of 0.6 or more. That is why no real series is read from its raw change count and each is judged against AR(1) surrogates.

Results

The ledger scores 9 of the 20 as held and 11 as not held, and one of the 9 held only because its rule could never fire.c1

The defect

The switching test used 19 surrogates, so its smallest p value was 0.05 and the rule "p below 0.05" could never fire; no claim about switching is made.c5 The switching share is 0 in every dataset by construction, and the prediction that it would be under 15 percent held for that reason alone. An exploratory rerun with "p at most 0.05" and at least 3 switches flagged 47 to 67 percent of people in the mood datasets and 54 percent of forecast questions. Those rates cannot be read as switching: Gaussian surrogates do not copy a bounded, skewed rating scale, and the control above shows the model reads level gaps from the histogram. A surrogate that keeps each series' own distribution of values is the test this needs, and it was not run.

Forecasts

In 238 forecast questions the drift test fired on 97 percent and 96 percent ended nearer the answer than they began, by a median 0.24 in probability, which is what a crowd converging on an outcome is expected to do.c2 Only 1.7 percent of questions were labelled stationary. We had predicted that steps would be the most common label, on the idea that news arrives as jumps; drift was, at 78 percent of questions against 20 percent for shift. The median question ran 126.5 days.

Mood

Table 1 and Figure 1 give the labels and test rates. On the two slider datasets the change-point test fired in 22 and 40 percent of people and the drift test in 26 and 43 percent, against about 5 percent per test for a stationary AR(1) series.c3 These shares rest on 113 and 70 people and have no intervals. We had predicted that more than half the people in every dataset would be labelled stationary, and that held in one dataset of four.

On the 1 to 7 and 1 to 5 scales the raw change-point rates of 47 and 70 percent fell to 18 and 12 percent once ties were broken, so most of those detections came from the rating scale.c4 A coarse scale gives runs of identical answers (a median 45 and 46 percent of consecutive prompts tie in these two datasets), a run of identical values has zero variance, and a Gaussian surrogate never produces one. DequantisingDefinition: dequantising signal processing Adding uniform random noise one scale step wide to values recorded on a coarse scale, so that identical neighbouring answers stop being exactly equal. Excludes any recovery of the finer value the person would have given on a continuous scale. full definition, adding uniform noise one scale step wide, removes the ties; it was an exploratory correction made after the run. On the sliders, where 3 to 4 percent of consecutive prompts tie, the rates barely moved (0.22 to 0.24 and 0.40 to 0.39).

Timescales and the sampling floor

Table 2 gives the fitted time constants. The median lies between 2 and 48 hours in each dataset, and across all 590 people the 5th to 95th percentile range runs from 0.54 to 109 hours, a factor of about 200. Between 13 and 40 percent of people sit at the sampling floor. We had predicted at least 20 percent in every dataset, which held in two.

Simulated people whose mood relaxes in 5, 15 or 30 minutes, sampled five times a day for 20 days with no measurement noise, were fitted at the sampling floor or with a noise share of 0.8 or more in 89, 98 and 89 percent of 100 runs, against a preregistered bar of 90 percent.c6 The prediction missed its bar by one run in a hundred at two of the three values. Its second rule held: the median correlation between consecutive prompts was 0.04, -0.02 and 0.01. Figure 2 shows the whole sweep. A true time constant of 1 hour gave the same 89 percent; at 3 hours the share fell to 22 percent, and at 12 and 48 hours to zero, with fitted values of 11.5 and 37.6 hours. The schedule measures time constants of about 3 hours and longer and folds everything faster into one floor. Sampling theory predicts this; the simulation sizes it for this schedule.

Three further timescale predictions did not hold. A model with two timescales beat one on each person's held-out prompts for 50 to 60 percent of people, where we had predicted at most half; people simulated with one timescale on the same prompt times picked two 46 to 51 percent of the time, so the comparison is close to a coin flip and supports no claim either way. In the 37 people with records of 60 days or more, the median share of variance arriving within a day was 0.72 (interquartile range 0.64 to 0.84) against a predicted range of 0.3 to 0.7, a narrow miss. A two-component mixture was preferred over one on that share (BIC -20.3 against -14.8), against our prediction of a continuum; a cluster of people at the floor beside a spread above it would give the same preference, and that was not tested. As predicted, 27 percent of those 37 people could not be told from their own shuffled series.

The other series

The two animation loops met two of their four predictions: every change point repeated at the same frame in the next loop, and every feature found repeated with the loop. A mode-finding method missed one loop's period because its window of 80 frames was shorter than the 288-frame loop. The forest inventory series, 14 and 12 annual values, are too short for any of the tests; a first run labelled them drifting through a software fault on short series, which was fixed and the faulty output kept. Oregon's mortality share was 0.077 to 0.096 from 2011 to 2020 and 0.125, 0.143, 0.153 and 0.178 from 2021 to 2024. Each year measures a different panel of plots, so this is a description and no test.

Discussion

The forecast result is the cleanest and the least surprising. A crowd's probability for the outcome that happens rises over a question's life, slowly more often than in jumps. Any stationary summary of a forecast series, such as one autocorrelation for the whole question, averages over a process that is changing throughout.

For mood the supported statement is narrower than our write-up first made it. On continuous sliders, a quarter to two fifths of people show a level change or a drifting coefficient beyond an AR(1) with Gaussian noise, each test taken alone. A rejection means "more than AR(1) with a Gaussian marginal", which a long-memory or skewed process also produces. On coarse rating scales the change-point test mostly detected the scale. A researcher fitting one autoregressive model per person to several weeks of slider data should expect it to be wrong in form for a sizeable minority, and should not use a variance-based change-point cost on a 5-point scale.

The sampling result agrees with the simulation literature cited above [5, 6]: a schedule of prompts hours apart cannot recover a process that runs in minutes. Our addition is the size for one common design. With five prompts a day, a person whose feelings turn over within the hour is indistinguishable from a person who is half noise. Measuring that person needs a continuous signal.

The defect has a general form. A surrogate count sets the smallest p value a test can return, and a threshold at or below that value makes the test silent. The count has to be chosen from the threshold.

Limitations

  • Eleven of 20 predictions did not hold, and one that held could not have failed. A further one, that the inventory series are too short to test, is a statement about series length.
  • The switching test could not fire. No switching result exists, in either direction.
  • The headline shares have no intervals. They rest on 113, 70, 34 and 373 people and 238 questions.
  • The surrogates copy mean, variance and lag-1 memory only, with Gaussian noise. Bounded probabilities and rating scales sit outside that family.
  • The tie correction and the switching rerun were exploratory and made after the results were seen.
  • The stationarity tests order prompts and ignore the gaps between them, including nights.
  • The aliasing result comes from simulation of one model and one schedule, and follows from sampling theory. It missed its own bar of 90 percent at two of three values.
  • That forecasts move toward the answer is expected, and the series was defined as the probability of the realised outcome.
  • Forest inventory years are different plot panels; those numbers are descriptive.
  • Scoring was done by our own code and our own reading of the result files, and was not blind.

Evidence

Mixed. Eleven of 20 predictions did not hold. The switching test used 19 surrogates, so its smallest p was 0.05 and its rule could not fire: no switching result exists. The aliasing prediction missed its 90 percent bar at two of three values (89, 98, 89 percent of 100 runs). The within-day variance share was 0.72 against an upper bound of 0.7. On 1 to 5 and 1 to 7 scales the change-point rates of 70 and 47 percent fell to 12 and 18 percent once ties were broken.

Figures

These are the paper's own figures, numbered as in the PDF, and each "Figure" reference in the text points here. The charts on this page redraw the same results from the result files and carry their own numbers.

Each prediction is scored as written. Values are read from the study's result files.

items.title: F39: Music with long ringing tails and dark spectra is rated calmer, and also less pleasant
items.description: Across 502 held-out music clips by 270 artists, sounds that ring on longer and lean toward low frequencies were rated lower in arousal, beyond loudness, genre and year. We forecast they would also be rated more pleasant; they were rated less pleasant instead.

What this means for a reader

Music that rings on and sounds dark is heard as calmer, across every genre in the set. It is also rated less pleasant. If you build a playlist to relax, music with these two properties was rated calmer, and it was also rated less pleasant; the study did not change the sound of any clip, so it does not show that adding them causes either. The ratings describe what listeners judged the music to express, and say nothing about what it made them feel.

Objection

Tail is a proxy for instrumentation and production style, since timbre was not held; DEAM is short clips with crowd perceived-emotion ratings. The register lists a third point, on where the audio copies came from, and its text is cut short there.

What would change the call. Replicate on a second rated corpus, add a blind listening test with tail manipulated at fixed instrumentation, and measure felt calm.

From the strongest objection recorded in our publication register.

Abstract

People often reach for music with long, ringing sustain and a warm, dark tone when they want to wind down. We asked whether those two properties of the sound go with how calm and how pleasant listeners judge a clip to be, beyond loudness, genre and year. On 1,744 rated 45-second clips from the DEAM dataset, we measured how long each note rings after its onset and how far the spectrum leans toward low frequencies, and tested the link on 502 clips by 270 artists kept out of all fitting. A calm index built from a longer tail and a darker spectrum correlates -0.394 with rated arousal (95% interval -0.476 to -0.304), with loudness, genre and year held fixed.c1 Adding the two measures raises held-out explained variance in arousal by 0.110 (0.034 to 0.182).c2 We forecast that the same sounds would be rated more pleasant; they were rated less pleasant, -0.375 (-0.455 to -0.280), and -0.227 with arousal also held.c3 In these ratings, calm sits closer to subdued than to content.
