Introduction and motivation

The acoustic side of musical emotion has mostly been studied on single notes. Eerola, Ferrer and Alluri [2] had listeners rate isolated instrument sounds for valence, tension and energy and found that features such as attack time and spectral brightness tracked those ratings. Korsmit and colleagues [3] pooled several such datasets and found that some acoustic links held across them and others did not. These studies hold the musical context fixed by removing it.

Reverberation has its own small literature. Mo, Wu and Horner [4] added reverberation to eight wind and bowed-string sounds and found that its length shifted their emotional character, most strongly toward romantic and mysterious and less toward sad. Wilkie and Harrison [5] varied reverberation time in recorded music heard over headphones and found that longer reverberation raised ratings of sublimity, nostalgia and wonder while leaving unease and vitality about the same.

We asked a question one step further from the laboratory: in full mixed music by many artists, does a longer ringing tail after each note and a darker spectrum go with lower rated arousal, beyond loudness and genre, on artists the analysis never saw? We also asked, more tentatively, whether the same sounds would be rated as more pleasant. The decision this informs is which acoustic controls a music tool can trust to move perceived calm, and what else they move with it.

Searches run on 9 November 2026 found the DEAM benchmark paper [1], the studies above and related work on isolated tones. They returned nothing that measures an onset-locked tail in full mixed music. That is what the searches returned; it does not show that no such study exists.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, a dated plan hash-locked before any result is seen, was written on 29 October 2026 and locked at 16:24 UTC. Acoustic features were extracted from the audio before the lock. No rating was joined to any feature before it; while checking copies of the annotation file, the first two rows (two clips) were seen and nothing else of the ratings.

The plan fixed the data, the measures that had passed an instrument check, the artist split, the controls, the predictions and the rule for each verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition, which is the pass or fail of one preregistered rule set read off by code. Every rule is fail-closed: a verdict passes only when all of its rules hold. The predictions were:

  • P1, primary: the calm index correlates negatively with arousal on the test clips, its interval excludes zero, and it lies below the 5th percentile of a shuffle control.
  • P2a and P2b: the tail alone correlates negatively with arousal, and the spectral slope alone positively, each with an interval excluding zero.
  • P3, stated as possible: the calm index correlates positively with valence, its interval excludes zero, and it lies above the 95th percentile of a shuffle control.
  • P4: adding the tail and the slope to the controls raises explained variance in arousal on the test clips, with an interval above zero and above the 95th percentile of a shuffle control.
  • P5: P1 still holds with tempo and spectral entropy added to the controls.

The forecasts written before the run were a P1 correlation near -0.15 (range -0.05 to -0.30) and a P3 correlation near +0.05, likely to fail. The same plan also held two questionnaire tests on music absorption and personality. Their values were seen before the lock through a test of the analysis code, so they are not blind tests, and they are left out of this paper.

One change came after the lock and before feature extraction: the audio loader switched from an FFT resampler to a polyphase one. The instrument check's synthetic clips are made at the analysis rate and never pass through the loader, so the check is unaffected.

Data and provenance

The data are DEAM, the MediaEval Database for Emotional Analysis in Music [1]. It holds Creative Commons music from the Free Music Archive, Jamendo and MedleyDB, with ratings from crowd workers. The release is licensed CC BY-NC, non-commercial use with attribution; this paper reports statistics only and redistributes no audio or ratings.

The ratings are arousal and valenceDefinition: arousal and valence psychology of emotion (the circumplex model) Two rating scales for emotion: arousal runs from calm to excited and valence from unpleasant to pleasant. In DEAM each is a nine-point scale averaged over crowd raters. Excludes named emotions such as sadness or nostalgia, which the ratings place only as points on the two scales. full definition: arousal runs from calm to excited and valence from unpleasant to pleasant, each on a nine-point scale averaged over raters for each clip. They measure perceived emotionDefinition: perceived emotion music psychology The emotion a listener judges the music to express, as opposed to the emotion the listener feels. Excludes felt or induced emotion, physiological response and any change in mood or symptoms. full definition, what a listener judges the music to express, and not what the listener feels.

We used the 1,744 clips of 45 seconds from the 2013 and 2014 rating rounds, by 899 artists. The 58 full songs from 2015 were left out because their length, rater pool and rating method differ. Genre comes from the dataset's metadata: 11 sampling genres, with one clip under another label pooled as Other.

The official host refused connections on the day of download. The audio came from a public mirror; the archive holds 1,802 files, the count the dataset paper gives, but there is no official checksum to compare it with. The per-clip annotations came from three independent public copies with identical bytes. The metadata is the official file, retrieved through the Internet Archive. The mirror's provenance is a limit, stated below.

Methods

Measures

Each clip was converted to mono at 22,050 Hz and cut to its first 45 seconds. The energy envelope is the root mean square over 256-sample windows at a 64-sample hop.

The onset-locked tailDefinition: onset-locked tail audio signal processing (our measure) For each note onset found in the energy envelope, the time constant of the envelope's decay from its peak to the next minimum, with the median taken over onsets. It follows whichever of the note's own decay and the room's decay is slower. Excludes the reverberation time of the room on its own, which this measure cannot separate in dense music. full definition is a decay time measured after each note onset. Onsets are envelope peaks at least 0.1 s apart and above the envelope's 60th percentile. For each onset, the log envelope from the peak to the next minimum is fitted by least squares against time, giving a slope bi. Each onset with a negative slope gives a decay time constant in seconds,

τi=−1bi(1)

and the tail Ttail is the median of τi over those onsets. This follows whichever of the note's own decay and the room's decay is slower. In dense music it cannot separate the two.

The spectral slopeDefinition: spectral slope audio signal processing The slope of log power against log frequency between 110 Hz and 5.5 kHz. A more negative slope means energy leans toward low frequencies and the sound is darker. Excludes pitch, loudness and the shape of the spectrum beyond its overall tilt. full definition s is the least-squares slope of log⁡10 power against log⁡10 frequency from a Welch spectrum, between 110 Hz and 5.5 kHz. A more negative slope means a darker sound.

The calm index combines the two, with each measure standardised by its mean μ and standard deviation σ on the training clips only:

C=ln⁡Ttail−μTσT−s−μsσs(2)

A higher C means a longer tail and a darker spectrum.

Split

Artists were put in a random order with a fixed seed, and 30 percent of them, with all their clips, form the held-out test setDefinition: held-out test set statistics and machine learning Data kept apart from everything that was fitted or standardised, here every clip by 30 percent of the artists, so that a result on it is a check on new material. Excludes data used to fit the model, choose a threshold or compute a scaling. full definition: 502 clips by 270 artists. The other 1,242 clips are the training set. Every verdict reads the test set.

Statistics

The controls in every confirmatory model are loudness in decibels relative to full scale, 11 genre indicators and rating year, with an intercept. The main statistic is the partial correlationDefinition: partial correlation statistics The correlation between two quantities after each has had the linear effect of a set of control variables removed by least squares. Excludes a causal effect, and any non-linear dependence on the controls. full definition: each of the two quantities is regressed on the controls by least squares, and the residuals ex and ey are correlated, with sums over the clips:

rxy=∑exey∑ex2∑ey2(3)

Residuals from a fit with an intercept have mean zero, so this is the ordinary correlation of the residuals.

The held-out R2 gainDefinition: held-out R2 gain statistics The share of variance in the test outcome explained by a model fitted on training data with the added measures, minus the same share for the model without them. Excludes the in-sample R2 of a fit, which can only grow as variables are added. full definition fits arousal on the training clips twice, once on the controls and once on the controls plus ln⁡Ttail and s, and scores both fits on the test clips:

R2=1−∑i(yi−ypred,i)2∑i(yi−ymean)2(4)
G=R12−R02(5)

where ypred is a fit's prediction for a test clip, ymean the mean test rating, R02 the test score of the controls-only fit, R12 that of the fit with the two measures, and G the gain.

Intervals are 95% intervalsDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition, the 2.5th to 97.5th percentiles of 2,000 cluster bootstrapDefinition: cluster bootstrap statistics A bootstrap that resamples whole groups, here artists with all their clips, so that clips by one artist count as one draw. Excludes a bootstrap over single clips, which treats one artist's clips as independent. full definition resamples of the test set, where whole artists are drawn with replacement.

Controls and planted checks

Instrument check on synthetic music

Before the lock, every measure was run as a planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition: synthetic music built so that the right answer is known. Each of 40 clips held 30 seconds of harmonic notes on a beat, with room decay time, note decay, attack, tempo, spectral tilt and wet mix set at random and varying at once. Each measure's median error was compared with the error of the same measure against shuffled targets. A measure counted as strong when it beat the shuffled targets' 5th percentile and its median error was at most half the shuffled median. The ratio of the two medians is in Figure 1.

The tail recovered the slower of note and room decay with an error ratio of 0.12 and a rank correlation of 0.95; the spectral slope recovered the planted tilt with 0.21 and 0.99.c4 The library's reverb-size measure failed in dense music (0.81), and the tail against room decay alone failed too (0.80), so room reverberation cannot be separated from note decay with these tools and enters no verdict. The best attack measure reached 0.55, short of strong, so attack enters no verdict either. A constant estimator, included as a false-success check, scored 1.00 and failed, as it must.

c4 observed, evidence for claim 4
The numbers in claim 4
0.12; 0.95; 0.21; 0.99 matches the result file, 2026-11-09
Chart 1
How well each sound measure recovers values planted in synthetic music.
Basis

Shuffle controls

Each controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition removes the structure under test and is scored the same way as the real data. For P1 and P3, the calm index was shuffled across test clips 1,000 times and the partial correlation recomputed each time; the spread of those draws is the null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition. For P4, the tail and slope rows were shuffled within the training set and within the test set, 1,000 times, and the whole fit repeated. Table 1 gives the bars.

Results

Figure 2 and Table 2 give the confirmatory results on the 502 test clips. A calm index built from a longer tail and a darker spectrum correlates -0.394 with rated arousal (95% interval -0.476 to -0.304), with loudness, genre and year held fixed.c1 That is far outside the shuffle range and about 2.6 times the size forecast. Each measure carries the link on its own: the tail at -0.301 and the slope at +0.324, where a higher slope means a brighter sound.

Adding the two measures raises held-out explained variance in arousal by 0.110 (0.034 to 0.182).c2 The controls alone explain 0.160 of the test variance. With tempo and spectral entropy added to the controls, the calm index still correlates -0.343 with arousal.

We forecast that the same sounds would be rated more pleasant; they were rated less pleasant, -0.375 (-0.455 to -0.280), and -0.227 with arousal also held.c3 P3 failed on all three of its rules. This is an honest nullDefinition: honest null research method (our usage) A working test that found no effect beyond a stated bound, a forecast that failed, or an error of our own found and fixed, reported with the same weight as a positive result. Excludes a void run, and a result left unpublished because it was negative. full definition of the forecast, reported with the same weight as the passes: arousal and valence correlate 0.54 on the test clips, so part of the valence drop rides on arousal, and the rest (-0.227, interval -0.312 to -0.123) does not.

Post hoc checks

The following were run after the verdicts and carry no verdict. In busy music the next onset cuts each tail short, so the tail could stand in for note rate. Note rate has a median of 4.9 events per second and correlates -0.17 with the log tail. With note rate added to the controls, P1 is -0.370 (-0.444 to -0.284) and the tail alone -0.285; with note rate, tempo and entropy all added, P1 is -0.324.

Inside each of the 11 genres, on the 1,743 clips they hold (one clip tagged Other is left out), the calm index correlates negatively with arousal, from -0.25 in hip-hop to -0.62 in international music.c5 Figure 3 shows each genre.

c5 observed, evidence for claim 5
The numbers in claim 5
11; 1,743; -0.25; -0.62 matches the result file, 2026-11-09
Chart 4
The same link inside each genre (post hoc, run after the verdicts).
Basis

On the whole sample, P1 is -0.414 and the valence correlation -0.395. Among exploratory measures on the test clips, the failed reverb-size measure reads in the same direction as the tail (partial correlation with arousal -0.237), and so does the envelope's autocorrelation decay (-0.198); neither can be read as room reverberation. Rise time shows no relation (0.024), which is a null of a weak instrument and says nothing about attack itself.

Discussion

The arousal result agrees with what single-note studies found for brightness [2] [3] and extends it to full mixes by many artists, on artists held out from fitting, with a tail measure checked on synthetic music before use. The size, about -0.39, is larger than we forecast. It survives tempo, spectral entropy and note rate, and holds inside every genre.

The valence result is the more interesting one. A reader might expect calm music to be rated pleasant. In DEAM it is rated less pleasant, and the drop is not only the shared variance with arousal. Wilkie and Harrison [5] found that longer reverberation raised sublimity and nostalgia and left unease and vitality about the same, and Mo, Wu and Horner [4] found reverberation moved instrument sounds toward romantic and mysterious and, less strongly, sad. Both fit a reading in which long dark tails carry a wistful or melancholy calm.

For a music tool, the practical reading is that a sustain or darkness control may move perceived calm and lower perceived pleasantness together, which a test that changes the sound would have to confirm. A tool that offers calm through these controls should say so.

The tierDefinition: tier our publication register How ready a finding is to publish: A candidate, B signal worth expanding (B* strong), C internal, D honest null worth reporting, E not reliable as it stands. Excludes a measure of how large or how true an effect is. full definition B* places this as a strong signal worth expanding. Three things would raise it: a second rated corpus, a listening test that changes the tail with instrumentation held fixed, and ratings of felt calm.

Limitation

What this means for a reader

Adding more of the same kind of measurement helps, then stops helping long before the data's own noise would stop it. The gap closes when something different arrives, most often a record of how the same thing behaved before. If a team says it can predict an outcome once it measures enough, ask how close its current model sits to the outcome's measurement noise, and what kind of variable it has not yet measured.

Objection

Ridge and logit may leave signal that a nonlinear model finds, so a stall may be the model class; datasets are a convenience sample; DEAM rater count is assumed and the ceilings are bounds.

What would change the call. Rerun with nonlinear learners and a preregistered tree ceiling on fresh splits; leave out the private image collection; add a domain from outside our own records.

From the strongest objection recorded in our publication register.

Abstract

A common hope says that measuring enough things about a system lets you predict it. We tested that hope on public data against the best score each target's own measurement noise allows. Variables were added in random orders and the model refitted and scored on held-out cases, for six targets with a measurable ceiling: tree growth, next-beep mood, music valence and arousal ratings, forecaster accuracy and a similarity task. Held-out skill rose with added variables in every target and beat a shuffled-target control in every target.c1 Only the similarity task, whose variables were learned from the same task, reached its ceiling (0.985 of the way); mood, valence, arousal and forecaster accuracy stopped at 0.65, 0.54, 0.46 and 0.18, and the tree ceiling estimator failed.c2 The largest gains came from a different kind of variable: past accuracy lifted forecasters from 0.131 to 0.360 and prior growth lifted trees from 0.396 to 0.639.c3 Both preregistered forecasts for the claim failed. Two toys with every variable known set hard limits: chaos returns forecast time only logarithmically in precision, and a published forecast that people react to can defeat itself.

Introduction and motivation

How predictable an outcome is, and how much of that predictability a model captures, are two separate questions. Salganik and colleagues [1] gave 160 teams a rich birth-cohort dataset and asked them to predict six life outcomes; the best predictions were only slightly better than a simple benchmark, and error depended more on which family was predicted than on the method. That study measured how far models got. It did not set the result against a ceiling from the outcome's own noise.

In neuroscience the noise ceilingDefinition: noise ceiling measurement theory and computational neuroscience The best held-out score any model could reach on a target, given how far repeated measurements of that same target disagree. It is estimated from the data's own repeats. Excludes the best score reached so far by any model, and a bound set by missing variables. full definition is routine: the best held-out score any model could reach on a target, given how far repeated measurements of that same target disagree. Lage-Castellanos and colleagues [2] compare ways to estimate it for brain responses. Hebart and colleagues [3] reported that their similarity model explained most of the explainable variance in human odd-one-out choices, against a ceiling set by repeated triplets.

For forecasters, Himmelstein, Atanasov and Budescu [5] found that psychometric traits predict future accuracy when little track record exists and that past accuracy takes over as it accumulates. That points to one kind of variable that may close a gap others leave open.

We asked whether held-out skill reaches the noise ceiling when enough measured variables are added, across unrelated domains in one design. Searches run on 9 November 2026 found the work above, and a preprint on the PISA 2022 school assessment [10] that reads predictive R2 against a ceiling set by measurement noise inside one domain. A search for a cross-domain comparison of skill curves against noise ceilings returned nothing closer; that is what the search returned, and it does not show that no such study exists. The decision this informs is where effort goes when a prediction stalls: more of the same variables, a different kind of variable, or acceptance of a hard limit.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, a dated plan hash-locked before any result is seen, was written on 29 October 2026 before any model in the study was fitted to real data. Data caches were built first and printed row counts only. Several of the datasets had been used in earlier studies of ours, which the plan states so that it is not mistaken for blindness.

The plan fixed the targets, variables, splits, models, ceilings and the rule for each verdictDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition, the pass or fail of one preregistered rule set read off by code. The predictions were:

  • P1, ceiling reached: a target is at ceiling when its all-variable held-out skill above chance is at least 0.8 of its ceiling above chance. Pass if at least 4 of the 6 targets with a ceiling are at ceiling.
  • P2, unmeasured variables: a target's plateau moves when its named strong variable adds at least 0.02 skill over all base variables and the result exceeds the upper 97.5th percentile of the fitted plateau. Pass if at least 3 of 7 targets move.
  • P3, chaos: in the Lorenz-63 toy, the forecast horizon is linear in the log of precision (linear R2 at least 0.98), its slope is within 25 percent of theory, and the gain over the last three decades is between 0.75 and 1.33 times the gain over the first three.
  • P4, reflexivity: five rules on a toy crowd, listed in Appendix A.
  • P5, overfitting control: every target beats its shuffled-target control, and a deliberately overfitted fit behaves as expected (Appendix A).

The plan also held an identification test on a private image collection. That test, and the seventh P2 target built on the same collection, are left out of this paper; the P2 count below includes that target because the verdict was computed over seven.

The corrected rerun

The first run, on 29 October 2026, gave forecaster accuracy a held-out R2 of -1.686. The cause was a pipeline fault: 84 of the 1,349 forecaster variables were nearly constant among the training forecasters, so their scaled values in held-out forecasters became enormous. A second preregistration file, hashed after the first run had been read, made one change: every scaled variable is clipped to the range -5 to 5. Domains, splits, seed, models and verdict rules stayed the same. The second run is the primary result. It is a corrected rerun and not a blind one. Outside forecasters, the two runs agree within 0.01.

Data and provenance

Five public sources supply six targets with a ceiling and one without:

  • Tree growth and tree death: the USDA Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis [8], remeasured trees in Washington and Oregon, a US government dataset. Growth is annual diameter growth of survivors from the second to the third measurement (73,553 trees); death is death between them (90,427 trees, 18.6 percent died). 42 variables measured at the second visit cover size, crown, damage, site, stand, location and species.
  • Mood: openESM dataset 0062 [9], experience sampling with repeated short questionnaires (beeps) during the day, licensed CC BY 4.0. Target: rated happiness at the next beep of the same day, from 31 items at the current beep (8,141 cases).
  • Music valence and arousal: DEAM static ratings [6], 1,744 clips, licensed CC BY-NC (non-commercial use with attribution); this paper reports statistics only. 22 variables: sound measures, genre flags and set flags.
  • Forecaster accuracy: Good Judgment Project data [7], licensed CC0. Target: each forecaster's mean per-question z-scored Brier scoreDefinition: Brier score forecast verification (meteorology) The mean squared difference between a probability forecast and the outcome coded 0 or 1. Lower is better. Excludes measures that score only whether the most likely outcome happened. full definition, the mean squared gap between a probability forecast and the 0 or 1 outcome, on the even half of their questions (2,120 forecasters with at least 10 scored questions in each half). 1,349 individual-difference variables.
  • Similarity triplets: THINGS odd-one-out choices with the 66 published object dimensions [4], used under the publisher's terms. In each triplet a person picks the image least like the other two; chance is one in three.

Methods

Curves

For each target the variables were added in 8 random orders and one informed order (by absolute training-set correlation with the target), at about 14 counts from one variable to all of them. At each count the model was refitted on training cases and scored on held-out cases. Held-out skillDefinition: held-out skill statistics and machine learning A model's score on cases kept apart from fitting: R2 for numbers, the area under the ROC curve for yes-or-no outcomes, and accuracy for triplet choices. Excludes the score on the data used to fit the model. full definition is R2 for numeric targets, AUCDefinition: AUC statistics (signal detection) The area under the ROC curve: the chance that a randomly chosen positive case is ranked above a randomly chosen negative one, with 0.5 for guessing. Excludes accuracy at any one threshold. full definition (the chance a random positive case is ranked above a random negative one) for tree death, and accuracy for triplets.

Models were ridge regressionDefinition: ridge regression statistics Least squares with a penalty on the size of the coefficients, chosen by leave-one-out error, so that many variables can be fitted without chasing noise. Excludes non-linear models such as boosted trees or neural networks. full definition with a leave-one-out penalty for numeric targets, L2 logistic regression for tree death and a conditional logit for triplets. Medians, scaling and clipping came from the training cases only. Held-out cases were whole plots for trees, each person's last 30 percent of beeps for mood, 30 percent of artists for music, 30 percent of forecasters, and between-subject repeated triplets for the similarity task.

Ceilings and shares

Each ceiling comes from the target's own repeats:

  • Mood, by parallel formsDefinition: parallel forms psychometrics Two items meant to measure the same thing, answered at the same time. Their correlation estimates reliability, here happy and cheerful at the same beep. Excludes the same item repeated later, which also picks up real change. full definition: the correlation of happy with cheerful at the same beep, over 11,472 beeps. If the two items differ in what they measure, this is a lower bound, which makes the ceiling easier to reach.
  • Forecasters, by split-half reliabilityDefinition: split-half reliability psychometrics The correlation between scores computed on two halves of the same items, here a forecaster's accuracy on the odd and the even questions. Excludes agreement between different people or different occasions. full definition: the correlation of accuracy on odd and even questions.
  • Similarity: leave-one-out majority agreement on 1,000 repeated triplets (36,401 trials).
  • Music, from rater spread, with sd the rater standard deviation of a clip, n the number of raters and m the clip's mean rating over clips:
c=1−mean(sd2/n)var(m)(1)

The number of raters was not stated in the files we had; n = 10 was assumed, with n = 5 reported beside it.

  • Tree growth: the error variance of a remeasured increment was estimated from the shrinking increments of survivors, on the assumption that true growth is never negative.

The share of ceilingDefinition: share of ceiling our usage Held-out skill above chance divided by the noise ceiling above chance. 1 means the model scores as well as the measurements allow. Excludes the raw skill, which is not comparable across targets. full definition puts targets on one scale, with s the held-out skill, s0 its chance level and c the ceiling:

q=s−s0c−s0(2)

For the four numeric targets with a valid ceiling, one minus R2 splits into measurement noise, 1−c, and reliable variance the variables do not reach, c−s.

Plateau fit

A saturating curveDefinition: saturating curve curve fitting The curve s(k) = a k / (k + h) fitted to skill above chance against the number of variables k, where a is the level it approaches. Excludes a forecast of skill with variables not in the dataset. full definition was fitted to skill above chance against the number of variables k:

s(k)−s0=akk+h(3)

It was fitted to the mean random-order curve, and to each of the 8 orders separately; the spread of a over the orders gives the plateau's interval. The fit bound was 2.0, and for curves that had not flattened the upper end of the interval reached it.

Strong variables

Each target had a strong variableDefinition: strong variable our usage in this study A variable of a different kind from the base set, named for each target before the run: past behaviour of the same unit, or a human rating of a related quantity. Excludes one more variable of the kind already in the base set. full definition named before the run, of a different kind from the base set: prior diameter growth for trees, the person's mean training happiness for mood, the other dimension's human rating for music, and accuracy on the other half of the questions for forecasters.

Toys with known answers

The Lorenz-63 system was run with an exact model from 100 states on its attractor, with the starting state measured with error δ per coordinate from 10−1 to 10−12. The forecast horizonDefinition: forecast horizon dynamical systems (chaos) The time until a forecast from a slightly wrong starting state differs from the truth by more than a set tolerance. In a chaotic system it grows with the logarithm of the starting precision. Excludes errors from a wrong model, which the toy does not have. full definition is the first time the error norm exceeds 1. Theory gives the slope per tenfold gain in precision as

ln⁡10λ≈2.54(4)

with λ = 0.906 the largest Lyapunov exponent.

The crowd toy tests a reflexive forecastDefinition: reflexive forecast economics and social science A published forecast that the forecast population reads and reacts to, so that publishing it changes the outcome it predicts. Excludes a forecast kept private from the people it describes. full definition, one that the forecast population reads and reacts to. Each of N members attends when ui+β(c−F)>0, where ui is the member's own taste, c a fixed threshold and F the published forecast of the attending share; β sets how strongly members react. The forecaster measures k members' tastes exactly. An unpublished forecast is never seen; a naive one is the unpublished forecast published anyway; a fixed-point forecast solves for the share that would attend given the forecast itself.

Controls and planted checks

Every target was refitted on shuffled training labels 20 times and scored on the real held-out labels. This controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition removes the link between variables and target. The 95th percentile of those 20 draws, the top of the null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition, is the bar each real score must clear. The similarity control starts its weights at 1, so a fit that stops early keeps the raw embedding similarity, and its bar sits above chance for that reason.

The Lorenz toy is a planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition for the chaos limit, since its answer is known from theory. A deliberate overfit forms a second check: 150 forecasters fitted by plain least squares with up to all 1,349 variables, which should fit the training data almost perfectly and fail held out.

The tree-growth ceiling estimator failed. It returned -3.96, because a few gross shrinkages dominate the mean of squared negative increments. It is kept as preregistered, and the tree target counts as not at ceiling.

Results

Held-out skill rose with added variables in every target and beat a shuffled-target control in every target.c1 The highest control bar among the numeric targets was 0.013 R2; tree death's was 0.531 AUC against 0.686, and the similarity task's was 0.439 accuracy against 0.642 on its validation triplets.

items.title: F508: Shannon's 1951 letter statistics hold on old and new English; his third-order value reads high
items.description: Shannon's first- and second-order entropy figures for English letters match ours within 0.12 bits on books from 1788 to 1925 and on present-day Wikipedia. His third-order figure sits 0.23 to 0.40 bits above ours, and an n-gram reader never gets near his 1.3 bits per letter.

What this means for a reader

Shannon's 1951 table is still quoted as a fact about English. The rows built from single letters and letter pairs hold on text two centuries apart. The row built from letter triples comes out about a third of a bit lower than his, so quote the higher rows with care. A reader that knows only letter counts stays well above his 1.3 bits per letter. His figure describes a human reader who brings knowledge of words and of the world.

Objection

Wikipedia is the only new text, so era, genre and topic stay tangled in every new-text row.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

In 1951 Claude Shannon published a table of how many bits each letter of printed English carries when the reader knows 0, 1 or 2 letters before it. We recomputed that table on three pooled corpora: books from 1788 to 1859, fiction from 1892 to 1925, and present-day Wikipedia featured articles, each reduced to 26 letters and a space. The single-letter and letter-pair rows match Shannon's within 0.12 bits on all three corpora.c1 His third-order value of 3.1 bits sits 0.39 bits above ours on the old books and 0.23 above ours on Wikipedia.c2 We also trained a letter-count reader on each corpus and scored it on held-out text. With the corrected split, the reader needs 1.63 to 2.41 bits per letter on its own kind of text and never reaches Shannon's 1.3.c3 Within fiction, a change of era costs the reader 0.10 and 0.25 bits per letter, and a change from fiction to The Federalist in the same era costs 0.44, so the preregistered claim that era costs more than genre failed.c4 A planted Markov text with known entropy was recovered within 0.004 bits.

Introduction

Shannon [1] described two ways to measure how predictable English is. The first counts letters. Let the text be reduced to 26 letters and a space, so 27 symbols. The N-gram entropyDefinition: N-gram entropy information theory, after Shannon 1951 The uncertainty of the next letter when the N minus 1 letters before it are known, averaged over the text. Shannon wrote it F with a subscript N, so F1 uses single-letter counts, F2 one letter of context and F3 two. Excludes the entropy of the language as a whole, which is the limit as N grows. full definition is the uncertainty of the next letter when the N minus 1 letters before it are known; F1 uses single-letter frequencies, F2 knows one letter back and F3 two. All are in bits per letterDefinition: bits per letter information theory The average number of binary digits needed to write down each letter of a text under a given model of the text. One bit halves the number of equally likely choices, so 4.75 bits per letter is the cost of picking blindly among 27 symbols. Excludes a count of bytes in a file, and any statement about meaning. full definition, the average number of yes-or-no answers needed per letter. Blind choice among 27 symbols costs 4.75 bits. His table for 27 symbols reads 4.76, 4.03, 3.32 and 3.1 for F0 to F3, and 2.14 bits per letter from word statistics. The second way asks a person to predict the next letter of a passage. From that experiment he put an upper bound near 1.3 bits per letter on the entropy of English when 100 letters of context are known.

Later work kept both routes. Cover and King [2] replaced guessing with betting, so a subject's stake on each letter gives a probability, and reported estimates near 1.3 bits per character. Brown and colleagues [3] built a word trigram model, measured its cross-entropy on a balanced sample of English and gave an upper bound of 1.75 bits per character. Takahira, Tanaka-Ishii and Debowski [4] compressed large corpora in six languages with prediction by partial matching [5] and extrapolated the code length to infinitely long text to estimate the entropy rate itself.

Those studies push the estimate of the entropy rate downward. Our question is narrower. Do the low rows of Shannon's table, which are easy to recompute, still hold on text of other eras and kinds? And when a reader built from letter counts is trained on one kind of text and reads another, which costs more, a change of era or a change of genre?

Preregistration and design

A preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition is a dated plan fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen. This study had two. The first was locked on 1 November 2026 at 08:13 UTC. It named the corpora, the statistics, the reader, the planted text, the control, nine numeric forecasts and the kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition, a rule that decides against the run with no judgement after it. The decision it informed was which claims in material we had saved still hold when the text or the reader changes, and so which ones we can reuse.

The first run had a fault of ours. The code promised in a comment to shuffle the books before splitting training text from test text and never did. The old corpus's test text was therefore all The Federalist, and the mid corpus's all Fitzgerald, so era was read through one book. We wrote a second preregistration to fix the split and locked it at 08:20 UTC the same day. It was not blind: it was written after the first run had been read. The first run stands as recorded, and both are reported here.

Claims and kill condition, as locked:

  • Claim 1, first run: the 1951 table holds on present data within 0.15 bits for F1, 0.2 for F2 and 0.3 for F3.
  • Claim 2, first run: the reader reaches 1.3 bits per letter. The forecast said it would not.
  • Claim, second run: era costs a reader more than genre does. The forecast said it would not.
  • Void if the reader misses the entropy of the planted text by more than 0.1 bits.

Data and provenance

The books are public-domain texts from Project Gutenberg [6]: The Federalist (1788), Austen (1813), Bronte (1847), Melville (1851) and Dickens (1859) make the old corpus; Doyle (1892), Joyce (1914 and 1916), Wodehouse (1920) and Fitzgerald (1925) make the mid corpus. The new corpus is a sample of Wikipedia featured articles [7], about 0.77 MB, fetched through the Wikipedia API on 1 November 2026. Wikipedia text is licensed CC BY-SA; we use it for statistics only and release no text from it. The source record names each file and its size; the text files themselves were not hashed at download, so a reproduction may draw slightly different editions.

Each text was cut to the Project Gutenberg start and end markers, lowercased, and every run of characters outside a to z was replaced by a single space. In the first run each corpus takes an equal slice from each of its books, 750,000 characters in all, and the first 600,000 train the reader. In the second run every book gives its first 80 percent to training and its last 20 percent to test, and the sets are kept apart by genre: old fiction (four novels), mid fiction (five works), old nonfiction (The Federalist) and new nonfiction (Wikipedia). Each set has 600,000 training characters, except Wikipedia with 588,712, and 100,000 test characters.

Shannon's own test passages are not openly available, so we compare against his printed table. The table values were recorded in the first preregistration from a scan of the 1951 paper.

Methods

The letter statistics

For a block bi of N minus 1 letters and a next letter j, the N-gram entropy is

FN=−∑i,jp(bi,j)log⁡2p(j|bi)(1)

with probabilities taken as relative frequencies in the pooled corpus. This is a plug-in estimateDefinition: plug-in estimate statistics An entropy computed by putting the observed relative frequencies of a sample straight into the entropy formula, with no correction for the size of the sample. Excludes corrected estimators that add a term for unseen or rare events. full definition: observed frequencies go straight into the formula with no correction for sample size. F0 is log⁡227, 4.755 bits.

The word-based figure divides the entropy of the word frequency distribution, Hw, by the mean number of characters per word including the following space, L:

Fw=HwL(2)

Shannon reached his 2.14 by extending a fitted Zipf's lawDefinition: Zipf's law quantitative linguistics The observation that the frequency of a word falls roughly in inverse proportion to its rank in the frequency list. Excludes an exact law that holds for every word or every text. full definition tail, the rule that a word's frequency falls in inverse proportion to its rank. We counted words directly.

The reader

The reader is a context modelDefinition: context model data compression and statistical language modelling A model that predicts the next symbol from counts of what followed the same few preceding symbols in training text, blending long and short contexts. Prediction by partial matching (PPM) is the classic form. Excludes models that use word meaning, grammar or knowledge outside the letter counts. full definition: it predicts the next letter from counts of what followed the same preceding letters in training text, in the manner of prediction by partial matching. It blends contexts of length 0 to 6. Starting from a uniform distribution over 27 symbols, each context length k with nk counts over dk distinct next letters updates the estimate as

pk(x)=ck(x)+dkpk−1(x)nk+dk(3)

where ck(x) is the count of letter x after that context. The reader is scored by its log lossDefinition: log loss information theory and machine learning; also called cross-entropy The average of minus the base-2 logarithm of the probability a model gave to the letter that came next, in bits per letter. It is the length of the code an ideal coder driven by the model would write. Excludes the share of letters guessed right, and the entropy of the text itself, which log loss can only bound from above. full definition, the average of minus log⁡2 of the probability it gave to the letter that came next:

R=−1n∑ilog⁡2q(xi|ci)(4)

over n letters of held-out textDefinition: held-out text statistics and machine learning Text kept apart from the text a model was trained on and used only to score it. Excludes any text whose counts entered the model. full definition, text the reader was not trained on. The first run scores 40,000 letters of each test text and the second 30,000.

The reader also plays Shannon's guessing gameDefinition: guessing game information theory, after Shannon 1951 A reader guesses the next letter in order of preference until right. The share of letters found at the first, second and later guesses gives an upper and a lower bound on the entropy. Excludes a direct measure of the probabilities a reader holds. full definition: it ranks the 27 symbols and we record the rank r of the true letter. With qr the share of letters found at rank r, Shannon's upper and lower bounds are

U=−∑rqrlog⁡2qr(5)
B=∑rr(qr−qr+1)log⁡2r(6)

Transfer penalties

A transfer penaltyDefinition: transfer penalty our usage, from machine learning practice on domain shift The extra log loss a reader pays on another kind of text compared with a reader trained on that kind of text, both scored on the same held-out passage. Excludes the difference in difficulty between two texts read by their own readers. full definition is the extra log loss a reader pays on another kind of text, against a reader trained on that kind, on the same held-out passage. With R(a,b) the log loss of the reader trained on set a reading the test text of set b,

D(a,b)=R(a,b)−R(b,b)(7)

The era penalty in fiction uses a and b from old and mid fiction. The genre penalty uses old fiction and The Federalist, which share an era.

Controls and planted checks

A planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition is data built so the right answer is known. Ours is a random order-2 Markov chainDefinition: order-2 Markov chain probability A random text in which each symbol depends only on the two symbols before it, through a fixed table of probabilities, so its entropy per symbol can be computed exactly. Excludes real text, whose dependence reaches further back. full definition over 27 symbols, 2,000,000 symbols long, with transition probabilities drawn from a Dirichlet distribution. Its entropy per symbol is 2.673 bits by eq. 1 with N of 3. A reader of context length 2 was trained on the first half of the chain and scored on 20,000 later symbols. It missed the true entropy by 0.004 bits, against a kill threshold of 0.1.c5 The void condition did not fire.

c5 observed, evidence for claim 5
The numbers in claim 5
0.004; 0.1 matches the result file, 2026-11-09
Chart 1
Does the reader measure an entropy that is known in advance?
Basis
observed: measured in this study, with a result file

A controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition is a version of the data with the structure under test removed and scored the same way. Here the held-out test text has its characters shuffled 20 times, 4,000 letters each, and the trained reader reads each shuffle. The real text should cost far less than any shuffle. In the first run the shuffles cost a mean of 8.51 bits per letter against 2.73 for the real Wikipedia text; in the second, 9.26 against 1.93 for old fiction. The shuffles cost more than 4.75 bits because the reader is confident and wrong on scrambled text. The real text beat all 20 shuffles in both runs. The p value from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition, p=(k+1)/(n+1) with k shuffles at or below the real loss out of n, is 0.048, the smallest value 20 draws allow.

Results

The table

Table 1 and Figure 1 set Shannon's table against ours. The first run computed the letter statistics on each pooled corpus.

The single-letter and letter-pair rows match Shannon's within 0.12 bits on all three corpora.c1 The largest of those gaps is F2 on Wikipedia, 0.120. His third-order value of 3.1 bits sits 0.39 bits above ours on the old books and 0.23 above ours on Wikipedia.c2 The first-run verdict on the old table failed on that row alone, and the verdict on the new table passed, since 0.228 is inside the 0.3 bound. The word-based figure is 0.29 to 0.39 bits below his. Words in the Wikipedia sample are longer, 5.92 characters with the space against 5.41 in the old books, and their frequency distribution carries 10.34 bits per word against 9.74.

The reader

In the first run the reader trained on the old corpus needed 2.13 bits per letter on the old held-out text, inside the forecast band of 1.85 to 2.35. Because of the faulty split, that held-out text was all The Federalist. The guessing game gave bounds of 1.34 and 2.35 by eqs. 6 and 5, and the reader's first guess was right on 58 percent of letters. The claim that this reader reaches 1.3 bits failed, as forecast.

The second run, with the split fixed, gives the matrix in Figure 2. With the corrected split, the reader needs 1.63 to 2.41 bits per letter on its own kind of text and never reaches Shannon's 1.3.c3 The Federalist is the easiest text for its own reader, 1.63, and Wikipedia the hardest, 2.41.

Table 2 gives the transfer penalties of the second run against their forecasts.

Within fiction, a change of era costs the reader 0.10 and 0.25 bits per letter, and a change from fiction to The Federalist in the same era costs 0.44, so the preregistered claim that era costs more than genre failed.c4 We forecast that failure. A mid-fiction reader on Wikipedia pays 0.92, where era, genre and topic all change at once.

Of the numeric forecasts, 4 of 9 held in the first run and 4 of 5 held after the fix. Appendix A lists each one.

Discussion

The low rows of Shannon's table describe English letters across two centuries of text. Single-letter frequencies and letter-pair statistics differ by 0.03 and 0.09 bits between the oldest books and Wikipedia. That is the part of the table a reader can quote.

F3 is different. Our value is lower than his on every corpus, by more than our forecast allowed on the old books. We have not found the cause. Two are open, and neither was tested. A plug-in estimate falls below the true value as the number of contexts grows against the sample, and 27 squared, 729, two-letter contexts is many for 750,000 characters if rare pairs matter. Shannon's F3 also rests on letter counts from other text than ours, and a difference in the source counts would move it. Either way the third row should be quoted with its source and method.

The word-based gap fits a difference of method. Counting words directly misses the long tail of rare words that a fitted Zipf curve adds, and a missing tail lowers the entropy. We did not refit his tail to confirm it.

The reader result agrees with the line of work after Shannon [2] [3]: letter counts alone do not reach a human reader's figure. Our context model sits at 1.63 to 2.41 bits per letter on held-out text. Shannon's 1.3 is a bound on a reader who knows words, grammar and the world.

The transfer result was the condition we most wanted to vary. A reader from one era of fiction reads another era at a cost of 0.10 to 0.25 bits, and the same reader reads The Federalist at 0.44. What a text is about and how it is argued changes letter statistics more than when it was written.

Limitations

  • Wikipedia is the only new text, so era, genre and topic stay tangled in every new-text row.
  • No large language model was used as a reader. That was the change we most wanted to make, and it stays open.
  • The word-based gap may come from Shannon's fitted Zipf tail against our direct count. We did not test that.
  • The cause of the F3 gap is unknown. Sampling bias in the plug-in estimate and a difference in his source counts are both candidates, and neither was measured.
  • Shannon's own test passages are not openly available, so the comparison is with his printed table.
  • The first run's split was faulty, and the second preregistration was written after reading the first run, so it is not blind.
  • Scoring was done by our own code and was not blind.

Evidence

Held. Real texts, one new source.

Figures

These are the paper's own figures, numbered as in the PDF, and each "Figure" reference in the text points here. The charts on this page redraw the same results from the result files and carry their own numbers.

What this means for a reader

Small studies have reported that people who were maltreated as children show weaker resting coupling between the amygdala and the prefrontal cortex. In 187 adults, with the test fixed in advance, we found no association of a size that would matter, and a much larger study found the same in 1,325 adults. Treat a strong resting-state version of the claim with caution. A weak effect is still possible, two trauma subscales gave inconclusive results, and other kinds of brain measurement were not tested.

Objection

An anatomical mask, a low-pass rule for head motion (framewise displacement) used outside the single-band data it was validated on, retrospective self-report, and no positive control showing the pipeline finds a known effect.

What would change the call. Add a second open sample or functional vmPFC mask to shrink the 0.10 to 0.20 gap; add a positive control.

From the strongest objection recorded in our publication register.

Abstract

A widely discussed idea holds that childhood maltreatment weakens the coupling between the amygdala, which responds to threat, and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, which helps regulate that response. We tested one resting-state form of the idea with the analysis fixed before any questionnaire value or image was seen. The data are the Transdiagnostic Connectome Project on OpenNeuro (CC0): 241 adults with and without psychiatric diagnoses, preprocessed in full, of whom 187 met the motion and questionnaire rules. Childhood trauma scores were unrelated to amygdala-vmPFC resting connectivity in 187 adults: partial r -0.006, 95% interval -0.152 to 0.140.c1 The 90% interval, -0.129 to 0.117, lies inside -0.20 to 0.20, so effects of 0.20 or larger in size are excluded at the preregistered bound.c2 A secondary region gave r -0.025. Shuffling the trauma scores 10,000 times placed the observed value at the 47th percentile. Fifteen exploratory sensitivity analyses moved the primary r between -0.081 and 0.081, and none reached an association.c3 The emotional-neglect and physical-abuse subscale analyses, r 0.081 and -0.081, are inconclusive because their 90% intervals touch 0.20.c4 Power to detect a correlation of 0.20 was 0.77, so true effects between 0.10 and 0.20 remain open.c5

Introduction

The amygdalaDefinition: amygdala neuroanatomy A pair of almond-shaped structures deep in the temporal lobes, one per hemisphere, involved in detecting threat and in emotional learning. Excludes its separate subnuclei, which the anatomical masks here do not distinguish. full definition and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC)Definition: ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) neuroanatomy The lower middle part of the frontal lobe, linked to the regulation of emotional responses. Here defined by the Harvard-Oxford label Frontal Medial Cortex. Excludes functional definitions from a task, and the dorsal and lateral prefrontal cortex. full definition form a circuit often linked to threat and its regulation. A common hypothesis is that maltreatment in childhood changes this circuit, and that the change shows up as weaker resting-state functional connectivityDefinition: resting-state functional connectivity neuroimaging The correlation over time between the blood-oxygen signals of two brain regions while a person lies in the scanner with no task. Excludes anatomical connections, activity evoked by a task, and the direction of any influence between regions. full definition between the two.

Birn and colleagues [2] studied 27 male combat veterans, 17 of them with PTSD, and modelled amygdala and hippocampus connectivity from childhood maltreatment, combat exposure and PTSD symptoms together. Their abstract reports that scores on the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ)Definition: Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) clinical psychology A 28-item adult self-report questionnaire about childhood experiences, scored as five subscales (emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional neglect, physical neglect) of 5 to 25 each and a total of 25 to 125, plus minimisation items that flag denial. Excludes records of maltreatment from the time it happened, and clinical diagnosis. full definition predicted lower amygdala connectivity to the vmPFC.

Goltermann and colleagues [3] tested the same family of claims in 1,325 adults (624 with major depression, 701 healthy controls), with the CTQ and regions chosen from earlier reports, among them the amygdala. Maltreatment was not associated with the connectivity of any region of interest in the full sample. Within the depressed group, maltreatment went with greater, not weaker, connectivity between the amygdala and dorsolateral frontal areas. The authors conclude that most earlier connectivity correlates of maltreatment did not replicate.

Our study adds a smaller, independent test on open data with one feature the larger study did not state in its abstract: a preregistered smallest effect of interestDefinition: smallest effect of interest statistics (equivalence testing) The size of effect, fixed before the data are seen, below which an effect is treated as too small to matter for the decision at hand. Here a correlation of 0.20 in size. Excludes a claim that smaller effects are zero. full definition and an equivalence test (two one-sided tests)Definition: equivalence test (two one-sided tests) statistics A test that supports the absence of a meaningful effect when the 90 percent interval of the estimate lies wholly inside the band set by the smallest effect of interest, which is the same as rejecting both edges of the band at the 5 percent level. Excludes a test of whether the effect is exactly zero. full definition in the form Lakens [4] describes for correlations. An equivalence test can support "no effect of a size that matters", which a non-significant result alone cannot.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition was frozen on 9 October 2026, before any phenotype value or image from the dataset was downloaded or viewed. Only file names, the dataset description and the CTQ definitions file had been read. Three choices were made at that point: an anatomical vmPFC, the full sample with no diagnostic filter, and a smallest effect of interest of 0.20 in size, about 4 percent shared variance.

The decision rule had three outcomes, fixed in advance:

  • Association: the 95 percent interval excludes 0 and, by a deviationDefinition: deviation research method (metascience) A dated, reasoned change to a preregistered plan, written into the plan's log, with the point in the study at which it was decided. Excludes a silent change to the analysis. full definition logged before any data were processed, the Holm correctionDefinition: Holm correction statistics (multiple testing) A step-down adjustment of p values across a family of tests that keeps the chance of any false positive in the family at the stated level. Excludes adjustment for analyses outside the declared family, such as the exploratory sensitivity checks. full definition-adjusted p across the two registered tests is below 0.05.
  • No meaningful association: the 90 percent interval lies wholly inside -0.20 to 0.20.
  • Inconclusive: neither.

The preregistration also stated that effects between 0.10 and 0.20 could be missed at the expected sample size, and that any write-up must say so.

Six deviations are logged in the preregistration, each dated with the point at which it was decided:

  • 1 to 3, on 9 October, before any participant was processed: keep aCompCor components up to five per mask when fewer are available; require the Holm-adjusted p for an association call; use each session's acquired field maps for distortion correction, with a field-map-free fallback where they do not match.
  • 4, on 10 October: a fallback preprocessing path if a software licence was not in place. It was not used; every participant went through one pipeline.
  • 5 and its correction 5a, on 10 October, after one participant's motion check and before any trauma or connectivity value was opened: the data are multiband with a 0.8 second repetition time, and breathing showed up as apparent motion. The motion rule became a 0.1 Hz low-pass filter on the motion parameters, with volumes censored above 0.1 mm, following Gratton and colleagues [5]. That rule was validated on single-band data, so here it runs outside its validated setting. Deviation 5 first specified a band-stop filter that did not remove the breathing signal; 5a replaced it.
  • 6, on 29 October, after preprocessing and before any trauma-connectivity value was opened, decided from counts of the questionnaire coding only: the dataset codes missing CTQ answers as 88, which the registered code did not list, so 88 became a missing code.

Data and provenance

The data are the Transdiagnostic Connectome Project, OpenNeuro dataset ds005237, snapshot 1.1.3 [1], released under CC0, a public-domain dedication. It is a transdiagnostic adult sample with up to four resting-state runs per participant. This paper reports group statistics only; per-participant tables were not published and no individual record appears here.

All 241 participants were preprocessed with fMRIPrepDefinition: fMRIPrep neuroimaging software An open preprocessing pipeline for functional MRI that corrects head motion and distortion, aligns images to a standard brain space and writes nuisance signals for later cleaning. Excludes the denoising and statistics that follow, which were run by our own code. full definition 25.2.6, with no processing errors. Of these, 230 had four runs, 6 had three and 5 had two. Distortion correction used acquired field maps for 198 participants and the field-map-free method for 43.

The analysed sample of 187 had a mean age of 33.4 years (SD 13.3). It included 112 women, 73 men and 2 people who reported another sex; 122 were scanned at one site and 65 at the other; 114 were in the patient group and 73 in the general-population group. The mean CTQ total was 43.0 (SD 17.3) on a scale of 25 to 125.

Methods

Regions

Regions came from the Harvard-Oxford atlasDefinition: Harvard-Oxford atlas neuroimaging A probabilistic atlas of cortical and subcortical regions in standard brain space. At a 50 percent threshold a voxel belongs to a region when at least half of the reference brains placed it there. Excludes regions drawn from each participant's own anatomy or from functional data. full definition at the 50 percent threshold in standard space: left and right amygdala combined; "Frontal Medial Cortex" for the primary vmPFC target; and "Subcallosal Cortex", the label closest to Brodmann area 25, as the pre-declared secondary target.

Denoising and motion

Each run was cleaned by regression of 24 motion parameters, aCompCorDefinition: aCompCor neuroimaging (denoising) Anatomical component correction: the main components of the signal in white matter and cerebrospinal fluid, where little neural signal is expected, are regressed out as noise. Excludes global signal regression, which removes the mean of the whole brain. full definition (up to five white-matter and five cerebrospinal-fluid components) and cosine drift terms, with no global signal regressionDefinition: global signal regression neuroimaging (denoising) Removing the average signal of the whole brain from every region before connectivity is computed. Excludes aCompCor and motion regression, which remove other nuisance signals. full definition in the primary analysis. Framewise displacementDefinition: framewise displacement neuroimaging (motion quality control) A summary of how far the head moved between two consecutive brain volumes, in millimetres, from the six rigid-body motion parameters. Excludes motion within a single volume. full definition was computed from low-pass filtered motion parameters, and censoringDefinition: censoring neuroimaging (motion quality control) Dropping single brain volumes whose head motion exceeds a threshold before connectivity is computed. Excludes dropping whole runs or whole participants, which follow separate rules. full definition removed volumes above 0.1 mm together with uncensored segments shorter than five volumes. A run was unusable with more than 20 percent of volumes censored, and a participant needed at least two usable runs.

Connectivity

For each usable run j, rj is the Pearson correlation of the mean denoised time series of the two regions. It is converted with the Fisher zDefinition: Fisher z statistics The transform z = artanh(r) of a correlation, which makes its sampling spread close to normal so that correlations can be averaged and given intervals. Excludes any change to the sign or ranking of correlations. full definition transform,

zj=12ln⁡1+rj1−rj(1)

and averaged over the participant's R usable runs:

Z=1R∑jzj(2)

The test

The exposure is the CTQ total, the sum of the five subscales. The statistic is the partial correlationDefinition: partial correlation statistics The correlation between two quantities after the linear effect of a set of covariates has been removed from both. Excludes adjustment for covariates that were not measured, and any statement about cause. full definition rp between CTQ total and Z, adjusting for age, sex, site, mean filtered framewise displacement and the number of retained volumes, which the result file records as k=6 model terms. Intervals use the Fisher transform of rp with standard error

SE=1n−3−k(3)

and run from zp−c·SE to zp+c·SE, transformed back to the correlation scale, with c 1.96 for the 95 percent interval and 1.645 for the 90 percent interval. With n=187 this gives the intervals in Table 1. Statistical powerDefinition: statistical power statistics The chance that a test detects an effect of a stated size, given the sample size and the threshold for significance. Excludes the chance that a detected effect is real. full definition uses the same normal approximation.

Controls and planted checks

The controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition shuffled CTQ totals across participants 10,000 times (seed 20261029) and recomputed the partial correlation each time, giving a null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition for both the primary and the secondary test. It shows where the observed value sits among values that carry no link by construction.

There is no positive controlDefinition: positive control experimental design A test of a known effect run through the same pipeline, to show that the pipeline can find an effect of the expected kind. Excludes shuffled controls, which show what no effect looks like. full definition. No known effect was planted in the data, and no planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition shows that this pipeline would find a connectivity effect of size 0.20 when one is present. The equivalence call rests on the interval width, which depends on the sample size and not on the pipeline's sensitivity. A pipeline that destroyed real signal would also produce a narrow interval around zero. This is the main weakness of the design.

Results

Of 241 participants, 17 were excluded for having fewer than two usable runs after motion censoring, 16 had no CTQ record and 21 were missing at least one subscale, leaving 187.

Childhood trauma scores were unrelated to amygdala-vmPFC resting connectivity in 187 adults: partial r -0.006, 95% interval -0.152 to 0.140.c1 The 90% interval, -0.129 to 0.117, lies inside -0.20 to 0.20, so effects of 0.20 or larger in size are excluded at the preregistered bound.c2 The decision is "no meaningful association". The secondary region gave the same decision (Table 1).

The unadjusted p values were 0.94 and 0.74. Under the shuffle control the primary value sat at the 47th percentile of 10,000 shuffles (two-sided permutation p 0.93) and the secondary at the 37th (p 0.73), as Figure 1 shows. The shuffled primary values ran from -0.119 to 0.124 between the 5th and 95th percentiles.

Power to detect a correlation of 0.20 was 0.77, so true effects between 0.10 and 0.20 remain open.c5 At the Holm-adjusted threshold the power was 0.68. The smallest correlation detectable with 80 percent power was 0.207. The chance that the equivalence test succeeds when the true correlation is zero was 0.71.

Fifteen exploratory sensitivity analyses moved the primary r between -0.081 and 0.081, and none reached an association.c3 Figure 2 draws all of them with the two registered tests; Table 2 in Appendix A lists them. Thirteen of the fifteen met the equivalence rule on the primary region. The emotional-neglect and physical-abuse subscale analyses, r 0.081 and -0.081, are inconclusive because their 90% intervals touch 0.20.c4 Their 90% intervals run from -0.041 to 0.201 and from -0.202 to 0.042. Each of these single subscales neither shows an association nor excludes one of 0.20.

The same sensitivity analyses were also run on the secondary region. Two of them were inconclusive there

What this means for a reader

When a paper or a model card reports how few bits a language model needs per character, ask what text it was measured on. On a famous public document, the number measures recall of that document as much as modelling of language. On text the models could not have seen, their lead over a classical compressor shrinks from about tenfold to under twofold. Check a compression figure on fresh text before reading it as either.

Objection

There is one unseen text. It is our own technical writing in one register, full of numbers and technical terms, and it was chosen after the headline numbers were seen. A set of fresh texts across registers is needed before the size of the memorisation share can be stated.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

A language model that predicts the next word well is also a compressor, and its compression rate is often quoted as a measure of how well it models text. We used two small open models, SmolLM2-360M and Qwen3-0.6B, as arithmetic coders and compared them with xz and with a PPM context model. SmolLM2 encodes the English Universal Declaration of Human Rights at 0.27 bits per character, and Qwen3-0.6B at 0.57.c1 The best classical coder, PPM trained on 5 million characters of Project Gutenberg, needs 1.99. We then added a control we had not planned: 30,000 characters of our own technical writing from October 2026, written after both models were released. On text written after their training, the two models need 1.59 and 1.66 bits per character.c2 Cold PPM, which has seen nothing, finds the unseen text only slightly harder than the declaration: 2.70 against 2.57 bits per character.c3 The models' advantage on the declaration therefore points at their having seen it; one fresh text cannot size that share. An arithmetic encoder and decoder round-tripped a 120-token passage exactly with both models.c5
