Introduction

A model that assigns a probability to each next symbol can drive an arithmetic coderDefinition: arithmetic coding data compression A method that turns a model's probability for each next symbol into a single binary number, so a symbol given probability p costs close to minus log2 p bits, and a decoder with the same model recovers the text exactly. Excludes codes that give each symbol a fixed whole number of bits, such as Huffman codes. full definition, which spends close to minus log⁡2p bits on a symbol given probability p and lets a decoder with the same model recover the text exactly. The better the predictions, the shorter the code. Delétang and colleagues [1] used this equivalence to show that large language models are strong general-purpose compressors, and pointed out that counting the model's own size changes the picture. Huang and colleagues [2] found that compression on external text corpora tracks benchmark scores almost linearly across about thirty public models, and proposed compression as an evaluation measure.

Compression on public text has a known weakness. If the text was in the training data, a model can predict it from memorisationDefinition: memorisation machine learning; in evaluation also called training-data contamination A model's ability to predict a specific text because that text, or close copies of it, was in its training data, as distinct from predicting text of the same kind it has not seen. Excludes any claim about how the model stores the text internally. full definition, recall of that text, and not from a general model of language. Li and colleagues [3] built an evaluation on this point: they measured compression on Wikipedia, news, code and arXiv text dated before and after each model's training cutoff and reported that the rate worsens after the cutoff for many models.

Our question is smaller and concrete. How many bits per characterDefinition: bits per character information theory and data compression The length of a compressed text in bits divided by the number of characters in the original. Lower is better, and 8 is the cost of plain one-byte text. Excludes bits per token or per byte, which divide by a different count. full definition do two small open models need on a famous public document, against classical compressors, and how much of the result survives on text written after they were trained?

Preregistration and design

This test is one part of a larger study of language as a code. Its preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, a dated plan fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen, is a forecast file written and hashed on 1 November 2026 at 03:14 UTC, before any measurement. A first work session wrote it and stopped with no measurement saved. A second work session wrote a file of scoring rules 13 minutes later, before computing anything, and ran every measurement after that. A point forecast holds if the measured value is within 25 percent of it, and an inequality forecast holds when the inequality is true.

For this part the forecast file fixed:

  • The bits per character on the English declaration: xz 3.0, PPM cold 2.4, PPM trained on Gutenberg 2.1, SmolLM2 1.2, Qwen3 1.0.
  • On a held-out Gutenberg book: xz 2.9, trained PPM 2.1, SmolLM2 2.0.
  • That SmolLM2 needs at least a billion characters to pay for its own size against xz, and trained PPM at most 200 million.
  • A kill condition, a rule that decides against the run with no judgement after it: if an arithmetic-coded round trip with a model is not exact, the model rows count only as ideal lengths and not as real codes.
  • Forecasts for the cost of sending known answers, and a shuffled-training control for PPM.

The unseen-text control was not in the forecast file. It was added after the declaration came in at 0.27 bits per character under SmolLM2, to test whether that number was memorisation. It is a post hoc controlDefinition: post hoc control research method A control added after the first results were seen. It can test an explanation but carries less weight than a control fixed in advance, because the choice of control could follow the result. Excludes controls named in the preregistration. full definition: it can test an explanation, and it carries less weight than a control fixed in advance.

Data and provenance

  • The English Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 10,637 characters after runs of whitespace were collapsed, from the udhr2 collection of translations distributed with NLTK [7]. The download's source address was not recorded and the archive carries no licence file, so its licence is not established. We report numbers only and release no text from it.
  • Lewis Carroll, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, characters 5,000 to 35,000, from the Project Gutenberg selection distributed with NLTK [8]. Public domain in the United States.
  • The training text for PPM: the first 5,000,000 characters of the other books in that selection, with Alice and the King James Bible left out.
  • The unseen text: 30,000 characters of an unpublished research log of ours, written in October 2026. It is not released. Its SHA-256 is 2248f9fa40d14608bc9b2932af537caa0b548722e16499532413ca020952850c, so a later release can be checked against it.
  • SmolLM2-360M [4], Hub revision f8027fd0, and Qwen3-0.6B [5], Hub revision c1899de2, both Apache-2.0, downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub on 31 October 2026 as safetensors with no remote code. The SmolLM2 weight file is 723,674,912 bytes and the Qwen3 file 1,503,300,328 bytes.

SmolLM2's technical report appeared in February 2025 and Qwen3's in May 2025 [4] [5]. That the unseen text was written after both models were trained rests on those dates and on the log's own dates.

Methods

Code length under a language model

Each text is split into tokensDefinition: token natural language processing The unit a language model reads and predicts, a whole word, part of a word or a single character taken from a fixed vocabulary of tens of thousands of pieces. Excludes a character or a byte. full definition, the word pieces a model reads, with the model's own tokenizer. Every token ti is priced at minus log⁡2 of the probability the model gave it after the tokens before it. The ideal code lengthDefinition: ideal code length information theory The sum over a text of minus log2 of the probability the model gave to each symbol that came next. A real arithmetic coder comes within a few bits of it. Excludes a measured file size, and any cost of storing the model. full definition of a text of C characters and T tokens is

b=1C∑i−log⁡2p(ti|t1,...,ti−1)(1)

in bits per character, with the sum over tokens 2 to T. The first token is priced at log⁡2V bits for a vocabulary of V tokens: 49,152 for SmolLM2 and 151,936 for Qwen3. Long texts are read in windows of 512 tokens that advance by 256, so every token after the first window is predicted from at least 256 tokens of context. The models ran in half precision on one GPU. Decoding the tokens gave back the exact original text for the declaration and Alice under both tokenizers.

A real code

An ideal length is only a claim until a coder achieves it. For each model, an arithmetic encoder turned the first 120 tokens of the declaration into a bit string, using a 64-token context, single precision weights on the CPU and probabilities rounded to integer frequencies out of 224. The decoder, given the bit string, the first token and the same model, rebuilt the 120 tokens. This is the kill condition in the design.

Classical coders

xzDefinition: xz data compression software A general-purpose file compressor using the LZMA method, which replaces repeated strings with references to earlier copies. Here at its strongest preset. Excludes any model of language beyond repeated byte strings. full definition is a general-purpose compressor that replaces repeated strings with references to earlier copies; it ran at its strongest preset, and its size in bits is divided by the number of characters. PPMDefinition: PPM data compression Prediction by partial matching, a compressor that predicts each character from counts of what followed the same preceding characters, falling back to shorter contexts when a longer one has not been seen. Here method C with exclusion and contexts of up to 5 characters. Excludes models with learned weights, such as neural language models. full definition, prediction by partial matching [6], predicts each character from counts of what followed the same preceding characters, here up to 5 characters back, with method C escapes and exclusion. A character never seen in any context costs log⁡2 of the number of Unicode code points. PPM cold starts empty and learns as it codes. PPM trained starts from counts over the 5,000,000 training characters and keeps learning as it codes; the counts are restored after each text.

Payback length

A compressor that must be sent along with the message pays for its own size. The payback lengthDefinition: payback length our usage, after the two-part code of minimum description length The number of characters a model must compress before the bits it saves over another compressor add up to the size of the model itself, when the model has to be sent along with the message. Excludes a compression ratio on one text, which ignores the cost of the model. full definition is the number of characters after which the bits saved over xz equal the model's size in bits:

N=8Sbxz−bm(2)

where S is the model's size in bytes and bxz and bm are bits per character under xz and under the model. For trained PPM, S is the training text compressed with xz, 1,458,524 bytes.

Cost of a known answer

For a prompt such as "The capital of Norway is" or "5 + 6 =", the cost of an answer is the code length of the answer's tokens given the prompt. Each prompt has a right answer and a wrong one. There are 20 capital-city prompts and 30 each of one-digit and three-digit sums.

Controls and planted checks

A controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition is a version of the data with the structure under test removed and scored the same way. Three serve here.

The round trip of the methods section is a check that the model rows are real codes. An arithmetic encoder and decoder round-tripped a 120-token passage exactly with both models.c5 The kill condition did not fire. The long-document figures remain ideal code lengths.

PPM was retrained on the same 5,000,000 characters with every character shuffled, and again with every word shuffled. On the declaration, character-shuffled training gave 3.59 bits per character, worse than cold PPM at 2.57, so the trained model's gain over cold is gone and more. Word-shuffled training gave 2.10 against 1.99 for normal training, a loss of a fifth of the gain. The context model gains from letter order inside words much more than from word order, as it should.

The unseen text is the control for prior exposure. A coder that has seen nothing, cold PPM, gives a measure of how hard each text is in itself.

Results

Table 1 gives every coder on every text, and Figure 1 draws the same numbers.

SmolLM2 encodes the English Universal Declaration of Human Rights at 0.27 bits per character, and Qwen3-0.6B at 0.57.c1 Against xz on the same text that is a tenfold and a fivefold lead. Our forecasts were 1.2 and 1.0, and both failed by far more than the 25 percent allowed. The Gutenberg book shows the same pattern more weakly: 0.89 under SmolLM2, against a forecast of 2.0.

On text written after their training, the two models need 1.59 and 1.66 bits per character.c2 SmolLM2 needs about six times the bits it needs on the declaration. Its lead over xz falls from tenfold to under twofold.

Cold PPM, which has seen nothing, finds the unseen text only slightly harder than the declaration: 2.70 against 2.57 bits per character.c3 xz finds it easier, 2.74 against 2.83. A sixfold jump for a language model on a text that classical coders find about as hard as the declaration points at prior exposure to the declaration.

Trained PPM does worse than cold PPM on the unseen text, 2.89 against 2.70 bits per character.c4 Its training on literary English helps on the declaration and on Alice and hurts on our technical writing.

Model size changes the ranking for short messages. By eq. 2, SmolLM2 pays for its 723,674,912 bytes against xz after 2.6 billion characters of Alice-like text, which held the preregistered bound of at least one billion. On the unseen text, where its lead over xz is 1.15 bits per character, the same arithmetic gives about 5 billion characters. Trained PPM pays back after 11.9 million characters of Alice-like text.

Figure 2 shows the cost of sending a known answer. A right capital city costs about 1 bit under either model, and a wrong one 18 to 20. A one-digit sum costs Qwen3 1.29 bits and SmolLM2 4.01, close to its 4.63 for a wrong sum. A three-digit sum costs 8.5 to 9.1 bits even when right, and a wrong one costs only about 5 bits more. The answer costs fit recall of capital cities and show no sign of reliable three-digit addition.

Appendix A sets every preregistered forecast for this part against its outcome.

Discussion

The headline number, 0.27 bits per character, is true of the declaration and says little about language. The declaration is copied widely on the public web, so we infer that it sits in the training data of both models, probably many times; we did not check their training sets. A model that has seen it often can code it from recall. The unseen text removes that route, and the lead over classical coders drops to what a model of language buys.

That residual lead is still real. On text neither model could have seen, both need about 1.6 bits per character against 2.70 to 2.89 for the classical coders. This agrees with the main claim of Delétang and colleagues [1] that language models are strong compressors, and with their point that the model's size belongs in the count: on fresh text, SmolLM2 needs billions of characters before it pays for itself against xz.

Our result fits the evaluation design of Li and colleagues [3], who score compression on text from after each model's training cutoff. It also bears on compression used as a measure of capability [2]. A corpus that overlaps the training data rewards recall, and two models can rank differently on recall than on language. Here the smaller model, SmolLM2, leads by a factor of two on the declaration and by 4 percent on the unseen text.

The trained PPM result is a smaller lesson of the same kind. Counts from Gutenberg books help on literary text and hurt on a technical log. A compressor's training text is part of its result, for a context model as much as for a neural one.

Limitations

  • There is one unseen text. It is our own technical writing in one register, full of numbers and technical terms, and it was chosen after the headline numbers were seen. A set of fresh texts across registers is needed before the size of the memorisation share can be stated.
  • The unseen text differs from the declaration in style as well as in novelty. Cold PPM finds the two about equally hard, which suggests the difficulty gap is small, but it does not remove the difference.
  • That the unseen text was written after the models were trained rests on its date. We have not checked whether it quotes public text.
  • The unseen text is not released, so no one else can rerun that row. Its hash is given so a later release can be checked.
  • Both models are small, 360 million and 600 million parameters. Larger models may memorise more.
  • The round trip covered 120 tokens. The long-document figures are ideal code lengths, and a real coder would add a few bits.
  • All declaration and Alice rows for the language models carry the same contamination.
  • The licence of the declaration file is not established; we report numbers only.
  • Scoring was done by our own code and was not blind.

Evidence

Held. Changes how to read common LLM compression numbers; needs a wider unseen set.

Figures

These are the paper's own figures, numbered as in the PDF, and each "Figure" reference in the text points here. The charts on this page redraw the same results from the result files and carry their own numbers.

What this means for a reader

If someone tells you that forests exposed to drought become hardened against the next one, ask for the test against a version of the drought record moved in time. Across a large public archive of tree rings, trees that had lived through an earlier drought grew less in the severe drought year and bounced back more afterwards, and the two roughly cancelled. At this scale, drought "priming" of trees is not shown.

Objection

The 95% interval reaches +0.090 in log resilience, a gain of about 9 percent. Small conditioning effects are not ruled out.

What would change the call. Add a baseline for autocorrelation (biological memory) and state the test's power.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

A common intuition holds that stress hardens: a tree that came through a dry spell should cope better with the next one. We tested that idea on 1,175 tree-ring sites in the contiguous United States, 65 species and 3,780 site-drought events, with the test written down and hash-locked before the run. A moderate drought four to eleven years earlier moved log resilience to a later severe drought by +0.039 (95% interval -0.011 to +0.090), inside a time-shift null whose 95th percentile was 0.065 (p 0.18).c1 The preregistered steeling test failed. A severe prior drought lowered growth in the drought year (resistance -0.087, p 0.006) and raised recovery after it by +0.096, so resilience barely moved.c2 Part of that recovery gain follows from how the indices are built. A rerun with drought taken from 0.5 degree gridded data on 1,097 sites gave +0.025 (-0.009 to +0.059), below its own time-shift 95th percentile of 0.038 (p 0.14).c3 The interval still allows a gain of up to about 9 percent in resilience, so small conditioning effects are not ruled out.

Introduction

The question comes from a broad idea about stress and adaptation: that a moderate earlier stress leaves an organism better prepared for a harder one. Applied to trees, we call this steelingDefinition: steeling psychology and stress biology, here applied to trees The idea that a moderate earlier stress leaves an organism better able to cope with a later, harder one. Here, that a tree which lived through a moderate drought loses less growth to a later severe drought. Excludes recovery from the same drought, and any gain that follows only from how the growth indices are computed. full definition. Trees make a good test, because each annual ring records growth, and public archives hold thousands of sites with records over a century long.

Forest ecology points mostly the other way. Anderegg and colleagues [1] examined stem growth after severe drought at 1,338 forest sites worldwide and reported a widespread drought legacyDefinition: drought legacy forest ecology Growth that stays below its expected level for one or more years after a drought ends. Excludes the loss of growth in the drought year itself. full definition: growth stayed low for one to four years after the drought, most often in dry ecosystems and in the pine family. Anderegg and colleagues [2] later asked whether forests acclimate to repeated droughts or become more vulnerable, and concluded that successive droughts are generally more damaging, with conifers the most affected. We read that paper at the level of its publisher page and press coverage.

The usual measures of drought response come from Lloret, Keeling and Sala [3], who proposed resistance, recovery and resilience indices from ring growth around a low-growth episode in ponderosa pine. Schwarz and colleagues [4] reviewed 82 studies that used these indices and listed cases where they mislead: a lagged growth minimum, depressed growth in the reference years before the drought, and repeated droughts. Their review bears on our result, because resilience equals resistance times recovery, so a weak drought-year ring raises recovery by arithmetic alone.

Our searches, run on 9 November 2026, found these and related studies on legacies and repeated drought. We did not find a study of this exact contrast, moderate earlier drought against later resilience, scored against a time-shifted drought record. That is a search result, not proof that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The design was written as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition and hash-locked on 29 October 2026 at 22:54 UTC, before any hypothesis value was computed. A smoke run (a short trial run that checks the code executes) at small sizes before the lock printed design counts only: 1,175 sites, 3,780 events, 65 species, 177 climate divisions, and the prior-drought group sizes. No coefficient was printed or read.

The locked file covers four tests, A to D. Tests B to D are simulations of a loaded rod, a small neural network and a Bayesian learner, and they say nothing about trees. This paper reports Test A, the only test on real data. Across all four tests the run returned 22 verdictsDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition, 10 passing and 12 failing.

Test A had four preregistered predictions, each a set of rules that must all hold:

  • A1, steeling: the moderate-drought coefficient is above 0, its Benjamini-HochbergDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics, multiple testing A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05. The adjusted value is called q. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call. full definition adjusted q is below 0.05, and it is above the 95th percentile of both nulls.
  • A2: the moderate-drought coefficient exceeds the severe-drought coefficient, with q below 0.05.
  • A3: resilience rises and then falls with drought dose, by the two-lines testDefinition: two-lines test statistics (Simonsohn 2018) A test for a rise-then-fall shape that fits one straight line on each side of a data-chosen break point and asks whether the first rises and the second falls, both significantly. Excludes a quadratic fit, which can report a peak where none exists. full definition, with a statistic above 1.96 and above its shuffle 95th percentile.
  • A placebo: grouping by a window after the event must not predict resilience (p at or above 0.05).

The forecast written before the run: A1 weak or null, A2 likely positive because severe drought leaves legacies, and A3 failing.

Data and provenance

Rings: standard chronologiesDefinition: standard chronology dendrochronology One yearly ring-width index for a site, made by removing each tree's age trend and averaging the trees, scaled so that an ordinary year is near 1. Excludes raw ring widths of single trees, and density or isotope records. full definition for the contiguous United States from the International Tree-Ring Data Bank [5], held by NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information as public data with a request to cite the contributors. Ring width only. Years from 1896 with at least 5 samples where a sample count exists; index values at or below 0 dropped.

Drought, main test: NOAA nClimDiv divisional Palmer Drought Severity IndexDefinition: Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) climatology and hydrology A monthly index of soil-moisture supply against demand built from temperature and precipitation. 0 is normal, -2 is moderate drought and -3 or lower is severe drought. Excludes a direct measurement of soil water, and drought indices built on precipitation alone. full definition, version 1.0.0 built on 6 October 2026 [6], US federal data with no restriction on use. Each site was placed in its climate divisionDefinition: climate division US climatology (NOAA) One of the regions into which NOAA splits the contiguous United States for climate records, each with one averaged monthly series per variable. Excludes a single weather station, and a regular grid cell. full definition by its coordinates, and the yearly drought value is the June to August mean of that division. The final sample is 1,175 sites, 65 species and 177 divisions, with 579 division drought years and 3,780 site-drought events.

Drought, rerun: the self-calibrating PDSIDefinition: self-calibrating PDSI (scPDSI) climatology A version of the Palmer index whose constants are fitted to each location's own climate, so that the thresholds mean similar rarity everywhere. Here taken from the CRU TS gridded product at 0.5 degree. Excludes the original Palmer index with fixed constants, and station measurements. full definition from CRU TS 4.10 at 0.5 degree, 1903 to 2025 [7] [8], released under the Open Database License 1.0 with attribution to the Climatic Research Unit, University of East Anglia. Each site takes the nearest cell with complete June to August data in at least 60 years, within 1 degree. This gave 1,097 sites, 64 species, 505 cells and 2,549 events.

A division averages over a large area, and a site sits at one point in it. The rerun exists to pay that debt. A 0.5 degree cell is closer to the site and is still not a station.

Methods

Events

A focal year t is a division year with June to August PDSI at or below -3. An event needs ring growth in years t−3 to t+3, no other severe year in t−3 to t−1 or t+1 to t+3, and drought data for the exposure window t−11 to t−4.

The Lloret indices

With gt the ring index in the drought year, Gpre the mean of the three years before and Gpost the mean of the three years after, the Lloret indicesDefinition: Lloret indices dendroecology Three ratios of ring growth around a drought year: resistance is the drought-year growth over the mean of the three years before, recovery is the mean of the three years after over the drought-year growth, and resilience is the mean after over the mean before. Excludes measures of tree death, and growth responses that unfold over more than three years. full definition are resistance, recovery and resilience:

Rt=gtGpre,Rc=Gpostgt,Rs=GpostGpre=Rt·Rc(1)

All three are analysed as natural logarithms. The product in eq. 1 matters later: a lower drought-year ring lowers Rt and raises Rc by the same factor.

Exposure groups

The exposure is the lowest June to August PDSI in years t−11 to t−4. An event is in the none group if that minimum is above -2, moderate if it lies above -3 and at or below -2, and severe if it is at or below -3. The groups held 986, 941 and 1,853 events. The dose is the larger of 0 and minus that minimum.

The model

For event i at site s in year t:

ln⁡Rs=βmMi+βsSi+γ1Dt+γ2Dpre+γ3Dpost+αs+τt+ϵi(2)

where Mi and Si mark the moderate and severe groups, Dt, Dpre and Dpost are the drought-year PDSI and the mean PDSI of the three years before and after, and αs and τt are site and year fixed effectsDefinition: fixed effects econometrics and statistics One free constant per site (or species) and one per calendar year in a regression, so that differences between sites and between years cannot be mistaken for the effect of the variable under test. Excludes random effects, which treat those constants as draws from one distribution. full definition. Species are constant within a site, so site effects absorb them; a model with species and year effects was reported as secondary. Standard errors are clusteredDefinition: clustered standard errors econometrics Standard errors computed so that events in the same climate division may be correlated with each other, which widens the interval when they are. Excludes ordinary standard errors that treat every event as independent. full definition by climate division. Resistance and recovery were fitted with the same model as secondary outcomes. The coefficient under test is βm.

In the rerun, the preregistered primary model used species and year effects in place of site effects, with the same covariates and the same clustering by division.

Shape in dose

For prediction A3, resilience with site, year and covariate effects removed and no group terms was set against the dose, and the two-lines test was applied. Its statistic is the smaller of the rising line's z and minus the falling line's z, so a large positive value means a rise and then a fall.

Controls and planted checks

Test A had no planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition: no synthetic forest with a known steeling effect was built and run through the model. The placebo window serves as the design check, together with three controlsDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition.

  • The time-shift nullDefinition: time-shift null time-series statistics, surrogate data A control in which each drought record is moved in time by a random offset of 20 years or more, with the end wrapped round to the start, and the events rebuilt. It keeps each record's own pattern of droughts and breaks its timing against the rings. Excludes shuffling single years, which also destroys the drought record's own pattern. full definition moves each division's PDSI record by a random offset of at least 20 years, wraps it, and rebuilds every event and group. It keeps each record's pattern of droughts and breaks its link with the rings. 200 draws. This is the null the preregistered rule binds.
  • The label-permutation nullDefinition: label-permutation null statistics A control in which the prior-drought labels are shuffled among each site's own events, keeping every drought date in place. Excludes a null that moves the droughts themselves. full definition shuffles the prior-drought labels among each site's own events, 500 draws. It keeps every drought date in place, so it is the weaker comparison.
  • The dose shuffle permutes residual resilience across dose for the two-lines test, 200 draws.
  • The placebo windowDefinition: placebo window statistics and econometrics The same test run with the exposure window placed after the event, years 5 to 12 later, where no causal effect is possible, so that any effect found there points to a flaw in the design. Excludes a control on the outcome data. full definition groups each event by drought in years t+5 to t+12, after the event.

Each p value from draws is the share of draws at or above the real value, with one added to the count and to the number of draws:

p=k+1n+1(3)

where k is the number of draws at or above the real value and n the number of draws. The real value is compared with the null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition's 95th percentile. The rerun used the same time-shift null on each grid cell's record, 200 draws.

Results

Table 1 gives the estimates, and Figure 1 draws the main ones. A moderate drought four to eleven years earlier moved log resilience to a later severe drought by +0.039 (95% interval -0.011 to +0.090), inside a time-shift null whose 95th percentile was 0.065 (p 0.18).c1 Its raw p was 0.128 and its adjusted q 0.166. A severe prior drought gave +0.009 (-0.039 to +0.057). Moderate minus severe was +0.030 (-0.014 to +0.074, q 0.214).

Figure 2 sets the moderate-drought estimate against the three null ranges. It sits inside the time-shift range in both runs and above the label-permutation range (95th percentile 0.020, p 0.004). The label permutation keeps each site's drought timing, so beating it says less, and the preregistered rule used the time shift.

The components explain the null in resilience. A severe prior drought lowered growth in the drought year (resistance -0.087, p 0.006) and raised recovery after it by +0.096, so resilience barely moved.c2 By eq. 1, a lower drought-year ring raises recovery by the same factor it lowers resistance, so the recovery gain is partly arithmetic and is not evidence of conditioning.

The placebo window was clean: drought after the event gave +0.006 (p 0.86).c4 No rise-then-fall shape appeared with dose. The two lines fell and then rose, neither significantly (z -0.89 and +0.81), and the statistic of -0.89 sat below its shuffle 95th percentile of 1.26. The mean residual resilience by number of moderate-drought years in the window was -0.007 for none (1,705 events), +0.005 for one (1,268), +0.008 for two (643), -0.019 for three (103) and +0.059 for four (44). These five groups hold 3,763 of the 3,780 events; the result file lists no group for the other 17.

What this means for a reader

A method that points the right way on real data has not yet shown it can be trusted, because it must also pass tests on built data where we choose the answer. Here a simple panel test pointed from summer to ring by a wide margin and reversed when time ran backwards, and still missed two of the checks we had fixed in advance, by less than two percentage points each. We report that as a failure, because a near miss promoted after the fact is how weak methods earn trust they have not earned.

Objection

The planted forward and reverse worlds used a positive prior-summer term, the wrong sign for most of these stands. The pass of the planted forward world at real strength is a pass on a world unlike the real one.

What would change the call. Our publication register records no condition that would raise or overturn this call.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Tree rings and summer temperature give a causal-direction test with a known answer: warmth shapes the ring, and the ring has no meaningful effect on the weather. An earlier round on 135 European sites found that a site-by-site transfer entropy estimator could not tell the two directions apart. In this second round we read lagged Granger tests across a panel of 161 held-out ring-width chronologies at or above 55 degrees north, under a plan hash-locked before any ring series was set against climate. On the high-pass series the panel direction index was +1.206 (95% interval +0.871 to +1.591), against a far-pairing 95th percentile of +0.213.c1 Reversing time flipped the index to -0.894.c2 Rings predicted the next summer at 6.8 percent of sites, below the no-coupling world's 7.8 percent and above the 95th percentile of the far-site pairing control, 6.2 percent.c5 Two binding first-difference checks failed by less than 0.02: the planted reverse world was called correctly at 58.4 percent of sites against a bar of 60 percent, and the shared-trend world's reverse rate was 0.117 against a limit of 0.10.c3 The kill condition written before the run therefore fired, and the instrument earned no standing in this round. The real-data asymmetry is reported as an exploratory reading.

Introduction

Methods that read causal direction from two time series are used across climate science and ecology, and Runge and colleagues [1] set out the conditions under which such readings can be trusted in the Earth sciences. A known-answer testDefinition: known-answer test measurement and method validation A test of a method on a case where the true answer is fixed by physics or by construction, so that any wrong reading is a fault of the method. Excludes agreement with another method, which can share the same fault. full definition asks a method to recover a direction that is fixed in advance. Summer warmth shapes ring width at cold sites, and a ring cannot set the next summer, so annual rings and summer temperature give one such test on public data.

The first round of this study, finding F132questioned, ran a nearest-neighbour transfer entropy estimator site by site on 135 European chronologies and failed: the two directions were detected at similar rates, time reversal made no difference, and a planted direction was misread at about half the sites. Its own account was low power at about 78 years of data and a ring-temperature correlation near 0.2.

This round changes that assumption. It reads the direction across a panelDefinition: panel statistics and econometrics A set of units, here tree-ring sites, each observed over time and analysed together so that one statistic summarises all of them. Excludes a verdict reached site by site, and a pooled regression that treats all years of all sites as one series. full definition of sites at once, where F132questioned asked each site for its own verdict. The tool is the Granger testDefinition: Granger test econometrics and time-series statistics A regression test of whether the past values of one series improve the prediction of another beyond that series' own past. Here an F test on lags 1 and 2. Excludes a test of same-year effects, and proof of a physical cause. full definition, the lagged regression test Granger introduced in 1969. Panel versions exist in econometrics: Dumitrescu and Hurlin [2] average per-unit Wald statistics into one panel test of non-causality. Our index is simpler and was written from that idea, not copied from their statistic: a mean difference of per-site z-scores, with its null drawn from far-site pairings.

Two parts of the literature bear on the design. Preprocessing can create or hide Granger causality. Florin and colleagues [3] reported spurious and missed causalities after filtering, Barnett and Seth [4] showed that Granger causality is unchanged by filtering in theory and that filtering in practice raises both error rates, and Anderson and colleagues [5] gave conditions under which filtering does and does not distort it. That is why the plan ran three preprocessing arms and why their disagreement matters. Second, the lag structure of boreal conifer growth is not simple. Tumajer and Lehejcek [6] found in white spruce a positive effect of summer temperature in the year of ring formation and a negative effect of the summer one year before, and Lloyd and colleagues [7] reported that the previous growing season's temperature and precipitation control growth at most of their interior Alaska sites. Our searches, run on 9 November 2026, found no panel Granger test of ring width against climate with planted worlds of known direction. That is a search result, not proof that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The plan was written as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition and hash-locked on 2 November 2026 at 09:42:37 UTC. Before the lock, the only facts read from the new data were outcome-free: the site count, the regions, the blocks, the series lengths, the distance to the nearest climate cell and the species. No ring series had been correlated, regressed or tested against any climate series. The estimator had been tested on synthetic autoregressive series only.

The plan named the assumption it changed from F132questioned and split the instrument's job into two readings scored apart. The first is reverse-route exclusion: past rings carry no lagged route into next year's summer temperature at the strength of the observed same-year coupling. The second is the forward reading: past summers add to next year's ring beyond the ring's own past. The plan forecast that the forward reading would lack power.

The kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition was written without room for judgement: if any binding checkDefinition: binding check research method, our usage A preregistered rule on a synthetic world that the instrument must pass before any reading of the real data counts. Under the kill condition a single failure removes all standing. Excludes power checks and limit checks, which were recorded but could not remove standing. full definition fails, or the reverse-route exclusion fails on real data, the instrument gets no standing and F132questioned's block on direction readings stands. Exclusion status needed every binding check and the exclusion rule to pass. Forward status needed, in addition, the planted forward world at real strength and the forward rule on real data.

One deviation was recorded before any result was seen. The first run stopped on a division by zero inside the precipitation arm, which is descriptive and decides no verdict. CRU precipitation at many of these cells is filled with climatology where stations are absent, and at four sites the June to August total is constant over the whole window. The fix returns a p value of 1 when the target's residual sum of squares is zero. No temperature series can reach that branch: temperature repeats for at most 2 years at any site. The plan, the verdicts and the seed were unchanged.

Data and provenance

Rings: standard ring-width chronologies from the International Tree-Ring Data Bank [8], held by NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information as public data with a request to cite the contributors. The selection rule was fixed in the build script before the lock: standard chronologies with no earlywood, latewood or density keyword, latitude at or above 55 degrees north, outside longitudes 12 W to 45 E so that no site falls in F132questioned's European region, years 1901 to 2025 with at least 5 samples, and a longest gap-free run of at least 60 years. This gave 161 sites: 100 in Canada, 45 in Alaska and 16 in Asia, in 77 two-degree blocks, with series of 60 to 115 years and a median of 89. The species are mostly white spruce, Picea glauca.

Climate: June to August mean temperature of the ring's year from the nearest land cell of CRU TS 4.10 [9] [10], released under the Open Database License 1.0 with attribution to the Climatic Research Unit, University of East Anglia. The nearest cell lay a median of 16.8 km from the site and at most 31 km. June to August precipitation was run as a descriptive secondary target.

Methods

The Granger pair at each site

For ring width Rt and summer temperature Ct at one site, the climate-to-ring test compares the full regression

Rt=c+a1Rt−1+a2Rt−2+b1Ct−1+b2Ct−2+et(1)

with the same regression without the two climate terms, by an F test on the same rows. The ring-to-climate test is the mirror, with the roles of R and C exchanged. Each p value becomes a z-scoreDefinition: z-score of a p value statistics The point of the standard normal distribution that leaves the p value above it, so that a smaller p gives a larger z. Here capped at 6. Excludes a standardised value of the data themselves. full definition, z=Q(1−p), where Q is the quantile function of the standard normal distribution, capped at 6. The site's direction statistic is

di=zf,i−zr,i(2)

where zf,i is the forward (climate to ring) score and zr,i the reverse one.

The panel index

The panel direction indexDefinition: panel direction index time-series statistics, our usage The mean over sites of d, the z-score of the climate-to-ring Granger test minus that of the ring-to-climate test. Positive values point from summer temperature to ring width. Excludes a test of significance at any one site. full definition is the mean over the N=161 sites:

D=1N∑idi(3)

Its 95% interval is a block bootstrapDefinition: block bootstrap statistics An interval made by resampling whole 2 degree blocks of sites with replacement, here 2,000 times, so that neighbouring sites that share climate move together and the interval is not too narrow. Excludes a bootstrap over single sites, and a binomial interval that treats sites as independent. full definition over the 77 two-degree blocks with 2,000 resamples. The detection rateDefinition: detection rate statistics, our usage The share of sites at which the Granger test in one direction gives p 0.05 or below. For synthetic worlds it is averaged over the draws. Excludes a rate corrected for testing 161 sites. full definition in each direction is the share of sites with p 0.05 or below. The same-year correlation between ring and temperature is reported and gives no direction.

Three preprocessing arms

Each pair of series was analysed three ways: through a high-pass filterDefinition: high-pass filter signal processing A filter that keeps fast variation and removes slow trends. Here each series minus a Gaussian smooth of width 10 years, then scaled to unit variance. Excludes first differences, which are reported as a separate arm. full definition (the primary arm, as in F132questioned), as first differencesDefinition: first differences time-series statistics Each year's value minus the previous year's, a second way to remove slow trends that weights the fastest changes most. Excludes the high-pass filter, which removes trends by smoothing. full definition, and raw, scaled only. The raw arm is descriptive and shows what a shared trend does.

Synthetic worlds

Each world is built per site from iAAFT surrogatesDefinition: iAAFT surrogate time-series statistics, surrogate data A copy of a series built by repeated rounds of Fourier phase randomisation and rank reordering, so that it keeps both the original spectrum, and with it the autocorrelation, and the original set of values, while its timing against any other series is lost. Excludes a shuffle of single years, which destroys the autocorrelation. full definition of that site's own series, five draws per site. In the planted forward world a surrogate St of the ring series receives the site's own climate:

Rt=St+aCt+0.4aCt−1(4)

At real strength a is the larger of the site's absolute same-year correlation on the high-pass arm and 0.1. In the planted reverse world a surrogate of the climate series receives the ring:

Ct=St+aRt+0.4aRt−1(5)

with the same a. The strong worlds use coefficients 0.6 and 0.3. In the no-coupling world both series are independent surrogates. In the common-driver world an autoregressive driver with coefficient 0.5 enters both series in the same year with weight 0.2. In the shared-trend world independent surrogates receive a common line and random walk before preprocessing.

For a world with a planted direction, direction accuracyDefinition: direction accuracy method validation, our usage The share of sites at which the sign of d matches the direction planted in a synthetic world. 0.5 is what a coin would give. Excludes whether the test at any site is significant. full definition is

A=mN(6)

where m is the number of sites whose di has the planted sign.

Far-site pairing and multiple testing

The far-site pairingDefinition: far-site pairing statistics, our usage A control in which each ring series is paired with the summer temperature of a random site at least 1,000 km away, so that real coupling is removed while both series keep their own form. Repeated 199 times. Excludes pairings with nearby sites, which share regional climate. full definition pairs each ring with the summer temperature of a random site at least 1,000 km away, 199 times, on the high-pass and first-difference arms. Every site had at least 65 partners at that distance. Its p value is the share of pairings at or above the real index:

p=k+1n+1(7)

with n=199, so the floor is 0.005. That floor sits under 0.0083, the smallest threshold the Benjamini-Hochberg correctionDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics, multiple testing A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05. The adjusted value is called q. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call. full definition at 0.05 over six tests can need, a lesson from F132questioned, where 20 pairings left a floor too high to correct. The six family p values are the two pairing tests, the real reverse rate on each of two arms against a binomial 5 percent, and two sign tests on the planted worlds at real strength.

Controls and planted checks

Every controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition and synthetic world ran in the same run as the real data. The planted checksDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition were split by role in the plan.

Binding checks, any failure fatal:

  • Planted reverse world seen, on the high-pass and first-difference arms: the upper end of its index interval below 0, and accuracy above 0.6.
  • No-coupling world, on both arms: forward and reverse detection rates at or below 0.10, twice the nominal 0.05.
  • Shared-trend world on first differences: both rates at or below 0.10.

Power and limit checks, recorded but not binding:

  • Strong planted forward world seen on high-pass: interval lower end above 0, accuracy above 0.55.
  • Planted forward world at real strength seen on high-pass: interval lower end above 0. Forecast to fail.
  • Shared-trend world on high-pass: both rates at or below 0.10. Forecast to fail, since F132questioned saw 0.126 and 0.170.
  • Common-driver world on high-pass: its index interval contains 0.

Real-data rules:

  • Exclusion: real reverse rate at or below 0.10 on both arms, and the real index above the planted reverse world's upper interval end on both arms.
  • Forward: real high-pass index above the pairing 95th percentile, with its interval lower end above 0. The same comparison on first differences.

The time-reversedDefinition: time reversal time-series analysis The same test run on both series read backwards in time. A method that reads direction from lag order should flip. Excludes a control on coupling strength. full definition real series were reported beside the rules and decide nothing.

Results

Table 1 gives the panel index and both detection rates in every world, and Figure 1 draws the index with its interval on the two binding arms. Synthetic worlds are averaged over five draws per site.

On the high-pass series the panel direction index was +1.206 (95% interval +0.871 to +1.591), against a far-pairing 95th percentile of +0.213.c1 The pairing mean was +0.047 and its 5th percentile -0.099, and no pairing reached the real value, so p is 0.005, the floor at 199 pairings. First differences gave +1.107 against a pairing 95th percentile of +0.186 (p 0.005), and the raw series +1.242 (+0.873 to +1.655). Climate predicted next year's ring at 39.8 percent of sites. Rings predicted the next summer at 6.8 percent of sites, below the no-coupling world's 7.8 percent and above the 95th percentile of the far-site pairing control, 6.2 percent.c5 The mean same-year correlation on the high-pass arm was 0.160, positive at 87.0 percent of sites.

Reversing time flipped the index to -0.894.c2 On first differences it flipped to -1.092 and on the raw series to -1.041. The shared trend pushed the high-pass index negative (-0.317) and the raw index further (-0.744, with rates 0.335 and 0.594), and the common driver gave -0.090 with an interval across zero. Neither confound produced a positive index like the real one.

Figure 2 sets every binding rule against its bar.

Two binding first-difference checks failed by less than 0.02: the planted reverse world was called correctly at 58.4 percent of sites against a bar of 60 percent, and the shared-trend world's reverse rate was 0.117 against a limit of 0.10.c3 Every high-pass binding check passed: the planted reverse world was called at 71.4 percent with its interval upper end at -0.303, and the no-coupling rates were 0.055 and 0.078. Every real-data rule passed, the power checks passed, including the planted forward world at real strength (interval lower end +0.073), and the shared-trend limit on high-pass failed as forecast (0.135 and 0.221). Under the kill condition one binding failure is enough. The instrument gets no standing from this round.

items.title: F76: How flat a spectrum is predicts forecast skill, but real series follow it loosely
items.description: A 1940s formula says how predictable a series can be from its spectrum alone. On 1,236 real series it ranked held-out forecast skill (rho 0.41) and held as a ceiling in about 94 percent of them, yet real series tracked it less tightly than copies with the same spectrum and scrambled phases.

What this means for a reader

Before you fit any forecasting model, you can compute from the data alone a rough upper limit on how much a linear forecast can help. On 1,128 real tree-ring series that limit sorted series by how forecastable they turned out to be (rank correlation 0.40); on the 106 mood series it did not (0.035), though less sharply than it does on idealised copies. Treat it as a ceiling with an error band: useful for deciding which series deserve modelling effort, unreliable as a promise about any one series.

Objection

Tree rings are 91 percent of series and arrive detrended; pooled rho may reflect group mix. Half-split AR estimation may explain the gap, and the bound is old.

What would change the call. Independent series families (M-competitions, climate, physiology), then explain the surrogate gap by nonstationarity, non-Gaussianity or AR estimation.

From the strongest objection recorded in our publication register.

Abstract

A classical result says how well any linear rule can forecast a stationary series one step ahead, using nothing but the series' spectrum: the flatter the spectrum, the less a forecast can win. We asked whether that ceiling, estimated on the first half of a real series, ranks and bounds the skill of a forecast on the second half. On 1,236 series (1,128 tree-ring chronologies, 106 experience-sampling mood series and two machine power logs) the design was hash-locked before any real-series statistic was computed. One minus spectral flatness ranked held-out one-step forecast skill with Spearman rho 0.414 (95% interval 0.361 to 0.461), against a time-shuffled control whose 95th percentile was -0.023.c1 80 of 1,236 series (6.5 percent, 5.2 to 8.0) beat the bound beyond estimation error, under the preregistered 10 percent kill.c2 Real series tracked the bound less tightly than copies with the same spectra: rho 0.414 against 0.568 to 0.628 on 39 phase-randomised surrogate sets.c3 A nonlinear analogue forecaster beat the bound in 6.4 percent of series, the same as its false rate of 6.3 percent on planted Gaussian series, so no predictability beyond the linear bound turned up.c4 All six primary verdicts passed and both secondaries failed. The bound works as a rough ceiling with an error band, not as an exact number for one series.

Introduction and motivation

The power spectrumDefinition: power spectrum time-series analysis and signal processing How a series' variance is spread over frequencies, from slow swings to fast jitter. Excludes the timing or phase of the swings, which the spectrum does not record. full definition of a series says how its variance spreads over frequencies, from slow swings to fast jitter. A series with all its variance in a few frequencies, like the phases of the Moon, is easy to forecast. White noise spreads its variance evenly and cannot be forecast at all. Spectral flatnessDefinition: spectral flatness signal processing (speech coding) and the theory of stationary processes The geometric mean of a power spectrum divided by its arithmetic mean. It is 1 for white noise and near 0 when a few frequencies hold most of the variance. Excludes flatness of the series itself in time, and measures that use the spectrum's entropy instead of its geometric mean. full definition, the geometric mean of the spectrum over its arithmetic mean, puts that contrast on a scale from 0 to 1.

The link to forecasting is exact for one class of series. For a weakly stationaryDefinition: weakly stationary probability and time-series analysis A series whose mean and autocovariance do not change over time. Excludes series with trends, level shifts or drifting variance, such as a machine whose load changes between the halves. full definition series, one whose mean and autocovariance do not change over time, the smallest one-step error variance any linear predictor can reach equals the exponential of the average log spectrum. We call this the Kolmogorov-Szego boundDefinition: Kolmogorov-Szego bound the theory of weakly stationary processes The smallest one-step error variance any linear predictor can reach on a weakly stationary series, equal to the exponential of the average log spectrum. One minus the flatness is therefore the most variance a linear one-step forecast can remove. Excludes nonlinear predictors on non-Gaussian series, multi-step forecasts, and series whose statistics drift over time. full definition. Divided by the variance, that error is the flatness, so one minus the flatness is the most variance a linear one-step forecast can remove. For Gaussian series the best linear predictor is the best predictor of any kind, so the bound then covers every forecaster.

Davis and Jones [1] turned the formula into an estimator: the average log periodogram plus a constant estimates the log of the innovation variance. Luati, Proietti and Reale [2] later generalised that estimator into a family they call the variance profile. In machine learning, Goerg [3] built Forecastable Component Analysis on a related quantity, the entropy of the normalised spectrum, and searched for the most forecastable combination of several series. Wang, Klee and Roos [4] proposed a spectral predictability score as a check made before any model is built and reported that it tracked the performance of several forecasting models on the M5 retail data.

Those works use spectral measures as indices of forecastability. We asked a narrower question about the bound itself. On real series that are not exactly stationary or Gaussian, does one minus flatness, estimated on the first half, rank the held-out skill of a linear forecast on the second half, and does it hold as a ceiling once estimation error is allowed for? And does it do so as well on real data as on Gaussian copies with the same spectra? The searches behind this section, run on 9 November 2026, did not return a test that sets real series against their own phase-randomised copies in this way. That is what the searches returned; it does not show that no such test exists.

Preregistration and design

The preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition was written on 29 October 2026 and hash-locked at 00:35:53 UTC on 30 October. Before the lock, two things had run: a smoke test (a short trial run that checks the code executes) on scrambled data, with every real series permuted in time and only counts and timings printed, and a calibration of the bound estimator on synthetic autoregressive series only. No statistic of an unscrambled real series was computed before the lock.

One change came before the lock and is disclosed in the locked file. The first estimator, a Welch spectrum with a log-bias correction, underestimated the true bound on synthetic series by 0.13, 0.12, 0.06 and 0.02 at lengths 60, 150, 300 and 1000. A Hann-tapered periodogram with the Euler-gamma log correction gave 0.07, 0.04, 0.02 and 0.01. The tapered periodogram became the primary estimator and both Welch forms became secondaries.

The decision the study informs was written in the same file: whether the flatness estimator is adopted into our study tooling as a predictability bound. It is adopted only if the planted check, the ranking test and the ceiling test all pass.

Kill conditionsDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition, without discretion:

  • The bound's rank correlation with skill at or below the 95th percentile of the time-shuffled control.
  • More than 10 percent of series beating the bound beyond estimation error.

The full set of preregistered verdictsDefinition: verdict research method (our usage) The pass or fail of one preregistered rule set against the run's numbers, read off by code. Excludes an interpretation written after reading the numbers. full definition and their rules is in Appendix A.

Data and provenance

Three kinds of series were read, without modification.

  • Tree rings: 1,128 ring-width index series from the International Tree-Ring Data Bank [6], standard chronologies for sites in the conterminous United States, each at least 200 years long with no gaps. Median length 398 years. These are public data from NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information, with credit to the contributors of each chronology. The site list was the one built for an earlier study of ours.
  • Mood: 106 experience-sampling mood series, each at least 100 prompts long, in prompt order, from four openESM datasets [7] (Westhoff, Bailon, Neubauer and Bayer), each released under CC BY 4.0. Median length 113 prompts.
  • Machine power: CPU package and GPU watts from one workstation, the longest unbroken run on a 1 second grid, 20,145 seconds each. These two logs are not public.

Tree-ring indices arrive already standardised by their chronology method, which removes slow growth trends before this study sees them. Mood series have night gaps that the prompt order ignores. Series whose training or test half was constant would have been dropped and counted; none was.

Methods

The bound

Each series of length n is split in half by time. On the training half, demeaned, the spectrum S(ω) is estimated with a tapered periodogramDefinition: tapered periodogram spectral estimation The squared Fourier transform of a series after its ends are faded with a Hann window, used as a raw estimate of the power spectrum at each Fourier frequency. Excludes smoothed or averaged spectrum estimates such as Welch's method, which we report only as secondaries. full definition Ij at the Fourier frequencies ωj. The Kolmogorov-Szego formula gives the smallest linear one-step error variance V1 through

ln⁡V1=12π∫ln⁡S(ω)dω(1)

with the integral taken over frequencies from −π to π, and the Davis-Jones form estimates the right-hand side from the periodogram as

ln⁡V1≈1m∑jln⁡Ij+γ(2)

where m is the number of frequencies used and γ≈0.5772 is Euler's constant, which corrects the downward bias of a log periodogram. With V the variance of the training half, the flatness and the bound are

r=V1V,b=1−r(3)

The forecast and its skill

An autoregressive modelDefinition: autoregressive model time-series statistics A linear forecast of the next value from a weighted sum of the last p values, with the weights fitted by least squares. P is the order. Excludes models with moving-average terms, external inputs or nonlinear terms. full definition is fitted by least squares to the mean-centred training half. Its order p runs from 0 to pmax, the smaller of 20 and one tenth of the training length, and is chosen by AICDefinition: AIC statistical model selection The Akaike information criterion, a fit score that adds a penalty of two per fitted parameter, used here to choose the autoregressive order. Excludes choice by held-out error, which would use the test half. full definition on a common sample, then refitted. On the test half the model forecasts each value from the true past, with the end of the training half as context. The one-step skillDefinition: one-step skill forecast verification One minus the mean squared error of one-step-ahead forecasts on the test half, divided by the test half's variance. 0 matches forecasting the mean and 1 is perfect. Excludes skill at longer horizons and skill measured on the data used to fit the model. full definition is

s=1−MVtest(4)

where M is the mean squared one-step error on the test half and Vtest its variance. Using the test half's own variance means a level shift between halves counts against skill.

Ranking

The ranking test is the Spearman rhoDefinition: Spearman rho statistics (rank correlation) The correlation between the ranks of two quantities across cases. 1 means the same order, 0 no relation of order. Excludes agreement in size, since two quantities can share an order and differ in scale. full definition between b and s over all series pooled, with a 95 percent interval from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of series.

The ceiling and estimation error

Skill estimated on a finite half and a bound estimated on the other half both carry error, so a series can beat the point bound by chance. The rule for a real breach uses the series' own surrogates. For each series, 39 phase-randomised surrogatesDefinition: phase-randomised surrogate nonlinear time-series analysis (surrogate data) A copy of a series with the same power spectrum and random Fourier phases, so it keeps the autocorrelation and is Gaussian and stationary by construction. Excludes shuffling in time, which also destroys the spectrum. full definition of the whole series, with the mean restored, go through the same pipeline, in the surrogate-data tradition of Theiler and colleagues [5]. With excess d=s−b, a violationDefinition: violation of the bound our usage in this study A series whose excess skill over the bound beats that of at least 38 of its own 39 phase-randomised surrogates, which happens to 5 percent of Gaussian stationary series by chance. Excludes a series whose skill merely exceeds the point bound, which estimation error makes common. full definition is a series whose d beats the excess of at least 38 of its 39 surrogates. The per-series p value is

pi=ki+140(5)

where ki is the number of surrogates whose excess is at or above the real one. For a Gaussian stationary series with that spectrum, violations occur 2 times in 40, or 5 percent, by chance. The share of violating series is reported with a Wilson intervalDefinition: Wilson interval statistics (binomial proportions) A 95 percent interval for a proportion that stays inside 0 and 1 and behaves well when the count is small. Excludes intervals from resampling. full definition.

The nonlinear check

Because the bound covers nonlinear forecasts only for Gaussian series, an analogue forecasterDefinition: analogue forecaster nonlinear time-series prediction (method of analogues) A forecast that finds the k past states most like the present one and averages what came next. It can follow nonlinear structure a linear model misses. Excludes trained nonlinear models such as neural networks. full definition was run beside the linear model. It works on the standardised series, chooses an embedding dimension from 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 on the last quarter of the training half, uses the square root of the library size as the number of neighbours, and takes its library from the training half only, at most the last 4,000 states. Its violations are counted by the same surrogate rule.

Multiple testing

A Benjamini-Hochberg correctionDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics (multiple testing) A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05. Excludes corrections that control the chance of any false call at all, such as Bonferroni. full definition at 0.05 runs over five p values: the pooled rho, the tree-ring rho, the mood rho, the binomial test that linear violations exceed 5 percent, and the same test for the analogue forecaster.

Controls and planted checks

Two controlsDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition and two planted checksDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition ran with the same pipeline.

The time-shuffled control permutes every series in time, which destroys both the spectrum and any forecastable structure, and recomputes the pooled rho; 100 draws. Its 95th percentile was -0.023, the cut a real rho must clear. The p value against it is counted as a p value from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition, so with 100 draws the smallest possible value is 1 in 101, or 0.0099.

The phase-surrogate control keeps each series' spectrum and makes it Gaussian and stationary. On those sets the bound should rank skill well and the violation rule should fire 5 percent of the time. Over the 39 surrogate sets the pooled rho ran from 0.568 to 0.628 (5th to 95th percentile, mean 0.595), and the mean violation rate of each set against the other 38 was 5.1 percent. The violation rule is calibrated.

Planted linear series: 300 Gaussian autoregressive series of order 1 to 4 with random stable roots and lengths drawn from the real tree and mood lengths, whose true bound is known analytically. The estimated bound correlated 0.925 with skill and 0.946 with the true bound, with a mean bias of -0.020 and a mean absolute error of 0.077. Their violation rate was 4.3 percent (2.5 to 7.3).

Planted nonlinear series: 50 noisy logistic maps of length 400, a deterministic nonlinear system that a linear forecast handles poorly. The analogue forecaster beat the linear bound in all 50, with median skill 0.987 against a median bound of 0.084, while the linear forecast violated in 6 percent. The nonlinear check can see nonlinear predictability when it is there.

Results

All 1,236 series were kept. Figure 2 sets the ranking against both controls and Table 1 gives the main numbers.

One minus spectral flatness ranked held-out one-step forecast skill with Spearman rho 0.414 (95% interval 0.361 to 0.461), against a time-shuffled control whose 95th percentile was -0.023.c1 The ranking passed the Benjamini-Hochberg correction. A separate permutation of the pairing between bound and skill gave p 0.0005.

Real series tracked the bound less tightly than copies with the same spectra: rho 0.414 against 0.568 to 0.628 on 39 phase-randomised surrogate sets.c3 The real value sits below every one of the 39 sets. Gaussian stationary series with the same spectra let the bound rank skill better than the real series do.

80 of 1,236 series (6.5 percent, 5.2 to 8.0) beat the bound beyond estimation error, under the preregistered 10 percent kill.c2 The rate sits above the 5 percent expected by chance (binomial p 0.013, which passed the correction), yet no single series survives a Benjamini-Hochberg correction across series: 0 of 1,236. With 39 surrogates the smallest p value one series can reach is 0.025, far above what that correction needs across 1,236 series, so no series could have passed and this line rules nothing out. Figure 3 shows the rates. Without the surrogate rule the bound would look much weaker as a ceiling: AR skill exceeded the point bound in 36.4 percent of real series and in 45.7 percent of planted Gaussian ones, where the bound is true by construction.

A nonlinear analogue forecaster beat the bound in 6.4 percent of series, the same as its false rate of 6.3 percent on planted Gaussian series, so no predictability beyond the linear bound turned up.c4 Its median skill was 0.044 below the linear model's. The secondary verdict for nonlinear excess failed.

Table 2 breaks the result down by kind of series.

Tree rings carry the pooled result: rho 0.396, p 0.0099, passing the correction, with a median AR order of 2. Mood gives rho 0.035 (p 0.19, failing the correction), because its bound, median 0.024, leaves almost nothing to rank, and its median skill is below zero. Both power series beat the bound. Their load drifts between the two halves, so they are not stationary, and the bound does not apply to them.

Two secondaries ran as planned. The spectral exponent alone, the slope of the log spectrum against log frequency on the training half, ranked skill at rho 0.394 against 0.414 for flatness, so that verdict failed; the two measures correlate at 0.697 and the result file gives no interval on their difference, so we treat them as close. On sensitivities, the Welch estimator with segments of one eighth of the series gave rho 0.399 with a lower median bound of 0.099, a second Welch rule gave 0.441, and linear detrending in place of demeaning gave 0.423.

A later round of our own, run on 30 October 2026 with its own preregistration, tested four drift-aware versions of the bound on a split of the same tree-ring and mood series, choosing on 649 development series and testing on 585. None beat the original, which was chosen. On the 585 test series the original gave rho 0.404 against 0.595 on surrogates. The gap between real and surrogate series repeated on a split of the same data, not on new series.

Discussion

The bound does two things on real series. It ranks them: series with peaked spectra in the first half are the ones a linear model forecasts best in the second half. And, read with its own surrogate envelope, it holds as a ceiling for about 94 percent of series. The cheap number is useful for triage, the use Wang and colleagues [4] propose for their spectral score.

The part worth more work is the gap. Real series rank less well than Gaussian stationary series with identical spectra. Three explanations compete, and this study does not separate them. Fitting a model on half a series adds estimation error, which the surrogates s

What this means for a reader

A meadow that looks plain to us is full of colour differences we cannot see. In this collection of surfaces, those hidden differences cluster between flowers and what surrounds them, which fits the old idea that flower colours are tuned to the animals that visit them. The ultraviolet channel is textbook, and earlier work used this same data to study flower signals. What this paper adds is a direct count of the differences a person misses, with a control for chance and a check of how far the count can be trusted. The direction can be trusted on two sets of surfaces; the exact size cannot.

Objection

The instrument check failed twice, with Weber noise and with photon noise, so the model is too fine for at least the bee. Only the direction of the ratio is claimed.

What would change the call. Pass the instrument check with noise values sourced for each species, then match backgrounds to each flower's own site and test behaviour.

From the paper's first stated limitation; our register records no separate objection.

Abstract

Two surfaces can look the same colour to a person and differ sharply to a bee, which sees ultraviolet. We asked where such hidden differences fall among 728 measured Australian surfaces: 221 flower petals and 507 rocks, bark and leaves. Each observer was modelled with the receptor-noise-limited model and published receptor curves. Among pairs a modelled human cannot separate, modelled bees and blue tits separate flower-background pairs more often than background-background pairs, and the separation ratio exceeded its label-shuffle 95th percentile in every condition tested: two noise models on the first set, and two on a second set of Californian flowers against North American soil and leaf litter.c1 The size of the ratio did not travel: for the bee it was 2.04 with Weber noise and 1.67 with photon noise added on the first set, and 45.6 on the second set, where the backgrounds are brown and alike.c2 A preregistered instrument check failed under both noise models: the model resolves finer wavelength steps than bees show in behaviour, so only the direction of the effect is claimed.c3
