Introduction

Each animal's colour vision rests on a few receptor classesDefinition: receptor class vision science One kind of light-sensitive cell in the eye, defined by the wavelengths it responds to. Humans have three cone classes, bees three including one for ultraviolet, blue tits four. Excludes the rods used in dim light, and the nerve cells that compare receptor signals. full definition. People have three cone classes, the honeybee three with one in the ultraviolet, and the blue tit four with one in the ultraviolet. Two surfaces can give the same signals in a person's cones and different signals in a bee's, so the bee tells apart what the person cannot.

The standard way to compute such differences is the receptor-noise-limited modelDefinition: receptor-noise-limited model visual ecology The model of Vorobyev and Osorio in which two colours can be told apart when the difference in log receptor signals is large compared with the noise in each receptor class. Brightness differences are left out. Excludes models of colour appearance, and any effect of pattern, motion or learning. full definition of Vorobyev and Osorio [1]. It treats colour as coded by comparisons between receptor classes and sets the threshold by the noise in each class. A distance of one just-noticeable difference (JND)Definition: just-noticeable difference (JND) psychophysics The unit of colour distance in the receptor-noise-limited model. A distance of 1 is treated as the threshold, so pairs at or below 1 count as indistinguishable for that observer. Excludes a measured threshold for a real animal on a real task. full definition is the threshold. The model was built to predict colour thresholds for animals whose eyes have been measured but whose thresholds have not.

The link between flower colour and pollinator vision has a long record. Chittka and Menzel [2] analysed 180 flower reflectance spectraDefinition: reflectance spectrum optics and visual ecology The share of light a surface reflects at each wavelength, here measured from 300 to 700 nm, which includes the ultraviolet below 400 nm. Excludes the colour a viewer sees, which also depends on the light and the eye. full definition and found that sharp steps in reflectance fall where bee-like insects discriminate best; their calculations of the best set of three receptors for telling flower colours apart matched the receptors measured in many Hymenoptera. Dorin, Shrestha, Garcia, Burd and Dyer [3] measured the surface set used here, flowers with rocks, minerals, bark and leaves from Australia, and found that the share of flowers with sharp spectral steps was an order of magnitude above the share among background samples. They argued that insect colour vision is older than flowers and was shaped by flight among rocks and plants, and that flowers evolved colours that stand out against that background.

This paper asks a narrower question that the model can answer directly. Among the pairs of surfaces a person cannot tell apart, does a modelled bee or blue tit tell apart flower-background pairs more often than background-background pairs? Searches we ran on 9 November 2026 found the work above and no direct count of this kind; that is what the searches returned, not proof that none exists.

Preregistration and design

The first study was written as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition on 29 October 2026 and locked at 01:27:38 UTC on 30 October. Before the lock, the code was run only on scrambled data, with every spectrum permuted across wavelength and the group labels permuted, and only keys, counts and timings were printed. The model was checked against its published closed forms on random numbers, to 4 times 10 to the power -16. No statistic of a real spectrum seen through any observer was computed before the lock.

The locked file names the data, the observers and their noise values with a grade for each source, the model, the measures, the hypotheses with their pass rules and kill conditionsDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition, the controlsDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition and the multiple-testing plan. This paper reports hypothesis H2, the flower test, with its secondary H2b and the instrument check V0. The same run tested other hypotheses about the information each observer carries; those are reported in the findings ledger and are not part of this paper.

H2 reads: among pairs one observer X cannot separate, the share another observer Y separates is larger for flower-background pairs than for background-background pairs. It was tested for four pairs of observers: human then bee, human then blue tit, dog then bee, and dog then blue tit. The kill condition: a ratio at or below 1, or inside the label-shuffle range. Each conditional share needs at least 20 pairs.

A second study, written after the first and locked at 02:40:37 UTC on 30 October, added photon noiseDefinition: photon noise physics of light detection The random variation in how many photons a receptor absorbs, which every real receptor has and which matters most when the catch is small. Added here as a term that falls with the catch. Excludes noise in the nerve cells after the receptors. full definition to the model, reran the instrument check, and repeated H2 on the first set and on a second set of surfaces. Its preregistration was hash-locked in the same way. Its result narrows this finding and is reported here as the replication.

Data and provenance

Set 1 is the 728 reflectance spectra of Dorin and colleagues [4], under CC0: 346 rocks and minerals, 96 bark, sticks and dry plant material, 65 green leaves, 153 insect-pollinated and 68 bird-pollinated flower petals, measured from 300 to 700 nm. The files were fetched from the Zenodo mirror of the Dryad deposit, because the Dryad file interface needed a token; the archive hashes equal those Dryad publishes.

Human cones are the CIE 2006 two-degree cone fundamentals, and the light is CIE standard illuminant D65, both under CC BY-SA 4.0 [5]. Bee, dog and blue tit receptor curves, blue tit ocular media and two natural lights come from the data inside the pavo 2.10.0 R package [6], under GPL version 2 or later; they were read with a pure-Python reader and no package code was run.

Set 2, used only in the replication, joins 512 flower spectra from Californian serpentine seeps (LeCroy and colleagues [7], CC0) with 41 eastern North American forest-floor backgrounds: 20 soils, 10 dry litter and 11 wet litter samples (Kraemer and Adams [8], CC0). Flowers and backgrounds come from different deposits and places.

Methods

The model

For a surface with reflectance R under light I, the quantum catchDefinition: quantum catch vision science The number of photons a receptor class absorbs from a surface, the sum over wavelength of reflectance times light times the receptor's sensitivity, here divided by the catch from a perfect white under the same light. Excludes the brightness a viewer reports. full definition of receptor class i with sensitivity Si is

Qi=∑λR(λ)I(λ)Si(λ)(1)

summed over wavelength λ in photon units. With von Kries adaptationDefinition: von Kries adaptation colour science Scaling each receptor class's catch by its catch from a white under the same light, a simple model of how eyes adjust to the colour of the light. Excludes adaptation that mixes signals between receptor classes. full definition, qi is Qi divided by the catch from a perfect white, and the receptor signal is fi=ln⁡qi. For two surfaces, let di be the difference in fi. For an observer with three receptor classes and noise e1, e2, e3, the colour distance in JND is

S2=(e1)2(d3−d2)2+(e2)2(d3−d1)2+(e3)2(d1−d2)2(e1e2)2+(e1e3)2+(e2e3)2(2)

Two- and four-class observers use the general form of the same model [1]. Brightness differences are left out.

Noise

In the first study each receptor's noise is a Weber fractionDefinition: Weber fraction psychophysics and vision science The noise in one receptor class as a fixed share of its signal, the same at every light level. We call a model with only this noise the Weber model. Excludes photon noise, which grows in relative size as the catch falls. full definition, a fixed share of its signal. The human values are 0.063, 0.028 and 0.020 for the short, middle and long cones, from a long-cone fraction of 0.02 and relative cone densities of 1 to 5 to 10. The bee values are 0.13, 0.06 and 0.12. The blue tit uses 0.1 for its long-wave class with relative densities 0.37 to 0.70 to 0.99 to 1. The dog uses 0.05 for its long-wave class with densities 1 to 9. The preregistration grades these sources: the human densities and fraction are from memory with low confidence, the bee and blue tit values from memory of published sources with moderate confidence, and the dog value assumed.

The replication adds photon noise:

(ei)2=(wi)2+1Niqi(3)

where wi is the Weber fraction above, qi the catch, and Ni the photon catch from the white per receptor and integration time. Ni is N scaled by each class's relative density, with N set to 10,000. That value is an order-of-magnitude memory with low confidence. Noise is evaluated at the mean catch of the pair.

The test statistic

A human-blind pairDefinition: human-blind pair our usage, after the metamer of colour science A pair of surfaces whose modelled colour distance for the human trichromat is at most 1 JND, so the model says a person cannot tell them apart by colour. Dog-blind pairs are defined the same way. Excludes pairs a person cannot tell apart by brightness, which the model does not test. full definition is a pair with S≤1 for the human model. Among the human-blind pairs, let PFB be the share of flower-background pairs with S>1 for the second observer, and PBB the same share among background-background pairs. The separation ratioDefinition: separation ratio our usage Among pairs one observer cannot separate, the share of flower-background pairs a second observer separates divided by the share of background-background pairs it separates. 1 means flowers gain nothing over the background. Excludes how far apart the pairs are for the second observer. full definition is

H=PFBPBB(4)

Dog-blind pairs are treated the same way. Flower-flower pairs are not counted.

Secondary test and named examples

H2b compares, for each flower, the median bee distance to all backgrounds between insect- and bird-pollinatedDefinition: insect- and bird-pollinated pollination ecology The dataset's labels for flowers whose recorded pollinators are insects only or birds only. Excludes flowers visited by both, which the dataset does not include in these groups. full definition flowers, with a one-sided label-permutation p value. Named examples were listed among human-blind flower-background pairs, with each surface's UV shareDefinition: UV share our usage A surface's mean reflectance below 400 nm divided by its mean reflectance from 400 to 700 nm. Excludes whether the ultraviolet forms a pattern on the petal. full definition.

Instrument check

The instrument checkDefinition: instrument check our usage; a known-answer test of the model against behaviour A preregistered test in which the model must reproduce published behavioural measurements, here the smallest wavelength step each observer can detect. If it fails, only ranks and ratios from the model are used. Excludes a test of the model against its own output, and a planted check on synthetic data. full definition, V0, asks the model for the smallest step in wavelength between two pure spectral lights that reaches 1 JND, in steps of 0.1 nm. In the first study the human minimum had to lie between 0.5 and 5 nm and the bee minimum between 1.5 and 12 nm, against behavioural values of about 1 to 2 nm for people and 4 to 5 nm for bees. In the replication the rules were tightened to a factor of 2 of the behavioural values at named wavelengths, for example a human step between 3 and 12 nm at 640 nm and a bee minimum between 2.25 and 9 nm. The behavioural values come from secondary sources and memory; the primary papers were not in hand. If V0 fails, absolute sizes from the model are not used.

Controls and planted checks

The control for H2 is a label shuffleDefinition: label shuffle statistics (permutation test) A control that randomly reassigns the flower and background labels over the same surfaces, here 500 times, and recomputes the separation ratio, which shows how large it gets when the labels carry no meaning. Excludes a shuffle of the spectra themselves. full definition: the flower and background labels are permuted over the same surfaces 500 times and the ratio recomputed. The null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition of the ratio has a mean near 1, as it should. A real ratio must exceed the shuffle's 95th percentile. The p value from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition is the share of shuffles at or above the real ratio, counted with one added to both counts, so with 500 draws the smallest possible value is 0.002. The p values were then put through the Benjamini-Hochberg correctionDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics, multiple testing A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call. full definition: over 7 tests in the first study and 14 in the replication.

Two code checks stand in for a planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition. The model's distances agreed with the published closed forms for two and three receptor classes to 4 times 10 to the power -16 on random inputs, and pavo's D65 equalled the CIE D65 to within 8 times 10 to the power -6. The instrument check is the known-answer test against behaviour. No surface set with a planted flower effect was run.

Results

The first study

Among pairs a modelled human cannot separate, modelled bees and blue tits separate flower-background pairs more often than background-background pairs, and the separation ratio exceeded its label-shuffle 95th percentile in every condition tested: two noise models on the first set, and two on a second set of Californian flowers against North American soil and leaf litter.c1 In the first study, with Weber noise, the bee separated 0.98 of 1,108 human-blind flower-background pairs and 0.48 of 3,892 human-blind background pairs, a ratio of 2.04 against a shuffle 95th percentile of 1.08. The blue tit separated 0.99 against 0.45, a ratio of 2.22 against 1.09. Among dog-blind pairs the ratios were 1.45 for the bee and 1.16 for the blue tit, each above its shuffle percentile. All four had p 0.002 and passed the correction (Table 1).

What this means for a reader

A tree-ring site that matches its local drought record only weakly is not a weak drought recorder in every sense. In the American West the trees carry most of the broad, regional pattern of summer drought and almost none of the local detail, as far as a gridded record that is itself smoothed can show. When a proxy is scored site by site, ask how much of its lost skill is lost in space rather than in time.

Objection

CRU interpolates precipitation with a 450 km decay distance, right where the filter opens, so low fine-scale coherence may be smoothing in the reference. Site clustering and noise fill the finest band.

What would change the call. Repeat with station or denser gridded data as reference, another region, a held-out fine-scale network.

From the strongest objection recorded in our publication register.

Abstract

Tree-ring records are often judged one site at a time, by comparing a site's yearly growth with the climate at that spot. We split that comparison by spatial scale as well as by time scale. The data are June to August drought from a gridded index, 399 one-degree cells in western North America from 1903 to 2025, and 664 tree-ring chronologies in the same box, complete from 1903 to 1980. In each of 30 cells of a grid of six spatial bands and five time bands we measured the share of the drought signal that the trees pass. The preregistered contrast between broad, slow scales and fine, fast scales was 0.64 (95% interval 0.62 to 0.68), against 95th percentiles of 0.22 for phase-randomised trees and 0.30 for trees moved to shuffled sites, with an adjusted p of 0.035.c1 Below 55 km the trees pass at most 0.004 of the drought signal in every time band, and above 460 km they pass 0.27 to 0.91.c2 Three tests on the drought field came back null. The drought field's covariance did not depart from a space part times a time partc3, no travel speed could be claimedc4, and broad and fine patterns lose their memory at the same rate, with a dispersion exponent of 0.02 (-0.12 to 0.17)c5. Measured against this gridded record, the trees act as a spatial filter; the grid is itself smooth, so the filter may belong partly to the grid.

Introduction

Tree rings are the main yearly record of drought before instruments. Cook, Meko, Stahle and Cleaveland [1] built a grid of summer drought reconstructions for the United States from a dense network of chronologies. Their method fits each grid point from the chronologies within a search radius, and they reported that a radius of 450 km worked best. The method is local by design. The reconstructed maps still kept the spatial features of drought, which the authors noted although the method was not built to be spatial.

The drought index in this study is the self-calibrating Palmer Drought Severity IndexDefinition: self-calibrating Palmer Drought Severity Index (scPDSI) climatology and hydrology A monthly drought index computed from temperature and precipitation through a simple soil water balance, with its constants calibrated to each location so values compare across places. Excludes a direct measurement of soil moisture or of streamflow. full definition, the scPDSI. Wells, Goddard and Hayes [2] built it so that the index's constants are fitted to each location and values compare across places. We use the gridded scPDSI distributed with CRU TS 4.10 [3] [4].

Averaging trees over larger areas raises the shared climate signal. Duchesne and colleagues [6] showed with forest inventory cores in Quebec that averaging at the stand level removes tree-level noise, that covariance among tree-ring signals falls with distance, and that reliable climate signals can be drawn at scales from 37 to 583,000 square km.

These studies treat space and time one at a time. A field that varies in both can hold structure neither view shows: a front that moves, patterns that fade faster at fine scales than at broad ones, or a filter that passes some combinations of scale and period and not others. This paper asks four questions at once. Does the drought field's covariance split into a space part times a time part? Do its anomalies travel? Do broad and fine patterns fade at different rates? And which combinations of spatial scale and period do the tree rings pass?

Preregistration and design

The design was written and hash-locked on 30 October 2026 at 04:20 UTC as a preregistrationDefinition: preregistration research method (metascience) A dated written plan for a study, fixed and hash-locked before any result is seen: the question, the data, the statistic, the controls, the forecasts and the kill conditions. Excludes a plan revised after looking at the outcome, and a protocol written only for the record after the run. full definition, before any outcome on the real data was computed. The real data had been built and only their counts printed: 399 cells by 123 years and 664 sites by 78 years. Development before the lock used synthetic fields only, and the preregistration lists every change made during that development.

The locked file names the data, the band edges, the four statistics, the synthetic fields, each controlDefinition: control statistics and experimental design A version of the data with the structure under test removed (for example shuffled or pooled), scored the same way as the real data, so the real score has something to beat. Excludes a comparison with a different dataset or with a published number. full definition, the forecasts and the pass rules. No unit, constant or rule changed after the lock. Each test passes only when the real statistic beats the 95th percentile of every scoring control, its adjusted p value is 0.05 or less, and, where named, its bootstrap interval sits above 0. A test that misses any rule fails, which makes each rule a kill conditionDefinition: kill condition research method (our usage, after Popper's falsification) A rule written in the preregistration that, when met, decides against the claim with no room for judgement after the run. Excludes reasons found after the run for setting a result aside. full definition.

Forecasts, written before the run: the covariance would be non-separable in both fields; travel would most likely be null or slow, under 100 km per year; the dispersion exponent would lie between 0 and 2, closer to the diffusion reading than the wave reading; and the tree filter test would pass.

Data and provenance

Drought: the June to August mean of the scPDSI from CRU TS 4.10 [4], 0.5 degree, 1903 to 2025, released under the Open Database License 1.0. The 0.5 degree cells between 125 and 100 W and 30 and 50 N were averaged to one-degree cells, keeping only one-degree cells with all four parts present in every year. This gave 399 cells and 123 years.

Trees: standard ring-width chronologiesDefinition: tree-ring chronology dendrochronology One yearly series for a site, built by dating many cores, removing each core's age and size trend and averaging the results into a dimensionless index. Excludes a single core's raw ring widths, and a climate reconstruction made from the series. full definition from the International Tree-Ring Data Bank [5], held by NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information as public data, with a request to cite the contributors. Every site in the same box with a gap-free index from 1903 to 1980 entered, which gave 664 sites and 78 years. Each site was paired with the June to August scPDSI of its nearest 0.5 degree cell with data in every year.

Every series had its linear trend removed and was scaled to unit variance. Positions were projected about 112.5 W and 40 N, in km. The input files and code were hashed into the run record before the run.

Methods

Bands in space and time

Let Kb be the matrix that smooths values on the sites with a normalised Gaussian of width σb, where σ1 to σ5 are 55, 95, 160, 270 and 460 km. Set K0 to the identity and K6 to zero. The space bandDefinition: space band signal processing on irregular sites, our usage The part of a field that varies between two spatial scales, taken as the difference of two Gaussian smoothings of the site values with the two scales as widths. The six bands add back to the field. Excludes an exact wavenumber, because the bands overlap and the sites are irregular. full definition b of a field x is

xb=(Kb−Kb+1)x(1)

for b from 0 to 5, so band 0 holds what varies below about 55 km and band 5 what varies above about 460 km, and the six bands add back to x. Each band is then split into five time bandsDefinition: time band spectral analysis The part of a yearly series whose period lies between two limits, kept by masking its Fourier transform. Excludes a moving average or a fitted trend. full definition by masks on the Fourier transform in time with edges at 1/32, 1/16, 1/8 and 1/4 cycles per year: periods over 32 years, 16 to 32, 8 to 16, 4 to 8 and 2 to 4 years. Each masked series is kept as a complex analytic signal.

The tree filter

For space band b and time band w, let ax and ay be the analytic signals of drought at the tree sites and of the trees. Summing over sites and years, with Sxy the sum of ax*ay and Sxx, Syy the sums of squared magnitudes, the passed share is the squared coherenceDefinition: squared coherence spectral analysis The share of one series' variance in a frequency band that a linear filter of the other series can account for, between 0 and 1. Here pooled over sites and years in each space and time band and called the passed share. Excludes a nonlinear dependence, and the size of the response, which the gain measures. full definition

γbw2=|Sxy|2SxxSyy(2)

The preregistered contrast C is the mean of γ2 over the four broad, slow cells (space bands 4 and 5, periods over 16 years) minus its mean over the four fine, fast cells (space bands 0 and 1, periods under 8 years):

C=14∑Lγbw2−14∑Fγbw2(3)

where L and F name those two sets of cells.

Separability

Let ρ(h,u) be the correlation between sites at distance h and time lag u, pooled over pairs in 100 km bins to 800 km and lags of 1, 2 and 3 years. A separable covarianceDefinition: separable covariance space-time statistics A covariance that factors into a function of distance times a function of time lag, so the spatial pattern of correlation has the same shape at every lag. Excludes fields whose anomalies travel or whose broad and fine patterns fade at different rates. full definition has ρ(h,u)=guρ(h,0). With gu fitted by least squares, the statistic is the sum of squared departures

D=∑h∑u(ρ(h,u)−guρ(h,0))2(4)

Travel

For site pairs within 1,200 km, the lag-one cross-correlation sij between site i in one year and site j in the next is pooled in 40 km offset cells and fitted as

sij=cρ0(|dij−v|)(5)

where dij is the offset between the sites, ρ0 the lag-zero correlation profile by distance, c a scale and v a velocity in km per year.

Dispersion

The decay rate of a pattern with wavenumber k is modelled as akβ, with power per log wavenumber proportional to k−q and white site noise. Each interior space band's autocovariance at lags 0 to 8 is predicted from the measured transfer of plane waves through that band on these exact sites and from the bias that linear detrending adds, and the four parameters are fitted to bands 1 to 4. The dispersion exponentDefinition: dispersion exponent physics of waves and diffusion The power beta in a decay rate that grows as the wavenumber to the power beta. Diffusion gives about 2, and fine and broad patterns that fade at the same rate give 0. Excludes a speed of travel, which the propagation test measures. full definition β is the result. Beside it, each band's e-folding time is reported.

p values, intervals and multiplicity

Each control was drawn 200 times, or 300 times for the separable surrogate. A test's p value is the larger of its scoring controls' p values from drawsDefinition: p value (from draws) statistics The share of control draws scoring at or above the real score, with one added to the count and to the number of draws, so it is never zero. Excludes a p value from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution. full definition,

p=k+1n+1(6)

with k the draws at or above the real value and n the draws. The seven real-data tests were adjusted together with the Benjamini-Hochberg correctionDefinition: Benjamini-Hochberg correction statistics, multiple testing A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call. full definition at q 0.05. Every 95% intervalDefinition: 95% interval statistics The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number. We report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. full definition comes from a moving-block bootstrapDefinition: moving-block bootstrap statistics An interval made by recomputing a statistic many times on years resampled in runs of consecutive years, here 10, so that year-to-year correlation is kept inside each run. Excludes resampling single years as if they were independent. full definition in time with blocks of 10 years.

Controls and planted checks

A planted checkDefinition: planted check research method; called a positive control in experimental science Data built so that the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show that the analysis can see the effect when it is there. Excludes any check made on the real data, which cannot show what the analysis misses. full definition ran in the same job before the real data were scored. Synthetic fields were built on the drought cell positions with 123 years, from 800 random plane waves plus white noise: a separable field, a wave field carried at 120 km per year toward 30 degrees, a diffusing field and pure noise. Five realisations of each were scored, and the instrument passed every rule. The separable field read as separable (median p 0.37 against a rule of at least 0.05), the planted wave's speed came back within 2.2 percent and its direction within 0.66 degrees, and the diffusion exponent read 1.88 against a rule of 1.7 to 2.3.c6 On the separable field the exponent read -0.01 and on the wave 0.81. Those are the readings a real exponent is compared against. The same checks on the tree positions with 78 years were reported and not scored; there the diffusion exponent read 1.64, below the scoring range.

c6 observed, evidence for claim 6
The numbers in claim 6
0.37; 0.05; 2.2; 0.66; 1.88; 1.7; 2.3 matches the result file, 2026-11-09
Chart 1
The design: one instrument, checked on planted fields, then four questions put to real drought and tree rings.
Basis
observed: measured in this study, with a result file

The real statistics faced these controls, each drawn many times to give a null distributionDefinition: null distribution statistics The spread of scores a control gives over many random draws. Its 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear. Excludes a theoretical distribution assumed rather than drawn from the data. full definition. Separability: a fitted separable field with the same lag-zero spatial covariance and pooled time autocovariance, and shuffled site coordinates. Travel: the lag-one matrix with its symmetric part kept and its antisymmetric part permuted across pairs in 100 km distance bins, and shuffled coordinates. Dispersion: shuffled coordinates and phase randomisationDefinition: phase randomisation time-series statistics, surrogate data A copy of a series with the same power spectrum and random Fourier phases, so it keeps the series' autocorrelation and loses its timing against any other series. Excludes shuffling years, which also destroys the autocorrelation. full definition of each site. The tree filter: phase-randomised trees, and tree series reassigned to shuffled sites. The last control keeps every tree's own spectrum and breaks only the link to its place.

Results

The tree filter

The preregistered contrast between broad, slow scales and fine, fast scales was 0.64 (95% interval 0.62 to 0.68), against 95th percentiles of 0.22 for phase-randomised trees and 0.30 for trees moved to shuffled sites, with an adjusted p of 0.035.c1 Figure 1 sets the contrast against both controls.

Figure 2 gives the passed share in all 30 cells. The share rises with spatial scale in every time band. Below 55 km the trees pass at most 0.004 of the drought signal in every time band, and above 460 km they pass 0.27 to 0.91.c2 Between 95 and 160 km they pass 0.07 to 0.11, and between 270 and 460 km 0.13 to 0.53. Time scale matters most at the broad end: above 460 km the share is 0.91 at periods over 32 years and 0.27 at 2 to 4 years. The phase-randomised control's mean share is at most 0.18, in that broadest and slowest cell.

The trees' own variance sits where their filter is closed. Figure 3 shows that 0.61 of the tree variance lies in the finest space band, against 0.12 for the drought index at the same sites.

The drought field

Table 1 gives all seven real-data tests. The drought field's covariance did not depart from a space part times a time partc3: its departure D was 0.0011 against a separable-surrogate 95th percentile of 0.0085 (p 0.72). The trees came back the same way (p 0.35). Both fields beat shuffled coordinates, which only shows that nearby sites are alike.

The drought fit for travel pointed 34.5 degrees north of east at 64.5 km per year and beat the antisymmetric shuffle (95th percentile 32 km per year). It did not beat shuffled coordinates, whose 95th percentile was 467 km per year, and no travel speed could be claimedc4: the bootstrap interval of the speed along the fitted direction ran from -41 to 242 km per year and the adjusted p was 0.66.

Broad and fine patterns lose their memory at the same rate, with a dispersion exponent of 0.02 (-0.12 to 0.17)c5. The e-folding times of the four interior bands were 0.76 to 0.83 years. Neither 1 nor 2 lies inside the interval, and the reading sits at the instrument's separable value, not at its wave or diffusion value. The trees' dispersion fit stopped at its lower bound of -1 and says nothing.

items.body_html:
Findings

Glossary

Each technical term on the findings pages, defined the way we use it: what we mean, the field the term comes from and what it excludes. A term shared across the findings has one definition; a term one study fixed for itself is defined in that study's scope. Each definition lists every page that uses it, and each use links back here.

401 terms, 478 scoped definitions, 717 first uses across 36 findings.

  1. 106-means rule

    In F14 history of optics; Newton's own rule in Opticks, Book II

    Newton's statement that the thickness goes as the secant of an angle whose sine is the first of 106 arithmetical means between the sines of incidence and refraction, counted from the bigger sine. Excludes the secant law, which uses the air angle alone.

    Used in F14, Newton's grazing-angle ring table follows his fitted rule, which runs 27% low at 85°extended

  2. 95% interval

    Across the findings statistics

    The range that holds the middle 95 percent of the bootstrap or control draws for a number; we report it beside the number. Excludes a statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability.

    Used in F27, Mood that lingers and mood that bounces back were not shown to be separate traits, F28, Forecasts people rate low are worse and more hedged, and people who skip more score betternarrowed in part, F32, Forecasters who skip questions score better, and the best filter reads the probability, F33, Cedar decline and water: observer site calls show no pattern either way, F39, Music with long ringing tails and dark spectra is rated calmer, and also less pleasantnarrowed in part, F97, Tree rings track the broad drought pattern in a gridded record and almost none of its local detail, F152, Finding missing links by shared neighbours lost to simple popularity on three corporaheld, F166, Our combined value formula lost to plain prospect theory on 11,759 risky choice problems, F172, A selection model shrinks the overstatement in published effects but cannot pick which replicateextended, F281, A home rerun of the GRB 090510 light-speed test, and sound waves that keep their own limitnarrowed in part, F320, A random split scores a stress classifier perfect on data with nothing to learnnarrowed in part, F329, In held-out private die-roll reports, about 45 percent read as honest, and this method cannot tell us whynarrowed in part, F362, Published 1 sigma error bars hold near nominal; a 95 percent interval needs 3 to 5 sigmanarrowed in part

  3. A-B-C ranking

    In F152 literature-based discovery, after Swanson

    Scoring an unlinked pair A and C by the intermediate concepts B that each is linked to; here a cosine over shared neighbours with each edge weighted down when both of its ends are popular. Excludes methods trained on known outcomes, and the expert reading that Swanson applied to each candidate.

    Used in F152, Finding missing links by shared neighbours lost to simple popularity on three corporaheld

  4. aCompCor

    In F50 neuroimaging (denoising)

    Anatomical component correction: the main components of the signal in white matter and cerebrospinal fluid, where little neural signal is expected, are regressed out as noise. Excludes global signal regression, which removes the mean of the whole brain.

    Used in F50, Childhood trauma scores showed no meaningful link to amygdala-prefrontal coupling in 187 adults

  5. acoustic horizon

    In F281 analogue gravity

    The place in a moving fluid where the flow speed equals the sound speed, so that sound travelling against the flow cannot get out; it mimics the horizon of a black hole. Excludes a gravitational horizon, and any place where the flow is slower than sound.

    Used in F281, A home rerun of the GRB 090510 light-speed test, and sound waves that keep their own limitnarrowed in part

  6. Adamic-Adar index

    In F152 network science

    A count of the neighbours two nodes share in which each shared neighbour is weighted by one over the logarithm of its own degree. Excludes the popularity discount on edges that the A-B-C score uses.

    Used in F152, Finding missing links by shared neighbours lost to simple popularity on three corporaheld

  7. adjoint

    In F204 linear algebra and inverse problems

    The partner of a linear map that carries vectors from the output space back to the input space so that the inner product of an output with a vector equals the inner product of the input with the partner's result. Excludes the inverse, which undoes the map; an adjoint exists for maps that cannot be undone.

    Used in F204, Backward and contrary checks caught 39 of 47 quiet faults in eight small simulated instruments

  8. AIC

    In F23 statistics (model selection)

    The Akaike information criterion, twice the number of fitted parameters minus twice the log-likelihood; between two models fitted to the same data the lower value is preferred, and a gap of 2 or more is the usual bar. Excludes a test that one model is true.

    Used in F23, Fungal hub trees mostly track sampling, cedar heartwood rots slowest, wind damage evades prediction

    In F76 statistical model selection

    The Akaike information criterion, a fit score that adds a penalty of two per fitted parameter, used here to choose the autoregressive order. Excludes choice by held-out error, which would use the test half.

    Used in F76, How flat a spectrum is predicts forecast skill, but real series follow it looselyheld

  9. Airy reflectance

    In F14 optics; named after George Airy

    The share of light power a thin layer reflects when every reflected and re-reflected beam inside it is summed, rather than only the first two. Excludes the two-beam approximation, and absorption in the glass.

    Used in F14, Newton's grazing-angle ring table follows his fitted rule, which runs 27% low at 85°extended

  10. aliasing

    In F38 signal processing

    The misreading that results when a process changes faster than it is sampled, so that the fast change appears in the record as something else, here as noise. Excludes measurement error in the instrument, which is present even with dense sampling.

    Used in F38, Forecasts drift, mood steps or drifts in many people; simulated five-a-day prompts miss fast emotion

  11. amygdala

    In F50 neuroanatomy

    A pair of almond-shaped structures deep in the temporal lobes, one per hemisphere, involved in detecting threat and in emotional learning. Excludes its separate subnuclei, which the anatomical masks here do not distinguish.

    Used in F50, Childhood trauma scores showed no meaningful link to amygdala-prefrontal coupling in 187 adults

  12. analogue forecaster

    In F76 nonlinear time-series prediction (method of analogues)

    A forecast that finds the k past states most like the present one and averages what came next; it can follow nonlinear structure a linear model misses. Excludes trained nonlinear models such as neural networks.

    Used in F76, How flat a spectrum is predicts forecast skill, but real series follow it looselyheld

  13. AR(1) process

    In F27 time-series statistics

    A series in which each value is the mean plus a fixed fraction of the previous value's distance from the mean, plus fresh random noise; the fraction is the single parameter. Excludes models with separate rates for small and large deviations, and models with measurement noise on top.

    Used in F27, Mood that lingers and mood that bounces back were not shown to be separate traits

    In F38 time-series statistics

    A series in which each value is the mean plus a fixed fraction of the previous value's distance from the mean, plus fresh random noise. Excludes steps, drifting coefficients, switching between states and long memory.

    Used in F38, Forecasts drift, mood steps or drifts in many people; simulated five-a-day prompts miss fast emotion

  14. area under the risk-coverage curve

    In F32 machine learning, selective prediction

    The mean risk over coverages from 10 to 100 percent in steps of 5, one number for a whole filter; lower is better. Excludes coverages below 10 percent.

    Used in F32, Forecasters who skip questions score better, and the best filter reads the probability

  15. area under the ROC curve

    In F152 statistics and machine learning

    The chance that a randomly chosen target scores above a randomly chosen non-target; 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect. Excludes how the top of the list performs, which precision in the top 200 measures.

    Used in F152, Finding missing links by shared neighbours lost to simple popularity on three corporaheld

  16. arithmetic coding

    In F515 data compression

    A method that turns a model's probability for each next symbol into a single binary number, so a symbol given probability p costs close to minus log2 p bits, and a decoder with the same model recovers the text exactly. Excludes codes that give each symbol a fixed whole number of bits, such as Huffman codes.

    Used in F515, A small language model squeezes the UDHR to 0.27 bits a character, and fresh text to 1.59

  17. arousal and valence

    In F39 psychology of emotion (the circumplex model)

    Two rating scales for emotion: arousal runs from calm to excited and valence from unpleasant to pleasant; in DEAM each is a nine-point scale averaged over crowd raters. Excludes named emotions such as sadness or nostalgia, which the ratings place only as points on the two scales.

    Used in F39, Music with long ringing tails and dark spectra is rated calmer, and also less pleasantnarrowed in part

  18. attenuation

    In F27 psychometrics

    The shrinking of an observed correlation toward zero when the measures that enter it are noisy. Excludes a true weak relation between the underlying quantities.

    Used in F27, Mood that lingers and mood that bounces back were not shown to be separate traits

  19. AUC

    In F23 statistics (signal detection)

    The area under the ROC curve: the chance that a randomly chosen damaged tree is ranked above a randomly chosen undamaged one, with 0.5 for guessing. Excludes how close the predicted probabilities are to the observed rates.

    Used in F23, Fungal hub trees mostly track sampling, cedar heartwood rots slowest, wind damage evades prediction

    In F47 statistics (signal detection)

    The area under the ROC curve: the chance that a randomly chosen positive case is ranked above a randomly chosen negative one, with 0.5 for guessing. Excludes accuracy at any one threshold.

    Used in F47, More variables raise prediction skill, yet most targets stall far below their noise ceiling

    In F320 statistics and machine learning

    The probability that a classifier gives a randomly chosen positive case a higher score than a randomly chosen negative case; 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect separation. Excludes accuracy at one threshold, and any statement about how well the scores are calibrated as probabilities.

    Used in F320, A random split scores a stress classifier perfect on data with nothing to learnnarrowed in part

  20. autoregressive model

    In F76 time-series statistics

    A linear forecast of the next value from a weighted sum of the last p values, with the weights fitted by least squares; p is the order. Excludes models with moving-average terms, external inputs or nonlinear terms.

    Used in F76, How flat a spectrum is predicts forecast skill, but real series follow it looselyheld

  21. average runtime (aRT)

    In F183 optimiser benchmarking, as defined in the COCO platform

    The evaluations spent by every run, successful runs counted up to their first success and failed runs in full, divided by the number of successful runs; infinite when no run succeeds. Excludes the plain mean of the successful runs' runtimes, which ignores the cost of failures.

    Used in F183, After we fixed our own bug, CMA-ES ranked first and two nature-inspired optimisers proved centre-biased

  22. b-file

    In F308 the OEIS

    A text file stored beside an OEIS entry that lists the sequence's index and term pairs much further than the entry's own data section, often to thousands of terms. Excludes the entry's data section, which holds only the first few dozen terms.

    Used in F308, Checking 213 OEIS recurrence conjectures against their b-files finds one failure, already knownnarrowed in part

  23. backward check

    In F204 our usage, from physics symmetries

    A test that runs an instrument model in reverse against itself, by time reversal, reciprocity, an adjoint identity or an inverse, and needs no reference value. Excludes a comparison with a known answer.

    Used in F204, Backward and contrary checks caught 39 of 47 quiet faults in eight small simulated instruments

  24. base rate

    In F152 statistics

    The share of all unlinked candidate pairs that are targets, the precision a random ranking would reach on average. Excludes the precision of any particular ranker.

    Used in F152, Finding missing links by shared neighbours lost to simple popularity on three corporaheld

    In F172 forecasting

    A forecast that gives every effect in a held-out field the same chance of replicating, the share that replicated in the training fields. Excludes any use of an effect's own statistics.

    Used in F172, A selection model shrinks the overstatement in published effects but cannot pick which replicateextended

  25. benefit-to-cost ratio

    In F190 social evolution

    The benefit b that one producer's goods give in total divided by the cost c it pays, written b/c. Excludes the net payoff to any one cell, which also depends on its neighbours.

    Used in F190, Our model of cooperation on a grid had been rewarding selfishness

  26. Benjamini-Hochberg correction

    In F63 statistics, multiple testing

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05; the adjusted value is called q. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call.

    Used in F63, Across 1,175 tree-ring sites, an earlier moderate drought did not detectably toughen treesnarrowed in part

    In F81 statistics, multiple testing

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call.

    Used in F81, Among colours people cannot tell apart, modelled bees and blue tits split flowers from backgrounds more oftennarrowed in part

    In F97 statistics, multiple testing

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call.

    Used in F97, Tree rings track the broad drought pattern in a gridded record and almost none of its local detail

    In F114 statistics, multiple testing

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call.

    Used in F114, How much summer warmth one tree ring remembers, measured in bits

    In F132 statistics, multiple testing

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05; the adjusted value is called q. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call.

    Used in F132, Transfer entropy could not tell which way climate and tree rings are linkedquestioned

    In F147 statistics

    A rule for many tests at once: rank the p values from smallest, and reject the k smallest when the kth is no larger than k over the number of tests times the chosen false discovery rate, here 0.05. Excludes a correction for one test, and the stricter Bonferroni rule.

    Used in F147, Kodak's own curves put modern colour negative at 0.6 to 4.9 percent quantum efficiencynarrowed in part

    In F166 statistics, multiple testing

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values into q values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call.

    Used in F166, Our combined value formula lost to plain prospect theory on 11,759 risky choice problems

    In F172 statistics, multiple testing

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05; the adjusted values are called q values. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call.

    Used in F172, A selection model shrinks the overstatement in published effects but cannot pick which replicateextended

    In F204 statistics (multiple testing)

    An adjustment of a family of p values that limits the expected share of false discoveries among the tests called significant. Excludes control of the chance of any single false discovery, which is the stricter Bonferroni aim.

    Used in F204, Backward and contrary checks caught 39 of 47 quiet faults in eight small simulated instruments

    In F320 statistics, multiple testing

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false discoveries stays at or below a chosen level q. Excludes control of the chance of even one false discovery, which is a stricter rule.

    Used in F320, A random split scores a stress classifier perfect on data with nothing to learnnarrowed in part

    In F329 statistics, multiple testing

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate q, here 0.05. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call.

    Used in F329, In held-out private die-roll reports, about 45 percent read as honest, and this method cannot tell us whynarrowed in part

    In F344 statistics (multiple testing)

    A rule that raises a set of p values to control the expected share of false discoveries among the tests called significant; the smallest raw p is multiplied by the number of tests and larger ones by less. Excludes an uncorrected p value read on its own when several tests were run.

    Used in F344, No cubic pattern in public Auger cosmic-ray directions, at sensitivity that sees only large onesnarrowed in part

    In F675 statistics, multiple testing

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05; the adjusted value is called q. Excludes the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call.

    Used in F675, A panel test read climate driving tree rings correctly, and our own rule still failed itnarrowed in part

  27. Benjamini-Hochberg correction

    In F76 statistics (multiple testing)

    A rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05. Excludes corrections that control the chance of any false call at all, such as Bonferroni.

    Used in F76, How flat a spectrum is predicts forecast skill, but real series follow it looselyheld

  28. BIC

    In F27 statistics (model selection)

    The Bayesian information criterion, a fit score that charges each extra parameter a penalty growing with sample size; the lower value is preferred. Excludes a test of whether either model is true.

    Used in F27, Mood that lingers and mood that bounces back were not shown to be separate traits

    In F147 statistics; the Bayesian information criterion

    A model score that adds a penalty for each fitted parameter to the misfit, lower being better, so that a more flexible model must earn its extra parameters. Excludes a test on held-out data.

    Used in F147, Kodak's own curves put modern colour negative at 0.6 to 4.9 percent quantum efficiencynarrowed in part

    In F166 statistics, model selection

    The Bayesian information criterion with the log-likelihood divided by the dispersion: a score that trades fit against the number of parameters, lower being better. Excludes an absolute test of a model, since it only compares models on the same data.

    Used in F166, Our combined value formula lost to plain prospect theory on 11,759 risky choice problems

    In F172 statistics, model comparison

    The Bayesian information criterion, minus twice the maximised log likelihood plus the number of parameters times the log of the number of rows; lower is better, and a difference of 10 is the usual bar for strong preference. Excludes a test of whether either model is right.

    Used in F172, A selection model shrinks the overstatement in published effects but cannot pick which replicateextended

  29. binding check

    In F675 research method, our usage

    A preregistered rule on a synthetic world that the instrument must pass before any reading of the real data counts; under the kill condition a single failure removes all standing. Excludes power checks and limit checks, which were recorded but could not remove standing.

    Used in F675, A panel test read climate driving tree rings correctly, and our own rule still failed itnarrowed in part

  30. binomial likelihood

    In F166 statistics

    Fitting by choosing the parameters under which the observed counts of B choices are most probable, treating each choice as an independent draw at the predicted rate; here five choices per listed participant. Excludes extra scatter between problems, which the dispersion handles.

    Used in F166, Our combined value formula lost to plain prospect theory on 11,759 risky choice problems

  31. biologically labelled method

    In F183 our usage for this study

    An optimiser whose published description is framed by an animal, plant or other organism, here slime mould, grey wolf, particle swarm, bee colony, ant colony and invasive weed. Excludes any claim that the method works the way the organism does.

    Used in F183, After we fixed our own bug, CMA-ES ranked first and two nature-inspired optimisers proved centre-biased

  32. bipartite network

    In F23 network science

    A network with two kinds of node, here trees and fungal genets, in which a link joins a tree to a genet found on at least one of its root tips and never joins two nodes of the same kind. Excludes a network of measured flows between trees.

    Used in F23, Fungal hub trees mostly track sampling, cedar heartwood rots slowest, wind damage evades prediction

  33. bit

    In F114 information theory

    The unit of information: one bit halves the uncertainty about an outcome, so a record that keeps b bits a year narrows each year's range of possible summers by a factor of 2 to the power b, as measured by its standard deviation. Excludes a count of stored numbers, and any statement about which way the dependence runs.

    Used in F114, How much summer warmth one tree ring remembers, measured in bits

  34. bits per character

    In F515 information theory and data compression

    The length of a compressed text in bits divided by the number of characters in the original; lower is better, and 8 is the cost of plain one-byte text. Excludes bits per token or per byte, which divide by a different count.

    Used in F515, A small language model squeezes the UDHR to 0.27 bits a character, and fresh text to 1.59

  35. bits per letter

    In F508 information theory

    The average number of binary digits needed to write down each letter of a text under a given model of the text; one bit halves the number of equally likely choices, so 4.75 bits per letter is the cost of picking blindly among 27 symbols. Excludes a count of bytes in a file, and any statement about meaning.

    Used in F508, Shannon's 1951 letter statistics hold on old and new English; his third-order value reads high

  36. block cross-validation

    In F114 statistics and machine learning

    The years are split into contiguous blocks, here five; each block in turn is held out, the model is fitted on the rest and scored on the held-out block. Excludes a score on the fitting years, and splits that scatter single years so that neighbouring years leak into the fit.

    Used in F114, How much summer warmth one tree ring remembers, measured in bits

  37. Bogoliubov dispersion

    In F281 condensed-matter physics (Bose-Einstein condensates)

    The frequency of small waves in a uniform condensate: equal to the sound speed times the wavenumber at long wavelength and rising faster, towards the free-particle law, at wavelengths near the healing length. Excludes sound in an ordinary gas or solid, whose dispersion is set by other physics.

    Used in F281, A home rerun of the GRB 090510 light-speed test, and sound waves that keep their own limitnarrowed in part

  38. bootstrap interval

    In F23 statistics

    An interval made by recomputing a number many times on units drawn with replacement from the data, here trees, logs or inventory plots, and keeping the middle 95 percent of the results. Excludes an interval that also covers doubt about the model's form.

    Used in F23, Fungal hub trees mostly track sampling, cedar heartwood rots slowest, wind damage evades prediction

    In F28 statistics

    Recomputing a statistic many times on forecaster-years resampled with replacement to read how much the estimate varies. Excludes an interval from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution.

    Used in F28, Forecasts people rate low are worse and more hedged, and people who skip more score betternarrowed in part

    In F32 statistics

    Recomputing a number many times on data resampled with replacement, here within strata or over questions, to see how much it varies. Excludes an interval from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution.

    Used in F32, Forecasters who skip questions score better, and the best filter reads the probability

    In F166 statistics

    Refitting a model many times on problems resampled with replacement to read how much an estimate varies. Excludes an interval from a textbook formula that assumes a distribution.

    Used in F166, Our combined value formula lost to plain prospect theory on 11,759 risky choice problems

    In F183 statistics

    An interval read from the spread of a statistic recomputed on many resamples, drawn with replacement, of the data; here 2,000 resamples of the 15 paired repeats, and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Excludes uncertainty from choices the resampling does not repeat, such as which test functions were picked.

    Used in F183, After we fixed our own bug, CMA-ES ranked first and two nature-inspired optimisers proved centre-biased

    In F281 statistics

    Resampling the data with replacement many times and recomputing the estimate each time, so that the spread of the recomputed values gives an interval for it. Excludes an interval taken from a formula that assumes a distribution.

    Used in F281, A home rerun of the GRB 090510 light-speed test, and sound waves that keep their own limitnarrowed in part

    In F362 statistics, resampling

    Redrawing the quantities of a table with replacement, here 300 times, and recomputing the coverage each time; the middle 95 percent of the recomputed values is the interval. Excludes uncertainty from the choice of editions or from shared inputs, which resampling quantities does not touch.

    Used in F362, Published 1 sigma error bars hold near nominal; a 95 percent interval needs 3 to 5 sigmanarrowed in part

  39. Brier score

    In F28 forecast verification, from weather forecasting

    The squared difference between the stated probabilities and the outcomes, here summed over the answer options in the Good Judgment Project form so it runs from 0 to 2; lower is better. Excludes questions left unanswered, which it does not score.

    Used in F28, Forecasts people rate low are worse and more hedged, and people who skip more score betternarrowed in part

    In F32 forecast verification, from weather forecasting

    The squared difference between the stated probabilities and the outcomes, here summed over the answer options in the GJP form so it runs from 0 to 2; lower is better. Excludes questions left unanswered, which it does not score.

    Used in F32, Forecasters who skip questions score better, and the best filter reads the probability

    In F47 forecast verification (meteorology)

    The mean squared difference between a probability forecast and the outcome coded 0 or 1; lower is better. Excludes measures that score only whether the most likely outcome happened.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

Two pen drawings of a person browsing in a room of bookshelves. The shelves fill the frame; each run of books is drawn as one repeated mark. Pale-green pencil perspective guides sit under the ink.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Ground: paper; green coloured-pencil guides (O). Palette leads #aaa496, #c1beb0, #d1cec4 (M).
  • Mark vocabulary (13 types, O): plain verticals; stacked short dashes; dot columns; line-and-dot; loops and curls; scallop rows; cross-hatched blocks; solid black blocks with white gaps; horizontal dash stacks; small open squares; forked marks; zigzag diagonal hatching; hooks.
  • Rule: one mark per shelf run, so the type of book is coded by mark (O).
  • Measures: spectral slope β 1.38 and 1.65 (rough, mark-dense, M); edge softness 1.6 to 1.9 (hard pen, M); texture wavelength 0.004 to 0.006 of width (the spine pitch, M).
  • Figure: one visitor per room, in the same pen (O).

The framework behind it

A mosaic whose tiles are marks, not colours: each tile carries a texture that stands for a kind of thing. It is a legend made of drawing, the same idea as a map's hatch patterns.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Cartography and geology maps: hatch and dot patterns encode rock and land types.
  • Textiles: weave structures named by their marks.
  • Musical notation: repeated marks as rhythm.
  • Halftone: dots standing for tone, here standing for kind.

Dual edge

Marks as categories invite reading meaning where none is fixed; a legend must travel with them. The drawings are someone's work; we take the mark idea, not the drawings.

What it is, and who made it

Three versions of a grid effect on a 15 s video: a poster grid, a 'style infection' that spreads a look cell to cell, and a temporal mosaic where cells show different moments.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

This is a reading method for dense philosophical texts, shown on Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, question 2, articles 1 to 3. Aliocha learned it in a course she names, "Leitura e interpretação de textos clássicos". She uses it only for reading that will be assessed academically. In her words, without it she would read "2 livros por ano".

The post is the method, and the four images show it in use:

  1. a notebook page that rewrites two objections as numbered premises and conclusions;
  2. 2. to 4. the printed page, annotated with circled conjunctions, colour highlights, cut marks and margin brackets.

Parts, layer by layer

The method, as stated (observed in the text).

  1. Structure. Split each argument into premises and conclusions, and often presuppositions.
  2. Movements. Decide whether arguments form a chain, a list (number them), or a turn, where the author moves from affirmative to negative.
  3. Conjunctions. They "indicate reversal of movement or continuity": they deny or confirm what came before.
  4. Active reading. Underline the main argument and the links between ideas. The aim is to reproduce the author's whole movement from conclusion to conclusion.

The notation, layer by layer.

LayerPartProperties (label)
L1 notebook (image 1)ruled page in a tablet notes app27 ruled rows at pitch 0.0289 of the height (M); labels P, C, pressuposto, 1º momento, 2º momento, numbered premises (O); yellow behind the labels (O)
L2 printed page (images 2 to 4)two columnsLatin original on the left, Portuguese on the right (O)
L3 colour code (images 3 and 4)highlighter inksyellow #c7bc75, blue #7eaed3, purple #875fa3, and teal #35555b where blue lies over yellow (M); yellow covers 0.255 and 0.398 of the two annotated columns (M)
L3 role mappingwhat each colour meansyellow is the first premise or proposition, blue the second premise or presupposition, purple the conclusion or objection (O). Purple marks a conclusion on page 164 and an objection on page 165, so colour codes a role within the current movement, not one global role (I)
L4 cut and circle marksI-beams, circles, bracketsI-beam bars split segments; 7 of them in objections 1 to 3 of article 2 (O, counted). Circled: portanto, mas, pois, nem, ora, assim (O). Margin labels: P¹, P², C, Pressuposto, 1 movimento, 2º movimento, Objeção, Corolário, Início do 2º (O)
marginaliawritten rules"As conjunções indicam mudança de movimento"; "Corolário. Conclusão acessória a outra conclusão"; "Estrutura diferente de tudo até agora" (O)

The argument under the notation. Each objection in article 2 has a fixed shape: a major premise, then Ora (Latin Sed) introducing the minor premise, then Logo (Latin Ergo) introducing the conclusion. Objection 3 nests: its minor premise is itself argued ("finite and infinite have no proportion") before the conclusion.

Text measures of her post (code).

  • Connectives found: 1 continuation and 4 condition.
  • Every condition hit is the Portuguese se or caso. In her text these are mostly the reflexive se ("se pode") and the noun caso, not conditionals.

The framework behind it

An argument has a grammar, and connectives are its function words. The method makes three structures visible:

  • Segments: premise, presupposition, conclusion.
  • Joints: the connective that opens a segment, with its role. The roles are conclusion (portanto, logo, ergo), minor (ora, scholastic sed), reversal (mas, sed, autem), continuation (além disso, praeterea) and cause (pois, quia, enim).
  • Movements: how segments link, as a chain, a list or a turn.

The colour, the cuts and the brackets are three encodings of the same tree, one per layer of attention. Reading actively means rebuilding that tree.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Logic and law: argument mapping (Toulmin's claim, data, warrant and rebuttal) and legal briefs that number premises. The scholastic article form (objections, sed contra, respondeo, replies) is the original template.
  • Linguistics: Rhetorical Structure Theory and the Penn Discourse Treebank. Both annotate discourse relations at connectives, which is the computational version of her circles.
  • Music: cadences. A conclusion connective works like a cadence, and mas works like a deceptive cadence that turns the line.
  • Code: control flow. Se is if, mas is else, logo is return. A reader's bracket is a block, and a movement is a call graph.
  • Our own work: Daylight's reading lens names techniques at spans. Articulate flags stock connectives as style. Neither yet reads the logic the connectives carry.

Dual edge

  • The lens can make weak arguments look rigorous. Marking portanto as a "conclusion" looks like validation, but a connective asserts a link; it does not prove one. The margin must say "the author marks this as following", never "this follows". That is our does-not-prove rule at the span.
  • It can be gamed. Persuasive writing borrows logical connectives to borrow authority ("therefore, clearly ..."). In Daylight the same spans that teach reading can flag connective inflation: many conclusion markers, few premises. That is a manipulation cue, and it stays behind the same gate.
  • It helps the readers the author named (2026-10-25: people who find communicating hard). It also risks replacing their reading with ours. The lens shows the joints and leaves the judgement to the reader, consistent with the canon: reveal the process, support the decision, don't make it.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

Four zine pages on composition for illustration: colour temperature, neutral against dynamic framing, depth planes, and horizon and mass in vertical frames.

Parts, layer by layer

  • DEPTH: foreground frames, midground holds the character and focal points, background sets the scene; "each plane has a job"; the foreground is often the smallest element and can be dropped (O).
  • Horizon and mass: where the horizon sits and how big the shapes are "make or break" a vertical composition; 50/50 splits are "a tough sell"; equal masses "feel too the same" (O).
  • Neutral and dynamic: neutral pose, camera and background connect to a character; dynamic ones build tension; the background sets focal length; mixing them carelessly causes dissonance (O).
  • COLOR TEMPERATURE, measured in CIE Lab from the page:
    • macro: sky (cool) b* −22.3; ground (warm) b* +42.4 (M);
    • micro swatches: pink-warm b* 10.4, cream 14.8, saturation band 13.4, orange cream 22.6, against the "cool" green a* −10.0, b* 11.0 (M): the cool swatch is greener, not bluer;
    • foliage: lit green a* −4.9, shadow a* +6.2 (M): the "red in the shadows" tip measured.

The framework behind it

A layer model with roles (planes that each do one job) and a property layer (temperature) that can be painted at two scales. For the fluid-medium framework: depth planes are strata, and temperature is a property field with a macro pattern and micro alternation.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Stage design: wings, actors and backdrop.
  • Atmosphere: aerial perspective cools and lightens with distance, the physics behind macro temperature.
  • Music mixing: front, middle and back of a mix, each with a frequency job.
  • Cartography: figure-ground and visual hierarchy.

Dual edge

Temperature rules are style rules from one studio tradition; applied everywhere they homogenise. Keep them as a dial, not a default. The zine is the author's own teaching material; credit it.

What it is, and who made it

A 1.4 s hand-drawn effects animation: a foot strikes water and a crown splash and droplets rise and fall on a perspective grid.

An effects animator's model of water: a few readable shapes (crown, droplets, ring) timed on a cycle, not a simulation.

What it is, and who made it

A UI card component: as cards are swiped, the next image appears through a spreading ink-like mask.

Parts, layer by layer

  • UI: rounded card, arrows, soft grey surround (O).
  • Reveal: an ink-edged mask grows from a point to fill the card (O).

The framework behind it

An image transition as a dye: the new image is the ink, the old one the water. The mask is a growing, noise-edged front.

  • Burn-in and dissolve transitions in film.
  • Infection spread on networks (a front with a noisy edge).

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

Four stills of a real-time pigment simulation: coloured rivulets branch, bead and ring across a gridded paper-coloured ground.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Ground: warm paper with a faint grid; palette leads #e5d6bc, #e0d2b8 (M).
  • Streams: branching rivulets in blue, red, orange, green, with beads along them and closed rings (O).
  • Edges: granular dark rims and lighter interiors (O).
  • Measures: spectral slope β 2.64, edge softness 4.55 (M).
  • Fluid reading: viscosity, surface tension, diffusion; additive pigment; tide lines and bubbles; processes advection, growth, sedimentation, bleed.

The framework behind it

Capillary flow on paper: pigment moves along wet paths, the path branches, surface tension pinches the stream into beads, and the drying edge leaves a darker line. 'Let it decide' names the method: set the laws and the drop, not the outcome.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Viscous fingering in Hele-Shaw cells.
  • River networks and leaf venation.
  • Lichtenberg figures (branching discharge).
  • Wicking in fabric.

Dual edge

Generative pigment flows are easy to mass-produce as decoration; the value is in the laws and the setting. Credit the author's method if we show the idea publicly.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

A 30 s visualisation of a round drum's vibration modes, with the post's history: Kac asked in 1966 whether the notes of a drum fix its shape; in 1992 two differently shaped drums were found that play exactly the same notes.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Drum: a gold rim on black; the membrane shows mode patterns in teal and gold (O).
  • Motion: mean speed 0.16 widths per second, coherence 0.53, vorticity share 0.52 (M): standing-wave flicker rather than a current.
  • Facts: Kac, "Can One Hear the Shape of a Drum?", American Mathematical Monthly, 1966 (high confidence). Gordon, Webb and Wolpert, isospectral planar domains, 1992 (high confidence). The disc is determined by its spectrum among planar domains, via heat-trace invariants (area, perimeter) (moderate-high confidence).

The framework behind it

A medium's shape sets its resonances (the Laplacian's eigenvalues), but the resonances do not always fix the shape. Sound as an additive therefore carries partial information about the vessel it sounds in.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Chladni plates: sand gathers on the nodal lines of a plate's modes.
  • Room acoustics: a room's modes colour every sound in it.
  • Spectral graph theory: a network's eigenvalues and when two networks share them.
  • Seismology: the Earth's normal modes reveal its interior.

Dual edge

Isospectrality is a clean warning about inference: identical outputs do not prove identical sources. That is our does-not-prove rule in mathematical form, and worth saying wherever we infer a cause from a signal.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

Two spreads of a brand reference book called "The Observing Mind", for a company named hermeneutic. Spread 1 is a mood board beside a large serif title. Spread 2 shows two symbol plates: an eye drawn as concentric rings (plate 11) and an atom of crossed orbits around a four-point star (plate 12).

Parts, layer by layer

  • Layout (O):
    • running heads in small tracked mono capitals (THE OBSERVING MIND on the left; CONCEPT or SYMBOL INSPIRATION on the right);
    • plates numbered ( 11 ) and ( 12 );
    • a keyword line at the foot of every spread: CONTEXTUAL, INTUITIVE, INTELLIGENT, DISCIPLINED, HUMAN;
    • a page number at the foot right;
    • two families: a light high-contrast serif and a mono.
  • Plate 11, the eye: an almond outline in several looped strokes around 4 to 5 concentric rings, chalk white on dark grain (O). From the centre, a line crosses bright strokes 9 times horizontally and 5 times vertically (M), so the lids add strokes sideways.
  • Plate 12, the atom: three tilted elliptical orbits crossing around a four-point star, in rough printed line (O).
  • Mood board (O): the ring eye, a dotted event sheet, a synesthesia card, a broken dashed ring, a starburst of arrows, two engraved hands, a card with smeared type, an embossed sheet.

The framework behind it

A reference book reads as a sequence of boards. Each spread has a running head (where you are), numbered plates (the evidence), and a keyword line (what it means). The motifs share one idea: a centre held by rings or orbits, which is how an observing mind is drawn.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Specimen books and type catalogues: a running head, numbered specimens and a caption line.
  • Scientific plates: numbered figures with a legend.
  • Our canon: the aperture and the luminous orb.
  • Physics: Bohr's atom, the orbits as a picture rather than the physics.
  • The concept layers' ring bridge (89 units in 11 mediums): ripples, drum modes, an iris, a halo.

Dual edge

A keyword line can tell the reader what to feel before they look. On our boards it should come from the measured concepts, not from adjectives.

What it is, and who made it

A game for drawing practice: walk a garden of 3D-scanned sculptures and sketch them, with a dynamic lighting mode for shading practice and model packs.

The framework behind it

A tool that turns light into the teacher: the same form under moving light shows how shading works. Light is the additive; the form is the medium.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Photographic lighting studies (one subject, many lights).
  • Museums with cast courts.

Learning tools can become engagement loops; the canon asks for tools that return time. A study tool should end when the drawing is done.
