items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

Acrylic washes on a pale ground: a turquoise field with dark round blots ringed at their edges and thin dark lines along the lower edge.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Ground: pale raw-looking ground showing at the borders (O).
  • Wash: thinned paint soaked into the ground; palette leads #557e7d, #9d8e6d, #6f8477 (M).
  • Blots: dark purple and teal discs with darker rims (O): pigment carried to the drying edge.
  • Measures: spectral slope β 3.05 (very smooth, M), edge softness 15.2 (soft, bled edges, M).
  • Fluid reading: diffusion, viscosity (thinned paint), opacity; additive pigment; tide lines; processes bleed, diffusion, sedimentation, layering.

The framework behind it

Soak-stain: the ground is part of the medium. Thin paint diffuses into it and deposits at the drying edge (the coffee-ring effect). Colour, edge and rim are set by how wet, how thin and how absorbent.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Coffee rings and watercolour backruns.
  • Chromatography: compounds travel different distances through paper.
  • River deltas: sediment drops where flow slows.
  • Tie-dye and batik.

Dual edge

Stain techniques read as calm and natural; used for data they can soften a hard number. Keep them out of anything that reports a value.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

Pink Noise is a book of poems by the Taiwanese poet Hsia Yu (夏宇).

  • Edition (from memory, moderate confidence): 2007, self-published, printed on transparent plastic sheets rather than paper.
  • How the poems were made (same confidence): English text found online was passed through translation software into Chinese, and both versions were printed.
  • What the saved images confirm:
    • the slipcase text names "Sherlock" and "the English";
    • the title lockup reads PINK NOISE / 粉紅色噪音 / Hsia Yü 夏宇.

The photographs were shared by @longtheriverrun, quoting @janjirasun. The photographers are not named, so credit them as unknown. @janjirasun's words: "the semi-transparent page layered on top of something super opaque, adds another layer of context to whatever is underneath". @longtheriverrun's words: "the densely set, heavy 明朝 type ... instills such a noisy, interferential affect".

Parts, layer by layer

Read it from the light inward.

LayerPartKey properties (label)
L0 lightroom light; back lightsoft top light (O); a hotspot behind the sheets in image 3, luma p99 0.862 (M)
L1 frosted slipcaseetched acrylic face; white printed essayplain face luma p50 0.851, saturation 0.095 (M); the polished edges glow (O); bilingual justified block, about 30 lines (O); printed area luma p50 0.727 (M)
L2 frosted coveretched face; title lockupluma p50 0.84 (M); PINK over NOISE in colliding high-contrast serif capitals, Chinese title in heavy Mincho (O)
L3 colour blocks behind the covermagenta block; dark striped blockmagenta through frost #a6677e, saturation 0.222 (M); dark block #3d666b, read as vertical bars because dense text lines blur into bands (M, O)
L4 clear Chinese sheetsblack sheet; magenta sheetblack ink #1e2c2b (M); magenta ink on clear film #ab6087 (M); lines flush right with ragged left starts (O)
L5 English sheetsroman serif textabout half the Chinese size (I); blurred one sheet down, luma p50 0.567 (M)
L6 ground and readerlinen; the reader's handlinen #e4d6ce, luma p50 0.854 (M); a red blur behind image 3 reads as a finger, so the reader becomes a layer (O, I)

Type as a layer.

  • The Mincho face: thick verticals, hairline horizontals, triangular stroke ends (uroko). Set heavy, its counters close up where lines overlap (O).
  • Density: in image 4 the row profile finds 26 dark-mark rows at a pitch of 0.0117 of the frame height (M).
  • Two inks (black, magenta) over two scripts (Latin, Han). The ink may encode which sheet, or which translation pass, a line belongs to. That reading is inferred and not confirmed.

How the layers interact.

  • Occlusion: a glyph hides what lies behind it, and clear film between glyphs hides nothing.
  • Blur grows with distance: print touching a frosted face stays sharp; print a few millimetres behind it turns to colour fields (I, from the optics of a diffuser).
    • The magenta measured through frost (#a6677e) against magenta on clear film (#ab6087) keeps its hue and loses value and edge. That comparison is weak, because it crosses two photographs.
  • Interference: dense Mincho rows are line grids. Where the loose sheet crosses the cover block at about 20 degrees (image 2, O), two grids beat against each other. That is the "interferential affect" the sharer names.
  • Reading order follows depth: the sharp top sheet reads first, and deeper sheets read as murmur (I).

The concept. Translation becomes physical layering, and the gap between two languages becomes a measurable depth. The title names the signal model: pink noise is 1/f, with equal energy per octave. Every scale carries the same weight, so no single sheet dominates the reading (I).

The framework behind it

A page is a stack of filters, and reading is a ray through the stack. Each layer has two parts:

  • a material: clear, frosted or opaque; its scatter radius; its tint;
  • a mark set: glyphs in one script and one ink.

What the eye sees at a point is the composite along the ray. A mark at depth d behind a diffuser is blurred by a kernel that grows with d.

Three parameters do most of the work:

  • the gap between sheets;
  • the scatter of each face;
  • the density of each sheet's line grid.

Meaning is assigned by depth: sharp is "said", blurred is "underneath", and crossing grids is "noise". The book is a hand-made instance of the compositing model behind every renderer: an over operator with a depth-dependent blur.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Cartography and anatomy: overlays and acetate atlases. Classic anatomy books layer skin, muscle and bone on clear sheets. The reader peels a body the way this book peels a translation.
  • Palimpsests: medieval parchment scraped and rewritten. Multispectral imaging recovers the under-text, which is depth recovery by another physics.
  • Audio: stacked takes, reverb as distance, and the noise floor. A quiet layer under a loud one is heard as texture before it is heard as words. Pink noise is the reference test signal.
  • Signal processing: frosted glass is a low-pass filter whose cutoff falls with distance.
  • Shoji screens and frosted bathroom glass: privacy by scatter, where presence shows but identity does not.
  • Version control: a diff view is two layers of text, one struck through and one added, read together.
  • Our own canon: "a witness you can see through who still changes the picture" (feed set 27 reading of glass).

Dual edge

  • For readers, the device can hide. Layering exposes translation's distortions, and the same stack can bury the source under the gloss so readers trust the sharp top sheet. A Daylight-style surface that layers "what was said" over "what was claimed" must keep the source sheet reachable and labelled. Depth must never decide credibility.
  • It is also a legibility cost. Dense, interfering type is beautiful and hard to read: hard for low vision, hard for dyslexic readers, and impossible for screen readers if rendered as an image. Any site use needs a plain text layer that assistive technology reads, consistent with the author's 2026-10-25 point about tools for neurodivergent people.
  • Machine translation as material can launder. Text run through a model reads as authored. If we use the method, the provenance of each sheet (source, model, date) belongs in the data, not on the page.

What it is, and who made it

Four paintings of sun glitter on dark wavelets, built from stacked horizontal strokes.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Palette: #ab9b7b, #877e64, #706753 (M).

Sun glitter: each wavelet facet that tilts the right way reflects the sun; the glitter path is where the tilt distribution allows it. The painter draws the facets as strokes.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

A 21 s shader: clouds trapped inside a rotating glass dodecahedron with a diffraction-grating surface, in a dark room under strip lights.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Object: a dodecahedron with rainbow-fringed faces (O).
  • Inside: soft white clouds (O).
  • Motion: mean speed 0.091, coherence 0.58, loop closure 7.8 (not a loop, M).
  • Fluid reading: refractive index, opacity; additive light; caustics; refraction.

The framework behind it

Two media in one object: a volume (cloud) inside a dispersive solid (grating glass). Light passes through both.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Snow globes and paperweights.
  • Holographic foil.
  • Ice crystals making halos.

Dual edge

Iridescent objects read as luxury; keep them where the optics mean something.

What it is, and who made it

Four photos of printed matter where translucent sheets lie over opaque ones: numbered colour bands, yellow vellum over pages, a translucent cover, large overlapping coloured characters.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Sheets: translucent printed layers over opaque print (O).
  • Type: large numerals and characters in overlapping colours (O).
  • Palette: #e2e3e5, #c7c4ca, #969bae (M); spectral slope 1.69 (M).

The framework behind it

Layer as context: the translucent page adds meaning to what lies under it without hiding it. The same sheet model as Pink Noise.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

Four views of paintings hung on pegboard: looking up from under water toward the surface, in teal and deep green, with branches or figures crossing the surface.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Palette: #304242, #1b2c2f against the white wall #e5dfd7 (M).
  • Depth: values darken and greens deepen toward the bottom of each canvas (O).
  • Surface: a lighter band where the surface is seen from below (O); refracted shapes above it (I).
  • Measures: wavelength 0.107, spectral slope 2.46, edge softness 7.75 (soft, M).
  • Fluid reading: refractive index, opacity, stratification; additive light; caustics and reflections; refraction, layering.

The framework behind it

The view from inside the medium: light enters through a bright window at the surface (Snell's window, inferred) and is absorbed with depth, red first, so the colour cools and darkens downward.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Underwater photography and diving.
  • Atmospheric perspective (the same absorption, in air).
  • Stained glass seen from inside a nave.

Dual edge

Immersion can overwhelm; a site that floods the view should let the reader surface.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

A full-body musculoskeletal model with 700 muscle-tendon units, 206 joints and 90 body segments. The 5 s clip shows the body moving beside a grid of muscle activations. The post says it is fully open source; the arXiv abstract says the model and controller will be released. The licence and code location are not verified here.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Elements: 700 muscle-tendon actuators, 206 joints, 90 rigid segments (O, post and paper).
  • Laws: muscle-tendon dynamics and rigid-body mechanics (inferred from the field; the paper names a hierarchical low-dimensional controller).
  • Display: an activation grid where each cell is one actuator and colour is activation (O): a live mosaic of control.
  • Motion: mean speed 0.019 widths per second, coherence 0.37 (M): small, articulated motion.

The framework behind it

Elements and laws: many small agents act on a medium through fixed laws, and the whole moves. For the fluid model, additives are the elements (ink, heat, text) and the properties are the laws (viscosity, diffusion, buoyancy).

The same idea in distant fields

  • Swarms and flocks: simple rules per agent, collective motion.
  • Orchestras: many players, one score.
  • Cellular automata: cells and update rules.
  • Puppetry: strings as actuators.

Dual edge

Body simulation at muscle level serves rehabilitation and robotics; the same control can drive persuasive synthetic humans. We take the elements-and-laws idea and the actuator mosaic, not the body.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

  1. "De A à Z" (French): a giant A crossed by Z strokes in translucent inks.
  2. Divisumma, signed by Herbert Bayer: ribbons of numbered colour tiles curling over a grey checker sheet.
  3. Divisumma 26: a hexagon filled with the digit string 1234567890 in three face colours on black.
  4. Elettrosumma 22: an isometric field of blocks with scattered digits.

Parts, layer by layer

1. De A à Z. Paper #fcf7eb. Inks measured alone: red #eb4324, cyan #04b2dd, yellow #fcc603, green #07ac3d, black #1a1b22. Every overlap is darker than both inks: transparent overprint. Ideal multiply gets lightness, misses hue by 14 to 21. Type: one A and parts of Z as flat planes; French body copy in a slab serif.

2. Elettrosumma 22. Edge-orientation peaks 35° and 143° (secondary 44°, 152°) from horizontal: steeper than isometric 30° (inferred dimetric, hand-drawn). Faces by area: coloured tops 0.235, light-grey sides 0.445, mid-grey sides 0.118, black 0.066, paper 0.134; light to mid side ratio 3.8 to 1. Eight top inks (observed). Single bold digits in the gaps.

3. Divisumma 26. Faces: pink, white, ochre on black. Line pitch 20 px of 1972 in the white face (autocorrelation 0.91); 19 px in the pink. Glyph advance about 12 px (weak, 0.51). Face boundaries near 127° to 145°. The string breaks: '13345' for '12345' in at least two lines (observed).

4. Bayer, Divisumma. Class shares: paper 0.19, light grey 0.28, mid grey 0.09, dark grey 0.04, black 0.20, colour 0.19. The S ribbon's bottom edge curvature runs +0.0087 to −0.0059 per px with an inflection near x 800; tightest radius 115 px (about 8% of the width); apparent height 92 to 399 px. Tile widths 88 to 89 px in the flat row and 26 to 47 px where the ribbon turns. Black teardrops fill the curls. Operators and digits ride the tiles and float on the grid.

The framework behind it

One framework seen three ways. Mosaic is the discretisation (blocks, glyph cells, tiles). Overprint is the optics: each ink a sheet with a transmission; overlap the product. Flow is the motion: tiles carried by a bending surface, the flow made visible by how tiles foreshorten. The fourth sheet adds error as grain: the misprinted digit proves the field is text.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Printing: CMYK overprint and trapping; the multiply blend mode in every compositor is the ideal case of image 1.
  • Crystallography: isometric block fields are the projection of a cubic lattice; the side-face shading is a one-light Lambert model.
  • Typesetting and early computing: fill patterns of repeated digits were how line printers made images (ASCII and typewriter art).
  • Fluid dynamics: Bayer's ribbon is a material line in a flow; its stretching and folding is how mixing is drawn (a Lagrangian view).
  • Textiles: woven ribbons with printed motifs that turn over show both faces, as the black teardrops do.

Dual edge

Mosaic as flow makes numbers look alive and friendly: Olivetti sold calculators with it. The same move can make figures look more orderly than the data behind them. Overprint can hide one layer inside another; a reading surface must keep each sheet separable. Copying Olivetti or Bayer forms directly would be a literal copy; the canon asks for the framework, not the look.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

The post has two layers of authorship:

  • Otto Piene, Red Eye Red, 1977, serigraph. These details come from the post caption. Piene (1928 to 2014) co-founded the ZERO group, and he made light ballets as well as smoke and fire paintings. Those biographical facts are from memory, high confidence.
  • Three colour studies by Meditations in Color, credited "by Pixel Symphony". Each study takes the print's palette through a historical colour system:
    • Josef Albers, Homage to the Square;
    • Wada Sanzō, A Dictionary of Color Combinations;
    • the Heian court's kasane no irome, colours of layered robes.

Parts, layer by layer

The print (image 1)

LayerPartProperties (label)
L1 groundorange-red fieldinks red #d24a2a and orange #d25c22 (M); flat screen-printed field, mottled with small round voids (O)
L2 dark markslash ring, iris rimdark #362e28 (M); ragged, flame-like strokes radiating around an oval (O); they look burned or blown, not brushed (I, consistent with Piene's fire works)
L3 pupilblack void, orange curlan orange form curls inside the black oval (O); radial colours from the centre run #413328 to #d35821 over 7 rings (M)
motifthe eye as aperturea radiant eye made by fire: the aperture and luminous orb of our canon (I)

Study 1: one centre on four grounds, after Albers (image 2)

  • Structure: four plates of four nested squares. The inner squares sit low, as in Albers (O).
  • One centre: #d84830 (M, named region "the centre, on the page"). The same hex appears at 0.162 of each plate's palette, measured in all four crops. The page does what its caption says: it shows one colour four times.
  • Grounds (M):
GroundLeading coloursContrast
I lighter#e4783c, #f06c24, #fe511f0.234
II darker#7e4030, #3d3024, #bf402f0.212
III warmer#ef6c25, #fe511f, #e950260.127
IV brighter#fe5120, #e95026, #e454310.063

Concentricity is highest on the darker ground (1.323), where the nested fields separate most.

  • Principle: simultaneous contrast. One chip reads differently on each ground (Albers, Interaction of Color, 1963).

Study 2: twos, threes and fours, after Wada (image 3)

  • Twelve colours, measured from the printed swatches (M):

The page prints its own hex codes under the swatches, but they are too small to read in this save (O). Our values carry JPEG error, so expect differences of a few units.

  • Combinations: 4 pairs, 4 triples and 4 quadruples (O). Each tile is labelled with its colour indices, such as "6·3", "1·10·8" or "4·6·2·8", and laid out as unequal bands and quarters.
  • Principle: a fixed, indexed palette. Harmony is a small set of indices, chosen and named.

Study 3: robes in layers, after kasane no irome (image 4)

  • Four robes, palettes measured (M):
RobeMeaning, seasonLeading colours
Kobaired plum, spring#fb5123
Momijimaple, autumn#834333, #c04d2a
Kuchibafallen leaves, autumn#bc5f19, #db5033
Sumizomeink-dyed, winter#3f3327, #c65825
  • Structure: a V collar shows 4 to 5 stacked colour bands, and the hem repeats them. A key of 4 to 5 small squares sits under each name, in layer order (O).
  • Principle: colour as a stack seen only at its edges, named for a season.

The study pages as a design system

  • A light orange serif for the artist and a darker serif for the work.
  • Small italic captions and tracked small capitals in grey (O).
  • One footer credit.

The framework behind it

One palette, three operators. The post is a decomposition engine made by hand:

  • The source artwork supplies a palette, here 12 colours.
  • Each historical colour system acts as an operator on that palette, and each tests a different claim:
    • Relational (Albers): a colour's appearance depends on its neighbour, so hold one colour and vary its ground.
    • Combinatorial (Wada): harmony lives in small indexed sets, so enumerate pairs, triples and quadruples.
    • Layered (kasane): colour is a stack seen at its edges, and the stack is named for a time of year.

The outputs are plates, not paintings. Each makes one claim checkable. That matches the canon's method: break a reference into parts, then recombine.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Music: a scale (the palette) run through harmonic systems. The same twelve tones serve as chords (Wada), as voicings over a pedal (Albers, one note against changing bass) and as layered instrumentation (kasane).
  • Chemistry: one compound's spectrum under different solvents. The solvent shifts what the "same" colour looks like, as the ground does in Albers.
  • Typography: one glyph set at many sizes and on many grounds in a specimen sheet. Our feed sets ask for this repeatedly (GAPS item 24, the specimen sheet).
  • Data visualisation: colour-blind and contrast audits put one palette through several perceptual models, and each plate is a test.
  • Textile and lacquer: kasane is a cousin of laminated glass and of lacquer built up in coats. The colour is the sum of the layers, and the edge is where the sum shows. That links to our glass and intaglio work, where the cut edge reveals the layers.

Dual edge

  • Reused palettes fake provenance. Extracting a master's palette and running it through prestige systems lends authority to anything painted in it. The plates must say whose palette, extracted how. Our records do; a published plate set must too.
  • Simultaneous contrast is a persuasion tool. The same effect that teaches Albers can make a chart's bar look larger or a warning look milder.
  • Seasonal naming is a cultural system. Kasane names carry court meaning. Using them as decoration without that context is a thin borrowing. The study pages credit the source; our plates should cite it too.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

Renders of London (Westminster and the Thames) and Shibuya in which streets and buildings bend along smooth curves, as if the city were a liquid surface. Three stills and a 24 s clip.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Source layer: Google Earth photogrammetry meshes with baked facade textures (O, from the post).
  • Deformation field: smooth, large-scale; rows of buildings follow it like streamlines (O). In the clip the camera drifts with mean speed 0.092 widths per second, coherence 0.41 (M).
  • Texture: where the field shears, facade pixels stretch into streaks (O). Measured stretch share (structure-tensor coherence over 0.6) 0.16 to 0.29 across the stills (M).
  • Bend: 3.5 to 4.1 degrees per 1% of width (M); controls 2.7 to 6.6 (hand-drawn shelves, Bayer ribbons, Elettrosumma blocks, Moran canyon). The measure does not separate this work: a reported null.
  • Light: photoreal daylight render; shadows follow the bent geometry (O).

The framework behind it

Advection applied to solid geometry: positions move through a velocity field while topology is kept. The look comes from two rules: deform vertices smoothly, and do not resample textures, so they stretch where the field stretches.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Geology: folded strata; rock flows over long times and the layers record the strain.
  • Glaciology: flow bands in glaciers.
  • Cartography: cartograms and fisheye maps bend a city for a reason (population, attention).
  • Film: the city-folding scene in Inception (from memory, a reference to check, not this work's source).

Dual edge

Bending a real city is a strong image of instability. Used on a news surface it could imply damage that did not happen. The data has a licence (Google Earth terms) that limits reuse; our version should use open map data.

What it is, and who made it

Four phone photos of framed Rembrandt etchings, one through a magnifying glass: deep blacks, light falling in shafts.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Medium: ink printed from an etched copper plate (O for etching; plate inferred).
  • Tone: dense crosshatching for darks, open paper for light (O).
  • Measures: spectral slope 2.59, edge softness 20.1 (soft, from photographing behind glass, M).
  • Fluid reading: opacity; additives acid and ink; erosion, sedimentation, layering.

The framework behind it

Etching: acid bites lines through a wax ground into the plate (erosion), ink settles in the bitten lines (sedimentation) and transfers under pressure. Tone comes from line density, as in our intaglio canon.

  • Photolithography in chip making.

items.body_html:
What it is, and who made it

Three tall frames of a website design for a private-network product: a dark ground, flower photographs, a node-graph overlay with coordinate and IP-style labels, one orange accent, a giant grotesk headline cropped at the frame, and numbered steps where the later steps are dimmed.

Parts, layer by layer

  • Ground: two darks, page #0e0e0e and card #1a1a1a (M); ground luma 0.098 (M).
  • Hot mark: orange #fc4b07 to #f94f0c (M). Area share 0.025 in frame 1, 0.285 in frame 2 (a full orange panel), 0.004 in frame 3 (M): one orange per view, from a thin bar to a whole panel.
  • Photography: orange and white blossoms cut out on the dark ground; inside some flowers a rectangle turns grey (O).
  • Graph overlay: thin white lines and small nodes over the photos, with boxed mono labels like coordinates and addresses (O). The overlay sits over the photograph and crosses petals and ground alike.
  • Type scale: headline line runs of 87 and 51 px in a 640 px wide frame; body lines 19 to 24 px of 1080; headline to body about 4 to 1 by line height (M). The headline is cropped at both edges ('ct anythi / ere.') (O).
  • Reading order: steps 1 and 2 at p99 luma 0.965, step 3 at 0.282 (29% of white), the small label above at 0.612 (M). Later steps wait in dim until reached (I).

The framework behind it

Three layers with three jobs: a living subject (flowers), a technical skin (the network graph and its labels) and a typographic voice (one huge cropped grotesk). Colour is rationed: one orange marks where to look. Brightness is used as reading order, so the page shows where the reader is.

The same idea in distant fields

  • Botanical specimen plates with labels and leader lines.
  • Air-traffic and network operations displays.
  • Swiss posters with cropped giant type.
  • Teleprompters and karaoke: the current line lit, the next dim.

Dual edge

Dimming future steps guides reading and can also hide terms the reader should see before agreeing; never dim anything a reader must consent to. The network graph over flowers reads as calm and natural; for a security product that softness can understate risk.
